stem: In the geophysical study of the Earth's interior, scientists classify sources of evidence into direct and indirect categories.
prompt: Although meteorites that reach the Earth's surface are solid, tangible specimens that can be physically analysed in laboratories, why are they classified strictly as an indirect source of information rather than a direct source?

opts.A: Their original mineralogical and isotopic composition is completely altered by intense atmospheric friction and ablation prior to impact.
opts.B: They represent volatile-rich remnants of outer solar system comets rather than differentiated rocky planetary interiors.
opts.C: Their magnetic and gravitational signatures cannot be correlated with terrestrial rocks found in the continental crust.
opts.D: The material recovered from them was never physically extracted from the Earth's own interior, serving instead as an extraterrestrial analogue formed during early solar system accretion.

core: Direct sources of information about the Earth's interior are restricted to physical materials derived directly from within the Earth, such as deep-earth mining rocks, scientific drilling cores, and volcanic magma. Meteorites, despite being tangible laboratory specimens, are classified as indirect sources because they did not originate inside the Earth, serving instead as compositional analogues from the protoplanetary nebula.

exp.why: Option D is correct because the classification into 'direct' and 'indirect' sources depends on whether the sample physically originated from the Earth's interior. Direct sources include surface rocks from mining areas, cores from deep ocean drilling projects (such as the Kola Superdeep Borehole), and molten magma/lava erupted during volcanic activity. Meteorites are solid bodies formed from the same nebular material and planetesimal differentiation processes as the proto-Earth; analysing iron-nickel and stony-iron meteorites provides powerful indirect insights into the composition of the Earth's mantle and core, even though the material is not extracted from the Earth itself. Option A is incorrect because only the thin outer crust (fusion crust) of a meteorite melts during atmospheric entry, leaving the interior pristine. Option B is incorrect because differentiated achondrites and iron-nickel meteorites originate from inner solar system asteroid cores/mantles, not comets. Option C is incorrect because chondritic and iron meteorites correlate closely with terrestrial geochemical and paleomagnetic models.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 3 (Interior of the Earth)

stem: With reference to the propagation mechanics of seismic body waves through the interior of the Earth, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Primary (P) waves propagate by vibrating rock particles perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation, creating alternating crests and troughs in the medium.
2. Secondary (S) waves are longitudinal waves that exert alternating compression and dilation parallel to the propagation axis without altering the shape of the rock.
3. Unlike P-waves, which can travel through gaseous, liquid, and solid media, S-waves can propagate only through materials that possess shear strength (rigidity).
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: P-waves are compressional (longitudinal) waves where particle motion is parallel to the direction of propagation, inducing volume changes across solids, liquids, and gases. S-waves are shear (transverse) waves where particle motion is perpendicular to propagation, requiring a non-zero shear modulus (rigidity) that exists only in solids.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it swaps the mechanics of P-waves with S-waves. Primary (P) waves are longitudinal (compressional) waves analogous to sound waves, in which rock particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation, producing alternating zones of compression (squeezing) and dilation (stretching) that change both volume and density.

Statement 2 is incorrect because Secondary (S) waves are transverse (shear) waves, not longitudinal waves. S-waves vibrate rock particles perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of wave propagation, creating troughs and crests that distort the shape of the rock medium without changing its volume.

Statement 3 is correct. P-wave velocity depends on both the bulk modulus (incompressibility) and shear modulus (rigidity), allowing P-waves to travel through solids, liquids, and gases since all fluids resist volume compression. S-wave velocity depends strictly on the shear modulus (rigidity); because fluids (liquids and gases) have zero shear rigidity and cannot sustain shear stress, S-waves can propagate only through solid media.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 3; GC Leong Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the generation and behaviour of seismic Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh waves) during an earthquake, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Surface waves originate directly at the subterranean hypocentre simultaneously with P and S waves, but arrive last at the seismograph due to their high frequency.
opts.B: Surface waves are generated when seismic body waves interact with the Earth's surface rocks, and they cause the maximum structural destruction due to their large amplitude and long wavelength.
opts.C: Rayleigh waves are the fastest among all seismic waves and induce purely horizontal side-to-side shearing of the ground without any vertical displacement.
opts.D: Unlike body waves whose velocity varies with the density and elasticity of the medium, surface waves travel at a uniform constant velocity across both continental and oceanic crust.

core: Surface waves do not originate directly at the subterranean focus (hypocentre); instead, they are generated when P and S body waves reach and interact with the free boundary of the Earth's surface. Characterised by low frequency, long wavelength, and large amplitude, they lose energy more slowly with distance than body waves and cause the severest ground displacement and structural collapse.

exp.why: Option B is correct. During an earthquake, energy released at the subterranean focus (hypocentre) radiates outward initially as body waves (P and S waves). When these body waves encounter the Earth's surface rocks, their interaction generates a new set of waves guided along the surface—namely Surface waves (L-waves, comprising Love and Rayleigh waves). Because surface waves spread in two dimensions along the surface rather than three dimensions through the interior, they maintain large amplitudes, long wavelengths, and long durations of shaking, making them the most destructive seismic waves. Option A is incorrect because surface waves do not originate at the subterranean hypocentre and are characterised by low frequency, not high frequency. Option C is incorrect because P-waves are the fastest seismic waves, and purely horizontal transverse shearing is characteristic of Love waves, whereas Rayleigh waves produce an elliptical retrograde rolling motion with both vertical and horizontal displacement. Option D is incorrect because surface wave velocity depends strongly on the elasticity, density, and thickness of the crust, travelling faster in denser oceanic crust than in continental crust and exhibiting wave dispersion.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 3; Savindra Singh Physical Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the propagation of seismic waves through the Earth's interior:
items: Statement-I: As seismic body waves propagate deeper into the Earth's mantle, their velocity generally increases, causing their ray paths to refract continuously and follow curved trajectories.

Statement-II: The propagation velocity of seismic waves is governed solely by an inverse relationship with rock density, as the incompressibility and rigidity of rocks remain constant throughout the mantle.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Seismic wave velocities depend on both the elastic moduli (incompressibility/bulk modulus K and rigidity/shear modulus μ) in the numerator and density (ρ) in the denominator. With increasing depth in the mantle, lithostatic pressure causes the elastic moduli of rocks to increase at a much faster rate than density, resulting in increasing wave velocity and upward-curving refracted ray paths.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Except within the partially molten Low Velocity Zone (asthenosphere), the velocity of both P and S waves generally increases with depth across the mantle due to increasing self-compression and mineral phase transitions. In accordance with Snell's law of refraction, as seismic waves pass into progressively higher-velocity layers at depth, they bend away from the normal, causing their ray paths to curve concavely upward toward the surface.

Statement-II is incorrect. Mathematically, P-wave velocity is Vp = sqrt((K + 4μ/3) / ρ) and S-wave velocity is Vs = sqrt(μ / ρ), where K is the bulk modulus (incompressibility), μ is the shear modulus (rigidity), and ρ is density. Although density (ρ) is in the denominator and increases with depth, the elastic moduli (incompressibility K and rigidity μ) do not remain constant; instead, they increase with depth under extreme lithostatic pressure at a rate much faster than density. It is this rapid increase in elastic stiffness relative to density that drives the increase in seismic velocity with depth.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 3; Alan Strahler Physical Geography

stem: With reference to seismic shadow zones and wave behaviour across the Core-Mantle Boundary (Gutenberg Discontinuity), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The shadow zone of S-waves covers a much larger total surface area of the globe than that of P-waves, extending continuously beyond an angular distance of 103° (or 105°) from the earthquake epicentre.
2. Upon crossing the Gutenberg discontinuity from the lower mantle into the outer core, P-waves experience a sharp increase in velocity that refracts them away from the 103° to 142° band.
3. Within the angular zone between 142° and 180° from the epicentre, both direct P-waves and direct S-waves are recorded by seismographs after traversing the core.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: At the Core-Mantle Boundary (2,900 km depth), the transition from the solid silicate lower mantle to the liquid iron-nickel outer core reduces shear rigidity to zero. This completely blocks S-waves beyond 103° (creating a shadow zone covering over 40% of the globe) and causes a sharp drop in P-wave velocity from ~13.7 km/s to ~8.1 km/s, refracting P-waves inward to leave a ring-shaped shadow zone between 103° and 142°.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Because the outer core is liquid and cannot transmit shear (S) waves, no direct S-waves are received anywhere beyond an epicentral angle of 103° (often rounded to 105° in introductory texts) all the way to the antipode (180°). Consequently, the S-wave shadow zone forms a continuous cap covering over 40% of the Earth's surface, which is substantially larger than the ring-like P-wave shadow band between 103° and 142°.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Upon crossing the Gutenberg discontinuity at ~2,900 km depth from the solid lower mantle into the liquid outer core, the shear modulus (μ) drops abruptly to zero and density jumps from ~5.5 g/cm³ to ~10 g/cm³. As a result, P-wave velocity drops sharply from approximately 13.7 km/s to 8.1 km/s (not an increase), causing the P-wave rays to refract sharply downward toward the centre of the core and leaving the 103°–142° surface belt unilluminated by direct P-waves.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Only P-waves (specifically PKP / PKIKP compressional phases) emerge in the zone between 142° and 180° from the epicentre after passing through the core. Direct S-waves are completely absorbed/blocked at the liquid outer core boundary and do not emerge in the 142°–180° zone.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 3 (Fig. 3.2 Earthquake Shadow Zones)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the propagation of seismic waves through the Earth's core:
items: Statement-I: The P-wave shadow zone located between 103° and 142° from an earthquake epicentre is not completely devoid of P-wave arrivals, as weak, delayed compressional signals are detected by sensitive seismographs within this belt.

Statement-II: Compressional waves travelling through the fluid outer core undergo sharp reflection and high-velocity refraction upon encountering the solid inner core boundary, deflecting a portion of their energy into the 103°–142° zone.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While a wholly liquid core would leave the 103°–142° shadow zone devoid of direct P-waves, Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann demonstrated in 1936 that weak, delayed P-waves do arrive inside this belt. These arrivals are caused by compressional waves reflecting off and refracting at higher velocities through a solid inner core (bounded at ~5,150 km depth).

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Although the annular belt between 103° and 142° from the epicentre receives no direct P-waves that merely graze the mantle or refract solely through the outer core, sensitive seismographs deployed since the 1930s consistently record weak, lower-amplitude compressional wave arrivals within this shadow zone.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. In 1936, Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann explained these anomalous P-wave arrivals inside the 103°–142° shadow zone by proving the existence of a solid inner core beginning at a depth of ~5,150 km (the inner core boundary, often termed the Lehmann or Bullen discontinuity). Because the inner core is solid, it possesses shear rigidity in addition to high bulk modulus, causing P-wave velocity to jump from ~10.3 km/s to ~11.2 km/s. Compressional waves entering the outer core are reflected (PKiKP) and strongly refracted (PKIKP) at this solid inner core boundary, bending upward to reach the surface within the 103°–142° shadow zone.

ref: Savindra Singh Physical Geography; Alan Strahler Introducing Physical Geography

stem: With reference to the internal structure of the Earth and seismic discontinuities, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Conrad Discontinuity : Transition zone between the upper mantle and the lower mantle
2. Mohorovicic Discontinuity : Boundary between the lower crust and the uppermost solid mantle
3. Repetti Discontinuity : Boundary between the upper felsic and lower mafic continental crust
4. Lehmann Discontinuity : Boundary between the liquid outer core and the solid inner core
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Seismic discontinuities mark depths where sudden changes in chemical composition, mineral phase, or physical state alter the bulk and shear moduli of rocks, causing abrupt refraction or reflection of seismic waves. From the surface downward, the five classic discontinuities are Conrad (intra-crustal), Mohorovicic (crust-mantle), Repetti (upper-lower mantle), Gutenberg (mantle-outer core), and Lehmann (outer-inner core).

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched (interchanged with Pair 3). The Conrad Discontinuity is a secondary intra-crustal seismic boundary found within the continental crust (at depths of 15 to 20 km) where P-wave velocity increases from ~6.0 km/s to ~6.5 km/s between the upper granitic/felsic crust (Sial) and the lower basaltic/mafic crust (Sima). It is generally absent in oceanic crust.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Discovered by Andrija Mohorovicic in 1909, the Mohorovicic (Moho) Discontinuity separates the lower crust (mafic gabbroic/basaltic rocks) from the uppermost solid mantle (ultramafic peridotite/dunite), marked by a sharp jump in P-wave velocity from ~6.9 km/s to ~8.1 km/s.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched (interchanged with Pair 1). The Repetti Discontinuity (located around 660–700 km depth at the base of the mantle transition zone) marks the boundary between the upper mantle and the lower mantle (mesosphere), where mineral phase transitions to perovskite/bridgmanite structures cause a steep velocity increase.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. While the Gutenberg Discontinuity at ~2,900 km separates the solid silicate lower mantle from the liquid iron-nickel outer core, the Lehmann Discontinuity at ~5,150 km depth separates the liquid outer core from the solid inner core, evidenced by a sudden increase in P-wave velocity and the re-emergence of weak shear-mode conversions.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; Savindra Singh Geomorphology Ch. 4

stem: As a seismic body wave propagates downward from a continental shield towards the Lehmann Discontinuity at the inner core boundary, in which sequence does it encounter the following internal zones and discontinuities?
items: 1. Seismic Low-Velocity Zone (Asthenosphere)
2. Conrad Discontinuity
3. Gutenberg Discontinuity
4. Repetti Discontinuity (Mantle Transition Zone)
prompt: Select the correct answer using the code given below (in order of increasing depth from the Earth's surface):
core: Tracking a seismic wave from a continental craton to the core requires integrating both compositional boundaries and mechanical/rheological zones by depth. Intra-crustal boundaries occur first, followed by the Moho, the upper-mantle asthenospheric low-velocity zone, the 410–660 km mantle transition zone, and finally the core-mantle and inner-core boundaries.

exp.why: Item 1 (Seismic Low-Velocity Zone / Asthenosphere) is encountered second in this list, between roughly 80 km and 200 km depth. A common sequencing error is placing the asthenosphere immediately below the upper crust or above the Mohorovicic Discontinuity (~35 km), forgetting that the rigid lithospheric mantle lies between the Moho and the asthenosphere.

Item 2 (Conrad Discontinuity) is encountered first at the shallowest depth of approximately 15 to 20 km within the continental crust, separating the upper felsic layer from the lower mafic layer well above the Mohorovicic Discontinuity (~35–40 km).

Item 3 (Gutenberg Discontinuity) is encountered fourth (deepest among the four items) at approximately 2,890–2,900 km depth at the Core-Mantle Boundary (CMB), where S-waves are completely blocked and P-waves drop sharply in velocity before eventually reaching the Lehmann Discontinuity at ~5,150 km.

Item 4 (Repetti Discontinuity / Mantle Transition Zone) is encountered third at approximately 660–700 km depth, marking the transition from the upper mantle (below the asthenosphere) into the high-viscosity lower mantle (mesosphere). Thus, the correct depth-wise order is 2 (15–20 km) -> 1 (80–200 km) -> 4 (660–700 km) -> 3 (2,900 km).

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; G.C. Leong Certificate Physical and Human Geography Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the compositional and rheological (mechanical) layering of the Earth's interior, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Mohorovicic discontinuity marks the rheological boundary between the brittle lithosphere and the mechanically ductile asthenosphere.
2. Although the crust and the uppermost part of the mantle differ in their mineralogical and chemical composition, they respond to tectonic stresses as a single rigid mechanical unit.
3. In the lower mantle (mesosphere), the effect of extreme confining pressure overrides the high temperature, keeping the silicate rock mechanically strong and solid down to the core-mantle boundary.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Geophysics classifies the Earth's interior along two distinct axes: chemical composition (Crust, Mantle, Core) and mechanical/rheological behaviour (Lithosphere, Asthenosphere, Mesosphere, Outer Core, Inner Core). The Mohorovicic discontinuity is strictly a compositional boundary within the rigid lithosphere, whereas the Lithosphere-Asthenosphere Boundary (LAB) is a deeper thermal/mechanical transition.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho) is a compositional boundary separating the silicate crust (felsic/mafic) from the ultramafic mantle (peridotite) at 7–70 km depth. The boundary between the rigid lithosphere and the ductile asthenosphere is the Lithosphere-Asthenosphere Boundary (LAB), which lies much deeper (at ~80–200 km depth) within the upper mantle.

Statement 2 is correct. Because temperatures down to ~1280°C–1300°C (the isotherm defining the base of the lithosphere) are cool enough to keep both crustal rocks and the uppermost mantle peridotite well below their melting point, both layers are welded together mechanically into a single rigid, brittle shell (the lithosphere) that forms tectonic plates.

Statement 3 is correct. Below the upper mantle transition zone (~660 km down to 2,900 km), the geothermal gradient rises more slowly than the pressure-dependent melting curve (solidus) of silicate perovskite (bridgmanite). Consequently, extreme lithostatic pressure locks the crystal lattice, making the mesosphere (lower mantle) solid and highly viscous.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; Tarbuck & Lutgens Earth Science Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the structural, compositional, and seismic characteristics of the Continental Crust and the Oceanic Crust, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Primary (P) seismic waves propagate at a higher average velocity through the continental crust than through the oceanic crust due to the greater thickness and silica enrichment of continental blocks.
2. In accordance with Airy's principle of isostasy, the Mohorovicic discontinuity lies at a much shallower depth beneath young fold mountain belts than beneath stable continental cratons.
3. Unlike the continental crust which is continuously destroyed at convergent plate margins, the oceanic crust preserves the oldest Archean rock assemblages on the Earth.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Seismic wave velocity is governed by the elastic moduli (incompressibility k and rigidity mu) relative to density (rho). Although oceanic crust is denser (~3.0 g/cm3) and thinner (5–10 km) than continental crust (~2.7 g/cm3, 35–70 km), its mafic basaltic-gabbroic mineralogy possesses substantially higher bulk and shear moduli, allowing P-waves to travel faster (~6.8–7.0 km/s) than in felsic continental crust (~6.0–6.2 km/s).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. P-wave velocity is higher in the oceanic crust (~6.8 to 7.0 km/s) than in the average continental crust (~6.0 to 6.2 km/s). Oceanic crust consists of mafic basalt and gabbro, which have much higher elastic stiffness (bulk modulus and shear modulus) that more than compensates for their higher density compared to silica-rich (felsic/granodioritic) continental rocks.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Airy's root-of-mountains hypothesis of isostasy, high-standing topographic masses like young fold mountains (e.g., the Himalayas and the Andes) are compensated by deep, buoyant crustal roots extending into the denser mantle. Therefore, the Mohorovicic discontinuity is deepest beneath young fold mountains (up to 65–75 km), moderate beneath cratons (~35–40 km), and shallowest beneath abyssal oceanic plains (~7–10 km).

Statement 3 is incorrect. It is the dense mafic oceanic lithosphere that is continuously created at mid-ocean ridges and recycled (subducted) into the mantle at oceanic trenches, leaving no in-situ oceanic crust older than ~180–200 million years (Jurassic). Conversely, low-density buoyant continental crust resists subduction and preserves Earth's oldest Hadean and Archean cratonic rocks (up to ~4.0 billion years old).

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3 & Ch. 4; Savindra Singh Geomorphology Ch. 4 & 5

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the propagation of seismic waves through the upper mantle:
items: Statement-I: Both Primary (P) and Secondary (S) seismic waves experience a marked drop in velocity and heightened attenuation upon entering the asthenosphere between approximately 80 km and 200 km depth, yet S-waves continue to propagate through this zone.
Statement-II: The asthenosphere consists of a continuous, completely molten magma ocean of liquid peridotite whose high temperature reduces its shear modulus to zero.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Asthenosphere corresponds to the Seismic Low-Velocity Zone (LVZ) at 80–200 km depth because the geotherm closely approaches the peridotite solidus, causing 1% to 5% interstitial partial melting along mineral grain boundaries. Because over 95% of the rock remains crystalline solid, its shear modulus (mu) is reduced but not zero, slowing down S-waves without blocking them.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Between roughly 80 km and 200 km depth (the asthenosphere / Gutenberg Low-Velocity Zone), seismic velocities drop noticeably (by ~5% to 8% for both P and S waves) and seismic energy is strongly attenuated (low quality factor Q). Crucially, however, S-waves are not stopped by the asthenosphere and continue to pass through to the deeper mantle.

Statement-II is incorrect. If the asthenosphere were a completely molten liquid layer with zero shear modulus (rigidity mu = 0), transverse S-waves would be completely blocked at 80 km depth just as they are blocked at the outer core (2,900 km). In reality, the asthenosphere is predominantly solid crystalline peridotite (>95–99% solid) near its melting point, containing only a tiny fraction (1–5%) of interstitial partial melt along grain boundaries that lubricates crystal deformation and lowers seismic velocity.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; Fowler, C.M.R. The Solid Earth: An Introduction to Global Geophysics

stem: With reference to the Mantle Transition Zone located between depths of approximately 410 km and 660 km inside the Earth, consider the following statements:
items: 1. This zone is marked by two sharp, step-wise increases in seismic wave velocities at depths of around 410 km and 660 km.

2. These abrupt seismic velocity jumps are caused primarily by a drastic change in bulk chemical composition from magnesium silicates in the upper mantle to iron-nickel metallic oxides in the lower mantle.

3. High-pressure mineral phases within this zone, such as wadsleyite and ringwoodite, can trap significant amounts of hydroxyl ions within their crystal lattices, acting as a major deep-earth reservoir of water.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The seismic discontinuities at 410 km and 660 km bounding the Mantle Transition Zone are isochemical polymorphic phase boundaries rather than compositional boundaries. Under immense lithostatic pressure, upper-mantle olivine ((Mg,Fe)2SiO4) rearranges its crystal lattice into denser polymorphs—wadsleyite (~410 km) and ringwoodite (~520 km)—before dissociating into bridgmanite (silicate perovskite) and ferropericlase at ~660 km.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Global seismic tomography and body-wave travel-time curves show two prominent, sharp step-increases (of ~5% to 7% each) in both P-wave and S-wave velocities at ~410 km and ~660 km depth, which define the top and bottom of the Mantle Transition Zone.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The bulk chemical composition across the upper mantle, transition zone, and lower mantle remains predominantly isochemical (ultramafic magnesium-iron silicates). The abrupt jumps in seismic velocity and density at 410 km and 660 km are driven by pressure-induced solid-state polymorphic phase transformations: olivine transforms into denser wadsleyite at ~410 km and ringwoodite at ~520 km, and subsequently breaks down into ultra-dense bridgmanite (magnesium silicate perovskite) and ferropericlase at ~660 km.

Statement 3 is correct. Unlike shallow olivine and lower-mantle bridgmanite which are nearly anhydrous, the crystal structures of wadsleyite and ringwoodite in the 410–660 km transition zone can incorporate up to 1% to 3% by weight of water (as structurally bound OH- ions), making the Mantle Transition Zone a vast internal reservoir holding water equivalent to several global oceans.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; Nature Geoscience & Fowler Solid Earth Geophysics

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the thermodynamic state and seismic behaviour of the Earth's core:
items: Statement-I: Across the Lehmann discontinuity at a depth of approximately 5,150 km, the Earth's core transitions from a liquid outer shell to a solid inner sphere even though ambient temperatures increase towards the centre of the Earth.

Statement-II: Primary (P) seismic waves experience an abrupt increase in velocity upon entering the inner core, which also exhibits cylindrical seismic anisotropy with waves travelling faster parallel to the Earth's rotational axis than parallel to the equatorial plane.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The phase transition from the liquid outer core to the solid inner core across the Lehmann discontinuity is governed by the intersection of the Earth's geothermal gradient (geotherm) with the iron-nickel melting point curve (liquidus), where extreme confining pressures (>330 GPa) elevate the melting point of iron above the ambient temperature. The resulting solid crystalline structure causes the observed jump in P-wave velocity and axial seismic anisotropy, making the seismic observation a consequence rather than the cause of solidification.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Although temperature increases with depth toward the Earth's centre (reaching ~5,400–6,000 K in the inner core), the melting point curve (liquidus) of the iron-nickel alloy rises more steeply with pressure than the actual geothermal gradient (geotherm). In the outer core, the geotherm lies above the iron liquidus (hence liquid), whereas at the Lehmann discontinuity (~5,150 km depth, ~330 GPa), the liquidus crosses above the geotherm, forcing iron to crystallize into a solid inner core.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I (Causal Reversal / T4). P-wave velocity jumps from ~10.3 km/s to ~11.1 km/s across the Lehmann discontinuity because the restoration of finite shear rigidity (shear modulus > 0) in a solid crystalline medium increases bulk wave velocity, and aligned hexagonal close-packed (hcp) iron crystals produce faster P-wave propagation along the spin axis. However, this seismic behaviour is the physical effect of the inner core being solid, whereas the thermodynamic reason for its solidity is the steeper slope of the pressure-dependent melting curve relative to the geotherm.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; Lowrie & Fichtner, Fundamentals of Geophysics (Core Thermodynamics & Geotherm-Liquidus Intersection)

stem: With reference to the generation of the Earth's magnetic field and the geodynamo mechanism, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Earth's main dipole magnetic field originates primarily from the permanent ferromagnetism of the solid iron-nickel inner core acting as a giant axial bar magnet.

2. Both thermal convection driven by heat loss across the core-mantle boundary and compositional buoyancy caused by the rejection of lighter elements during inner core crystallization power fluid motion in the outer core.

3. The Coriolis force resulting from the Earth's rotation organizes convective currents of electrically conducting liquid iron in the outer core into helical columns aligned roughly parallel to the spin axis.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Because temperatures throughout the Earth's core (>4,000 K) vastly exceed the Curie temperature of metallic iron (~1,043 K or 770°C), the core cannot sustain permanent ferromagnetism. Instead, the geomagnetic field is dynamically generated by a self-exciting fluid geodynamo in the liquid outer core, driven by thermo-compositional convection and organized into axial Taylor columns by the Coriolis force.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Ferromagnetic materials such as iron lose their permanent magnetization above their Curie temperature (~770°C at surface pressure) because thermal agitation randomizes magnetic domain alignment. Since temperatures in the Earth's core exceed 4,000–5,500°C, neither the outer nor the inner core can remain permanently magnetized.

Statement 2 is correct. The geodynamo is powered by thermo-compositional convection: secular cooling across the core-mantle boundary drives thermal convection, while the gradual freezing of the solid inner core expels lighter alloying elements (such as sulphur, oxygen, and silicon) into the base of the outer core, creating buoyant compositional plumes.

Statement 3 is correct. As buoyant parcels of electrically conducting liquid iron rise and sink in the outer core, the Coriolis force deflects their paths into corkscrew-like helical vortices (Taylor columns) aligned parallel to the Earth's rotational axis, inducing and sustaining an axial dipole magnetic field.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3 & 4;owler, The Solid Earth: An Introduction to Global Geophysics (Geodynamo Theory)

stem: With reference to paleomagnetism and geomagnetic polarity reversals, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Iron-bearing minerals such as magnetite in cooling basaltic lavas lock in the orientation of the ambient geomagnetic field only after cooling below their Curie temperature.
2. Geomagnetic polarity reversals occur with strict mathematical periodicity every 200,000 years and are accompanied by a corresponding flip in the Earth's physical axis of rotation.
3. The magnetic inclination preserved in ancient igneous rocks allows geologists to determine the paleolatitude at which the rock cooled.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Thermoremanent magnetization is acquired when ferromagnetic minerals cool below their Curie point, locking in both magnetic declination (direction to the magnetic pole) and inclination (which varies systematically with latitude from 0° at the magnetic equator to 90° at the magnetic poles). Geomagnetic polarity reversals are chaotic, aperiodic events within the fluid outer core that do not alter the Earth's rotational axis.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. When basaltic magma erupts and cools below the Curie temperature of magnetite (~580°C), the atomic magnetic domains become frozen in alignment with the prevailing geomagnetic field, preserving a permanent record called thermoremanent magnetization.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Geomagnetic reversals are stochastic (aperiodic) processes governed by non-linear fluid turbulence in the outer core; intervals between reversals vary wildly from tens of thousands of years to 'superchrons' lasting tens of millions of years (such as the ~37-million-year Cretaceous Normal Superchron). Furthermore, only the magnetic dipole flips—the Earth's physical spin axis remains unaffected.

Statement 3 is correct. Under the geocentric axial dipole hypothesis, the dip angle or magnetic inclination (I) of the magnetic field lines is mathematically tied to latitude (lambda) via tan(I) = 2 tan(lambda), enabling precise reconstruction of continental drift and paleolatitudes.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 4; Marshak, Earth: Portrait of a Planet (Paleomagnetism & Seafloor Spreading)

stem: With reference to gravity anomalies and isostatic mass distribution in the Earth's lithosphere, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Bouguer gravity anomalies measured over lofty young fold mountains such as the Himalayas are strongly negative because a deep, low-density sialic root displaces denser upper mantle material beneath the mountain chain.
2. Over deep oceanic basins, Bouguer gravity anomalies are strongly negative because the thin basaltic crust is overlain by a thick column of low-density seawater.
3. According to the Airy hypothesis of isostasy, variations in surface topography are compensated by lateral variations in the density of crustal columns that terminate at a uniform depth.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Bouguer gravity anomalies isolate subsurface density variations by correcting for elevation and the gravitational attraction of surface topography. Because high mountains are isostatically supported by deep, low-density granitic roots (~2.7 g/cm³) projecting into denser peridotitic mantle (~3.3 g/cm³), they exhibit strongly negative Bouguer anomalies, whereas ocean basins underlain by shallow dense mantle exhibit strongly positive Bouguer anomalies.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. After subtracting the gravitational attraction of the topographic rock mass above sea level (the Bouguer correction), gravity readings over the Himalayas reveal a large mass deficiency at depth caused by the thick (~70–80 km) low-density sialic crustal root displacing higher-density mantle rock, yielding a strongly negative Bouguer anomaly.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In marine gravity surveys, the marine Bouguer correction mathematically replaces the low-density seawater layer with rock of standard crustal density. Because the dense ultramafic mantle (peridotite, ~3.3 g/cm³) rises to within 5–7 km of the ocean floor (an 'anti-root'), oceanic basins exhibit strongly positive—not negative—Bouguer gravity anomalies.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Lateral density variations among crustal blocks terminating at a uniform depth of compensation is the postulate of the Pratt model of isostasy. In contrast, George Airy's model assumes that all crustal blocks have a uniform density (~2.7 g/cm³) and float in the denser mantle like icebergs, with higher mountains supported by deeper crustal roots.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; Savindra Singh, Physical Geography (Isostasy & Gravity Anomalies)

stem: With reference to the Earth's internal heat budget and dominant thermal transport mechanisms across interior layers, consider the following rows:
items: 1. Continental Crust : Dominated by thermal conduction : Highest volumetric concentration of heat-producing incompatible isotopes (U, Th, K)
2. Sub-lithospheric Mantle : Dominated by radiative and conductive transfer : Depleted of primordial heat and warmed exclusively by in-situ radiogenic decay
3. Liquid Outer Core : Dominated by convective heat transfer : Heat flux driven primarily by the radioactive decay of concentrated Uranium and Thorium alloys
prompt: In how many of the above rows is the given information correctly matched?
core: Incompatible radioactive elements (Uranium-238, Uranium-235, Thorium-232, and Potassium-40) have large ionic radii and high charges that prevent them from fitting into dense mantle silicates or metallic core alloys, concentrating them heavily in the granitic continental crust where rigid mechanics enforce conductive heat transport. Conversely, the mantle and outer core transport heat primarily by convection, with core heat derived from primordial accretion, gravitational differentiation, and latent heat of inner core crystallization rather than U/Th decay.

exp.why: Row 1 is correctly matched. Because the continental crust (and underlying lithospheric mantle) is mechanically rigid, it cannot convect, making thermal conduction the dominant heat transfer mode. Geochemically, U, Th, and K are large-ion lithophile (incompatible) elements that partition strongly into partial melts, giving the granitic continental crust the highest volumetric concentration of radiogenic heat production.

Row 2 is incorrectly matched. Across the sub-lithospheric mantle (asthenosphere and mesosphere), heat transport is overwhelmingly dominated by solid-state thermal convection (viscous creep of hot rock), as thermal conduction is orders of magnitude too slow over mantle thicknesses. Moreover, the mantle retains substantial primordial heat from planetary accretion and core heat flux alongside radiogenic heat.

Row 3 is incorrectly matched. Although heat transport in the liquid outer core is indeed dominated by vigorous fluid convection, Uranium and Thorium are strongly lithophile (silicate-loving) and chemically immiscible in liquid iron-nickel at planetary differentiation pressures. Thus, the core contains virtually no U or Th; its heat stems from primordial heat, gravitational energy released during core formation, and latent heat released as the inner core freezes.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3; Turcotte & Schubert, Geodynamics (Earth's Internal Heat Budget)

stem: With reference to direct and indirect geological analogues used to determine the composition of the Earth's interior, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Iron meteorites composed predominantly of iron-nickel alloys (kamacite and taenite) serve as compositional analogues for the Earth's differentiated metallic core.
2. Ultramafic peridotite xenoliths entrained in rapidly ascending kimberlite and alkali basalt magmas provide direct physical samples of the Earth's upper mantle.

3. Carbonaceous chondrites are highly differentiated meteorites that have undergone extensive partial melting and core-mantle segregation, making them compositional analogues for the upper granitic continental crust.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Geoscientists constrain the chemistry of the Earth's inaccessible interior by combining direct upper-mantle samples (peridotite xenoliths and ophiolite suites) with meteorite cosmochemistry. While iron meteorites represent the shattered metallic cores of differentiated planetesimals, carbonaceous chondrites are primitive, undifferentiated remnants of the early solar nebula that constrain the bulk composition of the entire Earth rather than its differentiated granitic crust.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Iron meteorites consist of crystalline iron-nickel alloys (kamacite and taenite) with minor sulphides (troilite), representing fragments of the metallic cores of early differentiated planetary embryos disrupted by collisions, and thus provide a close geochemical match for the Earth's core.

Statement 2 is correct. Xenoliths ('foreign rocks') of olivine- and pyroxene-rich peridotite ripped from the upper mantle walls at depths of 100–250 km and carried rapidly to the surface by volatile-rich kimberlite pipes or alkali basalts offer direct physical specimens of upper mantle mineralogy.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Carbonaceous chondrites are the most primitive, undifferentiated meteorites known; they never experienced planetary melting or core-mantle differentiation. Because their non-volatile elemental ratios closely match the solar photosphere, they represent the bulk starting composition of the solar nebula (Chondritic Uniform Reservoir), not the highly differentiated granitic continental crust.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3 (Interior of the Earth - Direct & Indirect Sources)

stem: With reference to the driving forces proposed by Alfred Wegener in his Continental Drift Theory (1912), consider the following statements:
items: 1. He attributed the equatorward movement of continents to the pole-fleeing force arising from the rotation of the Earth and its equatorial bulge.
2. He attributed the westward drift of the continents to the tidal force exerted by the gravitational attraction of the Sun and the Moon.
3. He proposed that sub-crustal thermal convection currents generated by radioactive decay in the mantle initiated the breakup of Pangaea.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Alfred Wegener relied solely on two external/rotational forces—the pole-fleeing force (for equatorward drift) and solar-lunar tidal force (for westward drift)—to explain continental movement. Sub-crustal thermal convection currents driven by radioactive heat in the mantle were postulated later in the 1930s by Arthur Holmes to overcome the mechanical inadequacy of Wegener's proposed forces.

exp.why: Wegener suggested that the movement responsible for the drifting of the continents towards the equator was caused by the pole-fleeing force (Polfluchtkraft), which relates to the centrifugal effect of the Earth's rotation acting on its equatorial bulge.

Wegener proposed that the westward movement of the continents (particularly the Americas) was caused by the tidal force due to the gravitational attraction of the Moon and the Sun, which he believed acted as a slow drag over millions of years.

Wegener was unaware of mantle convection currents. It was Arthur Holmes in the 1930s who proposed the Convection Current Theory, arguing that thermal differences generated by radioactive elements in the mantle drive sub-crustal convection cells capable of moving crustal masses.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4 (Distribution of Oceans and Continents); G.C. Leong Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following pairs regarding classical evidences offered in support of the Continental Drift Theory:
items: 1. Mesosaurus fossils : Distributed across all five Gondwana landmasses including Peninsular India, Australia and Antarctica
2. Gold-bearing placer deposits of the Ghana coast : Derived from gold-bearing veins located in the Brazilian plateau
3. Gondwana system of Tillites : Sedimentary deposits formed by ancient glaciation found across six distinct Southern Hemisphere landmasses and India
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: While Glossopteris flora and Gondwana Tillites show a pan-Gondwana distribution across India, Africa, Australia, Antarctica, and South America, Mesosaurus (a small Permian freshwater/brackish reptile) is restricted solely to two localities: the Southern Cape province of South Africa and the Iraver formations of Brazil. Similarly, Ghana's rich alluvial gold placers lack local source rock in West Africa and originate from the Brazilian plateau.

exp.why: Mesosaurus was a small reptile adapted to shallow brackish water whose fossil remains are found in only two regions worldwide: the Southern Cape province of South Africa and the Iraver formations of Brazil (presently separated by 4,800 km of ocean). It is the botanical fossil Glossopteris—not Mesosaurus—that is distributed across all Gondwana landmasses including India, Australia, Antarctica, South Africa, and Falkland Islands.

The occurrence of rich placer deposits of gold along the Ghana coast (West Africa) in the complete absence of any local gold-bearing parent rock in the region is explained by the fact that the gold-bearing veins are in Brazil, from where streams deposited the gold when the two continents lay side by side.

Tillite is a sedimentary rock formed out of deposits of glaciers. The Gondwana system of sediments from India has exact counterparts in six different landmasses of the Southern Hemisphere (Africa, Falkland Island, Madagascar, Antarctica, and Australia), proving prolonged shared palaeoglaciation.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4 (Distribution of Oceans and Continents)

stem: With reference to the post-World War II discoveries in ocean floor mapping and pre-Plate Tectonic theories, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Arthur Holmes postulated that thermal convection currents operating in the mantle are driven by heat generated from differential concentrations of radioactive elements.
2. Bathymetrical surveys of the ocean basins revealed that the deepest oceanic trenches are predominantly located along the central axes of the oceans, running parallel to the mid-oceanic ridges.
3. Radiometric dating established that rocks forming the crests of mid-oceanic ridges are substantially older than the rocks found in continental cratons.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Arthur Holmes (1930s) identified radioactive decay as the thermal engine driving mantle convection currents. Subsequent post-WWII ocean floor mapping revealed two critical anomalies that led to Seafloor Spreading: deep-sea trenches are situated near continental margins and island arcs (not in the centre of oceans), and oceanic crust is remarkably young compared to ancient continental rocks, with the youngest crust at the mid-oceanic ridge crest.

exp.why: In the 1930s, Arthur Holmes discussed the possibility of convection currents operating throughout the mantle portion, generated due to radioactive elements causing thermal differences in the mantle, providing a viable physical mechanism that Wegener lacked.

Contrary to early expectations, ocean floor mapping revealed that deep-sea trenches are not located in the middle of the ocean basins; instead, they are located very close to the continents and parallel to volcanic island arcs and fold mountain chains, particularly around the Pacific rim.

Radiometric dating showed the exact opposite: oceanic crust rocks are much younger than continental areas (nowhere older than 200 million years, vs up to 3,200+ million years for continental rocks), and rocks at the crest of the mid-oceanic ridges are the youngest of all, becoming progressively older away from the crest.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4 (Concept of Sea Floor Spreading & Ocean Floor Configuration)

stem: With reference to the geomorphology of the ocean floor and Harry Hess's Seafloor Spreading hypothesis, why are the rocks of the oceanic crust nowhere found to be older than about 200 million years, whereas continental cratons contain rocks over 3,000 million years old?

opts.A: Oceanic lithosphere is continuously created by basaltic volcanism at mid-oceanic ridges and eventually destroyed by subduction into the mantle at deep-sea trenches.
opts.B: Pre-Jurassic oceanic crust near the mid-oceanic ridge crests has been buried beneath several kilometres of abyssal marine sediments, rendering it inaccessible to deep-sea drilling.
opts.C: High hydrostatic pressure and hydrothermal acidity below the carbonate compensation depth chemically dissolve basaltic crust older than 200 million years.
opts.D: The ocean basins formed only after the breakup of Pangaea during the late Jurassic period, prior to which the Earth possessed a continuous sialic crust without oceanic floor.

core: Harry Hess (1961) explained the youthful nature of the ocean floor and the thinness of marine sediments through the seafloor conveyor-belt mechanism: constant volcanic eruptions at the crest of mid-oceanic ridges create new oceanic crust, while older denser oceanic lithosphere sinks and is consumed back into the mantle at oceanic trenches.

exp.why: Option A is correct because the oceanic crust operates on a geological recycling loop: new basaltic crust forms at divergent mid-oceanic ridges, spreads laterally on both sides, cools and densifies over time, and gets subducted into the asthenosphere at convergent deep-sea trenches within roughly 180–200 million years. Option B is incorrect because sediment cover at and near the mid-oceanic ridge crest is extremely thin or absent, thickening only as one moves away toward older crust. Option C is incorrect because the carbonate compensation depth dissolves calcareous oozes, not the underlying silicate basaltic crust. Option D is incorrect because pre-Jurassic oceans (such as Panthalassa and the Tethys) existed long before the breakup of Pangaea, though their ancient floors have since been subducted.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4 (Sea Floor Spreading - Harry Hess, 1961)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding palaeomagnetism and the evolution of ocean basins:
items: Statement-I: Oceanic crust on either side of the crest of a mid-oceanic ridge exhibits symmetrical, alternating stripes of normal and reversed magnetic polarity running parallel to the ridge axis.

Statement-II: Palaeomagnetic studies of ancient continental rocks reveal that the relative orientation of continents with respect to the Earth's magnetic poles has changed continuously over geological time.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The symmetrical zebra-like magnetic stripes of normal and reversed polarity parallel to mid-oceanic ridges (Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis) are caused by the combination of periodic geomagnetic polarity reversals and continuous bilateral seafloor spreading as basaltic lava cools below the Curie point—not by the gradual apparent polar wandering observed in continental rocks.

exp.why: Detailed magnetic surveys of the ocean floor on either side of mid-oceanic ridges revealed symmetrical mirror-image bands (anomalies) of normal and reversed magnetic polarity running parallel to the ridge crest, with rocks equidistant from the crest having identical ages and magnetic polarities.

Statement-II is factually true: palaeomagnetic measurements of continental rocks of different geological ages produce apparent polar wandering curves, demonstrating that continents have shifted relative to the magnetic poles. However, Statement-II does NOT explain Statement-I. The symmetrical alternating stripes of normal and reversed polarity on the ocean floor (Statement-I) are explained by the Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis: as new basaltic magma wells up at a mid-oceanic ridge and cools below its Curie temperature, magnetite crystals lock in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field, which periodically flips (geomagnetic reversals between North and South polarity) while the seafloor spreads laterally in both directions.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4; Savindra Singh Physical Geography (Palaeomagnetism & Seafloor Spreading)

stem: With reference to the Theory of Plate Tectonics, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike Wegener's hypothesis where only the sialic continents plough through the stationary ocean floor, Plate Tectonics postulates that both continents and ocean floors move as integral parts of rigid lithospheric slabs.
2. A tectonic plate is composed solely of continental or oceanic crust that glides horizontally over the Mohorovicic discontinuity.
3. The boundary of a major tectonic plate coincides with the geographical margin separating a continental landmass from its adjacent ocean basin.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: A tectonic (lithospheric) plate comprises both the crust and the rigid uppermost part of the mantle, varying in thickness from 5–100 km in oceanic parts to about 200 km in continental areas, and glides over the ductile asthenosphere rather than the Moho. Furthermore, most major plates carry both continental and oceanic lithosphere within the same plate, so continent-ocean coastlines (passive margins) rarely coincide with plate boundaries.

exp.why: Wegener considered continents to be freely moving sialic blocks ploughing through the underlying sima, whereas Plate Tectonics (McKenzie, Parker, and Morgan, 1967) established that continents are embedded within larger lithospheric plates and merely move along with the plate as a unified rigid unit.

A tectonic plate is not synonymous with the crust alone. It is a lithospheric slab comprising both the crust (continental and/or oceanic) and the rigid uppermost solid mantle below the Mohorovicic discontinuity. This entire lithosphere moves as a rigid unit over the mechanically weak, semi-molten asthenosphere.

Major tectonic plates (such as the Indo-Australian, North American, South American, African, and Eurasian plates) include both continental landmass and vast expanses of adjacent oceanic floor within the same rigid plate. Consequently, many continental coastlines (such as the Atlantic margins of the Americas and Africa or the coastlines of Peninsular India) are passive intraplate margins rather than plate boundaries.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4 (Plate Tectonics)

stem: With reference to the physical and compositional characteristics of the Earth's lithosphere, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The basaltic oceanic crust has a greater average thickness but a lower mean density compared to the granitic continental crust.

2. At convergent plate boundaries, continuous deep-mantle recycling via subduction occurs only in the oceanic lithosphere, because mature continental crust is too buoyant to sink into the denser asthenosphere.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Oceanic crust is thin (5–10 km) and dense (~3.0 g/cm³) due to its mafic (basaltic/gabbroic) composition, whereas continental crust is thick (35–70 km) and buoyant (~2.7 g/cm³) due to its felsic-to-intermediate (granitic/andesitic) composition. Because mature continental lithosphere remains permanently less dense than the underlying asthenospheric mantle (~3.3 g/cm³), only oceanic lithosphere undergoes continuous deep subduction.

exp.why: This statement reverses the thickness and density contrast between the two crustal types. Oceanic crust is significantly thinner (averaging 5 to 10 km) and denser (~3.0 g/cm³) because it is composed of mafic rocks rich in iron and magnesium (simatic/basaltic). Conversely, continental crust is much thicker (averaging 35 to 40 km, and up to 70 km beneath mountain belts) and less dense (~2.7 g/cm³) due to its sialic (granitic/granodioritic) composition.

As oceanic lithosphere cools and moves away from mid-oceanic ridges, its thickness and mean density exceed that of the underlying asthenosphere, driving slab pull and deep subduction. Mature continental crust, by contrast, is gravitationally buoyant relative to the mantle; when two continents collide after the intervening oceanic tract is consumed, subduction stalls and crustal thickening (orogeny) occurs instead of deep mantle recycling.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 3 & 4; Tarbuck & Lutgens, Earth: An Introduction to Physical Geology

stem: Consider the following pairs of Minor Tectonic Plates and their respective geographical locations:
items: 1. Cocos Plate : Between the Philippine Plate and the Indian Plate (North of New Guinea)
2. Caroline Plate : Between South America and the Pacific Plate
3. Fuji Plate : North-east of Australia in the south-west Pacific Ocean
4. Juan de Fuca Plate : Along the western margin of the North American Plate
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Minor tectonic plates predominantly occupy complex boundary zones around the Pacific Rim and the Indo-Australian margin. Accurate spatial mapping of the Cocos, Nazca, Caroline, Philippine, Fuji, and Juan de Fuca plates is essential to understanding regional subduction zones and volcanic arcs.

exp.why: The Cocos Plate is located in the eastern Pacific Ocean between Central America and the Pacific Plate (subducting beneath the Caribbean and North American plates to form the Central American Volcanic Arc). The minor plate located between the Philippine and Indian plates (north of New Guinea) is the Caroline Plate.

The minor plate situated between the western coast of South America and the Pacific Plate is the Nazca Plate (whose subduction beneath the South American Plate forms the Peru-Chile Trench and the Andes Mountains), not the Caroline Plate.

The Fuji Plate (or North Fiji micro-plate) is situated to the north-east of Australia in the south-west Pacific basin, within the complex convergence zone between the Pacific and Indo-Australian plates.

The Juan de Fuca Plate (a remnant of the ancient Farallon Plate) lies off the Pacific Northwest coast of North America (British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon) and subducts beneath the western margin of the North American Plate to form the Cascade Volcanic Arc.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4 (Distribution of Oceans and Continents)

stem: With reference to the geological processes operating along divergent plate boundaries, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Divergent plate boundaries are characterized by deep-focus earthquakes along a Wadati-Benioff zone accompanied by explosive calc-alkaline volcanism.

2. During the evolutionary transition from a continental rift such as the East African Rift Valley to a nascent linear sea like the Red Sea, the lithosphere undergoes progressive thickening due to horizontal compressional forces.

3. As seafloor spreading progresses along a mature mid-oceanic ridge, both the thickness of the overlying pelagic sediment cover and the mean density of the oceanic crust decrease steadily with increasing distance from the ridge crest.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Divergent plate boundaries are regimes of lithospheric extension, shallow normal-faulting seismicity, and decompression melting of the upwelling asthenosphere to yield low-viscosity tholeiitic basalt. As newly created oceanic lithosphere spreads laterally away from the ridge axis, it cools conductively, increases in density, subsides thermally, and accumulates progressively thicker marine sediments.

exp.why: Deep-focus earthquakes (down to 600–700 km along a Wadati-Benioff zone) and explosive calc-alkaline (andesitic/dacitic) volcanism are hallmarks of convergent subduction zones, not divergent boundaries. Because the lithosphere at divergent ridges is hot, thin, and under tensional stress, brittle fracture is confined to shallow depths (<15–20 km) via normal faulting, accompanied by quiet, effusive eruptions of low-viscosity basaltic lava.

Continental rifting (exemplified by the East African Rift evolving into the Red Sea proto-ocean) is driven by extensional tectonics and mantle upwelling, not horizontal compression. Under tensional stress, the continental lithosphere stretches and thins via normal faults (forming horst-and-graben topography) until it ruptures completely, allowing new basaltic oceanic crust to form.

At the ridge crest, the newly extruded oceanic crust is hottest, most buoyant (least dense), and virtually devoid of sediment cover. With increasing distance from the ridge crest, the oceanic crust becomes progressively older, cools conductively, contracts thermally to become denser, and accumulates a progressively thicker blanket of marine pelagic sediments.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4; G.C. Leong, Certificate Physical and Human Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the morphology of Mid-Oceanic Ridges:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the slow-spreading Mid-Atlantic Ridge which features a deep, rugged median rift valley, the fast-spreading East Pacific Rise exhibits a broad, smooth topographic swell lacking a prominent axial rift valley.

Statement-II: Fast-spreading mid-oceanic ridges experience much lower rates of decompression melting in the underlying asthenosphere, causing the axial crust to remain cold, thick, and structurally rigid against normal faulting.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The seafloor topography of mid-oceanic ridges is governed directly by spreading rate and thermal structure. Fast-spreading ridges have abundant magma supply and a hot, thermally buoyant axial zone that forms a broad swell without a deep graben, whereas slow-spreading ridges have intermittent magma supply and thicker brittle crust that fractures via steep normal faults to form a deep median rift valley.

exp.why: Slow-spreading ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Southwest Indian Ridge (spreading at 1–5 cm/year) display rugged topography with a steep, fault-bounded axial rift valley (1–3 km deep). In contrast, fast-spreading ridges such as the East Pacific Rise (spreading at >8–15 cm/year) have a wide, gently sloping axial high or topographic swell without a deep median graben.

This statement inverts the thermal and magmatic mechanism. Fast-spreading ridges experience much higher rates of mantle upwelling and decompression melting, sustaining a continuous, shallow axial magma lens. This high heat flux keeps the axial lithosphere warm, thin, buoyant, and ductile, preventing the development of large-offset normal faults and deep rift valleys.

ref: Tarbuck & Lutgens, Earth: An Introduction to Physical Geology; Savindra Singh, Physical Geography

stem: With reference to Oceanic-Continental convergent plate boundaries (Cordilleran-type subduction zones), consider the following statements:
items: 1. As the oceanic lithosphere descends into the mantle, marine sediments and oceanic crustal fragments are scraped off the downgoing slab to form an imbricated accretionary wedge along the inner wall of the deep-sea trench.
2. The primary mechanism generating magma beneath continental volcanic arcs such as the Andes is dry frictional melting of the subducting oceanic plate right at the shallow trench axis.

3. Partial melting and crustal assimilation as ascending magmas traverse the thick, silica-rich continental crust produce intermediate-to-felsic magmas that are more viscous and volatile-rich than mid-ocean ridge basalts.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: At oceanic-continental subduction zones, off-scraping of pelagic and terrigenous sediments builds an accretionary prism, while dehydration of the descending hydrous slab at depths of 80–120 km triggers flux melting in the overlying asthenospheric mantle wedge. Subsequent magmatic differentiation and crustal contamination within the overriding continental crust yield explosive andesitic-to-rhyolitic volcanic arcs.

exp.why: As the subducting oceanic plate bends and slides beneath the overriding continental plate, unconsolidated marine sediments and upper crustal slivers are sheared off and stacked by thrust faults against the leading edge of the overriding plate, creating a deformed accretionary wedge (or prism) bordering the oceanic trench.

Subduction zone magmatism is not caused by dry frictional heating at the shallow trench axis. Instead, as the hydrated oceanic crust descends to depths of roughly 80 to 120 km, increasing heat and pressure drive water and volatiles out of hydrous minerals in the slab into the overlying hot asthenospheric mantle wedge. This addition of water lowers the melting temperature (solidus) of the mantle peridotite—a process known as flux melting.

Although primary melts generated in the mantle wedge are basaltic, their ascent through the thick, buoyant, silica-rich continental crust involves fractional crystallization and assimilation of continental rocks (MASH processes), evolving the melt into viscous, volatile-rich andesitic, dacitic, and rhyolitic magmas.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 3 & 4; Alan Strahler, Introducing Physical Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Oceanic-Oceanic convergent plate boundaries:
items: Statement-I: Along the Mariana convergent boundary in the western Pacific, the Pacific Plate subducts steeply beneath the Philippine Sea Plate, forming the Mariana Trench and the Mariana Island Arc on the overriding Philippine Sea Plate.

Statement-II: When two oceanic plates converge, the geologically older oceanic lithosphere has undergone prolonged conductive cooling and thermal contraction away from its spreading ridge, making it thicker and denser than the younger, warmer oceanic plate.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In oceanic-oceanic convergence, relative plate age dictates subduction polarity because oceanic lithosphere cools, thickens, and increases in density as a function of the square root of its age. Consequently, the older, colder, and denser oceanic plate always subducts beneath the younger, warmer, and more buoyant oceanic plate.

exp.why: At the Mariana convergent margin, the ancient Jurassic-aged western Pacific Plate plunges steeply beneath the younger Cenozoic Philippine Sea Plate, creating the world's deepest oceanic trench (Mariana Trench) and generating the Mariana volcanic island arc on the overriding Philippine Sea Plate.

Because both plates share a mafic oceanic composition, the decisive factor determining which plate subducts is thermal density contrast governed by lithospheric age. Older oceanic lithosphere has cooled conductively for a much longer period since its formation at a spreading center, making its lithospheric mantle thicker, colder, and negatively buoyant compared to the younger oceanic plate, which directly explains why the older Pacific Plate subducts steeply beneath the Philippine Sea Plate.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 4; Tarbuck & Lutgens, Earth: An Introduction to Physical Geology

stem: With reference to the geological processes operating at Continental-Continental convergent plate boundaries, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The collision zone between two continental masses is frequently marked by an ophiolite-bearing suture zone representing remnants of a vanished ocean basin.

2. Because continental lithosphere is relatively buoyant compared to the underlying asthenosphere, convergence primarily results in crustal thickening, thrust faulting, and isostatic uplift rather than deep mantle subduction.
3. Present-day active stratovolcanoes are widespread along the Great Himalayan range due to the continuous deep subduction and flux melting of the Indian continental crust in the asthenosphere.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Continental-continental collision (such as the India-Eurasia collision) closes an intervening ocean basin along a suture zone (e.g., Indus-Yarlung Tsangpo Suture) and causes crustal doubling because buoyant felsic continental crust resists deep subduction into the dense mantle. Consequently, once the leading oceanic slab detaches (slab break-off), active subduction-driven arc volcanism ceases.

exp.why: Prior to continental collision, an oceanic basin (such as the Neo-Tethys Sea) separates the two landmasses. During closure and final welding of the continents along a suture zone (like the Indus-Yarlung Tsangpo Suture Zone), slivers of dense oceanic crust and upper mantle (ophiolites) are scraped off and obducted onto the continental margin.

Continental crust has a granitic/felsic composition with a lower average density (~2.7 g/cm³) compared to the ultramafic mantle (~3.3 g/cm³). Due to this high positive buoyancy, continental lithosphere cannot sink deeply into the asthenosphere; instead, compressive forces are accommodated by folding, imbricate thrust faulting (MCT, MBT, MFT), and doubling of crustal thickness (up to 70–80 km beneath Tibet).

Active stratovolcanoes are conspicuously absent along the Great Himalayan range. Pre-collisional calc-alkaline magmatism (seen in the Ladakh and Kohistan batholiths) occurred when the Neo-Tethyan oceanic lithosphere was subducting beneath Eurasia, but once continental collision occurred and the dense oceanic slab broke off, deep hydration and flux melting of the mantle wedge ceased.

ref: GC Leong Ch. 2 & 3; NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 4; Savindra Singh Geomorphology

stem: With reference to the mechanics of Transform Fault boundaries and oceanic Fracture Zones as formulated by J. Tuzo Wilson, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Along an oceanic fracture zone that offsets a mid-oceanic ridge, opposite plate motion and intense shallow-focus seismicity occur along the entire length of the linear scar, including the segments extending far beyond the offset ridge crests.

2. In a ridge-ridge transform fault system, the actual relative motion of the lithospheric blocks between the two offset spreading segments is in the direction opposite to the apparent geographical offset of the ridge crests.

3. Transform plate boundaries are not confined to oceanic crust; they can cut across continental lithosphere to link divergent or convergent boundaries, as exemplified by the San Andreas Fault and the Alpine Fault of New Zealand.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: J. Tuzo Wilson demonstrated that in a ridge-ridge transform system, only the segment strictly between the two offset spreading centers is an active transform fault where plates move in opposite directions and generate shallow earthquakes. Outside the ridge crests lie inactive fracture zones where adjacent seafloor belongs to the same plate and moves in the same direction.

exp.why: Active strike-slip shearing, opposite plate motion, and shallow-focus earthquakes occur strictly on the transform fault segment located between the two offset mid-oceanic ridge axes. Beyond the ridge crests, the linear topographic extensions are inactive 'fracture zones' where the crust on both sides belongs to the same lithospheric plate and moves in the same direction at nearly the same velocity, rendering them largely aseismic.

Because new seafloor spreads outward in both directions from each offset ridge segment, the relative slip between the two ridge crests is opposite to the apparent sense of offset that would be expected in a simple continental transcurrent fault. Furthermore, the distance between the two offset ridge axes remains constant over time as spreading continues.

Major transform faults frequently traverse continental lithosphere to connect other plate boundary segments. The San Andreas Fault connects the East Pacific Rise (divergent) in the south to the Juan de Fuca/Mendocino system in the north; the Alpine Fault in New Zealand links the Puysegur and Hikurangi subduction trenches; and the Dead Sea Transform links the Red Sea spreading center to the East Anatolian fault zone.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 4; Tarbuck & Lutgens Earth Science (Plate Tectonics)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the spatial and depth distribution of earthquakes across tectonic plate boundaries:
items: Statement-I: Deep-focus earthquakes originating at depths between 300 km and 700 km occur across both mid-oceanic divergent ridges and oceanic-continental subduction zones, continuing down to a depth of 1,200 km in the lower mantle.

Statement-II: Only cold, descending oceanic lithosphere at convergent subduction zones can retain sufficient structural integrity or undergo rapid high-pressure mineral phase transformations within the mantle transition zone before becoming completely ductile below approximately 700 km.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Intermediate (70–300 km) and deep-focus (300–700 km) earthquakes occur exclusively along dipping Wadati-Benioff zones at convergent subduction boundaries, never at divergent mid-oceanic ridges. Furthermore, no earthquakes have been recorded below ~670–700 km because the subducting slab heats up and deforms plastically in the lower mantle.

exp.why: Mid-oceanic divergent ridges and transform boundaries experience only shallow-focus earthquakes (typically < 30–70 km depth) because the high geothermal gradient at spreading centers makes the underlying asthenosphere too hot and ductile to store elastic strain. Moreover, even along convergent Wadati-Benioff zones, seismic activity terminates abruptly around 670–700 km and never extends to 1,200 km.

Deep-focus earthquakes (300–700 km) are restricted to Wadati-Benioff subduction zones because the rapidly descending oceanic slab remains much colder than the ambient mantle. In the mantle transition zone (410–660 km), sudden implosive mineral phase transformations (such as metastable olivine transforming into denser spinel/wadsleyite structures, known as transformational faulting) and dehydration embrittlement trigger deep seismic rupture until thermal equilibration renders the slab ductile below ~700 km.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 3 & 4; Savindra Singh Geomorphology

stem: With reference to the driving and resistive forces governing the motion of lithospheric plates, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Among the primary driving forces of plate tectonics, 'slab pull' generated by the negative buoyancy of cold, dense oceanic lithosphere sinking into the mantle at subduction zones is significantly stronger than 'ridge push' at mid-oceanic ridges.

2. 'Ridge push' is not a horizontal mechanical shove exerted by magma intrusion at the ridge axis, but rather a gravitational sliding body force acting across the elevated, thermally uplifted oceanic lithosphere as it cools and thickens away from the spreading center.
