Even when subjected to intense directed tectonic stress during regional metamorphism, pure quartzite and marble remain non-foliated (granoblastic) because they are essentially monomineralic rocks composed of equigranular quartz (SiO2) or calcite (CaCO3) crystals, lacking the platy sheet-silicates (micas, clays, chlorite) or prismatic amphiboles required to generate planar foliation.

This statement swaps the chemical and mineralogical pathways of mafic and felsic protoliths. Metamorphism is largely isochemical (preserving the bulk chemical composition of the parent rock aside from volatile loss). Mafic basalt (rich in iron, magnesium, and calcium, and deficient in free quartz) transforms into greenschist, amphibolite (composed mainly of hornblende and plagioclase), or eclogite. Conversely, felsic granite (rich in silica, quartz, and alkali feldspar) metamorphoses into granitic gneiss (orthogneiss).

When quartz sandstone metamorphoses into quartzite, elevated heat and pressure cause the original clastic quartz grains and silica cement to recrystallize and fuse into a tightly interlocking mosaic of quartz crystals. This process completely obliterates primary intergranular pore spaces, reducing porosity and permeability to near zero and making quartzite so compact that fractures cut directly across individual crystals rather than around grain boundaries.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 5; GC Leong Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the geological rock cycle and its manifestation across major Indian geological formations, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: In the crustal rock cycle, primary igneous rocks must first undergo surface weathering, erosion, and lithification into sedimentary strata before they can be transformed into metamorphic rocks.
opts.B: The Vindhyan Supergroup of Central India represents an ancient Archaean basement complex composed predominantly of high-grade plutonic charnockites and strongly foliated migmatites.
opts.C: The Deccan Traps represent a thick sequence of regionally metamorphosed argillaceous schists, whereas the Dharwar System consists of unaltered continental flood basalts erupted during the Cenozoic Era.
opts.D: The rock cycle operates as a non-linear system wherein plutonic igneous rocks can directly recrystallize into metamorphic orthogneiss, as seen in parts of the Archaean Peninsular Gneissic Complex, and existing metamorphic rocks can undergo further re-metamorphism.

core: The rock cycle is a multi-directional, non-linear web of crustal pathways driven by internal tectonic heat and external solar-driven weathering: igneous rocks can be directly metamorphosed into orthogneiss without an intermediate sedimentary stage, and pre-existing metamorphic rocks can undergo polymetamorphism or partial melting.

exp.why: Option D is correct because the rock cycle is not a rigid one-way circle. Igneous rocks (plutonic or volcanic) can be subjected directly to high temperature and directed tectonic stress deep within the crust to form metamorphic rocks (termed orthogneiss or ortho-amphibolite, as contrasted with paragneiss derived from sedimentary protoliths). Large tracts of the Archaean Peninsular Gneissic Complex in Southern India consist of tonalite-trondhjemite-granodiorite (TTG) plutonic protoliths that directly underwent regional metamorphism into orthogneiss, and existing metamorphic rocks frequently undergo further re-metamorphism (polymetamorphism). Option A is incorrect because igneous rocks do not need to pass through a sedimentary stage to become metamorphic rocks. Option B is incorrect because the Vindhyan Supergroup is a Proterozoic intracratonic sedimentary sequence dominated by horizontally bedded, largely unmetamorphosed sandstones, shales, and limestones, whereas charnockites and migmatites belong to the older Archaean granulite-gneiss basement. Option C is incorrect because it reverses the two formations: the Deccan Traps are Cretaceous-Paleogene continental flood basalts (extrusive igneous rocks), while the Dharwar System is an Archaean-Proterozoic volcano-sedimentary sequence rich in regionally metamorphosed schists.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 5; DR Khuller India: A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the exogenic geomorphic processes of weathering and erosion, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Weathering requires a mobile geomorphic medium such as running water or wind to transport disintegrated rock debris over short local gradients.
2. Unlike weathering, erosion necessarily involves the acquisition and transportation of rock debris through the kinetic energy of mobile geomorphic agents.
3. While weathering significantly aids erosion by weakening and fragmenting coherent bedrock, it is not a mandatory pre-condition for erosion to take place.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Weathering is strictly an in-situ (on-site) process involving the mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks with little or no motion of material, whereas erosion is a kinetic process driven by mobile geomorphic agents. Although weathering prepares the rock mantle for easier removal, both mass movements and erosion can operate directly on unweathered bedrock.

exp.why: Weathering is defined as the mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks in-situ (on-site) through the actions of various elements of weather and climate. Very little or no motion of materials takes place in weathering beyond minor gravity-induced settling; it does not require a mobile geomorphic transport medium.

Erosion involves the acquisition and transportation of rock debris. When massive rocks break into smaller fragments, mobile geomorphic agents like running water, groundwater, glaciers, wind, and waves use their kinetic energy to remove and transport the debris to other locations.

Weathering aids mass wasting and erosion by lowering the shear strength and coherence of rocks. However, a rock need not be weathered before it is eroded or undergoes mass movement; hence, weathering is not a mandatory pre-condition for erosion.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 6 (Geomorphic Processes)

stem: With reference to the mechanisms of chemical weathering in rocks, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Carbonation accelerates the breakdown of carbonate rocks because rainwater absorbs atmospheric and soil carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid that converts insoluble calcium carbonate into soluble calcium bicarbonate.

2. Hydration is a reversible physico-chemical process wherein minerals absorb water and expand in volume, generating internal stresses that cause mechanical fatigue and disintegration in the enclosing rock.
3. Reduction occurs predominantly in well-aerated vadose zones above the permanent water table, converting ferrous iron into reddish-brown ferric oxides.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Chemical weathering operates through solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation, and reduction. While oxidation occurs above the water table where atmospheric oxygen is readily available to rust iron-bearing minerals into red/yellow ferric oxides, reduction occurs below the water table in anaerobic, stagnant waterlogged conditions, turning ferric iron into bluish-grey or greenish ferrous compounds.

exp.why: Carbonation is the reaction of carbonate and bicarbonate ions with minerals. Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and soil air dissolves in rainwater to form weak carbonic acid (H2CO3), which reacts with limestone or chalk (CaCO3) to form soluble calcium bicarbonate, leading to karst dissolution.

Hydration is the chemical addition of water to a mineral (such as calcium sulphate taking up water to become gypsum). This reaction is reversible, and its repetition causes volume expansion and contraction, inducing fatigue and pore-space stress that splits rock grains.

The statement swaps Oxidation and Reduction. Oxidation takes place in well-aerated zones above the water table where there is ready access to oxygenated air and water, turning ferrous iron into red or brown ferric oxides. Reduction occurs when oxidized minerals are placed in an anaerobic environment without oxygen, usually below the water table in areas of stagnant water and waterlogged ground, changing the red colour of iron to greenish or bluish-grey.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 6; G.C. Leong Ch. 4

stem: Consider the following statements regarding physical weathering and associated landforms:
items: Statement-I: Large, smooth and rounded exfoliation domes develop in homogeneous plutonic rocks like granite when thick curved shells of rock spall off from the underlying bedrock.

Statement-II: In dry climates with high diurnal ranges of temperature, differential thermal expansion and contraction of surface rock layers generate internal shearing stresses that produce smooth-surfaced boulders known as exfoliation tors.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Exfoliation is a result description (flaking off of curved shells) rather than a single process. Large exfoliation domes (like those in granitic batholiths) form due to unloading and vertical pressure release upon the erosion of superincumbent rock layers, whereas smaller exfoliation tors form due to differential thermal expansion and contraction driven by diurnal temperature changes.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Continued erosion of overlying rocks removes the superincumbent load on deeply buried intrusive igneous rocks (such as granite batholiths). The resulting release of vertical confining pressure causes the upper layers of rock to expand radially and fracture roughly parallel to the ground surface, producing large, smooth, rounded exfoliation domes.

Statement-II is also factually correct, as diurnal temperature changes in dry climates cause the outer layers of boulders to expand and contract more rapidly than their cooler interiors, leading to stress-induced flaking and the creation of smooth-surfaced exfoliation tors. However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I because large exfoliation domes are formed by pressure release (unloading) rather than diurnal insolation heating, which penetrates only a few centimetres into rock.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 6 (Unloading and Expansion vs Temperature Changes)

stem: With reference to the physical weathering processes of frost wedging and salt crystallization, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Frost wedging operates at its maximum intensity in the permanently frozen interiors of polar ice sheets where temperatures remain continuously below the freezing point throughout the year.
opts.B: Salt crystallization is purely a chemical dissolution process that weakens silicate minerals without exerting any mechanical or physical pressure on the pore walls of host rocks.
opts.C: Frost wedging is most rapid in high-altitude and sub-polar periglacial environments experiencing frequent diurnal freeze-thaw cycles, whereas salt weathering is most effective in arid and coastal zones where alternating wetting and high evaporation promote crystal growth in rock pores.
opts.D: Among common sedimentary and igneous rocks, non-porous massive quartzite is the most susceptible to rapid disintegration by salt crystallization, whereas chalk and porous sandstone are the most resistant.

core: Frost wedging relies on the ~9% volumetric expansion of water upon freezing within rock fractures, making it most potent where temperatures frequently oscillate across 0°C rather than where water stays permanently frozen. Salt weathering is a powerful mechanical weathering mechanism in hot deserts and coastal zones, driven by thermal expansion, hydration, and crystallization pressure of salts within porous rocks.

exp.why: Option C is correct. Frost wedging requires repeated freezing and thawing of water trapped in rock cracks; hence, it is most rapid in glacial-margin, periglacial, and high-elevation middle-latitude mountains with frequent freeze-thaw cycles rather than permanently frozen polar interiors (making Option A incorrect). Salt weathering is a major physical weathering process in deserts and coastal areas where evaporation draws saline solutions to rock pores, and salts expand due to thermal heating, hydration, and crystallization (making Option B incorrect). Highly porous sedimentary rocks like chalk, limestone, sandstone, and shale are the most susceptible to salt crystal growth, whereas dense non-porous quartzite is highly resistant (making Option D incorrect).

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 6 (Freezing, Thawing and Frost Wedging; Salt Weathering)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding mass movements (mass wasting):
items: Statement-I: In geomorphology, mass movements are excluded from the strict category of erosion even though they involve the downslope transfer of massive volumes of rock debris from one place to another.
Statement-II: Although mass movements are much more active over weathered slopes than over unweathered rock, weathering is not a mandatory prerequisite for mass movements to occur.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Mass movements transfer rock debris downslope under the direct and sole driving force of gravity. They do not come under erosion because mobile geomorphic agents (running water, glaciers, wind, waves) do not participate directly in carrying the debris; instead, the debris itself moves downslope carrying air, water, or ice with it.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Even though there is a shift of materials from one place to another, mass movements do not come under erosion because no geomorphic agent like running water, glaciers, wind, waves, or currents participates directly in the process of carrying debris. Gravity is the sole driving force.

Statement-II is also correct: weathering aids mass movements considerably by reducing rock coherence, so mass movements are much more active over weathered slopes, yet unweathered steep bedrock can still fail under gravity. However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I; the reason mass movements are excluded from erosion is the absence of a transporting geomorphic agent (gravity acts directly), not the optional nature of prior weathering.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 6 (Mass Movements)

stem: With reference to the classification and mechanics of mass movements, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Solifluction is a slow-flowage mass movement characteristic of moist temperate and periglacial regions where water-saturated surface soil flows slowly downslope over an impermeable frozen or waterlogged substrate.

2. Unlike a debris slide or rockslide which involves rapid sliding without backward tilting, a slump is characterized by the slipping of one or several units of rock debris with a backward rotation with respect to the slope over a concave slip plane.
3. In the absence of vegetative cover and following heavy rainfall, thick layers of weathered materials get saturated with water and move rapidly down definite channels as mudflows.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mass movements are classified by rate of movement and water content into slow movements (creep, solifluction), rapid flows (earthflow, mudflow, debris avalanche), and landslides (slump, debris slide, rockslide, rockfall). The critical structural distinction among landslides is whether movement occurs with backward rotation along a concave plane (slump) or planar translation along bedding/joint planes without backward rotation (debris slide and rockslide).

exp.why: Solifluction involves slow downslope flowing of soil mass or fine-grained rock debris saturated or lubricated with water. It is especially common in moist temperate and periglacial areas where surface thawing of permafrost or heavy rain saturates the upper soil layer while the deeper permafrost or clay horizon remains impermeable, preventing downward percolation.

Within landslides, 'slump' refers to the slipping of one or several units of rock debris with a backward rotation with respect to the slope over which the movement takes place. By contrast, rapid rolling or sliding of earth debris without backward rotation is known as 'debris slide', and sliding of individual rock masses down bedding, joint, or fault surfaces is a 'rockslide'.

In the absence of vegetation cover and with heavy rainfall, thick layers of weathered materials get saturated with water and flow either slowly or rapidly down along definite channels as mudflows, looking like a stream of mud and often spilling out onto piedmont plains or roads.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 6; Savindra Singh Geomorphology

stem: With reference to fluvial erosional landforms formed during the youthful stage of a river, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A gorge is characterized by step-like side slopes where the valley is significantly wider at the top than at its floor, whereas a canyon has almost equal width at both its top and bottom.
2. Canyons commonly develop in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks where alternating layers of hard and soft strata undergo differential erosion.
3. Potholes are cylindrical depressions drilled into the rocky beds of hill streams through the rotational abrasion of pebbles and boulders caught in water eddies.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In the youthful stage, steep gradients drive dominant vertical downcutting (valley deepening) over lateral erosion, producing deep V-shaped valleys. Whether a valley evolves into a steep-walled gorge or a stepped canyon depends primarily on rock hardness, structural bedding, and regional aridity.

exp.why: This statement inverts the geometric distinction between a gorge and a canyon. A gorge is a deep, narrow valley with very steep to vertical walls that maintains almost equal width at its top and its floor, typically forming in massive hard rocks. Conversely, a canyon is characterized by step-like side slopes and is much wider at its top than at its bottom.

Canyons are variants of gorges that commonly form in horizontally bedded sedimentary strata (especially in arid or semi-arid regions like the Grand Canyon), where resistant sandstone or limestone layers form vertical cliffs and softer shale layers weather back into gentler slopes, creating a stepped profile.

Over rocky beds of fast-flowing hill streams, small shallow depressions trap pebbles and boulders. Swirling water currents (eddies) rotate these fragments like a drill (evorsion/abrasion), deepening and widening the depressions into cylindrical potholes; large and deep potholes at the base of waterfalls form plunge pools.

ref: NCERT Class XI: Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 7 (Landforms and their Evolution)

stem: With reference to river rejuvenation and associated landforms, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Incised meanders develop when a meandering stream flowing over a gentle gradient experiences rejuvenation due to regional tectonic uplift or a fall in sea level, accelerating vertical downcutting into the bedrock.

2. Unpaired river terraces found at different elevations on opposite banks are diagnostic of rapid, purely vertical incision without lateral channel migration, whereas paired terraces result from slow downcutting accompanied by continuous lateral shifting.
3. River terraces represent the dissected remnants of former valley floors or floodplains that have been abandoned as the stream incised to a lower base level.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Rejuvenation restores vertical erosive energy to a mature or senile river through a negative change in base level or tectonic uplift. The symmetry of the resulting river terraces (paired versus unpaired) records the relative ratio of vertical incision rate to lateral channel migration.

exp.why: While normal meanders form on gentle alluvial floodplains through lateral migration, incised (entrenched or ingrown) meanders occur when a pre-existing meandering stream is rejuvenated by tectonic uplift of the landmass or a eustatic drop in sea level, forcing the sinuous channel to cut deeply into the underlying bedrock.

This statement reverses the geomorphic origin of paired and unpaired terraces. Paired terraces occur at the same elevation on both sides of the river and indicate rapid vertical incision (due to rapid tectonic uplift or sudden discharge changes) where the river cuts down symmetrically before lateral shifting can destroy one floodplain margin. Unpaired terraces occur at unequal elevations on opposite banks and result from slow, progressive downcutting combined with lateral shifting of the meandering channel.

River terraces are step-like benches along the valley sides that mark former valley floor levels (either bedrock benches or older alluvial floodplains) left stranded above the active channel after vertical incision.

ref: NCERT Class XI: Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 7; Savindra Singh Geomorphology

stem: Consider the following statements comparing the morphology and depositional mechanics of Alluvial Fans and Deltas:
items: 1. Alluvial fans form at the piedmont zone where mountain streams experience an abrupt drop in gradient upon entering a plain, whereas deltas develop where a river approaches its base level at a standing body of water.
2. Alluvial fans in humid regions typically exhibit very steep, high cones with poorly spread debris, whereas those in arid and semi-arid climates form broad, low-angle cones with gentle gradients.
3. Compared to alluvial fan deposits, deltaic sediments exhibit markedly finer grain sizes and well-developed vertical and lateral stratification.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Both alluvial fans and deltas form when a drop in flow velocity reduces stream competence, triggering channel avulsion and distributary branching. However, climate controls the slope of alluvial fans, while subaqueous settling gives deltas superior sorting and stratification.

exp.why: Alluvial fans are terrestrial piedmont deposits created when a high-gradient mountain stream exits a narrow gorge onto a flat foothill plain and loses carrying capacity. Deltas are coastal or lacustrine deposits formed where a river enters a sea or lake at its ultimate or local base level.

This statement inverts the climatic control on alluvial fan morphology. In humid regions, abundant and sustained water discharge carries alluvium much further downslope, forming broad, low cones with gentle gradients from head to toe. In arid and semi-arid climates, ephemeral flash floods undergo rapid infiltration and evaporation upon leaving the mountain front, dumping coarse debris immediately to form steep, high cones.

Alluvial fans consist mostly of coarse, poorly sorted, and poorly stratified boulders, pebbles, and sands dumped rapidly at the mountain base. In contrast, deltaic sediments are well-sorted and distinctly stratified (into topset, foreset, and bottomset beds), with coarse material settling near the mouth and fine silts and clays carried further offshore.

ref: NCERT Class XI: Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 7 (Alluvial Fans and Deltas)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the hydrodynamics of meandering rivers:
items: Statement-I: In a meandering river channel, point bars are deposited along the inner convex bank (slip-off slope), whereas active undercutting and steep bank retreat occur along the outer concave bank.

Statement-II: As a river negotiates a meander bend, centrifugal force directs the maximum flow velocity toward the inner convex bank at the surface, triggering a bottom helicoidal current that sweeps coarse bedload toward the outer concave bank.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Meander migration is driven by corkscrew-like helicoidal flow within the channel bend. Centrifugal force pushes fast surface water against the outer concave bank, causing erosion and super-elevation, which in turn drives a compensating bottom current toward the inner convex bank where point bars accumulate.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Along a meander loop, the outer concave bank (cut-off bank) experiences intense hydraulic action and corrasion, forming a steep cliff-like bluff, while the inner convex bank experiences reduced velocity and sediment accumulation, forming gentle point bars (meander bars) on the slip-off slope.

Statement-II is incorrect because it reverses the direction of the centrifugal force and the helicoidal return flow. As water enters a curve, centrifugal force pushes the filament of maximum surface velocity toward the outer concave bank (not the inner convex bank). This slightly elevates the water surface at the outer bank, generating a transverse pressure gradient along the river bed that drives a bottom helicoidal current from the outer concave bank toward the inner convex bank, sweeping eroded bedload onto the slip-off slope.

ref: NCERT Class XI: Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 7; G.C. Leong Ch. 5

stem: With reference to river channel patterns and delta morphologies, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Braided river channels develop when a stream's sediment load exceeds its transport capacity and its banks are composed of easily erodible alluvium, causing the flow to split around shifting mid-channel bars.
2. A bird-foot delta develops only along coasts experiencing a macro-tidal range and strong longshore currents that focus coarse sand into elongated distributary fingers.

3. An arcuate delta is formed when a river empties into a deep, submerged river mouth where strong tidal currents continuously flush out sediment into narrow estuarine bars without forming a convex shoreline.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Delta geometry reflects the three-way interplay among river sediment input, wave energy, and tidal range. River-dominated coasts with fine clay loads form bird-foot deltas, wave-reshaped shallow shelves with multi-distributary coarse loads form arcuate deltas, and macro-tidal submerged river mouths form estuarine deltas.

exp.why: Braiding occurs when a stream experiences fluctuating discharge, a high bedload-to-suspension ratio, and weak, easily erodible banks. As lateral erosion widens the channel and reduces flow depth, competence drops, depositing longitudinal sand and gravel bars (eyots) that divide the stream into an interlacing network of channels.

A bird-foot (digitate) delta, exemplified by the Mississippi River, requires the exact opposite marine conditions: very weak wave action, a micro-tidal range, and a low-energy sheltered basin. Moreover, the river carries a high proportion of fine suspended clay that flocculates in seawater and seals the natural levees, preventing crevasse breaches and allowing a few main distributaries to build long, narrow fingers far out to sea.

This description pertains to an estuarine delta (such as the Narmada, Tapi, Seine, or Elbe), where a submerged river mouth is partially infilling with linear tidal sandbars. An arcuate (fan-shaped) delta, such as the Nile or Ganga-Brahmaputra, forms where numerous branching distributaries deposit porous sands and gravels into a shallow shelf, and moderate wave action smooths the outer perimeter into a convex arc.

ref: NCERT Class XI: Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 7; G.C. Leong Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the geological preconditions and erosional landforms of Karst topography, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Karst landforms achieve their most mature development in thick, highly porous, and unjointed chalk formations where rainwater can saturate the entire rock mass uniformly through primary pore spaces.
2. When several adjacent sinkholes or dolines enlarge through continued carbonation and roof collapse, they coalesce to form a compound elongated depression known as a uvala.
3. Lapies are corrugated ridges, grooves, and pinnacles carved on exposed limestone surfaces by differential solution along joints and crevices.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Karst topography is driven by carbonation-solution along planes of secondary permeability. Consequently, dense, crystalline, thinly bedded, and well-jointed limestone supports classic subterranean karst conduits and surface sinkholes, whereas highly porous chalk absorbs water like a sponge without concentrating flow.

exp.why: Ideal karst development requires soluble rock (limestone or dolomite) that is dense, compact, crystalline, thinly bedded, and extensively jointed, having low primary porosity. If the rock is highly porous and unjointed (like chalk), water percolates uniformly through primary intergranular pores across the entire rock body rather than concentrating along specific fracture lines and bedding planes, which prevents the excavation of distinct subterranean caverns and classic karst landforms.

Surface solution creates funnel-shaped depressions called sinkholes, which enlarge by subsurface roof collapse into dolines. When the dividing walls between several neighbouring sinkholes or dolines dissolve or collapse, they merge to form a larger, compound valley sink or elongated trench called a uvala.

As weakly acidic rainwater (carbonic acid) flows over bare, jointed limestone pavement, it selectively dissolves the rock along joints and fractures, transforming the smooth surface into an irregular, jagged terrain of sharp grooves, pits, and ridges termed lapies (or karren).

ref: NCERT Class XI: Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 7 (Groundwater and Karst Topography)

stem: In karst landscapes, underground depositional features (speleothems) such as stalactites, stalagmites, and pillars are formed when percolating groundwater enters open limestone caverns. Which one of the following chemical mechanisms primarily triggers the precipitation of solid calcium carbonate inside these caverns?

opts.A: A sudden increase in hydrostatic pressure inside the cavern that lowers the solubility of dissolved bicarbonate ions
opts.B: Rapid cooling of percolating geothermal groundwater upon contact with the colder subterranean rock walls
opts.C: Degassing of dissolved carbon dioxide and partial evaporation as calcium bicarbonate-rich water enters the lower carbon dioxide partial pressure environment of the cave
opts.D: Oxidation of dissolved calcium sulphate by subterranean chemosynthetic bacteria in the absence of sunlight

core: Speleothem deposition in karst caverns is governed by the reversible carbonation equilibrium between insoluble calcium carbonate and soluble calcium bicarbonate. When percolating water exited from narrow rock joints enters an open cavern with lower carbon dioxide partial pressure, CO2 degassing and partial evaporation reverse the reaction to precipitate calcite.

exp.why: Option C is correct because rainwater percolating through soil organic matter absorbs elevated levels of carbon dioxide (CO2), forming weak carbonic acid (H2CO3) that dissolves limestone (CaCO3) into soluble calcium bicarbonate [Ca(HCO3)2]. When this water emerges through fissures onto the ceiling of an air-filled cave where the partial pressure of CO2 is much lower than in the soil and rock pores, dissolved CO2 escapes (degasses) into the cave air alongside partial water evaporation, driving the reaction backwards to precipitate solid calcite (stalactites and stalagmites). Option A is incorrect because entering an open cavern lowers pressure rather than increasing it, and higher pressure actually increases CO2 solubility. Option B is incorrect because calcium carbonate exhibits retrograde solubility (it is more soluble in cold water than warm water), so cooling would promote dissolution rather than precipitation. Option D is incorrect because classic limestone speleothems are calcium carbonate precipitates driven by inorganic degassing, not bacterial oxidation of calcium sulphate.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7 (Landforms and their Evolution); G.C. Leong Ch. 8

stem: With reference to glacial erosional landforms, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Cirques are amphitheatre-like bedrock hollows at the heads of glacial valleys deepened by rotational ice movement, basal abrasion, and frost-wedging along the bergschrund.
2. Horns and arêtes are crescent-shaped ridges of sorted boulder clay deposited at the snout of retreating valley glaciers.
3. Fjords are funnel-shaped submerged coastal inlets formed when V-shaped fluvial valleys are drowned by post-glacial sea-level rise without prior glacial modification.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Alpine and high-latitude glacial erosion sculptures sharp upland bedrock features (cirques, arêtes, horns) and deep U-shaped troughs through plucking and abrasion. Submerged glacial troughs form steep-walled fjords with shallow rocky thresholds, which are genetically distinct from drowned fluvial Ria coasts.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Cirques (corries or cwm) are armchair-shaped or amphitheatre-like hollows excavated at the heads of valley glaciers due to rotational sliding of ice, abrasion of the rock basin floor, and intense plucking/frost-shattering along the deep crevasse (bergschrund) at the headwall. When the ice melts, water often collects in the over-deepened basin to form a cirque or tarn lake.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Horns (pyramidal peaks) and arêtes (knife-edged ridges) are high-altitude glacial erosional bedrock landforms created when two or more cirques erode headward into a mountain mass from opposite or radial sides. Crescent-shaped ridges of unsorted glacial till deposited at the snout of a glacier are terminal or end moraines.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Drowned V-shaped fluvial river valleys that were never glaciated form Ria coasts. Fjords are deep, steep-sided, U-shaped glacial troughs that were excavated below sea level by powerful valley glaciers before being submerged by marine transgression after deglaciation.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7; Savindra Singh Physical Geography Ch. 21

stem: Geomorphologists reconstruct the direction of ancient ice-sheet movement using asymmetric glaciated landforms. In this context, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A roche moutonnée is an elongated streamlined hill of unsorted glacial till featuring a steep, blunt upstream (stoss) slope facing the advancing ice and a gently tapering downstream (lee) slope.
2. A drumlin is an erosional bedrock landform characterized by a smooth, gently inclined upstream (stoss) face polished by abrasion and a steep, jagged downstream (lee) face shaped by plucking.

3. In a 'crag and tail' feature, a mass of resistant rock obstructs the advancing glacier on the upstream side and shields softer rock or glacial drift in its leeward shadow to form a gently sloping tail in the direction of ice flow.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Asymmetric glacial landforms serve as reliable directional indicators of paleo-ice flow, but erosional and depositional forms exhibit opposite slope profiles. A roche moutonnée (erosional bedrock) has a gentle abraded stoss side and a steep plucked lee side, whereas a drumlin (depositional till) has a steep blunt stoss side and a gently tapering lee tail.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it describes a drumlin rather than a roche moutonnée. A roche moutonnée is an erosional resistant bedrock mound in which the upstream (stoss) side is smoothed, striated, and gently inclined due to glacial ice abrasion, while the downstream (lee) side is steep, rough, and jagged due to glacial plucking (quarrying) induced by pressure-release refreezing.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it swaps the characteristics of a drumlin with those of a roche moutonnée. Drumlins are smooth, oval, elongated whale-backed hills composed of unsorted boulder clay (glacial till) deposited beneath active ice; their steeper, blunter stoss end points upstream against the ice source, while their gentler, narrower lee tail tapers downstream in the direction of ice advance.

Statement 3 is correct. A 'crag and tail' develops where a steep, resistant volcanic plug or hard bedrock knob (the crag) faces the oncoming glacier and protects the less resistant sedimentary strata or accumulated glacial till immediately behind it on the downstream (lee) side, creating a gently tapering ramp (the tail) aligned with the direction of ice movement.

ref: G.C. Leong Certificate Physical and Human Geography Ch. 6; Savindra Singh Physical Geography Ch. 21

stem: With reference to the sedimentological and geomorphic characteristics of glacial and glacio-fluvial deposits, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Terminal and ground moraines consist predominantly of well-sorted, horizontally stratified layers of rounded gravel and sand deposited by proglacial meltwater.
2. A medial moraine develops along the central zone of a compound glacier when two tributary valley glaciers coalesce and their adjacent lateral moraines join together.
3. Outwash plains (sandur) formed beyond the terminal moraine display distinct particle-size sorting and stratification because the glacial debris is reworked by braided meltwater streams.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Glacial drift is divided into unstratified glacial till dropped directly by melting ice and stratified fluvioglacial outwash deposited by meltwater streams. Because solid ice cannot sort debris by weight or density, moraines consist of chaotic, angular, unsorted till, whereas outwash plains contain water-sorted, layered sediments.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Terminal, lateral, medial, and ground moraines are formed by direct deposition from glacial ice without water sorting. Consequently, they are composed of glacial till (or boulder clay)—an unstratified, unsorted, heterogeneous mixture of angular rock fragments ranging in size from fine rock flour and clay to massive erratic boulders.

Statement 2 is correct. Lateral moraines form along the margins of a valley glacier from frost-shattered debris falling from valley walls. When two separate valley glaciers converge to form a single trunk glacier, their inner lateral moraines merge to create a dark ridge of debris running down the middle of the glacier known as a medial moraine.

Statement 3 is correct. Beyond the terminal moraine, meltwater emerging from the glacier snout spreads out in a network of braided glacio-fluvial streams to form an outwash plain (sandur). Because moving water loses competence progressively with distance, coarse gravels are deposited near the ice front while finer sands and silts are carried further downstream, producing sorted and stratified beds.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7; G.C. Leong Ch. 6

stem: Consider the following statements regarding fluvioglacial landforms:
items: Statement-I: Eskers are long, narrow, sinuous ridges composed of stratified sand and gravel that often run across hills and valleys at elevated levels above the present ground surface.

Statement-II: Rather than being deposited by meltwater streams flowing inside subglacial or englacial ice-walled tunnels, eskers are formed when isolated blocks of stagnant 'dead ice' buried in outwash plains melt away and cause the overlying drift to collapse.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Eskers are winding ridges of stratified fluvioglacial sand and gravel representing the inverted cast of subglacial or englacial meltwater tunnels after the confining ice walls melt away. Conversely, the melting of buried stagnant ice blocks in outwash plains creates depressions known as kettle holes or kettle lakes.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Eskers are steep-sided, winding ridges of water-sorted, stratified sand and gravel ranging from a few metres to tens of metres in height. Because the meltwater streams that deposited them flowed under hydrostatic pressure inside englacial or subglacial tunnels, eskers can climb over minor topographic undulations across the post-glacial landscape.

Statement-II is incorrect. Eskers are in fact formed by subglacial or englacial meltwater streams flowing inside ice-walled tunnels whose floors become choked with coarse stratified sediment; when the surrounding glacier ice melts away, the channel bed deposit is left standing as an elevated sinuous ridge. The melting of buried blocks of stagnant 'dead ice' in outwash plains causes the collapse of overlying sediment to form closed depressions called kettle holes (or kettle lakes), not eskers.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7; Savindra Singh Physical Geography Ch. 21

stem: Consider the following statements regarding aeolian geomorphic processes in hot deserts:
items: Statement-I: Mushroom rocks (pedestal rocks) develop narrow, deeply undercut bases and broad upper caps solely because capillary groundwater moisture chemically dissolves the lower bedrock while wind-borne sand abrasion operates uniformly at all heights above the desert floor.

Statement-II: During aeolian transport, coarse and heavy quartz sand grains responsible for intense mechanical abrasion move primarily by saltation within the lowest one to two metres above the ground surface, whereas only fine dust is carried higher in suspension.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Aeolian abrasion (sandblasting) is strongly height-restricted because coarse quartz sand grains have high mass relative to air density and travel via bouncing saltation trajectories mostly within 1 to 2 metres of the desert floor. This vertical concentration of kinetic energy undercuts rock outcrops near their base to sculpt mushroom (pedestal) rocks.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Wind-borne sand abrasion does not operate uniformly at all heights above the desert floor. On the contrary, the characteristic narrow neck and broad overhanging cap of a mushroom rock (gara or pedestal rock) result primarily from the severe vertical restriction of aeolian sandblasting, which is maximized within the lowest 1 to 2 metres above the ground.

Statement-II is correct. Because air has a much lower density and viscosity than water, wind cannot keep coarse quartz sand particles in high suspension. Instead, abrasive sand grains are transported via saltation (a series of short, low bounces) confined mostly within the lowest 1 to 2 metres above the desert floor, while finer silt and clay particles carried higher in suspension lack the mass to cause significant mechanical abrasion.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7; G.C. Leong Ch. 7

stem: With reference to aeolian erosional landforms in arid regions, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Yardangs are flat-topped, tabular ridges formed where horizontal layers of resistant caprock overlie softer rock strata, whereas Zeugen are streamlined ridges carved where alternating hard and soft rock strata dip steeply or stand vertically parallel to the prevailing wind.
2. Deflation hollows are created when persistent wind eddies scour and remove unconsolidated surface sediments, occasionally lowering the desert floor down to the groundwater table to form oases.

3. Dreikanter are specialized ventifacts exhibiting three wind-abraded and polished facets formed due to periodic shifts in wind direction or the undermining and overturning of pebbles on the desert floor.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Aeolian abrasion and deflation sculpt distinct bedrock morphologies depending on lithological structure: Zeugen develop in horizontal strata with a protective caprock, whereas Yardangs develop in steeply dipping or vertical alternating strata aligned parallel to the prevailing wind.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the structural geology of Yardangs and Zeugen. Zeugen are tabular, flat-topped ridges (up to 30 metres high) formed where horizontal strata of resistant caprock overlie softer, underlying rock layers; wind abrasion attacks the underlying soft layer along joints opened by frost or dew weathering. Conversely, Yardangs are steep-sided, streamlined, keel-like ridges formed where alternating bands of hard and soft rocks lie vertically or dip steeply parallel to the prevailing wind direction, allowing wind abrasion to excavate the softer corridors.

Deflation involves the lifting and blowing away of loose, fine-grained sand and dust by wind. Eddy currents excavate localized depressions called deflation hollows or blowouts. In great desert depressions (such as the Qattara and Bahariya depressions in Egypt), deflation lowers the surface until it intersects the capillary fringe or water table, where moisture binds the sediment against further wind removal and supports oasis ecosystems.

Ventifacts are stones or boulders on desert pavements that have been abraded, pitted, grooved, and polished by wind-driven sandblasting. When a rock develops three distinct curved, wind-worn facets meeting at sharp ridges—either because of seasonal shifts in prevailing winds or because the removal of sand beneath the pebble causes it to shift its centre of gravity and roll over—it is specifically termed a Dreikanter.

ref: GC Leong Ch. 7 (Arid or Desert Landforms); Savindra Singh Physical Geography Ch. 22

stem: Consider the following statements regarding aeolian depositional landforms:
items: 1. Barchans are crescent-shaped sand dunes formed in partially vegetated desert margins where the two horns point upwind against the prevailing wind, whereas parabolic dunes have their horns pointing downwind.

2. Transverse dunes are long, narrow sand ridges aligned parallel to the prevailing wind direction under a bi-directional wind regime, whereas Seif dunes form perpendicular to a gentle, unidirectional wind.
3. Loess deposits consist of homogeneous, non-stratified, and porous wind-borne silt accumulated extensively downwind of arid deserts or glacially outwashed surfaces.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Dune morphology is governed by sand supply, wind directionality, and vegetation cover: Barchan horns point downwind because their flanks advance faster than the taller central crest, whereas Parabolic dune horns point upwind because vegetation anchors the arms while the central blowout migrates downwind.

exp.why: Statement 1 swaps Barchans and Parabolic dunes. Barchans are crescentic dunes moving across bare, hard desert surfaces with a limited sand supply and constant unidirectional wind; their convex windward slope is gentle, their concave leeward slip-face is steep, and their two wings or horns point downwind (in the direction of wind movement) because the lower edges move faster than the high centre. Parabolic dunes form in semi-arid or coastal zones where sparse vegetation anchors the narrower arms while the central part is blown forward, causing the horns to point upwind.

Statement 2 swaps Transverse dunes and Seif (Longitudinal) dunes. Transverse dunes are asymmetrical ridges oriented perpendicular (at right angles) to the prevailing unidirectional wind where sand supply is abundant and vegetation is absent. Seif (or longitudinal) dunes are long, narrow, sword-shaped ridges aligned parallel to the resultant wind direction, typically developing where strong winds blow from two converging directions (bi-directional wind regime).

Loess is a terrestrial clastic sediment composed predominantly of wind-blown silt particles (20 to 50 micrometres) carried in suspension over long distances from desert interiors (such as the Loess Plateau of China, sourced from the Gobi and Ordos deserts) or Pleistocene glacial outwash plains. It is characteristically buff-coloured, calcareous, porous, friable, and lacks horizontal stratification, yet possesses vertical cleavage that allows it to stand in steep cliffs.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7 (Landforms and their Evolution); GC Leong Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following geomorphic features characteristic of an enclosed arid intermontane basin (Bolson):
items: 1. Bajada (Coalesced alluvial fans)
2. Mountain Front (Receding bounding scarp)
3. Playa (Central ephemeral lake bed)
4. Pediment (Gently sloping rock-cut surface)
prompt: If a geomorphologist traverses from the steep highland margin down towards the central floor of the basin, which one of the following represents the correct sequential order of these features?
core: An arid intermontane basin (Bolson) displays a classic four-part catenary sequence from the margin to the centre: the steep eroding Mountain Front meets the gently sloping bedrock Pediment at a sharp knickpoint (piedmont angle), which grades downslope beneath the depositional Bajada before terminating in the flat evaporite Playa.

exp.why: The Bajada occupies the third zone downslope from the mountain scarp. It is a continuous, undulating depositional apron of unconsolidated gravel, sand, and silt formed by the lateral coalescence of adjacent alluvial fans along the lower margin of the pediment.

The Mountain Front (bounding scarp) is the starting point (first zone) at the highland perimeter of the basin. It undergoes parallel scarp retreat driven by physical weathering, rill wash, and sheet floods.

The Playa occupies the lowest central floor (fourth zone) of the enclosed basin (bolson). Ephemeral runoff collects here after rare desert cloudbursts and rapidly evaporates, leaving behind flat beds of fine clay and precipitated evaporite salts (then called salinas or alkali flats).

The Pediment is the second zone, situated immediately below the mountain front and separated from it by an abrupt break of slope known as the knickpoint or piedmont junction. It is a gently inclined (1° to 7°) erosional bedrock surface carved by sheet wash and lateral planation, often veneered with a thin layer of transit alluvium.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7; Savindra Singh Physical Geography Ch. 22

stem: With reference to coastal geomorphology, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Tombolo : Isolated pillar of resistant bedrock left standing offshore after the collapse of a sea arch
2. Wave-cut Platform : Gently sloping littoral terrace built up by the accumulation of sand and shingle carried by constructive swash
3. Barrier Island : Elongated offshore ridge of unconsolidated sediment running parallel to the coast and separated from the mainland by a lagoon
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Coastal landscapes reflect the interplay between high-energy wave erosion on headlands (creating cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, and stacks) and longshore drift deposition in sheltered bays or gently shelving shores (creating spits, bars, tombolos, and barrier islands).

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. An isolated pillar of resistant bedrock left standing offshore after the roof of a sea arch collapses is a Sea Stack (which further erodes into a stump). A Tombolo is a depositional coastal landform consisting of a spit or bar of sand and shingle that connects an offshore island to the mainland (or connects two islands) due to wave refraction and convergence of longshore drift in the wave shadow behind the island.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. A Wave-cut Platform (or shore platform) is an erosional bedrock bench formed at the base of a receding sea cliff by the hydraulic action and corrasion (abrasion) of breaking waves between the high and low tide levels. The depositional terrace formed seaward of the wave-cut platform by the accumulation of eroded rock debris and sediment is called a Wave-built Terrace.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Barrier islands are long, narrow, offshore depositional ridges of sand running parallel to gently sloping coastlines, separated from the mainland shore by shallow lagoons, estuaries, or tidal marshes. They absorb wave energy and protect the mainland coast from storm surges.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7; GC Leong Ch. 10 (Coastal Landforms)

stem: Consider the following information regarding geomorphic landforms:
items: 1. Pediplain : Arid / Semi-arid Fluvio-Aeolian : Depositional plain formed by coalescing alluvial fans
2. Drumlin : Glacial : Erosional bedrock hummock smoothed on the stoss side and plucked on the lee side
3. Polje : Karst (Groundwater Solution) : Large, steep-sided, flat-floored structural and solutional depression
4. Esker : Glacio-fluvial : Sinuous depositional ridge of stratified sand and gravel laid down by subglacial meltwater streams
prompt: In how many of the above rows is the given information correctly matched?
core: Distinguishing erosional from depositional landforms across geomorphic regimes is vital: Pediplains are erosional bedrock plains formed by scarp retreat and pediment coalescence (unlike depositional bajadas), and Drumlins are depositional till mounds (unlike erosional roches moutonnées).

exp.why: Row 1 is incorrect. While a Pediplain is indeed formed in arid and semi-arid regimes by the combined action of sheet wash (fluvial) and wind (aeolian), it is an EROSIONAL plain, not a depositional plain. As conceptualized by L.C. King, a pediplain forms During the late stage of the arid geomorphic cycle when mountain fronts undergo parallel scarp retreat and adjacent rock-cut pediments coalesce, leaving behind only isolated residual hills (inselbergs or bornhardts). A depositional apron formed by coalescing alluvial fans is a Bajada.
Row 2 is incorrect. A Drumlin is a DEPOSITIONAL glacial landform—an elongated, oval-shaped hill (

Row 3 is correct. A Polje is the largest depression in a karst landscape, characterized by a vast, flat alluvial floor enclosed by steep limestone walls. It develops through the lateral coalescence of uvalas combined with structural (tectonic fault-guided) subsidence and solutional undercutting at the level of the local water table.

Row 4 is correct. Eskers are long, narrow, sinuous ridges composed of stratified, water-sorted sand and gravel deposited by meltwater streams flowing inside subglacial or englacial ice tunnels. When the enclosing glacier ice melts away, the choked channel bed is left standing as a winding embankment across the country.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 7; GC Leong Ch. 6, 7 & 8

stem: With reference to the origin and geomorphic evolution of distinct landforms across the Indian subcontinent, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Karewas of the Kashmir Valley are thick glacio-fluvial-lacustrine and aeolian deposits accumulated in a Pleistocene palaeo-lake and subsequently uplifted and dissected along the Pir Panjal flank.
opts.B: The Borra Caves of the Eastern Ghats and the Kutumsar Caves of Bastar are primary lava tubes formed during the Deccan Trap volcanic eruptions and later enlarged by mechanical exfoliation.
opts.C: The badland topography (ravines) of the Chambal basin is primarily an aeolian deflation landscape sculpted by desiccating winds blowing eastward from the Thar Desert.
opts.D: The Mawmluh Cave in Meghalaya, which houses the global stratotype marker for the Meghalayan Age, was carved by subglacial meltwater streams beneath Pleistocene alpine glaciers.

core: India exhibits diverse geomorphic landscapes: the Kashmir Karewas are Pleistocene glacio-lacustrine (and loessic) terraces; Borra, Kutumsar, and Mawmluh caves are classic limestone karst solution features; and the Chambal ravines represent severe fluvial gully erosion accelerated by neotectonic rejuvenation.

exp.why: Option A is correct: The Karewas (locally called Wudr) of the Kashmir Valley are unconsolidated, flat-topped terrace deposits (~1300–1800 m thick) consisting of sand, clay, silt, gravel, marl, and loess-paleosols. They were deposited in a vast Plio-Pleistocene primordial lake (Satisar) dammed by the tectonic uplift of the Pir Panjal range; subsequent tectonic uplift, draining of the lake through the Baramulla gorge by the Jhelum river, and fluvial dissection left them as fertile tablelands renowned for Zafran (saffron) cultivation. Option B is incorrect because the Borra Caves (Ananthagiri hills, Andhra Pradesh, drained by the Gosthani river) and Kutumsar Caves (Kanger Valley, Chhattisgarh) are classic Karst caves formed by chemical dissolution (carbonation) of Precambrian crystalline and stromatolitic limestones, not volcanic lava tubes. Option C is incorrect because the Chambal ravines (badlands) are a classic example of intense fluvial gully erosion and headward channel cutting into thick semi-arid Quaternary alluvium, triggered by neotectonic uplift of the Vindhyan forebulge and base-level lowering, not aeolian deflation. Option D is incorrect because Mawmluh Cave in Cherrapunji (Sohra), Meghalaya, is a solution karst cave carved in Eocene Sylhet limestone by heavy monsoonal water percolation, and its stalagmite speleothem (KM-2) serves as the Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) for the Meghalayan Age (beginning 4,200 years ago).

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 2 (Structure and Physiography); Geological Survey of India (Geo-tourism Sites)

stem: With reference to the thermal and structural characteristics of the troposphere and the tropopause, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The vertical thickness of the troposphere is significantly greater over the Equator than over the Poles due to vigorous convective uplift of heated air.
2. Because the equatorial region receives intense vertical insolation throughout the year, the temperature at the equatorial tropopause is substantially higher than that at the polar tropopause.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Although the equatorial surface is much warmer than the polar surface, the equatorial tropopause (~16–18 km) is significantly colder (around -80°C) than the polar tropopause (~8–10 km, around -45°C) because strong equatorial convection forces air to rise nearly twice as high under continuous normal lapse rate cooling (~6.5°C/km).

exp.why: Intense solar heating at the Equator generates powerful thermal convection currents that transport heat and turbulence up to 16–18 km, whereas cold, dense subsiding air over the Poles restricts the polar troposphere to a height of about 8–10 km.

Despite high equatorial surface temperatures (~27°C), the temperature drops continuously with altitude at the environmental lapse rate (~6.5°C per km) over a much greater vertical thickness (16–18 km). Consequently, cumulative cooling renders the equatorial tropopause much colder (around -80°C) than the shallower polar tropopause (around -45°C).

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 8; Savindra Singh Climatology

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the thermal structure and dynamics of the stratosphere:
items: 1. Within the stratosphere, the highest atmospheric temperature is recorded in the lower region between 20 km and 25 km where the absolute molecular concentration of ozone is at its maximum.
2. The positive temperature lapse rate in the stratosphere generates vigorous vertical convection currents that disperse atmospheric pollutants rapidly across altitudes.
3. Commercial jet aircraft cruise near the stratopause at an altitude of about 50 km to take advantage of high air density and minimal aerodynamic drag.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While ozone molecule density peaks in the lower stratosphere (20–25 km), temperature in the stratosphere peaks at the stratopause (~50 km, near 0°C) because upper stratospheric ozone intercepts unattenuated solar UV radiation first in much thinner air with lower heat capacity per unit volume.

exp.why: Although the maximum absolute density of ozone molecules occurs around 20–25 km, the highest stratospheric temperature (~0°C) is recorded at the stratopause (~50 km). Ozone at the top of the stratosphere absorbs the most intense incoming ultraviolet flux first, and because air density at 50 km is very low, the absorbed energy heats far fewer molecules per unit volume.

A temperature inversion (warmer air overlying cooler air) produces extreme vertical thermodynamic stability, which strongly suppresses vertical convection and turbulent mixing. Consequently, aerosols or volcanic gases injected into the stratosphere remain suspended for long periods.

Commercial jet aircraft cruise in the lower stratosphere and near the tropopause (around 10–12 km), not at the stratopause (50 km). At 50 km, air density is approximately 0.1% of sea-level density, which is far too thin to provide sufficient aerodynamic lift for wings or oxygen intake for jet turbine combustion.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 8; Barry & Chorley Atmosphere, Weather and Climate

stem: Consider the following atmospheric zones and phenomena:
items: 1. Formation of Noctilucent clouds
2. Formation of Nacreous clouds
3. Stratopause
4. Karman Line
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct vertical sequence of the above as one ascends from the Earth's surface into outer space?
core: Ascending from the Earth's surface, Nacreous (polar stratospheric) clouds form at 15–25 km, followed by the stratopause at ~50 km, Noctilucent (polar mesospheric) clouds near the mesopause at ~80–85 km, and finally the Karman Line at 100 km in the lower thermosphere.

exp.why: Noctilucent (night-shining) clouds, or Polar Mesospheric Clouds, are the highest clouds in Earth's atmosphere, forming in the upper mesosphere near the summer polar mesopause at an altitude of about 80–85 km where temperatures drop below -120°C.

Nacreous (mother-of-pearl) clouds, or Polar Stratospheric Clouds (PSCs), form in the lower stratosphere at altitudes of 15–25 km during extreme polar winter cooling (below -78°C) and play a catalytic role in polar ozone depletion.
The stratopause is the thermal boundary between the stratosphere and the mesosphere, located at an altitude of approximately 50 km.

The Karman Line is located at an altitude of 100 km above mean sea level (within the lower thermosphere) and serves as the internationally recognized boundary where aerodynamic flight gives way to orbital astrodynamics.

ref: WMO Cloud Atlas; Lutgens & Tarbuck The Atmosphere

stem: With reference to the thermodynamic and electromagnetic properties of the thermosphere and ionosphere, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Although kinetic temperatures in the thermosphere exceed 1,000°C due to high-energy solar radiation accelerating individual gas molecules, an object in the shade within this layer would not feel hot because extreme air rarefaction prevents significant conductive heat transfer.
2. All ionized layers of the ionosphere (D, E, and F layers) increase in electron density and reflectivity during the night due to the cessation of solar wind interference.
3. The disappearance of the D-layer after sunset enhances the long-distance skywave propagation of medium-wave (AM) radio signals.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In the extremely rarefied thermosphere, high kinetic temperature reflects rapid molecular velocity rather than high sensible heat content; meanwhile, in the ionosphere, cessation of solar radiation at night causes rapid ion-electron recombination in the denser D-layer, eliminating daytime AM radio absorption.

exp.why: Kinetic temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy (velocity) of gas molecules. While solar extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation accelerates isolated oxygen and nitrogen particles to high velocities (corresponding to >1,000°C), the gas density is so low that very few molecules collide with an object, resulting in negligible sensible heat transfer.

Photoionization in the ionosphere depends on incoming solar X-ray and EUV radiation. At night, in the absence of solar radiation, free electrons recombine with positive ions. Because air density is relatively high in the lowest layer (D-layer, 60–90 km), collision-driven recombination occurs rapidly after sunset, causing the D-layer to vanish and the E-layer to weaken significantly.

During the day, the D-layer absorbs and attenuates medium-wave (AM) radio frequencies due to frequent electron-neutral collisions. At night, once the D-layer disappears, AM radio waves travel unimpeded to the higher F-layer and reflect back to Earth as skywaves over much greater distances.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 8; Strahler Physical Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the compositional stratification of the Earth's atmosphere:
items: Statement-I: Despite contrasting vertical temperature gradients across the troposphere, stratosphere, and mesosphere, the relative volumetric proportions of major non-variable gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, and argon remain virtually uniform up to an altitude of about 80 to 100 km.
Statement-II: Below the turbopause, continuous macro-scale turbulent eddy diffusion mixes atmospheric gases much faster than gravitational molecular diffusion can segregate them by molecular weight.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The atmosphere is compositionally divided at the turbopause (~80–100 km) into the lower Homosphere—where turbulent eddy mixing homogenizes permanent gases regardless of molecular mass—and the upper Heterosphere, where a long mean free path allows gravitational molecular diffusion to stratify gases into concentric shells by weight.

exp.why: From the Earth's surface up to approximately 80–100 km (encompassing the troposphere, stratosphere, and mesosphere), the atmosphere constitutes the Homosphere, where dry air maintains a constant ratio of ~78.08% nitrogen, ~20.95% oxygen, and ~0.93% argon.

Statement-II explains Statement-I: Below the turbopause (homopause), atmospheric density is high enough that bulk turbulent mixing (eddy diffusion) dominates over diffusive separation, keeping gases uniformly blended. Above the turbopause (in the Heterosphere), turbulent mixing ceases and molecular diffusion under gravity separates gases into distinct layers from heaviest at the bottom (N2, O) to lightest at the top (He, H).

ref: Ahrens Meteorology Today; Barry & Chorley Atmosphere, Weather and Climate

stem: In the context of the Earth's radiation budget, which one of the following statements accurately explains the fundamental radiative principle governing the differential behaviour of incoming solar insolation and outgoing terrestrial radiation in the atmosphere?

opts.A: According to Wien's Displacement Law, the wavelength of peak radiation emitted by a blackbody is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, causing the cooler Earth to emit shorter wavelengths than the Sun.
opts.B: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour reflect the bulk of incoming shortwave solar radiation back into space while transmitting outgoing longwave terrestrial radiation unimpeded.
opts.C: The Earth's lower atmosphere is heated primarily from above through the direct absorption of incoming visible solar spectrum by diatomic nitrogen and oxygen molecules.
opts.D: Because the wavelength of maximum emission is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature of the radiating body, the Sun emits predominantly shortwave radiation to which greenhouse gases are largely transparent, whereas the cooler Earth emits longwave infrared radiation that matches the vibrational absorption bands of greenhouse gases.

core: Under Wien's Displacement Law (lambda_max = b/T), the hot Sun (~6,000 K) peaks in shortwave visible radiation (~0.5 micrometers) which passes easily through atmospheric greenhouse gases, whereas the cooler Earth (~288 K) emits longwave thermal infrared radiation (~10 micrometers) strongly absorbed by triatomic greenhouse gases, heating the troposphere from below.

exp.why: Option D is correct: Wien's Displacement Law states that the wavelength of maximum radiative emission is inversely proportional to the body's absolute temperature (T). Thus, solar radiation is concentrated in shortwave ultraviolet and visible bands (0.4–0.7 micrometers), to which CO2 and water vapour are largely transparent. The Earth re-emits energy as longwave infrared radiation (4–30 micrometers, peaking near 10 micrometers), which excites vibrational-rotational states in greenhouse gas molecules. Option A is incorrect because it inverts the inverse proportionality of Wien's law. Option B is incorrect because greenhouse gases transmit shortwave solar radiation and absorb (rather than reflect) longwave terrestrial radiation. Option C is incorrect because N2 and O2 are transparent to visible light, so the troposphere is heated primarily from below via terrestrial radiation, conduction, and latent heat.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 9 (Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature)

stem: With reference to the latitudinal and seasonal distribution of solar insolation across the Earth, consider the following statements:
items: 1. On the day of the June Solstice, the daily cumulative solar radiation received at the top of the atmosphere is higher at the North Pole than at the Equator.

2. Despite receiving maximum daily top-of-atmosphere insolation around the June Solstice, the North Pole records much lower net surface radiation than the tropics due to a longer atmospheric optical path and high cryospheric albedo.

3. At the Earth's surface, the highest mean annual insolation is received directly along the Equator rather than the subtropics because the Equator experiences the smallest annual variation in midday solar zenith angle.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Top-of-atmosphere (TOA) daily insolation depends on both solar elevation angle and daylight duration, allowing the 24-hour sunlit summer pole to exceed equatorial TOA insolation at the solstice. However, at the Earth's surface, atmospheric cloud attenuation causes maximum annual insolation to peak over clear-sky subtropical deserts rather than the cloudy Equator.

exp.why: Daily cumulative insolation at the top of the atmosphere (TOA) is a function of both the angle of incidence and the duration of daylight. On the June Solstice (around June 21), although the solar elevation angle at the North Pole is fixed at a modest 23.5 degrees, the Pole receives 24 hours of uninterrupted sunlight, compared to only 12 hours at the Equator. Consequently, the 24-hour integrated TOA solar energy at the North Pole (~500+ W/m2 daily average) surpasses that received at the Equator (~380 W/m2).

As solar rays enter the polar atmosphere at a low inclination angle (23.5 degrees at the solstice), they must traverse a substantially longer atmospheric path length (air mass) than nearly vertical tropical rays, suffering heavy depletion via scattering and absorption. Furthermore, the high surface albedo of polar sea ice and snow reflects 60% to 85% of the reaching shortwave radiation, keeping net surface thermal absorption low.

This statement ignores the critical contextual condition of atmospheric cloud cover. At the Earth's surface, maximum mean annual insolation is received over the subtropical high-pressure belts (around 20 to 30 degrees N/S, where major hot deserts lie) because descending air inhibits cloud formation. The Equator receives comparatively less surface insolation due to persistent deep convective cloud cover associated with the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), which reflects a large share of incoming shortwave radiation.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 9 (Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature); Strahler Physical Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the interplay between Earth's orbital mechanics and hemispheric seasonal temperatures:
items: Statement-I: Even though the Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion) during the Northern Hemisphere winter and farthest from the Sun (aphelion) during the Northern Hemisphere summer, the annual seasonal temperature contrast is greater in the Northern Hemisphere than in the Southern Hemisphere.

Statement-II: The much higher ratio of continental landmass to ocean area in the Northern Hemisphere results in lower average thermal inertia compared to the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere, overriding the ~7% seasonal insolation difference caused by Earth's orbital eccentricity.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Astronomically, Earth's elliptical orbit causes global insolation at perihelion (early January) to exceed that at aphelion (early July) by roughly 7%, which theoretically should make Northern Hemisphere winters milder and summers cooler than Southern Hemisphere counterparts. In reality, continental distribution and the contrasting specific heat capacities of land versus water reverse this expected pattern.

exp.why: Earth reaches perihelion (~147 million km from the Sun) around January 3 during Northern Hemisphere winter and aphelion (~152 million km) around July 4 during Northern Hemisphere summer. Despite receiving ~7% less top-of-atmosphere solar irradiance during its summer and ~7% more during its winter, the Northern Hemisphere experiences warmer average summers, colder average winters, and a significantly wider annual temperature range than the Southern Hemisphere.

The Northern Hemisphere comprises nearly 40% land, whereas the Southern Hemisphere is over 80% ocean. Land has a low specific heat capacity, remains opaque (concentrating heat in a thin top layer), and lacks vertical mixing or evaporative cooling comparable to oceans. Conversely, the vast Southern Ocean absorbs heat deeply through turbulent mixing and high specific heat capacity, moderating seasonal extremes and completely outweighing the astronomical eccentricity effect.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 9; Savindra Singh Climatology

stem: With reference to optical interactions of incoming solar radiation with atmospheric constituents, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Rayleigh Scattering : Selective scattering by gas molecules much smaller than the wavelength of visible light, causing the blue colour of the clear sky and reddish hues at sunset
2. Mie Scattering : Wavelength-independent scattering by large cloud water droplets and ice crystals that makes cumulus clouds appear bright white
3. Non-selective Scattering : Forward-dominant scattering by fine atmospheric aerosols, dust, and smoke particles whose diameters approximate the wavelength of incoming visible radiation
prompt: Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
core: The visual and radiative outcome of atmospheric scattering is governed by the ratio of particle diameter to radiation wavelength (the size parameter). Rayleigh scattering occurs when particles are much smaller than the wavelength, Mie scattering when particle sizes equal the wavelength, and Non-selective scattering when particles are much larger than the wavelength.

exp.why: Rayleigh scattering operates when atmospheric particles (primarily diatomic nitrogen and oxygen molecules, diameter ~0.0001 micrometres) are vastly smaller than the wavelength of visible light (0.4 to 0.7 micrometres). Scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength, scattering shorter blue wavelengths roughly ten times more efficiently than longer red wavelengths, giving the daytime sky its blue hue and leaving direct low-angle sunbeams red-orange at sunrise and sunset.

This description belongs to Non-selective scattering, not Mie scattering. Mie scattering occurs when spherical aerosols, pollen, smoke, and fine dust particles have diameters roughly equal to the wavelength of visible radiation, producing a muted whitish-grey glare or haze around the Sun rather than the bright white appearance of large-droplet clouds.

This description belongs to Mie scattering. Non-selective scattering is triggered by cloud water droplets and ice crystals (typically 5 to 100 micrometres in diameter) that are orders of magnitude larger than visible wavelengths; because they scatter blue, green, and red wavelengths with equal efficiency, dense unshaded clouds appear white.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch. 9; NCERT Class XI Geography Practical Work (Remote Sensing chapter on EMR interaction with Atmosphere)

stem: With reference to the surface albedo (shortwave reflectivity) of various terrestrial and marine environments, consider the following statements:
