Situated east of the Maikal Range and Kaimur-Rewa scarps, Baghelkhand contains both Vindhyan sandstones/limestones in the west and Gondwana coal-bearing strata (such as the Sohagpur and Singrauli coalfields) alongside ancient granites in the east. Physiographically, its central highlands separate the northward-draining Son river system from the southward-draining Mahanadi river system.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2; Khullar: India A Comprehensive Geography, Ch. 2 & 3

stem: With reference to the geomorphic and structural features of the Chota Nagpur Plateau, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 'Pat' lands in the western part of the plateau (such as Netarhat Pat) are high-level flat-topped mesas formed where Deccan-era basaltic lava flows overlying older crystalline rocks have weathered into thick caps of laterite and bauxite.

2. The Damodar River occupies a faulted rift trough (graben) that bifurcates the Chota Nagpur Plateau into the Hazaribagh Plateau in the north and the Ranchi Plateau in the south, preserving Permian-period Gondwana coal seams.

3. Owing to differential Tertiary uplift that raised its central granitic-gneissic peneplains in step-like tiers, the plateau exhibits a radial drainage pattern marked by rejuvenated waterfalls along its bounding scarps.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Chota Nagpur Plateau is a polycyclic, multi-tiered landscape where Tertiary uplift rejuvenated ancient Archean peneplains into distinct surfaces (the laterite-capped western 'Pat' mesas, the central Ranchi-Hazaribagh plateaus, and outer lower plateaus), cut across the middle by the coal-bearing Damodar rift graben.

exp.why: The 'Pat' region (locally meaning flat-topped tableland, averaging 900 to 1,100 m above sea level, such as Netarhat, Jamira, and Khamar Pats) lies in western Chota Nagpur. Here, outliers of Deccan Trap basaltic lava poured over the Archean gneissic basement and subsequently underwent intense tropical leaching to form thick lateritic and bauxite cappings.

The Damodar valley is a classic structural graben (rift basin) trending west-to-east through the middle of the Chota Nagpur Plateau. It separates the Hazaribagh Plateau on the north from the Ranchi Plateau on the south. Down-faulting during the Gondwana period allowed thick fluviatile-lacustrine sediments and glossopteris flora to accumulate and remain protected from sub-aerial erosion, creating India's premier coking and bituminous coal belt (Jharia, Bokaro, Karanpura, and Raniganj).

The Chota Nagpur Plateau experienced three phases of epeirogenic uplift synchronous with the Himalayan Tertiary orogeny, transforming an ancient peneplain into a stepped dome. Consequently, rivers such as the Damodar, Subarnarekha, North Koel, South Koel, and Barakar radiate outward in multiple directions (radial/centrifugal drainage) and plunge over steep plateau scarps as knickpoint waterfalls (such as Hundru on the Subarnarekha and Dassam on the Kanchi).

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2; Khullar: India A Comprehensive Geography, Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Meghalaya (Shillong) and Karbi Anglong Plateau:
items: Statement-I: Although the Meghalaya-Karbi Anglong Plateau is structurally a north-eastern extension of the Peninsular Indian block rather than a part of the Himalayan fold system, it stands physically separated from the main Chota Nagpur Plateau by a wide lowland gap.

Statement-II: Sharing the same Precambrian crystalline basement and Gondwana coal-bearing strata as the Chota Nagpur block, the plateau was isolated when crustal down-faulting along the Malda Fault between the Rajmahal and Garo Hills created a structural depression that was later filled by Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial sediments.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Meghalaya (Garo-Khasi-Jaintia) and Karbi Anglong Plateau shares the Archean gneissic-quartzitic lithology and Gondwana coal/mineral wealth of the Chota Nagpur Plateau; its apparent surface separation from the main Peninsular shield is due to tectonic subsidence along the Malda Fault (Garo-Rajmahal Gap) and subsequent Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial burial.

exp.why: Geologically and structurally, the Meghalaya Plateau (comprising the Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia Hills) and the contiguous Karbi Anglong (Mikir) Hills of Assam belong to the Precambrian Peninsular Indian shield rather than the young folded Tertiary Himalayas, even though a wide alluvial lowland separates them on the surface from the Chota Nagpur Plateau.

Like the Chota Nagpur Plateau, the Meghalaya-Karbi Anglong block is composed of ancient Archean quartzites, shales, schists, and granitoids overlain by Gondwana and Tertiary deposits rich in coal, limestone, iron ore, and uranium. During the Himalayan orogeny, tectonic down-faulting along the Malda Fault between the Rajmahal Hills and the Garo Hills created the Garo-Rajmahal Gap, which was subsequently filled by alluvial sediments of the Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers—directly explaining both its shared Peninsular structure and its surface separation stated in Statement-I.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2 (Structure and Physiography, p. 12–13)

stem: With reference to the geological origin and physiographic profile of the Western Ghats (Sahyadris), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Structurally, the Western Ghats are true fold mountains formed by Cenozoic compressional tectonics along the western continental margin of India.
2. They represent the faulted and uplifted western escarpment of the Peninsular plateau, presenting a steep, step-like cliff face towards the Arabian Sea and a gentle slope towards the east.
3. Unlike the Eastern Ghats, the Western Ghats form a comparatively continuous barrier and their average elevation increases progressively from north to south.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Western Ghats are not true folded mountains; they are the uplifted, faulted western edge (passive margin escarpment) of the Deccan tableland formed during the rifting of Madagascar from the Indian plate. Their elevation increases southward as the lithology transitions from eroded Deccan Trap basalts in the north to resistant Archaean charnockites and gneisses in the south.

exp.why: The Western Ghats are not true fold mountains like the Himalayas. They are block-like fault scarps (a passive continental margin escarpment) created when the western flank of the Peninsular block subsided and rifted away from Madagascar and the Seychelles during the Late Cretaceous-Eocene period.

Viewed from the west coast (Konkan and Malabar), the Sahyadris rise abruptly like a sheer wall or terraced staircase (hence the name 'Ghats' or steps) due to horizontal basaltic lava flows in the north, whereas from the eastern plateau side they appear as low, gently sloping hills.

The Western Ghats form an almost unbroken orographic wall breachable only through a few structural passes (Thalghat, Bhorghat, Palghat, Shencottah), and their elevation rises from north to south, culminating in Anamudi (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai Hills and Doddabetta (2,637 m) in the Nilgiris.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2 (Structure and Physiography); Majid Husain, Geography of India, Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following pairs of major mountain passes/gaps in the Western Ghats and the physiographic blocks or transport corridors associated with them:
items: 1. Thalghat (Kasara Ghat) : Connects Mumbai with Pune across the northern Sahyadris
2. Bhorghat : Connects Mumbai with Nashik and forms the principal route toward the Tapi valley
3. Palghat (Palakkad Gap) : Separates the Nilgiri Hills to the north from the Anaimalai Hills to the south
4. Shencottah Gap : Separates the Anaimalai Hills from the Palani Hills, connecting Kochi with Coimbatore
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: From north to south, the four principal breaches across the Western Ghats are Thalghat (Mumbai-Nashik), Bhorghat (Mumbai-Pune), Palghat Gap (between Nilgiri and Anaimalai Hills, linking Palakkad and Coimbatore), and Shencottah Gap (between Cardamom and Agasthyamalai Hills, linking Kollam and Madurai/Tenkasi).

exp.why: Thalghat (Kasara Ghat), located in the northern Sahyadris of Maharashtra, connects Mumbai (Kalyan) with Nashik (and onward to Agra/Kolkata), not Mumbai with Pune.
Bhorghat lies south of Thalghat in Maharashtra and serves as the critical rail and highway corridor linking Mumbai (Karjat/Khopoli) with Pune (Khandala/Lonavala) and the southern Deccan.

The Palghat (Palakkad) Gap is a major ~24-30 km wide tectonic and erosional shear zone in the Western Ghats that separates the Nilgiri Hills in the north from the Anaimalai Hills in the south, linking the Malabar Coast (Palakkad) with the Coimbatore plateau.

The Shencottah (Aryankavu) Gap is located much further south between the Cardamom Hills and the Agasthyamalai (Ashambu) Hills, providing the transport corridor between Kollam/Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala and Shencottah/Tenkasi/Madurai in Tamil Nadu.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2; Oxford School Atlas (Physical Map of Peninsular India)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the montane ecology of the Southern Western Ghats:
items: Statement-I: In the high-altitude rolling plateaus (above 1,800 metres) of the Nilgiri, Anaimalai, and Palani hills, stunted tropical montane evergreen forests ('Sholas') are strictly confined to sheltered folds and valleys, while the open convex hill slopes are dominated by montane grasslands.

Statement-II: During the winter months, radiative cooling produces severe nocturnal ground frost in exposed areas and desiccating winds sweep the convex ridges, preventing tropical tree seedlings from establishing outside the moisture-retaining, frost-protected valley depressions.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Shola-Grassland mosaic of the Southern Western Ghats sky islands is a dual-climax ecosystem maintained by micro-climatic partitioning. While sheltered stream valleys retain soil moisture and shield tropical evergreen trees from wind and frost, the open hill slopes experience winter nocturnal frost and dry winds that inhibit tropical tree recruitment and favour frost-tolerant C4 grasses.

exp.why: Statement-I accurately describes the characteristic 'Shola-Grassland' sky-island complex found above 1,800 m in the Nilgiris, Anaimalais (Eravikulam), and Palani hills, where dense, stunted evergreen Shola patches occupy concave valley heads and hollows amidst expansive rolling grasslands.

Statement-II provides the exact ecophysiological and micro-climatic mechanism behind Statement-I. Shola tree species are of tropical stock and cannot tolerate sub-zero ground frost or seasonal desiccation on exposed slopes during winter; only frost-hardy grasses survive there, whereas the sheltered valley folds retain moisture and buffer temperature extremes.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 5 (Natural Vegetation); Ecological Studies on Shola-Grassland Mosaic (IISc / ENVIS)

stem: With reference to the structural and lithological comparison between the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the northern half of the Western Ghats is largely composed of horizontal sheets of Cretaceous-Eocene Deccan Trap basalts, the Eastern Ghats represent an ancient Pre-Cambrian folded orogenic belt dominated by high-grade metamorphic rocks such as charnockites and khondalites.

2. Unlike the Western Ghats which act as the primary water divide of the Peninsula, the Eastern Ghats have been deeply eroded and dissected into discontinuous blocks by major east-flowing rivers that originate in the Western Ghats.

3. While the Western Ghats run closely parallel to the Arabian Sea coast throughout their length, the Eastern Ghats diverge significantly inland south of the Krishna valley to merge with the Western Ghats at the Nilgiri mountain knot.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Western and Eastern Ghats differ fundamentally in age, tectonics, and drainage interaction: the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt is a Proterozoic folded and metamorphosed terrain (charnockite-khondalite suite) dissected by major consequent rivers, whereas the Western Ghats represent a younger Cenozoic fault-scarp water divide.

exp.why: North of approximately 16 degrees North latitude (Goa), the Western Ghats are composed of horizontally bedded Deccan Trap basalts. In contrast, the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt (EGMB) is a Pre-Cambrian (Proterozoic) fold mountain system composed of granulite-facies metamorphic rocks, chiefly charnockites, khondalites, and granitic gneisses.

Because the Peninsular block tilts gently from west to east, major rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri rise in the Western Ghats (which serve as the continental water divide) and cut wide alluvial gaps across the older Eastern Ghats, reducing them to isolated hill ranges.

The Western Ghats maintain a fairly uniform proximity to the Arabian Sea coast, whereas the Eastern Ghats run parallel to the Bay of Bengal only in Odisha and northern Andhra Pradesh; south of the Krishna-Pennar delta, they swing southwestward through interior Tamil Nadu (Javadi, Shevaroy, Biligirirangan hills) to meet the Western Ghats at the Nilgiri Hills.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2; Geological Survey of India (Physiographic & Tectonic Divisions)

stem: Consider the following dissected hill ranges of the Eastern Ghats:
items: 1. Javadi Hills
2. Nallamala Hills
3. Palkonda Range
4. Shevaroy (Servarayan) Hills
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct spatial sequence of the above hill ranges from North to South?
core: Tracing the Eastern Ghats southward from the Krishna River across Andhra Pradesh into Tamil Nadu reveals a distinct sequence of faulted and eroded structural ridges: Nallamala Hills (between Krishna and Pennar), Palkonda Range (south of Pennar in Rayalaseema), Javadi Hills (northern Tamil Nadu), and Shevaroy Hills (Salem district, Tamil Nadu).

exp.why: The Javadi Hills (approx. 12.5 degrees North) lie in northern Tamil Nadu (Tirupattur, Vellore, and Tiruvannamalai districts) between the Palar and Ponnaiyar rivers, south of the Palkonda Range and north of the Shevaroy Hills.

The Nallamala Hills (approx. 15.0 to 16.2 degrees North) are the northernmost among the four, stretching across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana immediately south of the Krishna River up to the Pennar River basin.

The Palkonda Range (approx. 13.8 to 14.5 degrees North) is an arc-shaped hill range in southern Andhra Pradesh (Kadapa and Annamayya/Tirupati districts), situated south of the Nallamala Hills and the Pennar River.

The Shevaroy (Servarayan) Hills (approx. 11.8 degrees North, hosting Yercaud) are located further south in the Salem district of Tamil Nadu. Thus, the exact North-to-South order is Nallamala (2) -> Palkonda (3) -> Javadi (1) -> Shevaroy (4).

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2; Survey of India Physical Map of Southern Peninsula

stem: This mountain system of Peninsular India consists of a contiguous series of seven structural blocks stretching nearly 900 km from west to east. Tectonically, it functions as a classic horst (block mountain) flanked by two parallel rift valleys (grabens) on its northern and southern margins. While its western segments are composed of Deccan Trap basalts, its central segment exposes thick Gondwana sandstones where its highest peak is situated, and its eastern culmination forms a crescent-shaped basalt-and-bauxite plateau knot that exhibits classic radial drainage.
prompt: Which one of the following physiographic features is described in the passage above?

opts.A: The Vindhyan Scarplands and Kaimur-Bhanrer Range
opts.B: The Aravalli Horst and Delhi-Haridwar Ridge
opts.C: The Chotanagpur Plateau and Rajmahal Highlands

core: The Satpura Range ('Seven Folds') is a classic structural horst bounded by the Narmada Graben to the north and the Tapi Graben to the south. Stretching through the Rajpipla Hills, Gawilgarh Hills, Mahadeo Hills (containing Dhupgarh at Pachmarhi on Gondwana sandstones), and the Maikal Range, it culminates at the Amarkantak plateau knot where the Narmada, Son, and Johilla rivers radiate.

exp.why: Option D is correct because the Satpura-Maikal system comprises seven contiguous hill ranges (including Rajpipla, Gawilgarh, Mahadeo, and Maikal) forming an uplifted tectonic horst between the Narmada rift valley in the north and the Tapi rift valley in the south. Its highest peak, Dhupgarh (1,350 m) near Pachmarhi in the Mahadeo Hills, stands on Upper Gondwana (Pachmarhi) sandstones, while its eastern anchor, the Maikal Range, culminates at the Amarkantak plateau—a famous radial drainage dome giving rise to the Narmada, Son, and Johilla (and Mahanadi tributaries nearby). Options A, B, and C are incorrect as none of them lie as a horst between two parallel grabens with radial drainage at their eastern tip.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & Ch. 3; Savindra Singh, Physical Geography

stem: With reference to the comparative geomorphology of the Western Coastal Plain and the Eastern Coastal Plain of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Eastern Coastal Plain is predominantly a coast of structural submergence marked by drowned river valleys, the Western Coastal Plain is broadly an emergent coast characterized by prograding deltas.
2. The Western Coastal Plain is narrowest in its middle segment along the Karnataka coast and broadens progressively towards both its northern and southern extremities.
3. Owing to its emergent nature, gently sloping nearshore profile, and heavy deltaic sedimentation, the Eastern Coastal Plain affords fewer natural harbours than the Western Coast.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Western Coastal Plain (barring the Malabar segment) is a narrow, faulted coast of submergence where short, swift rivers form deep estuaries suited for natural harbours. Conversely, the Eastern Coastal Plain is a broader emergent coast where major east-flowing rivers build extensive deltas and shallow offshore sandbars, hindering natural deep-water harbour formation.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the geomorphic character of the two coasts. The Western Coastal Plain is primarily an example of a submerged coastal plain (caused by Neogene faulting along the Arabian Sea margin), where rivers form estuaries rather than deltas. Conversely, the Eastern Coastal Plain is a broader, emergent coastal plain where major Peninsular rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) build large, prograding deltas into the Bay of Bengal.

Statement 2 is correct. Squeezed tightly between the steep western escarpment of the Sahyadris and the Arabian Sea, the Western Coastal Plain narrows to scarcely 10–25 km along the Karnataka (Kannada/Karwar) coast, where the Western Ghats descend almost to the shoreline, but widens significantly towards the north (Gujarat/Kachchh-Kathiawar plains) and towards the south (Malabar coast of Kerala).

Statement 3 is correct. Because the Eastern Coastal Plain is an emergent coast receiving massive alluvial sediment loads, the adjoining littoral zone is shallow and lined with offshore bars, spits, and barrier beaches. Consequently, deep water remains far offshore, creating very few natural harbours (Visakhapatnam, protected by the Dolphin's Nose headland, being a notable exception) and requiring regular dredging for artificial ports like Chennai, Ennore, and Haldia.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2 (Structure and Physiography - The Coastal Plains)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the regional subdivisions of the Western Coastal Plain of India:
items: 1. Although the Western Coast is broadly classified as a coastline of submergence, its southern segment—the Malabar Coast—exhibits distinct geomorphic evidence of emergence, including barrier spits and enclosed lagoons locally known as Kayals.

2. The Kathiawar Peninsula features a radial drainage pattern originating from its central highlands, where Mount Girnar represents an igneous plutonic-volcanic complex rising above the surrounding Deccan Traps.
3. Along the Konkan and Kannada coasts, west-flowing streams are unable to form waterfalls because the Western Ghats descend towards the Arabian Sea in a gentle, low-gradient homoclinal slope.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Konkan and Kannada coasts are classic submerged faulted margins with steep western escarpments and high waterfalls, the Malabar Coast is a key geomorphic exception showing marine emergence (uplifted terraces, barrier bars, and Kayals). Further north, the Kathiawar Peninsula displays classic radial drainage from its central igneous highlands.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Unlike the Konkan and Karnataka coasts to its north, which are classic coastlines of submergence, the Malabar Coast (Kerala) is a compound coast exhibiting clear geomorphic evidence of emergence, such as uplifted marine benches, coastal sand dunes (Teris/strandlines), and long barrier spits that enclose shallow brackish lagoons and backwaters called Kayals (e.g., Vembanad and Ashtamudi).

Statement 2 is correct. The Kathiawar (Saurashtra) Peninsula is dominated centrally by the Mandav Hills and the Girnar massif. Mount Girnar is a classic circular intrusive plutonic and volcanic complex (comprising gabbro, diorite, syenite, and granophyre) older than or contemporaneous with the terminal Deccan volcanism. Rivers such as the Bhadar, Shetrunji, Machhu, and Ojat flow outward in all directions from these central highlands, forming a textbook radial drainage pattern.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Far from having a gentle slope, the western flank of the Sahyadris along the Konkan and Kannada coasts is a precipitous, fault-line escarpment. Short, swift west-flowing streams supplied by heavy orographic monsoon rainfall plunge abruptly down this steep scarp and rejuvenated bedrock knickpoints, carving deep gorges and spectacular waterfalls such as Jog (Gersoppa) Falls on the Sharavathi River, Dudhsagar Falls on the Mandovi River, and Unchalli Falls on the Aghanashini River.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & 3; Savindra Singh: Geomorphology (Coastal Geomorphology of India)

stem: Consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Even though the Narmada and the Tapi have long courses comparable to major east-flowing Peninsular rivers, they form estuaries rather than deltas at their mouths in the Gulf of Khambhat, similar to the short streams draining the western flank of the Sahyadris.

Statement-II: The general elevation of the Deccan Plateau tilts gently from west to east, causing the principal water divide of Peninsular India to run close to the Arabian Sea coast along the crest of the Western Ghats.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: West-flowing rivers—both the long rift-bound Narmada/Tapi and short Sahyadri streams—form estuaries instead of deltas because of low erodible silt yield in hard-rock troughs/steep scarps combined with high tidal/wave energy and coastal subsidence along the Arabian Sea. The eastward tilt of the Deccan Plateau explains why most Peninsular rivers flow into the Bay of Bengal, not why Narmada and Tapi fail to build deltas.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Despite their considerable lengths (Narmada ~1,312 km; Tapi ~724 km), neither river builds a prograding delta at its mouth in the Gulf of Khambhat. Instead, like the short, swift streams descending the western escarpment of the Sahyadris (such as the Mandovi, Zuari, Periyar, and Netravati), they form funnel-shaped estuaries.

Statement-II is also factually correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. The gentle west-to-east tilt of the Deccan block explains why major Peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal and why west-flowing Sahyadri rivers have small catchments. However, the reason why Narmada, Tapi, and Sahyadri rivers form estuaries rather than deltas is two-fold: (i) Narmada and Tapi flow through narrow, structurally controlled fault troughs (grabens) floored by hard crystalline and basaltic rocks that yield relatively less fine alluvial silt, while Sahyadri rivers descend steep gradients at high velocity; and (ii) they debouch into a structurally subsiding, macro-tidal coastal zone (especially the Gulf of Khambhat) where strong tidal currents and littoral drift sweep sediments offshore rather than allowing sub-aerial delta accumulation.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System - Peninsular Drainage)

stem: With reference to distinctive regional geomorphic and pedological units of the Indian Coastal Plains and adjoining lowlands, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Teri Sands : Red, iron-oxide-coated Quaternary aeolian dune complexes along the southeastern coast of Tamil Nadu
2. Kari Lands : Deep black, highly acidic peaty and marshy soils rich in undecomposed organic matter in the submerged coastal tracts of Kerala
3. Kayals : Raised coralline and miliolite limestone terraces formed by tectonic uplift along the Saurashtra littoral zone
4. Banni Plains : Low-lying, slightly saline-alkaline alluvial flats along the southern margin of the Rann of Kachchh supporting arid grasslands
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: India's coastal fringe hosts specialized micro-geomorphic units: haematite-stained Quaternary 'Teri' sand dunes in southeastern Tamil Nadu, acidic waterlogged 'Kari' peaty soils in Kerala's Kuttanad lowland, 'Kayal' brackish lagoons along the Malabar barrier coast, and the 'Banni' arid alluvial grassland flats bordering the Great Rann of Kachchh.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. 'Teri' sands (found prominently in Thoothukudi, Tirunelveli, and Ramanathapuram districts of southeastern Tamil Nadu) are coastal red sand dune complexes formed during the Quaternary period. Chemical weathering of heavy minerals like ilmenite and garnet in a warm semi-arid climate has released iron oxides (haematite), coating the quartz sand grains in a distinctive crimson-red hue.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. 'Kari' soils occur in the low-lying, waterlogged coastal depressions of Kerala (such as Kuttanad in Alappuzha and Kottayam districts). Formed under anaerobic, marshy estuarine conditions with submerged forest/mangrove biomass, these soils are black, heavy clay-rich peats containing 10–40% organic matter, free aluminium and ferrous sulphates, and extreme acidity (pH often dropping below 4.0).

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. 'Kayals' are not raised limestone terraces in Saurashtra; they are shallow brackish coastal lagoons and backwaters running parallel to the Malabar Coast in Kerala, separated from the Arabian Sea by wave-built sand spits and barrier bars. Raised Pleistocene calcareous marine deposits along the Saurashtra (Kathiawar) coast are instead known geologically as Miliolite limestone.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. The 'Banni' plains form an extensive belt of low-lying, flat alluvial and lacustrine sediments along the outer southern fringe of the Great Rann of Kachchh in Gujarat. Deposited historically by shifting Himalayan/Aravalli river courses prior to tectonic uplift (such as the 1819 Allah Bund earthquake), the inherently saline-alkaline clayey soils support one of Asia's largest tropical arid grassland ecosystems.

ref: ICAR: Soils of India; NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & Ch. 6 (Soils)

stem: Consider the following physiographic sub-units of the Peninsular Plateau:
items: 1. Chhattisgarh Basin
2. Gawilgarh Hills
3. Garhjat Hills
4. Maikal Range
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of the above physiographic units as one moves from West to East across Central and Eastern Peninsular India?
core: Traversing Peninsular India eastward along the ~21°N–22°N belt takes one from the basaltic Gawilgarh Hills of the central Satpura system (~77.3°E) to the Maikal Range (~81°E), down its steep eastern scarp into the saucer-shaped Chhattisgarh Basin (~82°E–83.5°E), and finally into the Archean crystalline Garhjat Hills of the Odisha Highlands (~84.5°E–86.5°E).

exp.why: The Chhattisgarh Basin (approx. 81.5°E to 83.5°E) is a saucer-shaped structural depression underlain by horizontally bedded Proterozoic (Cuddapah-equivalent) limestones, shales, and sandstones, drained by the upper Mahanadi and Seonath rivers. It lies immediately to the east of the Maikal scarp and to the west of the Garhjat Hills (while the Dandakaranya/Bastar Plateau lies to its south).

The Gawilgarh Hills (approx. 77.0°E to 77.8°E) form a prominent Deccan Trap horst ridge of the southern Satpura mountain system along the Maharashtra (Amravati)–Madhya Pradesh (Betul) border, lying between the Tapi-Purna valley and the upper Wardha basin. It is the westernmost among the four given features.

The Garhjat Hills (approx. 84.5°E to 86.5°E), also known as the Odisha Highlands, lie to the east of the Chhattisgarh Basin. Composed of ancient Archean granites, gneisses, charnockites, and iron-ore series metasediments (encompassing the Similipal, Keonjhar, and Bonai uplands), they form the easternmost unit in this sequence.

The Maikal Range (approx. 80.8°E to 81.5°E) forms the eastern crescentic culmination of the Satpura system along the Madhya Pradesh–Chhattisgarh border, culminating near the Amarkantak plateau. Its steep eastern escarpment forms the western boundary wall of the Chhattisgarh Basin, placing it directly between the Gawilgarh Hills to the west and the Chhattisgarh Basin to the east (correct West-to-East order: 2 - 4 - 1 - 3).

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2 (The Peninsular Plateau); Survey of India Physical Map of India

stem: With reference to the geological structure and physiography of the southern Deccan Plateau, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Karnataka Plateau is physiographically differentiated into the 'Malnad', a densely forested upland region dissected by deep valleys along the flank of the Sahyadris, and the 'Maidan', an open rolling plateau dotted with low granitic hills to its east.
2. The Baba Budan Hills situated within the Malnad tract belong to the Archean Dharwar metamorphic system and host high-grade banded iron formations.

3. The Telangana and Rayalaseema plateaus are predominantly underlain by ancient, relatively impermeable crystalline gneisses and granites, whose undulating terrain of alternating ridges and shallow valleys structurally favours cascading tank irrigation.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The southern Deccan Plateau comprises two distinct Archean litho-physiographic domains: the Dharwar metasedimentary schist belts of the dissected Karnataka Malnad (hosting rich banded iron formations like Baba Budan) and the extensive Peninsular Gneissic Complex of the Karnataka Maidan, Telangana, and Rayalaseema, whose impermeable rolling terrain naturally supports cascading tank irrigation.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Karnataka (Mysore) Plateau is divided into two distinct physiographic zones: (i) the western 'Malnad' (literally 'hill country' in Kannada), a 60–80 km wide belt bordering the Sahyadris characterized by heavy rainfall, dense forests, high ridges, and deep headward-eroded valleys; and (ii) the eastern 'Maidan', a lower, gently rolling rain-shadow plateau characterized by open plains interspersed with isolated granitic inselbergs, tors, and domes.

Statement 2 is correct. The crescent-shaped Baba Budan Hills in Chikkamagaluru district (containing Mulangiri, the highest peak in Karnataka at 1,925 m, and the adjacent Kudremukh-Kemmangundi belt) form part of the Archean Dharwar Supergroup—India's oldest metamorphosed sedimentary rock system. These greenstone-schist belts contain vast reserves of Banded Iron Formations (both magnetite-quartzites and high-grade haematite).

Statement 3 is correct. Both the Telangana and Rayalaseema plateaus are dominated by the Archean Peninsular Gneissic Complex (hard, unstratified granites and gneisses). Because crystalline basement rocks lack primary porosity and have negligible permeability outside weathered fractures, deep percolation is restricted and excavating long canals through hard rock is costly. Simultaneously, differential weathering has created an undulating 'ridge-and-valley' topography where low earthen bunds built across natural depressions trap seasonal monsoon runoff into interconnected cascading tanks (historically perfected as the Kakatiya 'golusukattu cheruvus').

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 2; D.R. Khullar: India - A Comprehensive Geography (Physiography & Irrigation)

stem: The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has classified Indian soils into categories corresponding to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Soil Taxonomy orders. Which one of the following statements accurately describes the areal distribution and pedogenic nature of these soil orders in India?

opts.A: Vertisols occupy the largest geographical area in India because of the extensive spread of the Deccan Trap basaltic plateau across peninsular states.
opts.B: Alfisols represent the dominant soil order across the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains due to the rapid development of mature argillic horizons in riverine silt.
opts.C: Entisols are highly weathered, iron-rich tropical soils with well-developed subsurface horizons found predominantly along the high-rainfall crests of the Western Ghats.
opts.D: Inceptisols, comprising weakly developed embryonic soils with incipient horizon differentiation across alluvial plains and mountain valleys, cover the largest percentage of India's geographical area, followed by Entisols.

core: Under the ICAR-adopted USDA Soil Taxonomy, Inceptisols (~39.74%) and Entisols (~28.08%) together account for over two-thirds of India's geographical area because young alluvial, coastal, and Himalayan slope deposits have weak or absent pedogenic horizon development. Mature orders like Alfisols (~13.55%) and Vertisols (~8.52%) occupy much smaller proportions.

exp.why: Option D is correct: According to the ICAR classification mapped to USDA Soil Taxonomy, Inceptisols (young, embryonic soils showing only the beginning or 'inception' of horizon development, widespread in the Indo-Gangetic alluvial plains and river valleys) cover the largest share of India's geographical area (approx. 39.74%), followed by Entisols (approx. 28.08%, very young soils lacking distinct genetic horizons beyond an ochric epipedon, such as active floodplains and sandy desert stretches). Option A is incorrect (T6) because Vertisols (expanding black clay soils) cover only about 8.52% of the total area. Option B is incorrect because Alfisols (approx. 13.55%) are mature leached red and lateritic forest soils with an argillic/kandic horizon, whereas the Indo-Gangetic plains are dominated by Inceptisols and Entisols. Option C is incorrect because Entisols are azonal, unweathered recent deposits, whereas highly weathered tropical soils with low base status on the Western Ghats belong to Ultisols or Oxisols.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 6 (Soils, ICAR Classification Table)

stem: With reference to the chemical composition and geomorphological subdivisions of Alluvial soils in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Alluvial soils of the Great Northern Plains are generally rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, while being severely deficient in potash and lime.
2. The older alluvium known as 'Bhangar' occupies higher interfluve terraces above the annual flood limit and contains impure calcium carbonate concretions called 'Kankar'.
3. The newer alluvium known as 'Khadar' is deposited annually by floodwaters and is enriched with fine silt and clay, making it more fertile than Bhangar.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Alluvial soils in India are chemically rich in potash and lime (derived from the weathering of diverse Himalayan crystalline and sedimentary rocks) but are characteristically deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus. Pedologically, older Bhangar terraces develop calcic 'Kankar' nodules due to seasonal capillary action, whereas younger Khadar floodplains receive fresh fine silt annually.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the chemical fertility profile of Alluvial soils. Alluvial soils are generally rich in potash and lime, but are deficient in nitrogen, phosphoric acid (phosphorus), and organic humus.

Statement 2 is correct. Bhangar represents the older alluvium forming slightly elevated terraces away from the active river channel above the flood level. Both Bhangar and Khadar contain calcareous concretions ('Kankar'), which are particularly prominent and consolidated in the older Bhangar profiles.

Statement 3 is correct. Khadar is the newer alluvium occupying the lower floodplains; it is replenished almost every year by fresh deposits of fine silt and clay during monsoon floods, conferring superior natural fertility without heavy fertilizer input.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 6 (Soils - Alluvial Soils)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Black Cotton Soils (Regur) of the Peninsular Plateau:
items: Statement-I: Black soils exhibit a distinct 'self-ploughing' character and sustain rainfed crops long after the cessation of monsoon rains due to a high proportion of 2:1 expanding-lattice montmorillonite clay minerals that swell to trap sub-soil moisture when wet and shrink to form deep wide cracks when dry.
Statement-II: Black soils of the Deccan Plateau are chemically rich in lime, iron, magnesia, and alumina, while remaining generally deficient in phosphorus, nitrogen, and organic matter.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The physical 'self-ploughing' and moisture-retention properties of Black Cotton Soils (Vertisols) are governed by their smectite/montmorillonite 2:1 expanding clay crystal lattice, which absorbs water between silicate sheets. Their bulk chemical nutrient profile—richness in lime, iron, magnesia, and alumina alongside deficiency in N, P, and humus—is an independent pedochemical trait that does not cause the physical swelling-shrinking mechanism.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Black soils (Regur/Vertisols) are very clayey and contain 2:1 expanding-lattice clay minerals (primarily montmorillonite/smectite). During the rainy season, water molecules enter the interlayer spaces of the clay lattice, causing the soil to swell and become sticky and impermeable, which slows evaporation and retains sub-soil moisture for dryland crops like cotton and citrus fruits. In the dry season, moisture loss causes shrinkage and wide surface cracks (self-ploughing), allowing surface soil to fall into the cracks and aerate the profile.

Statement-II is also correct. Chemically, black soils derived from weathered Deccan Trap basalt are rich in lime, iron, magnesia, and alumina, and also contain potash, while lacking phosphorus, nitrogen, and organic matter. However, this macro-nutrient composition does not explain the physical swelling-shrinking and moisture-trapping mechanics described in Statement-I, which are already explained by clay mineralogy.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 6 (Black Soils)

stem: With reference to the origin, distribution, and properties of Red and Yellow soils in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Red soils develop predominantly over the basaltic lava flows of the north-western Deccan Plateau under conditions of heavy tropical rainfall.
2. The soil exhibits a yellow colour in its anhydrous ferric oxide state on well-drained uplands, and turns reddish when the iron oxide undergoes hydration in poorly drained low-lying pockets.
3. The coarse-grained Red soils occurring on dry upland ridges are significantly richer in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus than the fine-grained Red and Yellow soils found in lowland valleys.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Red soils develop on ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks (granites and gneisses) in low-rainfall zones encircling the eastern and southern Deccan Plateau. Their reddish hue comes from wide diffusion of anhydrous ferric oxide, which turns yellow upon hydration (forming limonite) in moist or poorly drained depressions.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Red soils develop on crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks (such as Archaean granites and gneisses) in areas of comparatively low rainfall in the eastern and southern parts of the Deccan Plateau, whereas the basaltic lava flows of the north-western Deccan Trap give rise to Black (Regur) soils.

Statement 2 reverses the chemical hydration states. The soil develops a reddish colour due to a wide diffusion of anhydrous iron (ferric oxide, Fe2O3) in crystalline and metamorphic rocks, and it looks yellow when the ferric oxide occurs in a hydrated form (limonite) in higher-moisture or poorly drained pockets.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Red and Yellow soils are generally poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus across their range. Furthermore, while the fine-grained red and yellow soils normally found in fertile lowland plains and valleys are comparatively fertile, the coarse-grained soils found in dry upland areas are poor in fertility.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 6 (Red and Yellow Soil)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the pedogenesis and agronomic characteristics of Laterite soils in India:
items: 1. Intense leaching caused by alternating wet and dry tropical monsoon seasons washes away iron and aluminium oxides from the upper soil horizon, leaving behind a topsoil enriched in silica and lime.

2. Because bacterial and microbial decomposers thrive rapidly in the high temperatures of humid tropical regions, humus is quickly consumed, leaving Laterite soils poor in organic matter and nitrogen.
3. Red laterite soils in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala are well-suited for tree crops like cashew nut.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Tropical laterization is fundamentally a process of desilication: heavy monsoon rainfall leaches soluble bases (lime) and silica downward out of the soil profile, leaving behind residual, insoluble sesquioxides of iron and aluminium in the upper horizon. Rapid microbial decomposition under high tropical temperatures further depletes humus.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the chemistry of tropical leaching (laterization). Under conditions of high temperature and heavy monsoon rainfall with alternating wet and dry periods, lime and silica are leached away (desilication) from the topsoil, while insoluble iron oxide and aluminium compounds (sesquioxides) are left behind and accumulate in the upper profile.

Statement 2 is correct. Although laterite soils often develop under tropical forest vegetation, the humus content of the soil is removed fast by bacteria that thrive well in high temperatures. Consequently, these soils are poor in organic matter, nitrogen, phosphate, and calcium.

Statement 3 is correct. While laterite soils are not naturally fertile for intensive field crops without heavy manuring and irrigation, red laterite soils in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala are widely and successfully used for tree crops like cashew nut, as well as tea and coffee on hilly slopes in Karnataka and Kerala.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 6 (Laterite Soil)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Arid (Desert) soils in western Rajasthan:
items: Statement-I: Arid soils in western Rajasthan are severely deficient in both nitrogen and mineral phosphate, rendering them permanently infertile even when assured canal irrigation is provided.

Statement-II: High evaporation and scanty rainfall in arid climates prevent the chemical leaching of native mineral phosphates, while downward increases in calcium content form a sub-surface 'Kankar' horizon that restricts water infiltration and keeps soil moisture available in the root zone when irrigated.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike humid tropical soils where rainfall leaches mineral salts, Arid soils retain normal levels of mineral phosphate (comparable to fertile alluvial soils) while lacking only water, humus, and nitrogen. Furthermore, their sub-surface calcareous 'Kankar' pan restricts deep percolation Losses, making them highly productive once canal irrigation is supplied.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. While Arid soils are deficient in nitrogen and humus (due to sparse vegetation and rapid dry oxidation), their phosphate content is normal and comparable to that of alluvial soils. When irrigation is made available—as seen in the Indira Gandhi Canal command area of western Rajasthan—these soils become readily productive and support vibrant agriculture.

Statement-II is correct. Because of the dry climate, high temperature, and accelerated evaporation, chemical leaching is minimal, preserving mineral phosphates and soluble salts in the profile. Additionally, the lower horizons of the soil are occupied by 'Kankar' layers because of the increasing calcium content downwards; this Kankar pan restricts water infiltration so that when irrigation is provided, soil moisture is sustainably retained for plant growth.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 6 (Arid Soils)

stem: With reference to the pedogenesis and reclamation of Saline and Alkaline (Usara) soils in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In intensive canal-irrigated tracts of semi-arid northwestern India, a rise in the shallow water table coupled with high potential evapotranspiration draws dissolved sodium, calcium, and magnesium salts upward through capillary action.
2. Sodic (alkaline) soils suffer from severe deflocculation and loss of soil structure because excess exchangeable sodium ions disperse clay micelles, drastically reducing water infiltration.

3. To chemically reclaim alkaline soils, agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) is extensively applied to replace exchangeable sodium, whereas gypsum (calcium sulphate) is primarily added to neutralize highly acidic lateritic soils.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Secondary salinization in Green Revolution canal command areas occurs via capillary rise of dissolved salts under high evaporation, while sodic dispersion of clay is chemically reclaimed using gypsum (calcium sulphate) rather than agricultural lime.

exp.why: In semi-arid and arid canal-irrigated regions (such as Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh), seepage from unlined canals and flood irrigation raises the water table. During dry periods, intense solar radiation and high potential evapotranspiration draw mineralized groundwater upward through soil capillaries; as the water evaporates, soluble salts of sodium, calcium, and magnesium precipitate as a white surface crust (Reh, Kallar, or Thur).

When exchangeable sodium exceeds 15% of the Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) and soil pH rises above 8.5, the large hydrated radius of sodium ions forces clay platelets apart (deflocculation/dispersion). This destroys soil aggregates, seals soil pores, causes surface crusting, and severely impedes water infiltration and root aeration.

The chemical amendments are reversed. Gypsum (hydrated calcium sulphate, CaSO4.2H2O) is applied to reclaim alkaline/sodic soils because calcium ions replace exchangeable sodium on the clay complex, forming soluble sodium sulphate (Na2SO4) which can then be leached out with fresh water and subsurface drainage. Conversely, agricultural lime (calcium carbonate or dolomite) is applied to raise the pH and neutralize the acidity of lateritic, podzolic, and peaty soils.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 6 (Soils); ICAR Handbook of Agriculture

stem: With reference to the Peaty and Marshy soils of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. These soils accumulate up to 40 to 50 percent organic matter because prolonged anoxic waterlogging suppresses the aerobic microbial decomposition of plant residues.
2. Locally known as Kari soils in the backwater tracts of Kerala, they are predominantly strongly alkaline in reaction due to the submergence of decaying vegetation in stagnant waters.
3. Besides the coastal deltaic marshes of the Sundarbans and Odisha, patches of peaty and marshy soils also occur in the northern districts of Bihar and the Almora belt of Uttarakhand.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Peaty and marshy (Kari) soils form under waterlogged anaerobic conditions that preserve 40-50% organic matter, making them heavy, black, and strongly acidic (often acid-sulphate) rather than alkaline.

exp.why: In areas of heavy rainfall, high humidity, and poor drainage, dense vegetative growth is followed by waterlogging. The resulting oxygen-depleted (anoxic) environment inhibits aerobic bacteria and fungi from mineralizing humus, leading to the accumulation of 40-50% partially decomposed organic matter (peat).

Peaty soils (known as Kari soils in Kuttanad and adjoining districts of Kerala) are heavy, black, and strongly acidic (often with pH dropping between 3.5 and 5.0), not alkaline. They frequently behave as acid-sulphate soils because accumulated iron sulphides (pyrite) oxidize upon drainage to form sulphuric acid, alongside humic and fulvic organic acids, and exhibit free aluminium and ferrous iron toxicity.

Peaty and marshy soils are not restricted to coastal environments. While widespread in the Kottayam and Alappuzha districts of Kerala, coastal Odisha, Tamil Nadu, and the Sundarbans of West Bengal, inland marshy and peaty soils also occur in the flood-prone depressions of North Bihar (such as Darbhanga and Muzaffarpur) and poorly drained valley hollows of the Almora district in Uttarakhand.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 6; Khullar India: A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the pedogenic processes operating in the Forest and Mountain soils of the Himalayas as compared to the tropical highlands of Peninsular India, which one of the following statements accurately describes the mechanism of 'Podzolization'?

opts.A: Intense leaching of silica under warm, humid monsoonal conditions leaves behind a residual accumulation of iron and aluminium sesquioxides in the upper topsoil horizon.
opts.B: Upward capillary migration of calcium and magnesium bicarbonates under sub-humid conditions precipitates an indurated kankar pan within the root zone.
opts.C: Percolation of strongly acidic organic leachates under cool, humid coniferous forest cover mobilizes and translocates iron and aluminium sesquioxides downward into the B-horizon, leaving a bleached, silica-rich ash-grey topsoil.
opts.D: Reduction and mobilization of ferric iron into ferrous compounds under permanently waterlogged anaerobic conditions produces a bluish-grey sticky clay horizon.

core: Podzolization (cheluviation) is the exact geochemical inverse of tropical laterization: under cool, humid coniferous forests, acidic humic leachates strip iron and aluminium oxides from the topsoil and leave behind an ash-grey, silica-rich eluvial A-horizon.

exp.why: Option C is correct because Podzolization occurs in cool, humid high-altitude Himalayan coniferous zones (such as under pine, deodar, and spruce forests). Resin-rich conifer needles decompose slowly into strongly acidic mor humus. Percolating organic acids chelate and leach iron and aluminium sesquioxides downward into the illuvial B-horizon, leaving behind insoluble quartz (silica) in a characteristic bleached, ash-grey eluvial A-horizon. Option A describes Laterization (desilication), which operates in warm tropical highlands like the Western Ghats where silica is leached out and iron/aluminium oxides remain in the topsoil. Option B describes Calcification in semi-arid zones. Option D describes Gleization in waterlogged bogs.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 6; Savindra Singh Physical Geography (Pedogenesis)

stem: With reference to the mechanics and geomorphological progression of soil erosion by water in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Sheet erosion removes thin, uniform layers of nutrient-rich fine topsoil across gentle slopes during heavy downpours without carving conspicuous channels, making it more insidious to agricultural productivity than localized gully erosion.

2. In the sequential progression of water erosion, gully erosion directly precedes rill erosion, as deep vertical ravines gradually flatten out into shallow micro-channels that can be obliterated by normal tillage.

3. The extensive badland (ravine) topography of the Chambal basin is driven by deep headward gully incision into thick, unconsolidated quaternary alluvial deposits subjected to intense monsoonal runoff and a deeply incised local river base level.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Water erosion progresses sequentially from raindrop splash to sheet, rill, and finally gully/ravine erosion; sheet erosion is the silent destroyer of fertile topsoil, while gully incision creates badland topography in unconsolidated alluvium.

exp.why: Sheet erosion takes place on bare, gentle slopes when rainfall intensity exceeds the infiltration capacity of the soil. Overland sheet flow detaches and washes away the finest, most fertile colloidal clay and organic humus particles uniformly across the field. Because it leaves no dramatic scars initially, it often goes unnoticed by farmers until subsoil exposure severely degrades crop yields.

The hydrodynamic sequence is reversed. Water erosion progresses from Splash erosion to Sheet erosion, then to Rill erosion, and finally to Gully (and Ravine) erosion. Rills are small, shallow finger-like micro-channels formed when sheet flow concentrates into rivulets; they are shallow enough to be smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage. When rills are neglected, they coalesce, deepen, and widen into permanent Gullies that cannot be crossed or obliterated by normal agricultural implements.

The Chambal, Yamuna, and Mahi basins exhibit severe ravine (Kotar/Biihad) topography because thick, erodible alluvial deposits lie significantly above the deeply incised channel of the trunk river (strengthened by slow neotectonic uplift of the Vindhyan foreland). Concentrated monsoonal downpours trigger rapid headward gully erosion and bank slumping as tributaries cut down sharply to meet the lower base level of the Chambal River.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 6; G.C. Leong Certificate Physical and Human Geography

stem: With reference to engineering and agronomic soil conservation practices across different soil groups in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Strict contour bunding, which impounds surface runoff completely along lines of equal elevation, is most effective in deep Black Cotton soils (Vertisols) of high-rainfall zones because their high clay content prevents structural breaching.

2. Graded bunding, which incorporates a slight longitudinal channel gradient along the bund, is specifically designed for low-permeability deep black soils or regions receiving high rainfall to safely drain away excess surface runoff.
3. Bench terracing is primarily recommended as a soil conservation measure on very gentle alluvial plains with slopes of less than 2 percent, where agronomic strip-cropping cannot be practiced.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Soil conservation engineering must match soil hydraulic conductivity: permeable Red and Alluvial soils in low-rainfall zones suit strict Contour Bunding, whereas impermeable swelling Vertisols and high-rainfall zones require Graded Bunding to prevent waterlogging and bund breaching.

exp.why: Strict contour bunding (which impounds all runoff behind level earthen embankments) is suitable only for permeable Red, Lateritic, and light Alluvial soils in low-to-medium rainfall areas (<600-800 mm). In deep Black Cotton soils (Vertisols), smectite clay swells upon wetting and renders the soil nearly impermeable; impounding water causes prolonged waterlogging that suffocates crops, while dry-season shrinkage cracks weaken the earthen bunds and cause catastrophic breaching during heavy monsoonal rains.

Graded bunding constructs earthen bunds or channels with a gentle longitudinal slope (typically 0.1% to 0.4%) leading into vegetated grassed waterways. This allows excess rainwater that cannot infiltrate into slow-draining Vertisols (or excess runoff in regions receiving >800 mm rainfall) to flow off at non-erosive velocities without ponding or breaching the bunds.

Bench terracing (converting a steep slope into a series of level or nearly level step-like platforms) is an intensive engineering measure practiced on steep hill slopes ranging from 16% to 33% (such as in the Himalayas, Nilgiris, and Meghalaya plateau). On very gentle slopes of less than 2 percent, simple agronomic practices such as contour ploughing, mulching, and strip-cropping are sufficient and cost-effective.

ref: ICAR Handbook of Agriculture (Soil & Water Conservation Engineering); NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 6

stem: Consider the following table matching specific physiographic sub-regions of Peninsular India with their parent lithology, soil group, and characteristic crop ecology:
items: 1. Malnad & Coorg Highlands : Archaean gneisses and charnockites weathering under heavy monsoonal rainfall into well-drained acidic Lateritic and Forest loams : Shade-grown Arabica and Robusta coffee with cardamom
2. Malwa Plateau : Cretaceous Deccan Trap basalt weathering into deep, moisture-retentive Vertisols (Regur soils) : Soybean, cotton, and rainfed wheat
3. Rayalaseema Plateau : Pleistocene aeolian coastal quartz sands coated with ferric oxide (Teri sands) : Cashew nut and palmyra palm plantations
4. Tirunelveli Teri Belt : Semi-arid Archaean granite-gneiss complex weathering into friable, gravelly Red Alfisols : Rainfed groundnut and coarse millets
prompt: Which of the rows given above are correctly matched?
core: Peninsular India's agro-ecological zoning is governed by the interplay of parent rock and climate: Deccan basalt forms moisture-retentive Vertisols on the Malwa Plateau, wet Western Ghats gneisses form acidic lateritic/forest loams in Malnad, interior rain-shadow granites form Red Alfisols in Rayalaseema, and oxidized coastal dunes form Teri sands in Tirunelveli.

exp.why: The Malnad and Kodagu (Coorg) highlands along the dissected leeward and windward slopes of the Karnataka Western Ghats consist of ancient Archaean gneisses and charnockites subjected to >2000 mm of rainfall. They develop well-drained, slightly acidic lateritic and humus-rich forest loams on undulating slopes that prevent waterlogging around roots, ideal for shade-grown coffee, pepper, and cardamom.

The Malwa Plateau (spread across western Madhya Pradesh and southeastern Rajasthan) is floored by Deccan Trap basaltic lava flows. Weathering under semi-arid to sub-humid conditions has produced deep, dark Vertisols rich in montmorillonite clay that retain subsoil moisture well into the rabi season, supporting India's premier soybean belt alongside cotton and unirrigated wheat.

The descriptions of Row 3 and Row 4 are interchanged. The Rayalaseema Plateau (southern Andhra Pradesh) is an interior, semi-arid rain-shadow plateau underlined by Archaean granites, gneisses, and Cuddapah formations that weather into porous, gravelly Red Alfisols (with localized black soil pockets), supporting drought-hardy rainfed groundnut, finger millet (ragi), pearl millet, and pulses.

The Teri coastal belt of Tirunelveli and Thoothukudi districts in southeastern Tamil Nadu consists of Pleistocene wind-blown (aeolian) red sand dunes where quartz grains are coated with oxidized ferric iron (hematite) derived from weathered ferruginous minerals. These drought-prone coastal red dunes support palmyra palms, cashew nut, and localized horticulture rather than interior granite-gneiss groundnut farming.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 2 & Ch. 6; Tiwari India: A Regional Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the evolution of the Himalayan drainage system:
items: Statement-I: Trans-Himalayan rivers such as the Indus, the Sutlej, and the Brahmaputra cut across the lofty Greater Himalayan range through deep, steep-sided gorges.

Statement-II: These rivers represent antecedent drainage systems that existed prior to the Cenozoic uplift of the Himalayas and maintained their original courses by continuously downcutting their valleys at a pace matching the rate of tectonic uplift.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Antecedent rivers like the Indus, Sutlej, Kosi, and Brahmaputra pre-date the folding of the Himalayan ranges. As the mountains rose episodically during the Cenozoic Era, vertical fluvial incision kept pace with tectonic uplift, carving deep transverse gorges across the mountain barrier.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The Indus (near Bunji/Gilgit), the Sutlej (near Shipki La), and the Brahmaputra (near Dihang/Namcha Barwa) originate north of the Great Himalayan axis in the Tibetan plateau and cut right across the highest crystalline axis of the Himalayas through spectacular, steep-walled canyons.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Unlike consequent rivers whose flow direction is determined after a mountain slope forms, antecedent rivers are older than the geological structures they traverse. Because the rate of vertical downcutting (corrasion) by these moisture-fed and glacier-fed rivers matched the gradual tectonic uplift of the Himalayas, they preserved their pre-existing paths rather than being ponded or deflected permanently.

ref: NCERT Class XI 'India: Physical Environment', Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Savindra Singh Physical Geography

stem: With reference to the geographical course of the Indus River mainstem, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It originates from a glacier near Bokhar Chu in the Kailash mountain range, where it is known as 'Singi Khamban'.

2. Throughout its northwestward traverse across the Union Territory of Ladakh, the mainstem of the Indus flows in a structural trough bounded by the Karakoram Range to the north and the Ladakh Range to the south.
3. Near the western syntaxial bend of the Himalayas, it carves a deep gorge around the Nanga Parbat massif before turning southward.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indus rises near Bokhar Chu in the Kailash range and enters Ladakh at Demchok, flowing northwestward in a structurally controlled valleyalong the Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone between the Ladakh Range to the north and the Zanskar Range to the south, before curving sharply around Nanga Parbat.

exp.why: The Indus originates from a glacier near Bokhar Chu in the Tibetan region at an altitude of about 4,164 m in the Kailash mountain range. In Tibet, it is known as 'Singi Khamban' or the Lion's Mouth.

In Ladakh, the mainstem of the Indus flows in a northwest direction between the Ladakh Range (to its north/northeast) and the Zanskar Range (to its south/southwest), cutting across the Ladakh Range near Dungti. It is the Shyok River—a right-bank tributary—that flows between the Karakoram and Ladakh ranges.

After flowing northwestward through Ladakh and Baltistan, the Indus cuts across the Great Himalayan range, carving a very deep gorge (nearly 4,500–5,200 metres deep) near Bunji just north of the Nanga Parbat peak, following the western syntaxial bend southward towards Attock.

ref: NCERT Class XI 'India: Physical Environment', Ch. 3 (Drainage System)

stem: With reference to the tributaries of the Indus River in its upper and middle mountain reaches, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Zanskar and the Suru rivers join the Indus on its right bank during its northwestward traverse through Ladakh.
2. The Shyok River, fed by the Siachen Glacier via the Nubra River, joins the Indus as a left-bank tributary.
3. The Gilgit, the Hunza, and the Kabul rivers are right-bank tributaries of the Indus River system.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Because the Indus flows from southeast to northwest through Ladakh, rivers draining northward from the Great Himalayas and Zanskar range (such as the Zanskar and Suru) join its left bank, whereas rivers draining southward from the Karakoram and Hindu Kush (such as the Shyok, Gilgit, and Kabul) join its right bank.

exp.why: Facing downstream along the southeast-to-northwest flow of the Indus in Ladakh, left is to the southwest and right is to the northeast. The Zanskar River (which meets the Indus at Nimmu) and the Suru River (joined by the Dras and Shingo rivers) flow northward from the Zanskar and Great Himalayan ranges and therefore join the Indus on its left bank.

The Shyok River originates from the Rimo Glacier and receives the Nubra River (which originates from the Siachen Glacier). Flowing south and then northwest along the northern flank of the Ladakh Range, the Shyok meets the Indus on its right bank near Keris (east of Skardu).

The Gilgit River (along with its major tributary, the Hunza) drains the western Karakoram and joins the Indus on its right bank near Bunji. Further downstream near Attock, the Kabul River—along with other western hills rivers like the Khurram, Tochi, and Gomal—also joins the Indus on its right bank.

ref: NCERT Class XI 'India: Physical Environment', Ch. 3; Survey of India Physical Map of Ladakh

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the fluvial geomorphology of the Jhelum River:
items: Statement-I: The Jhelum River flows in a straight, non-meandering channel across the Kashmir Valley and begins to form meanders only after entering the alluvial plains of Punjab.

Statement-II: In the Kashmir Valley, the local base level provided by Wular Lake and the flat lacustrine sediments left behind by a prehistoric palaeo-lake substantially reduce the channel gradient of the Jhelum River.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Although meandering is typically a mature-stage feature on low-altitude floodplains, the Jhelum exhibits classic meandering within its youthful mountain stage across the Kashmir Valley because thick Karewa lacustrine deposits and the local base level of Wular Lake create an exceptionally gentle valley floor gradient.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Despite being in its youthful stage inside a high-altitude intermontane basin bounded by the Great Himalayas and the Pir Panjal Range, the Jhelum River develops prominent, sweeping meanders across the Kashmir Valley around Srinagar before flowing into Wular Lake and subsequently cutting a steep gorge near Baramulla.

Statement-II is correct. During the Pleistocene epoch, the entire Kashmir Valley was occupied by a vast palaeo-lake (Satisar), of which present-day Wular and Dal lakes are remnants. As this lake drained and left behind unconsolidated, flat-lying fluvioglacial and lacustrine deposits (Karewas), the local base level of erosion checked vertical downcutting and drastically lowered the river's longitudinal slope, promoting lateral shifting and meandering.

ref: NCERT Class XI 'India: Physical Environment', Ch. 3 (Page 22 Box on Jhelum Meanders)

stem: With reference to the Chenab River system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Like the Indus and the Sutlej, the Chenab is a trans-Himalayan river that originates across the international border in the Tibetan plateau before entering Himachal Pradesh.
2. It is formed by the confluence of two headstreams, the Chandra and the Bhaga, at Tandi in the Lahaul and Spiti valley, where it flows between the Great Himalayas and the Pir Panjal range.
3. It is the largest tributary of the Indus in terms of water discharge, and the Marusudar River is its largest right-bank tributary.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike the trans-Himalayan Indus and Sutlej, the Chenab originates entirely within India near the Bara Lacha La pass in Himachal Pradesh via its two headstreams—Chandra and Bhaga—which unite at Tandi to form the largest tributary of the Indus.

exp.why: The Chenab is not a trans-Himalayan river originating in Tibet. Both of its headstreams—the Chandra and the Bhaga—rise on opposite sides of the Bara Lacha La pass in the Zanskar range completely within the Lahaul and Spiti district of Himachal Pradesh, India.

The Chandra and Bhaga streams meet at Tandi near Keylong in the Lahaul and Spiti district to form the Chandrabhaga (Chenab). From Tandi, it flows northwestward through the structural trough between the Great Himalayan range to the north and the Pir Panjal range to the south before entering the Pangi valley and Kishtwar.

The Chenab is the largest tributary of the Indus River, flowing for about 1,180 km before joining the Indus system (as the Panjnad). The Marusudar River, which originates from the Nunkun glacier region and flows through the Warwan and Marwah valleys to join the Chenab at Bhandarkoot in Kishtwar, is the largest tributary of the Chenab.

ref: NCERT Class XI 'India: Physical Environment', Ch. 3 (Drainage System)

stem: With reference to the Ravi and the Beas rivers of the Indus system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both the Ravi and the Beas originate in close proximity to the Rohtang Pass in Himachal Pradesh and carve deep gorges across the Dhauladhar range.
2. Prior to entering the plains, the Ravi drains the longitudinal valley lying between the Zanskar Range and the Great Himalayan Range.
3. Among the five rivers of the Panjnad system, the Beas is the only river whose entire course from source to confluence lies exclusively within India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Both the Ravi and the Beas rise near the Rohtang Pass in the Kullu hills and breach the Dhauladhar range through gorges, while the Beas remains the only Panjnad river confined entirely to Indian territory, terminating in the Sutlej at Harike.

exp.why: The Ravi rises west of the Rohtang Pass in the Kullu hills of Himachal Pradesh and cuts a gorge across the Dhauladhar range, while the Beas originates from the Beas Kund near the Rohtang Pass at an elevation of 4,000 m and cuts through the Dhauladhar range, forming spectacular gorges at Kati and Larji.

Flowing westward through the Chamba valley of Himachal Pradesh, the Ravi drains the area lying between the southeastern part of the Pir Panjal range and the Dhauladhar range (both in the Lesser Himalayas), not the valley between the Zanskar and Great Himalayan ranges.

While the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, and Sutlej all cross the international boundary into Pakistan, the Beas flows entirely within India through Himachal Pradesh and Punjab before merging with the Sutlej at the Harike wetland near Kapurthala.

ref: NCERT Class XI 'India: Physical Environment', Ch. 3 (Drainage System)

stem: With reference to the course and drainage characteristics of the Sutlej river, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Originating from the Rakshastal lake in Tibet where it is known as Langqen Zangbo, it is an antecedent river that cuts across the Great Himalaya and enters India near the Shipki La pass.
2. Shortly after entering Himachal Pradesh, it is joined at Khab by the Spiti river, which drains the cold desert valley of Spiti and meets it as a right-bank tributary.
3. Before emerging onto the Punjab plains, it cuts a deep gorge across the Dhauladhar range at Bhakra, after having already merged with the Beas river upstream of the Gobind Sagar reservoir.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Sutlej is the only trans-Himalayan tributary among the five rivers of the Panjnad, entering India via Shipki La and receiving the Spiti river at Khab before cutting the Naina Devi Dhar (Shiwalik range) at Bhakra. Its confluence with the Beas occurs downstream in the Punjab plains at Harike, not upstream of Bhakra.

exp.why: The Sutlej originates in the Rakshastal lake (at an altitude of ~4,555 m) near Lake Manasarovar in Tibet, where it is called Langqen Zangbo. It flows northwestward along the Kailash-Zanskar trough for nearly 400 km roughly parallel to the Indus before cutting an antecedent gorge through the Great Himalaya and Zanskar ranges to enter Himachal Pradesh through the Shipki La pass.

The Spiti river originates from the Kunzum range in Lahaul and Spiti district, drains the rain-shadow cold desert of the Spiti valley, and joins the Sutlej as a major right-bank tributary at Khab (near Namgia) in Kinnaur district shortly after the Sutlej enters India.

At Bhakra, the Sutlej cuts a narrow gorge across the Naina Devi Dhar range of the Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas), not the Dhauladhar range (which is pierced upstream near Rampur-Largi). Furthermore, the Beas river does not merge with the Sutlej upstream of the Gobind Sagar reservoir; it joins the Sutlej much further downstream at Harike in the Punjab plains.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Khullar: India A Comprehensive Geography, Ch. 4

stem: Consider the following river confluences belonging to the Indus drainage system:
items: 1. Confluence of the Zanskar river with the Indus
2. Confluence of the Shyok river with the Indus
3. Confluence of the Jhelum river with the Chenab
4. Confluence of the Ravi river with the Chenab
prompt: What is the correct sequence of the above river confluences when arranged geographically from North to South?
core: Because the Indus flows from southeast to northwest through the Ladakh trough before taking its syntaxial bend around Nanga Parbat, its downstream confluence with the Shyok (~35.2° N) lies further north than its upstream confluence with the Zanskar at Nimmu (~34.2° N). In the southern plains, the Chenab successively receives the Jhelum at Trimmu (~31.1° N) and the Ravi further south (~30.5° N).

exp.why: The Zanskar river flows north-northeast to join the Indus from the left bank at Nimmu in Ladakh at approximately 34°10' N latitude. Because the Indus flows northwestward between the Ladakh and Zanskar ranges, Nimmu lies upstream of the Shyok confluence but geographically further south.

The Shyok river originates from the Rimo Glacier in the Karakoram and flows northwestward before joining the Indus as a right-bank tributary at Keris (east of Skardu in Baltistan) at approximately 35°14' N latitude, making it the northernmost among the four confluences.
After emerging from the Pir Panjal and flowing along the Potwar-Salt Range margin, the Jhelum joins the Chenab at Trimmu (Jhang district) at approximately 31°08' N latitude.

The Ravi joins the combined waters of the Chenab and Jhelum further south near Ahmadpur Sial (Sidhnai stretch) at approximately 30°33' N latitude. Hence, the exact North-to-South geographical sequence is 2 - 1 - 3 - 4.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3; Survey of India Physical Map of Jammu, Kashmir & Ladakh

stem: With reference to the major hydro-electric and irrigation projects situated in the Indus river basin in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Ratle Hydroelectric Project : Chenab River
2. Pakal Dul Hydroelectric Project : Jhelum River
3. Shahpurkandi Dam Project : Beas River
4. Dul Hasti Power Station : Kishanganga River
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Under the Indus Waters Treaty framework, India operates major run-of-the-river hydroelectric projects along the Chenab basin (Salal, Baglihar, Dul Hasti, Ratle on the Chenab mainstem; Pakal Dul on its tributary Marusudar) and Jhelum basin (Uri on Jhelum; Kishanganga on Kishanganga/Neelum), while storage and barrage projects like Ranjit Sagar and Shahpurkandi lie on the Eastern river Ravi.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The 850 MW Ratle Hydroelectric Project is a run-of-the-river concrete gravity dam project situated on the mainstem Chenab River at Drabshalla in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The 1,000 MW Pakal Dul (Drangdhuran) Hydroelectric Project is located on the Marusudar River, which is the largest right-bank tributary of the Chenab River in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir, not on the Jhelum River.
