Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. The Shahpurkandi Dam Project is constructed on the Ravi River (an Eastern River under the Indus Waters Treaty) in Pathankot district of Punjab, just downstream of the Ranjit Sagar (Thein) Dam, not on the Beas River.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. The 390 MW Dul Hasti Power Station is a run-of-the-river project situated on the Chenab River in Kishtwar district, whereas the Kishanganga Hydroelectric Project is located on the Kishanganga (Neelum) tributary of the Jhelum River in Bandipora district.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3; Central Water Commission (CWC) Indus Basin Atlas

stem: With reference to the geological evolution of the Himalayan drainage systems during the Pleistocene epoch, which one of the following statements accurately explains the dismemberment of the ancient watershed into the distinct Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra drainage basins?

opts.A: Subsidence of the Aravalli-Delhi Ridge created a structural trough that captured the headwaters of the Yamuna and Sutlej, while the uplift of the Rajmahal-Garo tract deflected the Brahmaputra southwards.
opts.B: Reactivation of the Main Boundary Thrust diverted the antecedent Indus system eastward into the Indo-Gangetic foredeep, until marine transgression through the Bengal basin carved the Malda Gap by headward erosion.
opts.C: Uplift of the Potwar Plateau along with the Delhi Ridge acted as a water divide separating the Indus and Ganga systems, while mid-Pleistocene down-thrusting of the Malda Gap between the Rajmahal Hills and the Meghalaya Plateau diverted the Ganga and Brahmaputra systems toward the Bay of Bengal.
opts.D: Crustal upwarping of the Malda-Kishanganj fault zone detached the Peninsular plateau from the Shillong massif, forcing the erstwhile westward-flowing Tsangpo to reverse its course along the Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone.

core: Geomorphological evolution of the Himalayan foredeep involved two pivotal Pleistocene tectonic events: (1) uplift of the Potwar Plateau and the Delhi Ridge (Ambala-Saharanpur water divide), which severed the continuity between the Indus and Ganga drainage systems, and (2) down-thrusting (faulting/subsidence) of the Malda Gap between the Rajmahal Hills and the Meghalaya (Garo) Plateau, which funnelled the Ganga and Brahmaputra into the Bay of Bengal.

exp.why: Option C is correct. During the Miocene-Pliocene epochs, alluvial sedimentation occurred along the Himalayan foredeep (hypothesized by E.H. Pascoe and G.E. Pilgrim as the Shiwalik or Indo-Brahm drainage). In the Pleistocene epoch, tectonic upheaval in the western Himalayas, specifically the uplift of the Potwar Plateau (Delhi Ridge / Ambala-Saharanpur divide), acted as a structural barrier separating the Indus drainage to the west from the Ganga drainage to the east, with the Yamuna shifting eastward to join the Ganga. Simultaneously, during the mid-Pleistocene period, tectonic down-thrusting (subsidence) of the Malda Gap between the Rajmahal Hills and the Meghalaya Plateau lowered the base level and diverted both the Ganga and Brahmaputra systems southward into the Bay of Bengal. Options A and D are incorrect because the Delhi Ridge experienced uplift (not subsidence) and the Malda Gap experienced down-faulting/subsidence (not uplift/upwarping). Option B is incorrect because the Malda Gap is a tectonic down-faulted trough rather than a feature carved solely by marine headward erosion.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Evolution of the Himalayan Drainage, p. 24); Savindra Singh: Physical Geography

stem: With reference to the 'Panch Prayag' (five sacred confluences) along the course of the Alaknanda river in Uttarakhand, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Vishnuprayag : Confluence of Alaknanda and Dhauliganga
2. Nandaprayag : Confluence of Alaknanda and Nandakini
3. Karnaprayag : Confluence of Alaknanda and Mandakini (originating near Chorabari glacier)
4. Devprayag : Confluence of Alaknanda and Bhagirathi (originating at Gaumukh)
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Moving downstream from Satopanth glacier, the Alaknanda forms the Panch Prayag consecutively with the Dhauliganga at Vishnuprayag, the Nandakini at Nandaprayag, the Pindar at Karnaprayag, the Mandakini at Rudraprayag, and finally the Bhagirathi at Devprayag to form the mainstem Ganga.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The Alaknanda rises at the confluence and foot of the Satopanth and Bhagirath Kharak glaciers in Uttarakhand and first meets the Dhauliganga (White Ganga) at Vishnuprayag in Chamoli district.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Downstream of Vishnuprayag, the Alaknanda is joined by its left-bank tributary, the Nandakini river (originating from the Nanda Ghunti glacier on the rim of Nanda Devi Sanctuary), at Nandaprayag.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. At Karnaprayag, the Alaknanda is joined by the Pindar river (which originates from the Pindari glacier in Bageshwar district) as a left-bank tributary. The Mandakini river (also called Kali Ganga, originating from the Chorabari glacier near Kedarnath) joins the Alaknanda as a right-bank tributary further downstream at Rudraprayag, not at Karnaprayag.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. At Devprayag in Tehri Garhwal district, the Alaknanda meets the Bhagirathi river (which originates from the Gaumukh snout of the Gangotri glacier), and hereafter the combined river is known as the Ganga.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (The Ganga System, p. 25)

stem: With reference to the hydro-geography of the Bhagirathi sub-basin in the Garhwal Himalayas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Bhagirathi rises at the Gaumukh snout of the Gangotri glacier and is joined near Bhaironghati by the Jadh Ganga (Jahnavi), a tributary that originates across the international border in Tibet.
2. The Bhilangana river, which originates from the Khatling glacier, joins the Bhagirathi as a left-bank tributary at Old Tehri, the site of the Tehri Dam reservoir.
3. At the Devprayag confluence, the Bhagirathi is hydrologically considered the main stem of the Ganga because it carries a significantly larger annual water discharge than the Alaknanda.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Bhagirathi (fed by Gangotri glacier, trans-border Jadh Ganga at Bhaironghati, and Bhilangana at Old Tehri) is culturally revered as the primary source stream of the Ganga, the Alaknanda is hydrologically the main stem at Devprayag because of its substantially larger catchment area and greater annual water discharge.

exp.why: The Bhagirathi originates from the Gaumukh ice cave at the terminus of the Gangotri glacier (~3,900 m) in Uttarkashi district. Near Bhaironghati (just west of Gangotri), it receives the Jadh Ganga (also called Jahnavi), an antecedent trans-border tributary that originates in Zanda County of Tibet (north of Mana Pass) and cuts through the Great Himalaya into Uttarkashi.

The Bhilangana river rises from the Khatling glacier in Tehri Garhwal district and flows southwestward to join the Bhagirathi from the left bank at Ganeshprayag (Old Tehri), where the Tehri Dam reservoir impounds the combined waters of both rivers.

Although the Bhagirathi is traditionally and mythologically regarded as the source stream of the Ganga, in strict hydrological terms the Alaknanda is the main stem at Devprayag. Because the Alaknanda drains a much wider glaciated catchment (encompassing Kamet, Nanda Devi, Trisul, and Chaukhamba massifs via the Dhauliganga, Nandakini, Pindar, and Mandakini), it brings roughly twice the mean annual water discharge of the Bhagirathi to the Devprayag confluence.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3; Central Water Commission (CWC) Ganga Basin Report

stem: With reference to the Himalayan catchment of the Yamuna River system, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Before the Yamuna River breaches the Shiwalik hills near Paonta Sahib to enter the plains, the main Yamuna stream originating from the Yamunotri glacier carries a larger volume of water than any of its Himalayan tributaries.
Statement-II: The Tons River, which rises on the northern slopes of the Bandarpunch range and drains the Har-ki-Dun valley, joins the Yamuna near Kalsi as its largest Himalayan right-bank tributary.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Although the Yamuna is the master consequent stream of its basin, its Himalayan right-bank tributary, the Tons (Tamasa), drains a larger snow-fed catchment around the Bandarpunch massif and carries nearly twice the water volume of the main Yamuna at their confluence near Kalsi in the Dehradun valley.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Within the Himalayan catchment upstream of the Paonta Sahib gorge through the Shiwaliks, the main Yamuna stream (originating from the Yamunotri glacier on the southwestern slopes of Bandarpunch) actually carries less water than its principal Himalayan tributary, the Tons River. At their confluence near Kalsi (Dakpathar) in the Doon valley, the Tons contributes nearly twice the water discharge of the main Yamuna channel.

Statement-II is correct. Formed by the confluence of the Supin and Rupin streams draining the Har-ki-Dun valley and the northern slopes of the Bandarpunch range in Uttarkashi, the Tons flows through a deep gorge along the Himachal Pradesh-Uttarakhand border and joins the Yamuna as its largest Himalayan right-bank tributary near Kalsi, upstream of where the Giri (left-bank) and Asan rivers join near Paonta Sahib.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Khullar India A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the Peninsular tributaries of the Ganga-Yamuna drainage system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The northeastward flow of rivers such as the Chambal, Betwa, and Son into the Gangetic trough is the result of river capture by antecedent Himalayan streams rather than the structural tilt of the northern Peninsular block.
2. The Chambal, Betwa, Ken, and Peninsular Tons (Tamsa) rivers, which originate along the Vindhyan-Kaimur scarps, empty directly into the Yamuna River upstream of Prayagraj.
3. The Banas and the Rihand are direct right-bank tributaries of the Yamuna that drain the Bundelkhand gneissic plateau.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The north- and northeast-flowing rivers of the northern Peninsular foreland (Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken, Tons/Tamsa, and Son) follow the structural northward tilt of the Indian craton toward the Himalayan foredeep; while the Chambal, Sind, Betwa, and Ken join the Yamuna, the Peninsular Tons and Son empty directly into the Ganga.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The northward and northeastward flow of the Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken, and Son rivers is controlled by the regional structural slope (tilt) of the northern Peninsular craton and the Vindhyan-Malwa forebulge toward the subsiding Indo-Gangetic foreland basin, not by headward river capture by antecedent Himalayan streams.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While the Chambal, Sind, Betwa, and Ken join the Yamuna directly as right-bank tributaries upstream of Prayagraj, the Peninsular Tons (Tamsa)—which rises at Tamakund in the Kaimur range of Madhya Pradesh—flows northeastward to join the Ganga directly at Sirsa (downstream of Prayagraj), just as the Son joins the Ganga directly near Patna.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Neither the Banas nor the Rihand is a direct tributary of the Yamuna. The Banas originates in the Khamnor Hills of the Aravalli Range and joins the Chambal as a left-bank tributary near Rameshwaram in Rajasthan, whereas the Rihand originates in the Matringa Hills of Chhattisgarh and joins the Son River as a right-bank tributary in Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Singh Savindra Physical Geography

stem: With reference to the Ramganga and the Gomti rivers, two major left-bank tributaries of the Ganga, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both the Ramganga and the Gomti are snow-fed Lesser Himalayan rivers that cut deep gorges across the Shiwalik range before entering the Rohilkhand plains.
2. Before emerging into the Gangetic plains near Najibabad, the Ramganga flows through the Patli Dun valley inside Jim Corbett National Park and joins the Ganga near Kannauj.
3. The Gomti originates from a marshy lake (Fulhar Jheel) in the Terai belt of Pilibhit and flows entirely through the Indo-Gangetic alluvial plains before joining the Ganga near Saidpur.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Left-bank tributaries of the Ganga exhibit three distinct physiographic origins: trans-Himalayan/Great Himalayan glacier-fed rivers (Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi), Lesser Himalayan spring-fed rivers (Ramganga), and alluvial Terai/groundwater-fed plain rivers (Gomti, Varuna).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Neither river is snow-fed from permanent glaciers, and the Gomti does not originate in the Himalayas at all. The Ramganga rises in the non-glaciated Dudhatoli crystalline range (around 3,100 m) of the Lesser Himalayas in Garhwal and is fed by mountain springs and monsoon rainfall, whereas the Gomti is a purely alluvial, groundwater- and lake-fed river originating in the Terai plains of Uttar Pradesh.

Statement 2 is correct. After originating in the Dudhatoli range of Pauri Garhwal, the Ramganga flows through the longitudinal tectonic valley of Patli Dun inside Jim Corbett National Park, breaches the Shiwalik range at the Kalagarh gorge, enters the plains near Najibabad, and finally joins the Ganga on its left bank near Kannauj.

Statement 3 is correct. The Gomti originates from Gomat Taal (Fulhar Jheel) near Madho Tanda in Pilibhit district of the Terai region. Flowing sluggishly across the alluvial plains past Lucknow, Sultanpur, and Jaunpur, it joins the Ganga as a left-bank tributary at Kaithi near Saidpur in Ghazipur district.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Khullar India A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Ghaghara (Karnali) River system:
items: 1. Unlike the Indus and the Brahmaputra, the Ghaghara originates on the southern slopes of the Lesser Himalayas and does not form any antecedent gorges across the Great Himalayan range.
2. The Sharda (Kali) River originates from the Milam glacier in the Kumaon Himalayas and flows along the India-Nepal border before joining the Ganga directly near Kannauj.
3. Although the Ghaghara is the longest tributary of the Ganga, its annual water discharge at its confluence with the Ganga is smaller than that of the Yamuna.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Ghaghara (known as Karnali in Nepal) is a trans-Himalayan antecedent river originating near the Mapchachungo glacier close to Lake Mansarovar; augmented by the Sharda (Kali/Saryu) and Rapti rivers, it is the largest tributary of the Ganga by water volume, whereas the Yamuna is the longest.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Ghaghara (Karnali) is a trans-Himalayan river that originates from the glaciers of Mapchachungo on the Tibetan Plateau near Lake Mansarovar. Flowing southward into western Nepal, it cuts deep antecedent gorges across the Great Himalayas and the Shiwalik hills (Chisapani gorge) before entering the Indian plains.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While the Sharda (Kali or Mahakali) originates in the Milam glacier/Kalapani region of the Kumaon Himalayas and demarcates the international boundary between Uttarakhand and Nepal, it does not join the Ganga directly. Instead, after entering the plains at Tanakpur/Banbasa, it joins the Ghaghara River at Brahmaghat in Uttar Pradesh.

Statement 3 is incorrect because it reverses the hydrological relationship between the Yamuna and the Ghaghara. The Yamuna (approx. 1,376 km) is the longest tributary of the Ganga, whereas the Ghaghara (approx. 1,080 km) is the largest tributary of the Ganga in terms of annual water volume/discharge when it joins the Ganga at Revelganj near Chhapra in Bihar.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Majid Husain Geography of India Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the Gandak and the Burhi Gandak rivers draining the plains of North Bihar, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Gandak River is formed by the union of the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli rivers draining the central Nepal Himalayas between the Dhaulagiri and Mount Everest massifs, and enters the Bihar plains at Triveni (Valmikinagar).
2. Like the Gandak, the Burhi Gandak is a trans-Himalayan river that cuts an antecedent gorge across the Great Himalayas in Nepal before entering India.
3. Flowing southeastward roughly parallel to and east of the Gandak, the Burhi Gandak joins the Ganga downstream of the Gandak-Ganga confluence.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Gandak (Narayani) is a major antecedent Himalayan river cutting the deep Kali Gandaki gorge between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna in Nepal, the Burhi Gandak originates entirely within India in the Someshwar Hills (Shiwaliks) of West Champaran and occupies an older abandoned course of the Gandak.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Gandak (known as the Sapta Gandaki or Narayani in Nepal) is formed by seven Himalayan tributaries—principally the Kali Gandaki (which carves the deep Andha Galchi gorge between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna) and the Trishuli—draining the region between Dhaulagiri and Mount Everest. It enters the plains of Bihar at Triveni in Champaran (Valmiki Tiger Reserve) and joins the Ganga at Sonpur/Hajipur opposite Patna.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Unlike the Gandak, the Burhi Gandak is neither a trans-Himalayan river nor does it originate in Nepal. It originates entirely within India from the Chautarwa Chaur springs near Bishambharpur in the Someshwar Hills (the Shiwalik range) in West Champaran district of Bihar, fed by rainwater and sub-Himalayan springs.

Statement 3 is correct. The Burhi Gandak flows southeastward across North Bihar along an older abandoned channel of the Gandak, running roughly parallel to and east of the present Gandak river through Champaran, Muzaffarpur, Samastipur, and Begusarai before joining the Ganga near Khagaria, well downstream of the Gandak-Ganga confluence at Sonpur.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Khullar India A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the Kosi (Saptakoshi) River system and its geomorphological behaviour in the North Bihar plains, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Upon emerging from the Chatra Gorge into the plains of North Bihar, the Kosi River remains confined within a single deeply incised meander belt because its low sediment load promotes vertical downcutting rather than lateral aggradation.

Statement-II: The Saptakoshi is formed in eastern Nepal by the confluence of the trans-Himalayan Arun River with the Sun Kosi and Tamur rivers north of the Mahabharat Range, carrying an immense load of glacial and tectonic-erosional silt from the high Himalayas.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Draining the highest peaks of the world (Everest, Kanchenjunga, Makalu) via the Arun, Sun Kosi, and Tamur headwaters, the Kosi exits the Chatra Gorge with one of the highest suspended sediment loads in the world; the abrupt drop in gradient causes rapid channel bed aggradation, braiding, and frequent westward avulsions across its vast alluvial mega-fan.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Far from remaining confined in a deeply incised single meander channel, the Kosi is a classic braided river that builds a massive, low-gradient convex alluvial mega-fan upon exiting the Chatra Gorge. Because of the sudden loss of stream velocity and its enormous suspended silt load, the river rapidly aggrades (chokes) its own bed, causing recurrent breaches and lateral course shifts (avulsions) of over 120 km from east to west across North Bihar over the last two centuries.

Statement-II is correct. The Kosi (Saptakoshi) is formed by seven Himalayan streams organized into three main tributaries—the trans-Himalayan Arun (which originates in Tibet north of Mount Everest and cuts a deep antecedent gorge), the Sun Kosi from the west, and the Tamur from the east—which unite at Triveni north of the Mahabharat Range in eastern Nepal before cutting through the Chatra Gorge.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Kale V.S. Landscapes and Landforms of India

stem: With reference to the hydro-geography of the Lower Ganga Basin, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Mahananda, which originates in the Darjeeling hills, is the easternmost left-bank Himalayan tributary of the Ganga mainstem.
2. The Bhagirathi-Hooghly distributary bifurcates from the Ganga mainstem upstream of the Rajmahal Hills in Bihar before flowing southward into West Bengal.
3. Moving from north to south along the right bank of the Bhagirathi-Hooghly river, its plateau tributaries join in the sequential order of Damodar, Ajay, Mayurakshi, and Rupnarayan.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In the lower Ganga basin, the Mahananda joins as the final left-bank Himalayan tributary near the India-Bangladesh border, after the Ganga swings around the Rajmahal Hills and bifurcates downstream of Farakka into the Padma and the Bhagirathi-Hooghly. The Bhagirathi-Hooghly subsequently receives several rain-fed Chotanagpur Plateau tributaries on its right bank in the north-to-south order of Mayurakshi, Ajay, Damodar, Rupnarayan, and Haldi.

exp.why: The Mahananda rises in the Paglajhora area near Kurseong in the Darjeeling hills of West Bengal, flows through the Siliguri corridor, Bihar (Purnia/Katihar), and Malda district, and finally joins the Ganga (Padma) at Godagari in Bangladesh as its easternmost left-bank Himalayan tributary.

The Ganga first bends southward around the northeastern edge of the Rajmahal Hills (Jharkhand) and only bifurcates downstream of the Farakka Barrage near Giria/Dhulian in Murshidabad district of West Bengal into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly (flowing south through West Bengal) and the Padma (flowing southeast into Bangladesh).

Moving from north to south (upstream to downstream) along the right bank of the Bhagirathi-Hooghly, the Chotanagpur Plateau tributaries join in the order of Mayurakshi (near Kalna/Katwa upstream), Ajay (at Katwa), Damodar (at Falta), Rupnarayan (at Geonkhali), and Haldi (at Haldia). The statement reverses the relative positions of Mayurakshi, Ajay, and Damodar.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Majid Husain: Geography of India, Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following tributaries of the River Ganga:
items: 1. Gandak
2. Ghaghara
3. Gomti
4. Punpun
5. Son
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct upstream-to-downstream (west-to-east) sequence in which these rivers confluence with the mainstem of the Ganga?
core: Between eastern Uttar Pradesh and central Bihar, left-bank Himalayan rivers and right-bank Peninsular rivers interleave closely as they join the Ganga mainstem. Specifically, around the Patna metropolitan stretch, the Ghaghara joins upstream near Chhapra, followed by the Son just west of Patna, the Gandak directly opposite Patna at Hajipur, and the Punpun east of Patna at Fatuha.

exp.why: The Gandak (a left-bank Himalayan tributary entering Bihar near Valmikinagar) joins the Ganga mainstem at Sonpur/Hajipur directly opposite Patna (~85°11'E), making it fourth in the sequence.
The Ghaghara (a left-bank trans-Himalayan tributary) joins the Ganga near Revelganj/Chhapra in Bihar (~84°36'E), downstream of the Gomti but upstream of the Son, making it second in the sequence.

The Gomti (a left-bank alluvial-plain tributary originating in Gomat Taal, Pilibhit) joins the Ganga near Saidpur/Kaithi in Ghazipur district of Uttar Pradesh (~79°10'E), making it the furthest upstream (first) among the given rivers.

The Punpun (a right-bank plateau tributary originating in Palamu district of Jharkhand) joins the Ganga at Fatuha, about 25 km east/downstream of Patna (~85°18'E), making it fifth (furthest downstream) in the sequence.

The Son (a major right-bank Peninsular tributary originating at Amarkantak) joins the Ganga near Maner/Danapur just west of Patna (~84°52'E), placing its confluence between the Ghaghara (upstream) and the Gandak (downstream), making it third in the sequence.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Oxford School Atlas: Ganga Basin Map

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Brahmaputra river system:
items: Statement-I: In its Tibetan course, the Yarlung Tsangpo carries a comparatively small volume of water and minimal silt despite flowing for over 1,100 km parallel to the main Himalayan range.
Statement-II: Near Namcha Barwa, the river takes a sharp syntaxial bend and carves a deep, steep-gradient gorge across the Eastern Himalayas before emerging into India as the Siang.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The hydrological contrast between the Tibetan course (Yarlung Tsangpo) and the Indian course (Siang/Brahmaputra) is driven by climatic and topographic transitions across the Himalayan barrier. While the Tibetan course is cold, arid, and placid due to the rain-shadow effect of the Himalayas, the Indian course becomes turbulent and heavily silt-laden due to intense orographic monsoon rainfall and steep gorge gradients.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct: As the Yarlung Tsangpo flows eastward along the Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone in southern Tibet at an altitude of 3,500–4,000 m, it traverses a cold and dry rain-shadow region leeward of the Great Himalayas. Because precipitation and surface runoff are very low and the longitudinal channel gradient in the middle Tibetan valley is relatively gentle, the river carries a small volume of water and very little silt.

Statement-II is also correct: Around the eastern syntaxial bend at Namcha Barwa (7,755 m), the river makes a hairpin U-turn and cuts a deep, tumultuous gorge across the Eastern Himalayas to enter Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang (Dihang). However, Statement-II describes what happens at the downstream exit of Tibet and does not explain why the river has low water volume and silt in its upstream Tibetan course (which is explained by Tibet's cold, arid rain-shadow climate).

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System, p. 26)

stem: With reference to the headwaters and formation of the Brahmaputra river in Northeast India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. After emerging from the foothills of the Eastern Himalayas near Pasighat, the Siang flows into the Assam valley and becomes known as the Brahmaputra after its confluence with the Dibang and the Lohit near Sadiya.
2. While the Dibang originates near the Keya Pass in the Mishmi Hills of Arunachal Pradesh, the Lohit is a trans-boundary river that originates in eastern Tibet before entering India.
3. Both the Dibang and the Lohit join the Siang-Brahmaputra mainstem as major right-bank tributaries before the river enters the braided plains of Upper Assam.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Brahmaputra assumes its name in the Upper Assam plains near Sadiya/Kobo where three major headstreams—the Siang (Dihang), the Dibang, and the Lohit—converge. Because the Siang turns southwestward to flow down the Assam Valley toward the Bay of Bengal, rivers joining it from the eastern and southern hills (including both the Dibang and the Lohit) enter on its left bank.

exp.why: The Siang (Dihang) emerges from the Abor Hills of the Eastern Himalayas into the plains at Pasighat in Arunachal Pradesh. Flowing southwestward to the Kobo/Sadiya tri-junction in Upper Assam, it merges with the Dibang and the Lohit, beyond which the combined braided channel is officially known as the Brahmaputra.

The Dibang originates near the Keya Pass on the Indo-Tibetan border in the Mishmi Hills (Dibang Valley district of Arunachal Pradesh). The Lohit (known as Zayul Chu in its upper course) rises in the Kangri Garpo range of eastern Tibet (Zayul region) and enters India at Kibithu in Anjaw district, carving through the Mishmi Hills.

Looking downstream along the southwestward-flowing Siang-Brahmaputra mainstem, the Himalayan foothills to the north/northwest constitute the right bank, whereas the Mishmi and Patkai ranges to the east/southeast constitute the left bank. Both the Dibang and the Lohit join the Siang from the east/southeast as left-bank tributaries.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Khullar: India A Comprehensive Geography

stem: With reference to the northern (right-bank) tributaries of the Brahmaputra river, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Subansiri is the largest tributary of the Brahmaputra and is an antecedent trans-Himalayan river that originates in the Tibetan Plateau.
2. The Kameng, known as the Jia Bhoreli in Assam, originates in the Kingdom of Bhutan and forms the natural interstate boundary between Assam and West Bengal.
3. Unlike the Subansiri, the Manas river is entirely a southern-slope cis-Himalayan stream whose catchment is confined within Bhutan and Assam without crossing the Great Himalayan axis.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The northern (right-bank) tributaries of the Brahmaputra descend steeply from the Himalayas, carrying heavy silt loads and flash-flood discharges. Among them, both the Subansiri and the Manas (via its Lhobrak/Kuri Chhu headstream) are antecedent trans-Himalayan rivers rising in Tibet, whereas the Sankosh (not the Kameng) forms the interstate boundary between Assam and West Bengal.

exp.why: The Subansiri is the largest tributary of the Brahmaputra (contributing roughly 10% of its total discharge). It is an antecedent trans-Himalayan river whose headstreams (Loro Chu, Nye Chu, and Char Chu) rise in the Tibetan Plateau north of the Great Himalayan crest before cutting a deep gorge through the Miri Hills of Arunachal Pradesh to join the Brahmaputra at Jamugurihat/Lakhimpur.

The Kameng (Jia Bhoreli in Assam) originates from a glacial lake below Mount Gori Chen on the border of Tawang and West Kameng districts in Arunachal Pradesh (not Bhutan) and joins the Brahmaputra near Tezpur. It is the Sankosh river (rising in northern Bhutan) that forms the natural interstate boundary between Assam (Dhubri/Kokrajhar) and West Bengal (Alipurduar/Cooch Behar).

The Manas river system is also a trans-Himalayan antecedent system: its major eastern headstream, the Lhobrak (Kuri Chhu), originates in southern Tibet north of the Great Himalayan range, cuts across the main Himalayan axis into Bhutan, merges with the Mangde Chhu and Drangme Chhu, and enters India through the Manas National Park before joining the Brahmaputra near Jogighopa.

ref: NCERT Class XI: India Physical Environment, Ch. 3; Central Water Commission (CWC): Brahmaputra Basin Report

stem: Consider the following pairs of rivers in the Brahmaputra basin and their associated geographical features:
items: 1. Burhi Dihing : Originates in the Patkai Hills of Arunachal Pradesh and joins the Brahmaputra on its left bank
2. Dhansiri (South) : Originates from the Laisang Peak in Nagaland and flows along the eastern boundary of Kaziranga National Park
3. Kopili : Originates in the Dafla Hills of the Eastern Himalayas and joins the Brahmaputra on its right bank near Tezpur
4. Dikhow : Bifurcates from the Brahmaputra mainstem near Jakhalabandha as a southern anabranch and rejoins the main river near Guwahati
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Unlike the glacier-fed northern Himalayan tributaries, the southern (left-bank) tributaries of the Brahmaputra—such as the Burhi Dihing, Dikhow, Dhansiri, and Kopili—are rain-fed rivers originating in the Patkai, Naga, Barail, and Meghalaya ranges with meandering courses across the southern Assam valley.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched: The Burhi Dihing originates in the Patkai Hills (Changlang/Tirap districts of eastern Arunachal Pradesh), flows westward through the coal and oil belt of Margherita, Digboi, and Naharkatiya, and joins the Brahmaputra on its left bank at Dihingmukh south of Dibrugarh.

Pair 2 is correctly matched: The (South) Dhansiri originates from the Laisang Peak in southwest Nagaland, flows northward separating the Naga Hills from the Karbi Anglong plateau through Dimapur and Golaghat, and forms the eastern boundary of Kaziranga National Park before joining the left bank of the Brahmaputra at Dhansirimukh.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched: The Kopili is the largest left-bank (south-bank) tributary of the Brahmaputra in Assam. It originates in the Saipung/Borail range on the Meghalaya Plateau (Jaintia Hills)—not the Dafla Hills of the Eastern Himalayas—and joins the Kolong/Brahmaputra on the south bank near Hatiamukh.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched: It is the Kolong river that bifurcates as a southern anabranch/distributary from the Brahmaputra near Jakhalabandha in Nagaon district and rejoins the Brahmaputra near Kajalimukh (west of Guwahati). The Dikhow is a left-bank tributary that originates in the Naga Hills (Zunheboto district of Nagaland) and flows past Sivasagar to join the Brahmaputra at Dikhowmukh.

ref: Majid Husain: Geography of India, Ch. 3 (The Brahmaputra System); Assam State Gazetteer

stem: Which one of the following statements accurately describes the hydro-geomorphology and historical drainage evolution of the Teesta River system?

opts.A: Originating from the Pahunri and Zemu glacial systems in North Sikkim, it receives the Rangeet as its major right-bank tributary along the Sikkim–West Bengal border and underwent a catastrophic late-18th-century avulsion that shifted its outflow from the Ganga system to become a right-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh.
opts.B: It is an antecedent trans-Himalayan river rising on the Tibetan Plateau north of the Great Himalayan divide, cutting through the Nathu La pass before joining the Padma River directly as a left-bank tributary in Bangladesh.
opts.C: Along with the Jaldhaka and Torsa rivers, its catchment spans Bhutan, India, and Bangladesh, where its piedmont alluvial fans form the western geographical boundary of the fluvio-lacustrine Karewa formations.
opts.D: Following the 1787 flood-induced avulsion, it abandoned its prehistoric eastward course into the Brahmaputra and permanently captured the lower channel of the Mahananda to drain directly into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly distributary.

core: The Teesta originates within Sikkim from the Tso Lhamo/Pahunri and Zemu glacial systems, receives the Rangeet on its right bank at Melli, and famously shifted in the 1787 flood from draining southward into the Ganga (via the Atrai-Karatoya-Punarbhaba channels) to draining southeastward as a right-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) in Bangladesh.

exp.why: Option A is correct: The Teesta rises in North Sikkim at Tso Lhamo (Chho Lhamo) lake fed by the Pahunri and Zemu (via Lachen and Lachung headstreams) glaciers. Cutting deep gorges across the Sikkim Himalayas, it receives its largest right-bank tributary, the Rangeet (originating from the Rathong glacier in West Sikkim), at Melli/Teesta Bazaar along the Sikkim–West Bengal border. Prior to the catastrophic flood of 1787, the Teesta bifurcated across northern Bengal into the Punarbhaba, Atrai, and Karatoya rivers to drain southward into the Ganga (Padma) system; in 1787, massive sediment choking and tectonic tilting triggered a major channel avulsion that diverted the Teesta southeastward through an abandoned channel into the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) near Fulchhari in Bangladesh. Option B is incorrect because the Teesta originates entirely within India (Sikkim) south of the international border with Tibet and joins the Jamuna (Brahmaputra), not the Padma. Option C is incorrect because the Teesta basin lies entirely within India and Bangladesh (not Bhutan) and marks the western boundary of the Eastern Himalayan Duars (not Kashmir Karewas). Option D is incorrect because the 1787 avulsion shifted the river from the Ganga system to the Brahmaputra system, not the reverse.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Khullar, India: A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 4

stem: With reference to the Barak–Meghna river system in Northeast India and Bangladesh, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Barak River originates in the Manipur Hills south of the Japvo peak and flows southwestward through Manipur before executing a sharp hairpin bend at Tipaimukh upon its confluence with the Tuivai River.
2. After traversing the Cachar plains of Assam, the Barak cuts northward across the Meghalaya Plateau to join the Brahmaputra as a left-bank tributary near Dhubri before entering Bangladesh.

3. Near the India–Bangladesh border in the Karimganj district of Assam, the Barak bifurcates into two major channels—the Surma and the Kushiyara—which later rejoin inside Bangladesh to form the Meghna River system.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Barak River rises near Liyai Kullen in the Manipur Hills, executes a hairpin bend at Tipaimukh (confluence with the Tuivai), flows westward through the Cachar plains of Assam south of the Meghalaya Plateau water divide, and splits at Haritikar/Karimganj on the India–Bangladesh border into the Surma and Kushiyara rivers.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The Barak rises near Liyai Kullen village in the Senapati district of Manipur (on the southern slopes of Mount Japvo near the Nagaland-Manipur border). It initially flows southwestward through the structural ridges of Manipur until it reaches Tipaimukh on the Manipur-Mizoram-Assam tri-junction, where it receives the northward-flowing Tuivai River and makes an abrupt nearly 180-degree hairpin bend northward into the Cachar plains.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Meghalaya (Shillong) Plateau and the North Cachar Hills (Barail Range) form the prominent upland water divide separating the Brahmaputra basin to the north from the Barak (Meghna) basin to the south. The Barak never cuts across the Meghalaya Plateau to join the Brahmaputra in Assam; instead, it flows westward through the Cachar valley of southern Assam directly into Bangladesh, where the combined Surma-Kushiyara (Meghna) eventually meets the Padma (the joint Ganga-Brahmaputra stream) near Chandpur.

Statement 3 is correct: Near Bhanga/Haritikar in the Karimganj district of Assam along the India–Bangladesh border, the Barak bifurcates into two main distributaries: the northern branch is the Surma (which flows past Sylhet) and the southern branch is the Kushiyara. These two channels subsequently reunite in the Sylhet tectonic depression (Haor basin) of Bangladesh as the Kalni/Meghna before joining the Padma.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 3; Central Water Commission (CWC) Barak and Others Basin Report

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the fluvial geomorphology of the Brahmaputra River:
items: Statement-I: In its traverse through the Assam Valley between Sadiya and Dhubri, the Brahmaputra develops one of the world's most intensely braided multi-thread channel patterns characterized by shifting mid-channel sandbars (chars) and riverine islands.

Statement-II: Majuli Island in the upper Assam Valley is hydrologically enclosed between the main channel of the Brahmaputra to its south and the Kherkutia Xuti anabranch combined with the lower Subansiri River to its north.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The extreme braiding of the Brahmaputra in Assam is driven by an abrupt drop in longitudinal channel gradient combined with massive coarse sediment supply from seismically active, friable Eastern Himalayan catchments and flashy monsoonal discharge, whereas Statement-II merely describes the specific hydrographic boundary channels of Majuli Island.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct: As the Dihang (Siang) debouches from the Eastern Himalayas near Sadiya and joins the Dibang and Lohit to form the Brahmaputra, its longitudinal slope drops abruptly across the gentle 720-km-long Assam Valley. Coupled with enormous monsoonal peak flows and massive coarse bedload eroded from the friable, seismically active Eastern Himalayan syntaxial zone, the river loses sediment-carrying capacity, depositing vast mid-channel sandbars (chars) and splitting into an intensely braided network.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I: Majuli, the largest permanent riverine island in the Assam Valley, was formed through historical channel avulsions (notably in the mid-18th century when the Brahmaputra shifted southward to capture the lower Burhi Dihing course). Today, Majuli is bounded on the south by the main stem of the Brahmaputra and on the north by the Kherkutia Xuti (an anabranch spill channel of the Brahmaputra) joined by the lower Subansiri River. However, this local hydrographic configuration of Majuli's bounding channels is a result of avulsion/anabranching and does not causally explain why the entire Brahmaputra exhibits intense braiding from Sadiya to Dhubri.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 2 & 3; Savindra Singh, Physical Geography (Fluvial Geomorphology)

stem: With reference to the drainage-controlled structural and depositional landforms across the three divisions of the Himalayas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Karewas of the Kashmir Valley are thick Pleistocene fluvio-lacustrine and glacio-fluvial deposits flanking the Pir Panjal range, which have been deeply dissected into flat-topped terraces by the Jhelum River and its left-bank tributaries.

2. Longitudinal 'Dun' valleys in the Himachal and Uttarakhand Himalayas evolved when the tectonic uplift of the Shiwalik range temporarily impounded rivers descending from the Lesser Himalayas, leaving behind wide gravel-filled structural troughs drained axially by tributaries such as the Asan and the Suswa.

3. The 'Duars' of the Eastern Himalayas between the Teesta and Sankosh rivers are structurally enclosed synclinal valleys trapped behind a continuous, high-relief Shiwalik barrier that prevents Himalayan rivers from debouching directly onto the northern Bengal plains.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Western and Central Himalayas feature lacustrine Karewas (Indus/Jhelum basin) and Shiwalik-bounded structural Duns (upper Ganga-Yamuna and Indus basins), the Eastern Himalayas between the Teesta and Sankosh lack a distinct Shiwalik ridge due to intense monsoonal erosion and tectonic overthrusting, replacing Duns with coalescing piedmont alluvial fans called Duars.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: Karewas are thick (~1,300–1,800 m) unconsolidated Plio-Pleistocene lacustrine (lake-bed), fluvio-glacial, and aeolian loessic deposits laid down in the paleo-lake 'Satisar' when the rising Pir Panjal range impounded the Kashmir basin. Subsequent drainage of the lake through the Baramulla gorge and incision by the Jhelum and its Pir Panjal left-bank tributaries (such as the Vishav, Rambiara, Romshi, and Doodhganga) dissected these deposits into elevated tablelands ideal for saffron (Zafran) cultivation.

Statement 2 is correct: Longitudinal Duns (such as Dehra Dun, Kotli Dun, and Patli Dun) occupy tectonic synclinal depressions between the Lesser Himalayas (to the north) and the Outer Himalayas/Shiwaliks (to the south). As the Shiwaliks uplifted during the late Cenozoic, Himalayan rivers were temporarily dammed into lakes that filled with coarse boulders, gravels, and conglomerates. Once the trunk rivers (Ganga and Yamuna) cut antecedent gorges through the Shiwaliks, the lakes drained, leaving longitudinal flat-bottomed valleys drained axially by streams like the Asan (flowing west into the Yamuna) and the Suswa/Song (flowing east into the Ganga).

Statement 3 is incorrect: In the Eastern Himalayas (Sikkim, Darjeeling hills, and Bhutan foothills from the Teesta to the Sankosh/Dhansiri), the Shiwalik range is largely absent or obliterated over an ~80–90 km stretch because the Main Boundary Thrust (MBT) overrides the Main Frontal Thrust (MFT) and intense orographic monsoonal rainfall feeds torrential rivers (Teesta, Jaldhaka, Torsa, Raidak, Sankosh) that rapidly erode the soft outer foothills. Consequently, instead of enclosed synclinal Dun valleys trapped behind a Shiwalik ridge, these rivers debouch directly from the Lesser Himalayas onto the plains to form vast, coalescing piedmont alluvial fans known as the 'Duars'.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 2 (Structure and Physiography); Majid Husain, Geography of India Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the trans-boundary political geography of the Himalayan river basins, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both the Ghaghara (Karnali) and the Kosi (via its Arun headstream) are trans-Himalayan antecedent systems whose river basins span three countries—originating on the Tibetan Plateau in China, traversing Nepal, and joining the Ganga in India.
2. The Teesta River is a tri-national river basin whose upper glacial headstreams rise in the Tibetan Autonomous Region of China and pass through western Bhutan before entering India and Bangladesh.

3. Unlike the Indus and the Sutlej—which originate in the Kailash–Manasarovar region of Tibet (China) before traversing India and Pakistan—the Jhelum, Chenab, and Ravi originate entirely within Indian territory and have mainstem courses shared only between India and Pakistan.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Only antecedent trans-Himalayan rivers rising north of the Great Himalayan divide on the Tibetan Plateau—such as the Indus, Sutlej, Ghaghara (Karnali), Gandak (Trishuli), Kosi (Arun), and Brahmaputra—span three or more nations, whereas rivers rising on the southern slopes of the Great or Lesser Himalayas within India (such as the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Teesta) have mainstems confined to at most two countries.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The Ghaghara originates near the Mapchachungo glacier south of Lake Manasarovar in Tibet (China), cuts through western Nepal as the Karnali, and enters Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in India as the Ghaghara (Saryu). Similarly, the Kosi's primary trunk stream, the Arun (Phung Chu)—along with the Sun Kosi (Poiqu) and Tamakoshi—rises on the Tibetan Plateau in China north of the Great Himalayan crest (Mount Everest–Makalu–Kanchenjunga massifs), cuts deep antecedent gorges across eastern Nepal to form the Saptakoshi, and enters Bihar in India to join the Ganga. Both basins thus span China, Nepal, and India.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Teesta River is exclusively a bi-national (two-country) river basin shared between India and Bangladesh. It originates entirely within the state of Sikkim in India (at Tso Lhamo/Pahunri and Zemu glaciers south of the Indo-Tibetan international watershed divide), flows through Sikkim and West Bengal in India, and enters Bangladesh to join the Jamuna (Brahmaputra), without touching either China or Bhutan.

Statement 3 is correct: Within the Indus system, only the Indus mainstem (rising near Bokhar Chu in the Kailash range) and the Sutlej (rising at Rakshastal near Manasarovar) originate in Tibet (China) and traverse three countries (China, India, and Pakistan). By contrast, the Jhelum (rising at Verinag in Jammu & Kashmir), the Chenab (formed by the Chandra and Bhaga near Bara Lacha La in Himachal Pradesh), and the Ravi (rising near Rohtang Pass in the Kullu hills of Himachal Pradesh) originate entirely within India and flow into Pakistan, sharing their mainstem courses strictly between two countries.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 3; Ministry of Jal Shakti / Indo-Nepal & Indus Waters Treaty Basin Profiles

stem: With reference to the comparative hydrological regimes and seasonal discharge dynamics of the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra river systems, which one of the following statements is scientifically correct?

opts.A: The Brahmaputra basin derives the highest percentage of its annual runoff from glacial and snowmelt among the three systems because the Yarlung Tsangpo flows for over a thousand kilometres across the high-altitude Tibetan Plateau.
opts.B: Unlike the Ganga and Brahmaputra, the Indus River system experiences its highest monthly discharge in January and February coinciding with the peak arrival of extra-tropical Western Disturbances over the Northwestern Himalayas.
opts.C: The Indus system relies on the highest proportional contribution of snow and glacial meltwater fed by winter Western Disturbances, whereas the Brahmaputra exhibits a prolonged high-flow regime triggered sequentially by spring snowmelt, heavy pre-monsoon convective-orographic rainfall in the Assam valley, and the Southwest Monsoon.
opts.D: Among the three Himalayan drainage basins, the Ganga River in its middle plains exhibits the lowest seasonal variability between dry lean-season and peak-monsoon discharge due to uniform summer rainfall received from both Peninsular and Himalayan tributaries.

core: Hydrologically, the Indus has the highest snow and glacial melt share (~40–50% of annual runoff) because the Karakoram and Western Himalayas accumulate massive winter snowpacks from Western Disturbances against an arid downstream plain, whereas the Brahmaputra experiences an early and prolonged high-flow regime driven by spring snowmelt followed by heavy April–May pre-monsoon Nor'westers (Bordoisila) and intense Southwest Monsoon rainfall.

exp.why: Option C is correct: Among the three Himalayan river systems, the Indus basin has the highest proportional contribution of snow and glacial meltwater (accounting for roughly 40–50% of its total annual flow), because the Karakoram, Hindu Kush, and Western Himalayas contain the largest extra-polar glacier volume and receive heavy winter/spring snowfall from mid-latitude Western Disturbances, while its lower plains are semi-arid to arid. Conversely, the Brahmaputra exhibits a remarkably prolonged high-flow season starting as early as April–May: spring snowmelt in the Eastern Himalayas seamlessly overlaps with intense pre-monsoon convective-orographic thunderstorms (Bordoisila / Nor'westers) in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, and Meghalaya before reaching its massive Southwest Monsoon peak (June–September). Option A is incorrect because the Tibetan reach of the Yarlung Tsangpo lies in the cold, dry rain-shadow north of the Himalayas and contributes a relatively small fraction of total runoff compared to the immense monsoonal rainfall captured inside India; hence rainfall dominates the Brahmaputra's total water yield (~70–75%+). Option B is incorrect because during January–February, sub-zero temperatures lock precipitation as snow and ice in the upper Indus basin, making winter the lean-flow period; peak Indus discharge occurs in July–August when summer thermal melting coincides with monsoonal incursions. Option D is incorrect because the Ganga in its middle plains (and its Peninsular tributaries) suffers severe dry-season lean flows during April–May prior to the June monsoon onset, resulting in a very sharp lean-to-peak discharge ratio.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 3 (River Regimes); ICIMOD Himalayan Cryosphere and Hydrology Assessment

stem: With reference to the geological evolution of the Peninsular drainage system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The subsidence of the western flank of the Peninsular block during the early Tertiary period led to its submergence below the sea and disturbed the symmetrical plan of the original river systems on either side of the Western Ghats.

2. The upheaval of the Himalayas was accompanied by trough faulting in the northern flank of the Peninsular block, creating rift valleys through which the Narmada and the Tapi flow and fill the original crustal cracks with their detritus materials.
3. A slight tilting of the Peninsular block from the south-east towards the north-west during the Tertiary period oriented the major drainage system of the plateau towards the Bay of Bengal.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Three major geological events in the distant past shaped the present drainage systems of Peninsular India: early Tertiary subsidence of the western flank, Himalayan-era trough faulting creating the Narmada-Tapi grabens, and a slight tectonic tilt of the Peninsular block from north-west to south-east.

exp.why: During the early Tertiary period, the western flank of the Peninsula subsided, leading to its submergence below the Arabian Sea. This disturbed the symmetrical plan of the river on either side of the original watershed (the Western Ghats), leaving short, swift streams on the western coastal slope.

The upheaval of the Himalayas subjected the northern flank of the rigid Peninsular block to subsidence and consequent trough faulting. The Narmada and the Tapi flow in these fault troughs (grabens) and have filled the original cracks with their own detritus materials, explaining the lack of extensive alluvial and deltaic deposits along their courses.

The slight tilting of the Peninsular block during the same geological period occurred from the north-west to the south-east direction (not from south-east to north-west). This NW-to-SE tilt gave a general south-easterly orientation to the entire major drainage system (such as the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri) towards the Bay of Bengal.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the coastal geomorphology of Peninsular rivers:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the east-flowing rivers of the Peninsular plateau, the major west-flowing rivers such as the Narmada and the Tapi build extensive arcuate deltas rather than estuaries at their mouths.

Statement-II: The west-flowing Peninsular rivers traverse hard Precambrian and Deccan Trap rock beds along steep gradients or structural fault troughs with a relatively limited silt load, and enter a coast characterized by a steep offshore slope and strong tidal scouring.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: West-flowing Peninsular rivers form estuaries rather than deltas because their courses over hard basaltic/crystalline rock beds yield low sediment loads, and the submerged western coast experiences high tidal energy and steep coastal gradients that sweep away riverine alluvium.

exp.why: West-flowing rivers of the Peninsular plateau, including the Narmada and the Tapi as well as the short Western Ghats coastal streams, do not form deltas at their mouths; instead, they form estuaries. It is the east-flowing rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) that form extensive deltas along the Bay of Bengal coast.

West-flowing Peninsular rivers neither carry vast quantities of fine silt—because they flow rapidly through hard Deccan Trap basalt and crystalline rocks or structural rift valleys—nor encounter a shallow, low-energy depositional shelf at their mouths. Strong tidal currents in the Gulf of Khambhat and along the submerged western coast disperse sediments into the deep sea, favoring estuary formation.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; G.C. Leong Ch. 7 & 10

stem: With reference to the Godavari river system and its tributary network, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Indravati and the Sabari originate in the Eastern Ghats region and join the Godavari as major left-bank tributaries.
2. The Manjra and the Pravara flow from the north to join the Godavari as its principal left-bank tributaries.
3. Unlike its left-bank tributaries which are short and seasonal, the right-bank tributaries of the Godavari are far more numerous and collectively drain more than two-thirds of the entire basin.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: The Godavari basin exhibits strong hydrographic asymmetry: its left-bank tributaries (Purna, Penganga, Wardha, Wainganga/Pranhita, Indravati, and Sabari) are much larger and more numerous than its right-bank tributaries (Pravara, Mula, Manjra, and Maner).

exp.why: Both the Indravati (originating in Kalahandi district of Odisha in the Dandakaranya/Eastern Ghats) and the Sabari (originating in the Sinkaram hills of the Eastern Ghats in Koraput district, Odisha) flow south-westward to join the Godavari on its left bank.

The Manjra (rising in the Balaghat range) and the Pravara (rising in the Western Ghats in Ahmadnagar district) are major right-bank tributaries that join the Godavari from the south, whereas the Purna, Penganga, Wardha, Wainganga (Pranhita), Indravati, and Sabari are left-bank tributaries.

In the Godavari river basin, it is the left-bank tributaries (especially the Pranhita, Indravati, and Sabari systems draining higher-rainfall regions of central and eastern India) that are far more numerous and voluminous, whereas the right-bank tributaries drain the drier Deccan plateau and are fewer in number, with the Manjra being the only major long right-bank tributary.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; India-WRIS Godavari Basin Report

stem: With reference to the Pranhita and Indravati sub-basins of the Godavari river system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Indravati River originates in the Dandakaranya range of the Eastern Ghats in Odisha and flows westward across Chhattisgarh before joining the Godavari at the tri-junction border of Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, and Telangana.
2. The Penganga River flows independently across the Vidarbha plateau to join the Godavari mainstream directly upstream of Nanded, without merging into the Wardha-Wainganga river system.
3. The Pranhita River is formed by the confluence of the Purna and the Maner rivers and joins the Godavari on its right bank.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Pranhita is the largest tributary of the Godavari by discharge and drainage area; it is formed by the combined waters of the Penganga, the Wardha, and the Wainganga rivers joining the Godavari on its left bank at Kaleshwaram.

exp.why: The Indravati rises in the Kalahandi district of Odisha in the Dandakaranya range of the Eastern Ghats, flows westward through Bastar district in Chhattisgarh (forming the Chitrakote Falls), and turns south along the Maharashtra-Chhattisgarh border to join the Godavari near Somnoor Sangam/Kaleshwaram downstream at the tri-junction of Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, and Telangana.

The Penganga does not join the Godavari mainstream directly. Instead, the Penganga flows eastward to join the Wardha River, and subsequently the Wardha and the Wainganga unite to form the Pranhita River, which then empties into the Godavari.

The Pranhita River is formed by the confluence of the Wardha and the Wainganga rivers (along with the Penganga) and joins the Godavari on its left bank at Kaleshwaram. The Purna is a separate left-bank tributary in Maharashtra, while the Maner is a right-bank tributary in Telangana.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; CWC Godavari Basin Atlas

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the lower course of the Godavari River:
items: Statement-I: In its lower reaches, the Godavari River carves a deep gorge across the Papi Hills (Papikondalu) of the Eastern Ghats before emerging onto the coastal plains near Rajamahendravaram, where it divides into the Gautami and Vasishta distributaries flanking the Coringa mangrove ecosystem.

Statement-II: The gorge across the Papi Hills is a classic example of young Himalayan-type antecedent drainage formed because the Eastern Ghats underwent rapid orogenic folding and uplift during the late Quaternary period after the Deccan Traps were erupted.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: After crossing the Gondwana trough of the Pranahita-Godavari graben, the Godavari cuts a deep gorge through the Precambrian Papi Hills (Eastern Ghats) and bifurcates past Polavaram and Rajamahendravaram into the Gautami and Vasishta branches to build a wave-dominated lobate delta supporting the Coringa mangroves.

exp.why: After receiving the Indravati and Sabari, the Godavari cuts across the Eastern Ghats through a deep, scenic gorge in the Papi Hills (Papikondalu). Below Rajamahendravaram (Dowlaiswaram Barrage), the river splits into two primary distributaries—the Gautami Godavari on the east (which supports the Coringa mangrove sanctuary near Kakinada Bay) and the Vasishta Godavari on the west.

The Eastern Ghats are ancient Precambrian/Proterozoic denuded mountains, not young Quaternary fold mountains uplifted after the Deccan volcanism. The Godavari cuts through the Eastern Ghats via the structurally controlled Pranahita-Godavari rift graben and ancient superimposed/rejuvenated Peninsular drainage mechanisms rather than late-Quaternary Himalayan-style orogeny.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & 3; Savindra Singh Physical Geography

stem: With reference to the Krishna river basin, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Bhima River joins the Krishna from its right bank in Karnataka, whereas the Koyna River joins the Krishna from its left bank at Karad in Maharashtra.
2. The Musi River, which originates in the Ananthagiri Hills and flows through the city of Hyderabad, is a left-bank tributary of the Krishna River.
3. The Ghataprabha, the Malaprabha, and the Tungabhadra all originate in the Western Ghats and join the Krishna River as right-bank tributaries.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In the Krishna river system, the major left-bank tributaries draining the northern Deccan plateau are the Bhima, Dindi, Musi, Paleru, and Munneru, while the major right-bank tributaries rising in the Western Ghats are the Koyna, Panchganga, Dudhganga, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, and Tungabhadra.

exp.why: The bank orientations are reversed. The Bhima River rises in the Bhimashankar hills of the Western Ghats and flows south-eastward to join the Krishna as its longest left-bank tributary near Raichur, whereas the Koyna River flows southward and then turns east at Helwak to join the Krishna from its right bank at Karad (known as Preeti Sangam).

The Musi River originates in the Ananthagiri Hills near Vikarabad in Telangana, flows eastward through Hyderabad, and turns south to join the Krishna River on its left bank at Vadapally in Nalgonda district.

The Ghataprabha, the Malaprabha, and the Tungabhadra (formed by the Tunga and Bhadra rivers rising at Gangamoola in the Western Ghats of Karnataka) all drain eastward across the Karnataka plateau and join the Krishna on its right bank.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; India-WRIS Krishna Basin Atlas

stem: With reference to the major tributaries of the Krishna River system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Tunga and Bhadra rivers both originate near Gangamoola in the Varaha Parvata of the Western Ghats and unite at Koodli in Karnataka to form the Tungabhadra River.
2. The fertile Raichur Doab lies between the main channel of the Krishna River to the north and the Tungabhadra River to the south.
3. Among the Tungabhadra and Bhima rivers, only the Bhima flows through the State of Maharashtra before merging with the Krishna River.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Krishna River basin is asymmetrically fed by two dominant sub-basins: the Bhima from the north-west (left bank, draining Maharashtra and Karnataka) and the Tungabhadra from the south-west (right bank, draining Karnataka and bordering Telangana/Andhra Pradesh), enclosing the historic Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra channels.

exp.why: The Tungabhadra is formed by the confluence of two headstreams, the Tunga and the Bhadra, both of which rise near Gangamoola on the eastern slopes of the Varaha Parvata in the Western Ghats (Chikkamagaluru district, Karnataka). They flow through steep valleys before uniting at Koodli near Shivamogga in Karnataka.

The Raichur Doab is the triangular interfluve located in Karnataka and Telangana, bounded strictly by the Krishna River on the north and the Tungabhadra River on the south up to their confluence at Sangameswaram (near Alampur) in the Kurnool-Jogulamba Gadwal border region.

The Bhima River originates near Bhimashankar in the Western Ghats (Pune district, Maharashtra) and flows south-eastward across Maharashtra and Karnataka before joining the Krishna as a major left-bank tributary near Raichur. In contrast, the Tungabhadra is entirely a southern right-bank tributary whose course lies within Karnataka and along the Karnataka-Telangana-Andhra Pradesh border, never entering Maharashtra.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Majid Husain, Geography of India, Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the hydrological regime of the Peninsular rivers:
items: Statement-I: Unlike other major east-flowing Peninsular rivers such as the Godavari and the Krishna, the Cauvery River maintains a comparatively perennial flow throughout the year with much lower seasonal fluctuation in water discharge.

Statement-II: The upper catchment of the Cauvery basin in the Western Ghats receives rainfall from the South-West Monsoon during summer, whereas its lower catchment in Tamil Nadu receives substantial rainfall from the retreating North-East Monsoon during winter.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While most Peninsular rivers are strictly seasonal because their catchments depend almost exclusively on the South-West Monsoon, the Cauvery exhibits a unique bimodal hydrograph due to the complementary geographical orientation of its upper catchment (Karnataka/Kerala) to the summer monsoon and its lower catchment (Tamil Nadu) to the winter North-East Monsoon.

exp.why: Most Peninsular rivers (such as the Narmada, Tapi, Mahanadi, Godavari, and Krishna) are exclusively rain-fed by the summer South-West Monsoon and experience severe dwindling of discharge during the dry winter and pre-monsoon months. The Cauvery is a notable exception, carrying water throughout the year with comparatively subdued seasonal discharge variability.

Statement-II provides the exact climatological mechanism behind Statement-I. The Cauvery rises in the Brahmagiri hills (Kodagu district, Karnataka), where its upper basin receives heavy rainfall from the Arabian Sea branch of the South-West Monsoon (June to September). When the South-West Monsoon withdraws, the lower catchment in Tamil Nadu receives heavy precipitation from the North-East Monsoon (October to December) picking up moisture over the Bay of Bengal, thereby sustaining river discharge across both monsoon seasons.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System), p. 28

stem: With reference to the Cauvery River system and its channel morphology, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Kabini River originates in the Western Ghats of Karnataka and joins the Cauvery as a major left-bank tributary, whereas the Hemavati joins it from the right bank.
2. The Bhavani, Noyyal, and Amaravati rivers join the Cauvery as right-bank tributaries in its middle and lower reaches.

3. In its course across the Mysore plateau and the Tamil Nadu plains, the Cauvery bifurcates thrice into two streams and reunites downstream, forming the riverine islands of Srirangapattinam, Shivanasamudram, and Srirangam.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Understanding the spatial orientation of the Cauvery basin requires distinguishing its northern left-bank tributaries (Harangi, Hemavati, Shimsha, Arkavathi) draining the Karnataka plateau from its southern right-bank tributaries (Lakshmana Tirtha, Kabini, Suvarnavathi, Bhavani, Noyyal, Amaravati) draining Wayanad, the Nilgiris, and the Anaimalai-Palani hills.

exp.why: The bank orientations and origins are swapped. The Kabini (Kapila) originates in the Wayanad district of Kerala (from the confluence of the Panamaram and Mananthavady rivers) and flows eastward into Karnataka to join the Cauvery as a major right-bank tributary at Tirumakudalu Narasipura. Conversely, the Hemavati originates in the Western Ghats in Chikkamagaluru district of Karnataka and joins the Cauvery as a left-bank tributary near Krishnarajasagara.

After descending from the Karnataka plateau via the Hogenakkal Falls and passing through the Stanley Reservoir (Mettur Dam), the Cauvery receives the Bhavani (draining the Nilgiris/Silent Valley region), the Noyyal (draining the Velliangiri hills), and the Amaravati (draining the Anaimalai-Palani hills) all from its southern (right) bank in Tamil Nadu.

A distinctive geomorphological feature of the Cauvery is its repeated structural bifurcation around resistant crystalline outcrops and alluvial splits, reunite-and-divide braiding that creates three famous riverine islands in succession from west to east: Srirangapattinam and Shivanasamudram in Karnataka, and Srirangam (between the Kollidam/Coleroon and the Cauvery branches) near Tiruchirappalli in Tamil Nadu.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; D.R. Khullar, India: A Comprehensive Geography, Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the Mahanadi River system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Mahanadi originates from the Amarkantak Plateau in Madhya Pradesh and drains a radial basin in its upper reaches before entering Odisha.
2. The Seonath, Hasdeo, and Mand rivers join the Mahanadi as right-bank tributaries, whereas the Ong, Tel, and Jonk rivers join it from the left bank.
3. Before building its delta at the Bay of Bengal, the Mahanadi cuts across the Vindhyan escarpment to form the Satkosia Gorge in Chhattisgarh.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Mahanadi drains the saucer-shaped Chhattisgarh structural basin—producing a classic centripetal drainage pattern in its upper course—before breaching the Eastern Ghats in Odisha through the Satkosia Gorge.

exp.why: The Mahanadi does not originate on the Amarkantak Plateau (which is the source of the Narmada, Son, and Johila). Instead, the Mahanadi rises near Sihawa in the Dhamtari district of Chhattisgarh (northern foothills of the Dandakaranya). Moreover, because the Chhattisgarh plain is a saucer-shaped structural depression rimmed by the Maikal range, Chotanagpur plateau, and Bastar hills, the upper Mahanadi and its tributaries form a centripetal (inward-converging) drainage pattern rather than a radial one.

The tributary bank orientations are reversed. The Seonath (Shivnath), Hasdeo, Mand, and Ib flow from the north and north-west to join the Mahanadi as major left-bank tributaries. Conversely, the Jonk, Ong, and Tel flow from the south and south-west to join the Mahanadi as right-bank tributaries.

The Satkosia Gorge (a 22-km long superimposed gorge and notified Tiger Reserve/Ramsar site) is carved by the Mahanadi where it cuts across the Eastern Ghats in Odisha (spanning Angul, Boudh, Cuttack, and Nayagarh districts), not across the Vindhyan escarpment in Chhattisgarh.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; India-WRIS Basin Report: Mahanadi Basin

stem: This east-flowing Peninsular river rises near the northern foothills of the Dandakaranya region and initially flows northward before turning east to drain a saucer-shaped structural basin bordered by the Maikal Range on the west. After being impounded by one of the longest earthen dams in the world, it breaches the Eastern Ghats through a deep 22-kilometre gorge and finally forms an extensive delta, where its southern distributaries—the Daya and Bhargavi rivers—supply freshwater to the northern sector of Chilika Lake. Which one of the following rivers is described above?
core: The Mahanadi is uniquely characterized by its Sihawa origin in the Dandakaranya foothills, its saucer-shaped Chhattisgarh basin, the Hirakud Dam near Sambalpur, the Satkosia Gorge across the Eastern Ghats, and its deltaic distributaries (Kuakhai, Daya, and Bhargavi) feeding the northern marshes of Chilika Lake.

exp.why: Option A (Mahanadi) matches every physiographic and hydrological clue: (1) it rises near Sihawa in Dhamtari district (Chhattisgarh) on the northern edge of Dandakaranya; (2) it drains the saucer-shaped Chhattisgarh basin bounded by the Maikal Range on the west; (3) it is impounded by the Hirakud Dam (the longest major earthen dam in the world) near Sambalpur; (4) it carves the 22-km Satkosia Gorge across the Eastern Ghats; and (5) at Naraj near Cuttack, it bifurcates into deltaic branches including the Kathajodi and Kuakhai, which further split into the Daya and Bhargavi rivers that discharge freshwater into the northern sector of Chilika Lake. Option B (Brahmani) is formed by the confluence of the Sankh and South Koel rivers at Vedvyas (Rourkela) and is impounded by the Rengali Dam. Option C (Subarnarekha) rises on the Ranchi Plateau in Jharkhand and forms an independent estuary/delta without connecting to Chilika Lake. Option D (Godavari) rises at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra and drains into the Bay of Bengal in Andhra Pradesh.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; CWC Mahanadi Basin Profile

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Narmada River system:
items: 1. It originates on the western flank of the Amarkantak Plateau and flows westward in a structural rift valley bounded by the Vindhyan escarpment in the north and the Satpura block mountain in the south.
2. Because its main channel and short tributaries are guided by rectilinear fault lines and rock joints, the Narmada basin exhibits a characteristic trellis drainage pattern.
3. The Tawa River, which originates in the Vindhyan Range, is the longest right-bank tributary of the Narmada.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Narmada flows through a structurally controlled graben (rift valley) between the Vindhyan scarp and the Satpurahorst, receiving short, fault-guided tributaries at nearly right angles (trellis pattern), with the Tawa joining from the Satpura/Mahadeo hills in the south as its longest left-bank tributary.

exp.why: The Narmada rises on the western flank of the Amarkantak Plateau in Madhya Pradesh (at an elevation of about 1,057 m) and flows westward against the general eastward tilt of the Peninsular plateau because its course is confined within a down-faulted rift valley (graben) flanked by the Vindhyan escarpment to the north and the Satpura block mountain to the south.

Because the Narmada flows through a narrow, elongated structural trough bounded by steep scarps, its tributaries are relatively short and descend steeply from the flanking ranges along fractures and joints to join the trunk stream almost at right angles, creating a textbook trellis (and locally rectangular) drainage pattern.

Since the Narmada flows from east to west, tributaries joining from the south (Satpura side) are left-bank tributaries, while those joining from the north (Vindhyan side) are right-bank tributaries. The Tawa River originates in the Mahadeo Hills of the Satpura Range (Chhindwara/Betul region of Madhya Pradesh) and flows northward to join the Narmada at Bandarbhan in Narmadapuram (Hoshangabad) district, making it the longest left-bank tributary of the Narmada. Major right-bank tributaries from the Vindhyan side include the Hiran, Barna, Kolar, Man, Hatni, and Orsang.

ref: NCERT Class IX Contemporary India-I, Ch. 3; NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the Tapi (Tapti) river system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It originates near Multai on the Betul plateau and flows westward through a structural trough flanked by the Satpura range to its north and the Ajanta and Satmala hills to its south.
2. The Purna, Girna, and Panjhra are among its principal left-bank tributaries draining the northern Deccan plateau.
3. Although its drainage basin is shared across three states, the largest proportion of its catchment area lies within Madhya Pradesh.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Tapi is the second-largest west-flowing Peninsular river, occupying a fault trough south of the Satpura block mountain. Although it originates in Madhya Pradesh (Betul plateau), nearly 79% of its drainage basin lies in Maharashtra (Khandesh and Vidarbha regions), with major left-bank tributaries like the Purna, Girna, Panjhra, and Bori joining it from the Ajanta-Satmala uplands.
