exp.why: The Tapi originates near Multai in the Betul district of Madhya Pradesh at an elevation of about 752 metres. It flows westward through a rift valley bounded on the north by the Satpura range and on the south by the Ajanta and Satmala hills.

Unlike the short, torrential right-bank streams descending steeply from the southern scarp of the Satpuras (such as the Aner and Gomai), the Tapi receives extensive left-bank tributaries from the northern Deccan plateau, notably the Purna, Vaghur, Girna, Bori, and Panjhra.

While the Narmada has the overwhelming majority (nearly 87%) of its basin in Madhya Pradesh, the Tapi basin has a very different spatial distribution: approximately 79% of the Tapi catchment area lies in Maharashtra, about 15% in Madhya Pradesh, and the remaining 6% in Gujarat.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System); CWC Basin Reports

stem: Which one of the following Peninsular rivers originates on the northern slopes of the Vindhya Range, executes a prominent U-shaped northward loop through the Vagad region of southern Rajasthan—thereby intersecting the Tropic of Cancer twice—before flowing southwestward to empty into the Gulf of Khambhat?
core: The Mahi is the only river in India that cuts across the Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N latitude) twice due to the distinct inverted-U geometry of its course across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Gujarat. Its trajectory is controlled by the structural slope of the Malwa-Vindhyan plateau and the southern Aravalli flanks.

exp.why: The Mahi river rises in the Vindhya Range in Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh (near Minda village). Flowing initially northward across the Tropic of Cancer, it enters the Banswara and Dungarpur districts (Vagad region) of southern Rajasthan, where the Aravalli-Mewar uplands deflect its course sharply southwestward, causing it to cross the Tropic of Cancer a second time as it enters Gujarat and drains into the Gulf of Khambhat. By contrast, the Sabarmati rises in the Aravallis of Udaipur district north of the Tropic of Cancer and crosses it only once while flowing south; the Luni remains entirely north of the Tropic of Cancer until its terminal deltaic marshes in the Rann of Kachchh; and the Banas is an east-flowing tributary of the Chambal entirely north of the Tropic of Cancer.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; GC Leong & Majid Husain Geography of India

stem: With reference to the west-flowing drainage systems of northwestern Peninsular India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Sabarmati river originates in the Aravalli hills of Mewar and drains into the Gulf of Khambhat, the Luni forms an endorheic drainage system that dissipates in the Rann of Kachchh without reaching the open sea.
2. The Luni river originates as a hyper-saline stream in the Sambhar Lake basin and progressively turns into a freshwater river downstream of Balotra due to dilution from Aravalli tributaries.
3. The Wakal, Hathmati, and Vatrak are tributaries of the Sabarmati river, whereas the Jawai, Sukri, and Jojari are tributaries of the Luni river.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Luni and Sabarmati both originate in the Aravalli Range but exhibit contrasting hydrological regimes: the Sabarmati reaches the Arabian Sea via the Gulf of Khambhat, whereas the Luni is an ephemeral, inland (endorheic) river of the Thar Desert whose water is fresh in its upper reaches and turns brackish downstream of Balotra due to halite-rich desert soils.

exp.why: The Sabarmati originates in the Aravalli hills of Udaipur district (Mewar region) in Rajasthan and flows southwestward for about 371 km into the Gulf of Khambhat. The Luni rises near Pushkar in two branches (the Saraswati and the Sagarmati) and terminates in the marshy plains of the Rann of Kachchh without an open marine outlet, making it an inland/endorheic drainage system.

This statement reverses the actual hydro-chemical gradient of the Luni. The Luni does not originate in Sambhar Lake; it rises near the Pushkar valley of Ajmer as a freshwater stream (known locally as Sagarmati) and remains sweet/fresh for its first ~100 km down to Balotra (Barmer district). Downstream of Balotra, the river turns progressively brackish and saline because it flows over halite- and gypsum-rich desert soils of the Thar basin.

The Sei, Wakal, Harnav, Hathmati, Meshwo, and Vatrak are important tributaries of the Sabarmati river. The Lilri, Guhiya, Bandi, Sukri, and Jawai are left-bank tributaries of the Luni rising from the western slopes of the Aravallis, while the Jojari is the only major right-bank tributary of the Luni.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System)

stem: Consider the following east-flowing rivers of Peninsular India located between the Hooghly estuary and the Godavari delta:
items: 1. Brahmani
2. Subarnarekha
3. Vansadhara
4. Baitarani
5. Rushikulya
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of the above rivers when arranged from North to South along the eastern coast?
core: Between the Damodar-Hooghly mouth and the Godavari delta lies a distinct series of independent east-flowing Peninsular rivers draining the Chotanagpur Plateau, Odisha Highlands, and Eastern Ghats. Their exact North-to-South order is Subarnarekha, Burhabalanga, Baitarani, Brahmani, Mahanadi, Rushikulya, Bahuda, Vansadhara, and Nagavali.

exp.why: The Brahmani (1) is formed by the confluence of the Sankh and South Koel rivers near Rourkela in Odisha. Its basin lies immediately south of the Baitarani basin and north of the Mahanadi basin, placing it third from the north among the given rivers.

The Subarnarekha (2) originates near Nagri on the Ranchi Plateau in Jharkhand and enters the Bay of Bengal near Talsari in Balasore district of northern Odisha (~21.5°N), making it the northernmost river in the list.

The Vansadhara (3) originates in the Eastern Ghats near the Kalahandi-Rayagada border in southern Odisha and enters the Bay of Bengal at Kalingapatnam in Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh (~18.3°N), making it the southernmost river in the list.

The Baitarani (4) rises in the Gonasika/Guptaganga hills of Keonjhar district in northern Odisha. It flows south of the Subarnarekha and north of the Brahmani before joining the Brahmani distributary system near Dhamra (~20.8°N), placing it second from the north.

The Rushikulya (5) rises in the Daringbadi hills of the Eastern Ghats in Kandhamal district (Odisha) and drains into the Bay of Bengal near Ganjam/Puruna Bandha (~19.3°N), south of the Mahanadi-Brahmani system and north of the Vansadhara, placing it fourth from the north. Thus, the exact North-to-South sequence is 2 - 4 - 1 - 5 - 3.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; Oxford School Atlas

stem: Consider the following pairs of east-flowing Peninsular rivers and their associated physiographic origins or features:
items: 1. Pennar : Originates in the Nandi Hills and carves the Gandikota Gorge across the Erramala Hills
2. Vaigai : Originates in the Shevaroy Hills of the Eastern Ghats and drains into the Bay of Bengal near Pichavaram
3. Vellar : Originates in the Varusanadu Hills of the Western Ghats and empties into the Palk Strait
4. Subarnarekha : Originates on the Ranchi Plateau and forms the Hundru Falls along its course
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Smaller east-flowing Peninsular rivers exhibit strong structural control: the Pennar cuts discordantly across Cuddapah quartzite ridges (Erramala and Nallamala ranges) after rising in the Nandi Hills, while in Tamil Nadu the Vellar rises in the Shevaroy-Kalrayan hills of the Eastern Ghats and drains near the Pichavaram mangroves, whereas the Vaigai rises in the Varusanadu Hills of the Western Ghats and empties into the Palk Strait.

exp.why: The Pennar (Uttara Pinakini) rises in the Chennakesava hills of the Nandi Hills range in Chikkaballapura district of Karnataka (which also gives rise to the Palar and Ponnaiyar rivers). Flowing across Rayalaseema in Andhra Pradesh, it carves the spectacular Gandikota Canyon through the horizontal quartzites of the Erramala Hills before draining into the Bay of Bengal near Nellore.

The Vaigai river does not originate in the Eastern Ghats; it rises in the Varusanadu Hills (an eastern spur of the Periyar Plateau in the Western Ghats) in Theni district of Tamil Nadu, flows past Madurai, and empties into the Palk Strait near the Pamban Bridge in Ramanathapuram district.

The Vellar (Northern Vellar) originates in the Shevaroy and Kalrayan hills of the Eastern Ghats in Tamil Nadu (formed by the confluence of the Vasishta Nadi and Sweta Nadi) and empties into the Bay of Bengal at Parangipettai (Porto Novo) immediately north of the Pichavaram mangrove forest. Pairs 2 and 3 have been interchanged.

The Subarnarekha originates near Nagri village on the Ranchi Plateau in Jharkhand. Along its descent off the scarps of the Ranchi Plateau, it forms the 98-metre-high Hundru Falls before entering West Bengal and Odisha.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; Savindra Singh Physical Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the drainage regime of extreme southern Peninsular India:
items: Statement-I: The Tamiraparani (Thamirabarani) is a perennial river that originates in the Agastyamalai hills and flows entirely within Tamil Nadu before draining into the Gulf of Mannar.

Statement-II: Because the southern Western Ghats act as a continuous orographic barrier against the Arabian Sea branch, the upper catchment of the Tamiraparani is cut off from South-West monsoon precipitation and derives its annual discharge from the retreating North-East monsoon.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike most rivers of the Tamil Nadu plains (such as the Vaigai or Gundar) which are seasonal because they lie strictly in the rain-shadow of the South-West monsoon, the Tamiraparani is perennial because its headwaters in the Agastyamalai (Pothigai) range near the Shencottah gap intercept moisture from both the South-West and North-East monsoons.

exp.why: The Tamiraparani rises on the Agastyarkoodam peak of the Pothigai (Agastyamalai) hills on the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats in Tirunelveli district and flows for about 128 km through Tirunelveli and Thoothukudi districts into the Gulf of Mannar, making it the only major perennial river whose entire course lies within Tamil Nadu.

If the Tamiraparani basin were cut off from the South-West monsoon and received rainfall solely during the retreating North-East monsoon (October–December), it would be an ephemeral or seasonal river like the Vaigai. In reality, the southern extremity of the Western Ghats around the Agastyamalai hills and the adjoining Shencottah (Aryankavu) pass is narrow and notched by low-altitude saddles, allowing moisture-laden winds of the Arabian Sea branch of the South-West monsoon (June–September) to spill over into the upper catchment of the Tamiraparani and its tributaries (such as the Karaiyar, Servalar, and Manimuthar). This dual-monsoon replenishment sustains its perennial flow throughout the year.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 & Ch. 4; India-WRIS Basin Atlas

stem: With reference to the West-flowing rivers of Kerala, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Periyar River originates in the Anamalai hills and flows westward through the Palghat (Palakkad) Gap to empty into the Arabian Sea at Ponnani.
2. The Bharathapuzha is the longest river in Kerala and carries the largest annual volume of water discharge among all rivers in the State.
3. The Pamba River originates in the Wayanad Plateau of northern Kerala and drains directly into the Ashtamudi Kayal.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Among Kerala's 41 West-flowing rivers, the Periyar (244 km) is the longest and has the largest discharge volume, whereas the Bharathapuzha (209 km, second longest) drains the structurally controlled Palghat Gap and empties at Ponnani. In southern Kerala, the Pamba originates in the Peerumedu plateau (Pulachimalai) and drains into the Vembanad Kayal.

exp.why: It is the Bharathapuzha (also called the Ponnani River or Nila), not the Periyar, that originates near the Anamalai hills, flows westward through the tectonic Palghat (Palakkad) Gap, and empties into the Arabian Sea at Ponnani. The Periyar originates much further south in the Sivagiri peaks of the Sundaramala/Cardamom Hills along the Tamil Nadu border and bifurcates at Aluva to drain into the Vembanad-Kodungallur backwater system and the Arabian Sea.

The Periyar (approximately 244 km long) is the longest river in Kerala and carries the largest annual discharge volume in the State, earning it the epithet 'Lifeline of Kerala'. The Bharathapuzha (approximately 209 km long) is the second-longest river in Kerala; because a large part of its catchment lies within the comparatively drier Palghat Gap corridor, its annual runoff is significantly smaller than that of the Periyar.

The Pamba River originates at Pulachimalai in the Peerumedu plateau of the Western Ghats in Idukki district (south-central Kerala), not in the Wayanad Plateau of northern Kerala (which is drained primarily by the east-flowing Kabini). Furthermore, the Pamba drains into the southern arm of the Vembanad Kayal through the Kuttanad deltaic region, whereas the Ashtamudi Kayal receives the Kallada River.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage System); Khullar's India: A Comprehensive Geography, Ch. 4

stem: Consider the following pairs of prominent waterfalls of the Western Ghats and the West-flowing rivers on which they are situated:
items: 1. Dudhsagar Falls : Mandovi (Mahadayi) River
2. Jog (Gersoppa) Falls : Sharavathi River
3. Gokak Falls : Kalinadi (Kali) River
4. Magod Falls : Netravathi River
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Steeply graded West-flowing rivers descending the rejuvenated Western Ghats escarpment carve spectacular plunge waterfalls such as Dudhsagar (on the Mandovi), Jog (on the Sharavathi), and Magod (on the Bedti/Gangavali). In contrast, waterfalls like Gokak are located on East-flowing tributaries of the Krishna system on the Deccan plateau slope.

exp.why: Dudhsagar Falls is a four-tiered waterfall situated on the West-flowing Mandovi (Mahadayi) River in Goa near the Karnataka-Goa border, where the river plunges down the steep Western Ghats escarpment before forming an estuarine network with the Zuari via the Cumbarjua canal.

Jog (Gersoppa or Mahatma Gandhi) Falls is situated on the West-flowing Sharavathi River in Shivamogga/Uttara Kannada districts of Karnataka, where the river plunges nearly 253 metres down the Western Ghats scarp in four cascades (Raja, Rani, Roarer, and Rocket) before draining into the Arabian Sea at Honnavar.

Gokak Falls is situated in Belagavi district on the East-flowing Ghataprabha River, which is a right-bank tributary of the Krishna River draining toward the Bay of Bengal. The West-flowing Kalinadi (Kali) River in Uttara Kannada is associated with Lalguli Falls (and Sathodi Falls on its tributary).

Magod Falls is formed by the West-flowing Bedti (also known as Gangavali) River in Uttara Kannada district of Karnataka, not by the Netravathi River (which flows further south through Dakshina Kannada to join the Arabian Sea near Mangaluru).

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3; GC Leong & Majid Husain Geography of India (Drainage Systems)

stem: With reference to the Peninsular rivers that flow northward to join the Ganga-Yamuna drainage system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Chambal, Betwa, and Ken rivers fail to enter the adjacent Narmada rift valley because the Vindhyan range forms an asymmetrical cuesta with a steep southern escarpment facing the Narmada and a gentle northern dip-slope tilting toward the Yamuna.

2. Although the Son originates on the Amarkantak plateau close to the headwaters of the Narmada, its north-eastward trajectory toward the Ganga is structurally guided by the strike of the Kaimur escarpment.
3. Unlike the antecedent Himalayan rivers, these north-flowing Peninsular tributaries are geologically younger streams that originated after the Pleistocene alluviation of the Indo-Gangetic foredeep.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The northward drainage of the Malwa and Bundelkhand rivers (Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken) is controlled by the asymmetrical tilt of the Vindhyan-Malwa block, whose steep southern scarp blocks entry into the Narmada trough while its gentle northern dip slope leads to the Yamuna. These Peninsular rivers are geologically much older than the Himalayan drainage and the Pleistocene Indo-Gangetic alluvial plains.

exp.why: The Vindhyan range is not a symmetrical fold mountain but an asymmetrical tectonic cuesta/escarpment. Its southern face drops steeply into the Narmada fault trough, acting as a sharp water divide that prevents rivers rising just a few kilometres north of the scarp (such as the Chambal and Betwa on the Malwa plateau) from flowing south into the Narmada, compelling them to follow the regional northward dip-slope toward the Yamuna.

The Son rises on the Amarkantak plateau near the Narmada's source, flows north initially, and then encounters the steep Kaimur range (the eastern continuation of the Vindhyan system). Blocked to the north, the Son follows a structural strike valley along the southern foot of the Kaimur escarpment toward the north-east before directly joining the Ganga near Patna.

The north-flowing Peninsular rivers (Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken, and Son) are geologically much older than the Himalayan rivers and the Pleistocene Indo-Gangetic alluvial plain. They represent ancient Gondwana/Peninsular streams that originally drained northward toward the Tethyan margin and were subsequently integrated as right-bank tributaries of the evolving Yamuna-Ganga foredeep axial drainage.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & 3; K.S. Valdiya, Aspects of Tectonics: Focus on South-Central Asia

stem: With reference to the centrifugal (radial) drainage pattern associated with the Amarkantak Plateau at the junction of the Vindhya, Satpura, and Maikal ranges, which one of the following statements is geologically and hydrologically correct?

opts.A: The Narmada, the Son, and the Johilla originate in close proximity on the Amarkantak dome and diverge in different directions, whereas the main trunk of the Mahanadi originates further south in the Sihawa hills bordering the Chhattisgarh basin.
opts.B: The Narmada and the Tapi originate on opposite flanks of the Amarkantak plateau and flow westward through parallel rift valleys into the Gulf of Khambhat.
opts.C: The Son and the Ken radiate northward from the Amarkantak plateau to join the Yamuna as its principal right-bank tributaries.
opts.D: The Mahanadi and the Godavari share a common radial water divide with the Narmada at the summit of the Amarkantak plateau.

core: The Amarkantak plateau (at the crest of the Maikal Range) is the classic textbook example of a radial drainage dome in Peninsular India, from which the Narmada flows west, the Son flows north/north-east, and the Johilla (a tributary of the Son) flows north-west before curving into the Son. Although northern tributaries of the Mahanadi basin drain the southern Maikal slopes, the main Mahanadi river originates much further south near Sihawa in Dhamtari district of Chhattisgarh.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because the Amarkantak dome exhibits classic radial (centrifugal) drainage where the Narmada (westward into its rift valley), the Son (northward and then north-eastward to the Ganga), and the Johilla (a tributary of the Son) originate within a few kilometres of each other. While several left-bank sub-tributaries of the Mahanadi system (such as the Hasdeo and Arpa) drain the southern slopes of the Maikal-Amarkantak highlands, the main Mahanadi channel originates near Sihawa in Dhamtari district (Chhattisgarh), well south of Amarkantak. Option (B) is incorrect because the Tapi originates at Multai in Betul district (Satpura range), not Amarkantak. Option (C) is incorrect because the Son joins the Ganga directly (not the Yamuna) and the Ken originates in the Kaimur/Bhander hills of Katni district. Option (D) is incorrect because the Godavari originates at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 3 (Drainage Patterns); Savindra Singh, Physical Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the continental water divide and West-flowing rivers of Peninsular India:
items: Statement-I: Along parts of the Karnataka plateau, the continental water divide between the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal drainage systems has migrated east of the highest topographic crest of the Western Ghats due to river piracy by high-gradient West-flowing streams.

Statement-II: The Narmada and the Tapi flow westward to the Arabian Sea without breaching the Western Ghats escarpment because their courses are confined within structurally controlled East-West fault troughs flanking the Satpura block to the north of the Sahyadri range.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In the central Sahyadris (Uttara Kannada and Shivamogga), short West-flowing rivers like the Kali, Bedti, Aghnashini, and Sharavathi have cut back across the main escarpment crest via vigorous headward erosion—driven by steep western gradients and intense orographic monsoon rainfall—capturing the gentler headwaters of East-flowing plateau rivers and shifting the water divide eastward. While Statement-II accurately describes the tectonic rift control of the Narmada and Tapi flanking the Satpura horst further north, that structural mechanism does not explain the geomorphic headward capture along the Karnataka Sahyadris in Statement-I.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The Western Ghats are an asymmetrical faulted escarpment with a very steep western face and a gentle eastern dip-slope (Deccan plateau). Because the short West-flowing streams (such as the Sharavathi, Kali, Bedti/Gangavali, and Aghnashini) descend a steep gradient over a short distance to sea level and receive massive orographic rainfall on the windward slope, they possess immense kinetic energy for headward erosion. Over geological time, they have breached the original topographic crest-line, captured sluggish east-flowing tributaries of the Krishna-Tungabhadra system (producing elbows of capture and recessed gorge waterfalls like Jog), and pushed the functional water divide slightly east of the highest ridge.

Statement-II is also correct, as the Narmada and Tapi lie north of the Western Ghats (Sahyadri) cordillera and owe their westward flow against the general eastward tilt of the Peninsula to tectonic down-faulting along East-West grabens flanking the Satpura horst (the Narmada between the Vindhya and Satpura blocks, and the Tapi south of the Satpura block). However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: the eastward migration of the water divide in Karnataka is explained by differential stream power (steep western scarp gradient plus intense windward rainfall driving headward erosion), not by the Satpura rift tectonics.

ref: Kale, V.S. & Vaidyanadhan, R., Landscapes and Landforms of India (Springer); NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & 3

stem: With reference to the interaction between the Peninsular river systems and the Western and Eastern Ghats, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Pennar have breached and dissected the Eastern Ghats into discontinuous hill blocks, none of the major East-flowing Peninsular rivers cuts completely across the Western Ghats cordillera from west to east.
2. The Pennar River originates in the Nandi Hills of the Karnataka plateau and breaches the Eastern Ghats ranges through the Gandikota gorge before draining into the Bay of Bengal.
3. The Kaveri River cuts across the Nallamala and Velikonda ranges of the Eastern Ghats before bifurcating into the Kollidam and Kaveri branches at the head of its delta.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Because the Peninsular block tilted south-eastward during the Cenozoic Himalayan collision, major East-flowing rivers originate along the eastern flank of the continuous Western Ghats water divide (never cutting completely through the Western Ghats from west to east) and flow across the plateau to breach the older, heavily denuded Eastern Ghats through antecedent/superimposed gorges such as Satkosia (Mahanadi), Bison Gorge (Godavari), Vijayawada gap (Krishna), and Gandikota (Pennar).

exp.why: The Western Ghats form a continuous tectonic escarpment and primary continental water divide; all major East-flowing rivers of the Deccan (Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, Kaveri) originate on its eastern slopes or adjacent plateau uplands and flow eastward down the regional tilt—none of them originates on the western coastal strip to cut across the entire Western Ghats barrier from west to east. Conversely, these mighty rivers have repeatedly breached the ancient Eastern Ghats, eroding them into isolated, discontinuous hill ranges.

The Pennar (Uttara Pinakini) rises in the Nandi Hills (Chikkaballapur district of Karnataka), flows through the Cuddapah basin of Andhra Pradesh where it carves the famous Gandikota gorge across the Erramala hills, and subsequently passes through gaps in the Velikonda/Palkonda ranges of the Eastern Ghats to enter the Bay of Bengal near Nellore.

The Nallamala and Velikonda ranges are parts of the Eastern Ghats located in Andhra Pradesh (within the Krishna and Pennar drainage domains), far to the north of the Kaveri basin. The Kaveri descends from the Karnataka plateau into Tamil Nadu through the Hogenakkal falls region flanked by the southern hill complexes (Biligirirangan, Melagiri, Shevaroy/Servarayan, and Kollimalai-Pachamalai hills) before bifurcating at Srirangam (Grand Anicut/Upper Anicut) into the northern Kollidam (Coleroon) and southern Kaveri branches.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & 3; Oxford School Atlas (Physical Map of South India)

stem: With reference to the geological controls on drainage patterns across Peninsular India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Over the homogeneous crystalline gneisses and horizontal Deccan Trap basalt flows of the Godavari and Krishna plateaus, rivers predominantly develop a dendritic drainage pattern.

2. Along the faulted Vindhyan-Satpura troughs drained by the Narmada and Tapi and the folded metamorphic belt of the Singhbhum region, streams exhibit trellis and rectangular drainage patterns governed by structural joints and faults.

3. In the saucer-shaped Chhattisgarh basin, tributaries of the upper Mahanadi descending from the surrounding Maikal, Bastar, and Raigarh highlands converge inward before the trunk stream exits eastward through a narrow gorge.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Drainage geometry in Peninsular India reflects the underlying lithology and structural tectonics: uniform crystalline or horizontal basaltic surfaces foster tree-like dendritic networks, whereas faulted rift margins and folded belts impose rectilinear or trellis alignments. Localized structural depressions like the Chhattisgarh plain induce inward basin convergence before the master stream breaches the eastern rim.

exp.why: A dendritic (tree-like) pattern develops where the underlying rock offers uniform resistance to erosion and lacks strong structural control. Both the Archaean gneisses/granites of the southern Peninsula and the flat-lying basaltic lava sheets of the Deccan Traps allow tributaries to join the main streams at acute angles without systematic fault-line deflection.

In the Narmada-Tapi rift valleys, short tributaries descending the steep Vindhyan and Satpura scarps join the trunk rivers nearly at right angles along master fractures, creating rectangular and trellis patterns. Similarly, in the folded Dharwarian rocks of the Singhbhum plateau, alternating resistant ridges and softer strike valleys guide streams into a trellis geometry.

The Chhattisgarh plain is a structural depression underlain by Cuddapah-age sedimentary strata rimmed by higher crystalline plateaus. Tributaries such as the Seonath, Hasdeo, Mand, and Pairi flow inward from the surrounding highlands toward the central axis of the upper Mahanadi before the unified river cuts across the Eastern Ghats through the Satkosia Gorge.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Savindra Singh Physical Geography

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the hydrological characteristics of Peninsular river basins in India:
items: Statement-I: In the Peninsular component of the National Perspective Plan for river interlinking, the lower Godavari basin is classified as a chronically water-deficit basin requiring net water transfer from the middle Krishna and Pennar basins.

Statement-II: While large tracts of the middle Krishna and Pennar basins lie in the semi-arid leeward rain-shadow of the Western Ghats, the vast left-bank catchment of the Godavari lies directly along the north-westward track of Bay of Bengal monsoon depressions.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In the Peninsular River Development Plan, the Godavari basin is the principal water-surplus donor basin, whereas the Krishna, Pennar, and Cauvery basins are water-deficit recipient basins. This asymmetry arises because the Godavari's left-bank tributaries (Pranhita, Indravati, Sabari) intercept heavy rainfall from Bay of Bengal monsoon depressions, whereas the middle Krishna and Pennar catchments suffer from the Western Ghats rain-shadow effect.

exp.why: Under the National Perspective Plan prepared by the National Water Development Agency (NWDA), the Godavari basin (particularly its lower sub-basin fed by the Indravati and Sabari at Inchampalli and Polavaram) has a substantial assessable water surplus and acts as the primary donor basin to transfer water southward into the water-deficit Krishna, Pennar, and Cauvery basins.

Although the upper Godavari in Maharashtra lies in the leeward zone of the Sahyadris, more than half of the Godavari's total discharge is contributed by its left-bank tributaries (Wainganga-Pranhita, Indravati, and Sabari) draining eastern Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha, which lie directly along the main corridor of low-pressure monsoon depressions moving inland from the Bay of Bengal.

ref: National Water Development Agency (NWDA) Peninsular Component; India-WRIS Basin Reports

stem: With reference to the coastal and deltaic wetlands associated with Peninsular river systems, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Kolleru Lake is a brackish-water coastal lagoon located south of the Krishna delta and fed directly by the main distributaries of the Pennar river.
2. Pulicat Lake is an inland freshwater oxbow lake formed by the shifting distributary channels of the Cauvery river in the Thanjavur delta.
3. Chilika Lake lies immediately south-west of the Mahanadi delta and receives seasonal freshwater inflow from the Daya and Bhargavi distributaries of the Mahanadi system.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Along the eastern coast of India, rapid progradation of major river deltas has created distinct coastal wetlands: Kolleru is a freshwater inter-deltaic depression trapped between the advancing Godavari and Krishna deltas, whereas Chilika and Pulicat are brackish barrier-spit lagoons located on the margins of the Mahanadi and Swarnamukhi-Arani coastal plains respectively.

exp.why: Kolleru Lake is a large, shallow freshwater lake (not a brackish lagoon south of the Krishna delta) situated in the inter-deltaic depression between the Godavari and Krishna deltas in Andhra Pradesh. It is fed directly by seasonal streams such as the Budameru and Tammileru along with irrigation channels, and drains into the Bay of Bengal via the Upputeru outlet.

Pulicat Lake is India's second-largest brackish-water coastal lagoon, straddling the border of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu along the Coromandel Coast, separated from the Bay of Bengal by the barrier island of Sriharikota. It is fed by the Arani, Kalangi, and Swarnamukhi rivers, and has no hydrographic connection to the Cauvery delta.

Chilika Lake is a pear-shaped brackish-water lagoon on the Odisha coast situated just south-west of the Mahanadi delta. Its northern sector receives massive seasonal freshwater and silt inflows from the Daya and Bhargavi rivers, which branch off from the Kuakhai distributary of the Mahanadi river system.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment; Ramsar Sites of India Compendium (MoEFCC)

stem: Consider the following pairs of Peninsular waterfalls, the rivers on which they are located, and their physiographic settings:
items: 1. Shivanasamudram Falls : Cauvery River descending the rejuvenated edge of the Mysore Plateau
2. Chitrakote Falls : Subarnarekha River descending the eastern scarps of the Ranchi Plateau
3. Hundru Falls : Indravati River cutting across the Vindhyan scarps of the Bastar Plateau
4. Gokak Falls : Narmada River plunging over the Amarkantak basaltic rim in the Maikal Range
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Despite the senile, graded profile of most Peninsular valleys, prominent waterfalls mark rejuvenated fault scarps and lithological knickpoints across the plateau margins—such as Shivanasamudram on the Cauvery, Chitrakote on the Indravati, Hundru on the Subarnarekha, Gokak on the Ghataprabha, and Kapildhara on the Narmada.

exp.why: Shivanasamudram Falls is formed by the Cauvery River as it bifurcates into the Gagana Chukki and Bharachukki branches and plunges across the faulted, rejuvenated crystalline edge of the Mysore Plateau in Karnataka.

Chitrakote Falls (often called the Niagara of India due to its horseshoe breadth) is located on the Indravati River (a major left-bank tributary of the Godavari) in the Bastar Plateau of Chhattisgarh, not on the Subarnarekha River.
Hundru Falls is located on the Subarnarekha River where it descends the rejuvenated scarp edge of the Ranchi Plateau in the Chota Nagpur region of Jharkhand, not on the Indravati River in Bastar.

Gokak Falls is located on the Ghataprabha River (a right-bank tributary of the Krishna) plunging over Kaladgi sandstone cliffs in Belagavi district of Karnataka. The waterfall on the upper Narmada descending the Amarkantak rim in the Maikal Range is Kapildhara Falls.

ref: D.R. Khullar India: A Comprehensive Geography; Geological Survey of India Geotourism Sites

stem: Consider the following west-flowing rivers of Peninsular India:
items: 1. Narmada
2. Tapi
3. Mahi
4. Sharavathi
5. Zuari
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of the mouths of the above rivers into the Arabian Sea from North to South?
core: Rivers draining into the eastern side of the Gulf of Khambhat follow a clear North-to-South latitudinal progression of their estuaries: Mahi near the northern head of the Gulf (~22°13' N), followed southward by the Narmada near Bharuch (~21°38' N) and the Tapi near Surat/Hazira (~21°06' N). Further south along the Konkan and Kanara coasts lie the estuaries of the Mandovi-Zuari in Goa (~15°25' N) and the Sharavathi at Honnavar in Karnataka (~14°18' N).

exp.why: The Narmada River forms a wide estuary entering the Gulf of Khambhat near Bharuch/Aliabet at approximately 21°38' North latitude, lying south of the Mahi mouth and north of the Tapi mouth.
The Tapi River empties into the Gulf of Khambhat near Surat/Hazira at approximately 21°06' North latitude, south of the Narmada estuary.
The Mahi River enters the northern head of the Gulf of Khambhat near Kamboi at approximately 22°13' North latitude, making its mouth the northernmost among the five listed rivers.
The Sharavathi River drains into the Arabian Sea at Honnavar along the Uttara Kannada coast of Karnataka at approximately 14°18' North latitude, making it the southernmost among the listed rivers.
The Zuari River empties into the Arabian Sea at Mormugao Bay in Goa at approximately 15°25' North latitude, lying south of the Gulf of Khambhat estuaries and north of the Sharavathi estuary.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3; Oxford School Atlas

stem: With reference to the comparative basin size and interstate hydrographic spread of Peninsular rivers, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In terms of total drainage basin area within India, the Mahanadi basin is larger than both the Narmada basin and the Cauvery basin.
2. Besides Maharashtra, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh, the hydrographic catchment of the Godavari river system also extends into parts of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Karnataka.
3. Unlike the Godavari and Krishna basins, the drainage basin of the Cauvery river is confined exclusively to the states of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Among Peninsular river basins, the descending order of catchment area is Godavari (~3.13 lakh sq. km) > Krishna (~2.59 lakh sq. km) > Mahanadi (~1.42 lakh sq. km) > Narmada (~0.99 lakh sq. km) > Cauvery (~0.81 lakh sq. km) > Tapi (~0.65 lakh sq. km). Because drainage divides follow topographic ridges rather than political boundaries, both the Godavari and Cauvery basins encompass multiple riparian states through their outer tributaries.

exp.why: According to Central Water Commission (CWC) basin data, the Mahanadi drainage basin covers approximately 1,41,589 sq. km, making it the third-largest Peninsular river basin after the Godavari and Krishna, and significantly larger than both the Narmada basin (98,796 sq. km) and the Cauvery basin (81,155 sq. km).

The Godavari basin (3,12,812 sq. km) spans seven states and one UT: Maharashtra (~48.6%), Telangana and Andhra Pradesh (~23.4%), Chhattisgarh (~10.9% via the Indravati), Madhya Pradesh (~10.0% via the upper Wainganga, Pench, and Wardha), Odisha (~5.7% via the Sabari/Kolab and upper Indravati), Karnataka (~1.4% via the Manjira river in Bidar district), and Puducherry (Yanam).

The Cauvery basin (81,155 sq. km) is not confined solely to Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; it also extends into Kerala (accounting for about 3.5% of the basin through the Kabini, Bhavani, and Pambar sub-basins in Wayanad, Palakkad, and Idukki districts) and the Union Territory of Puducherry (Karaikal region in the lower delta).

ref: Central Water Commission (CWC) Watershed Atlas of India; NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the classical thermal concept and the modern dynamic theory of the Indian Monsoon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Differential land-sea thermal heating between the Asian landmass and the Indian Ocean is sufficient by itself to explain the sudden burst and intra-seasonal breaks of the Southwest Monsoon.

2. According to Flohn's Dynamic Theory, the Southwest Monsoon winds over India are genetically the planetary Southeast Trade Winds of the Southern Hemisphere that have crossed the equator and undergone Coriolis deflection.
3. During the boreal summer, the northward migration of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) establishes the Monsoon Trough over the Indo-Gangetic Plains.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Halley's classical thermal theory treats the monsoon as a giant land-sea breeze driven solely by differential heating, Flohn's dynamic theory explains it as the seasonal migration of planetary wind belts and the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) coupled with upper-tropospheric circulation changes.

exp.why: Edmond Halley's classical thermal concept (1686) cannot explain why the Southwest Monsoon does not commence in May when continental temperatures over northwestern India are at their peak, nor can a static land-sea thermal contrast explain the abrupt 'burst' of the monsoon, its spatial variations, or intra-seasonal dry 'breaks'. These features are governed by dynamic upper-tropospheric jet streams and planetary wave shifts.

Hermann Flohn (1951) demonstrated that as the solar zenith and thermal equator shift northward in summer, the Southeast Trade Winds of the Southern Hemisphere are drawn across the geographic equator into the Northern Hemisphere. Once north of the equator, the Coriolis force deflects them to their right, transforming them into moisture-laden equatorial westerlies (Southwest Monsoon winds).

During June–September, the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) shifts northward to roughly 20°N–25°N over the Indo-Gangetic Plains, where it is known as the Monsoon Trough—a zone of low pressure where deflected southwesterly maritime winds converge with tropical easterlies.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4; Savindra Singh Climatology

stem: With reference to the role of the Tibetan Plateau and the Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) in the Indian Summer Monsoon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. During summer, the Tibetan Plateau acts as an elevated mid-tropospheric heat source through sensible heating over its arid western region and latent heat release over its southeastern sector.
2. Intense summer heating over the Tibetan Plateau generates a persistent upper-tropospheric cyclonic low-pressure cell that draws in the Tropical Easterly Jet from the western Pacific Ocean.
3. A stronger and more persistent Tropical Easterly Jet over Peninsular India is positively correlated with active Southwest Monsoon conditions over the Indian subcontinent.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mid-tropospheric diabatic heating over the Tibetan Plateau expands the overlying air column to create an upper-tropospheric thermal anticyclone (Tibetan High), whose diverging southern outflow is deflected by the Coriolis force to form the Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ).

exp.why: At an average elevation of 4,500 metres, the Tibetan Plateau receives intense insolation during summer. Its dry western expanse transfers sensible heat directly to the middle troposphere, while cumulus convection over its humid southeastern margin releases substantial latent heat of condensation.

While heating creates a shallow thermal low at the surface of the plateau, warming of the air column causes vertical expansion of isobaric surfaces aloft, creating a powerful upper-tropospheric anticyclonic high-pressure cell (the Tibetan High at 200–100 hPa)—not an upper-air cyclonic low. Air diverging southward from this Tibetan High is deflected westward by the Coriolis force to generate the Tropical Easterly Jet.

As shown by P. Koteswaram (1958), upper-tropospheric divergence on the left entrance and right exit flanks of the Tropical Easterly Jet promotes low-level convergence and vertical ascent over India, whereas its subsidence over the Mascarene region strengthens the cross-equatorial monsoon flow.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4; Koteswaram (1958) Tellus

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the onset of the Southwest Monsoon over India:
items: Statement-I: Even though intense solar heating establishes a deep surface thermal low over northwestern India by May, the sudden 'burst' of the Southwest Monsoon does not occur as long as the southern branch of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet (STWJ) remains positioned south of the Himalayas.

Statement-II: The southern branch of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet maintains upper-tropospheric convergence and dynamic subsidence of air over northern and northwestern India, which caps surface convection and prevents the vertical ascent of maritime winds.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The southern branch of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet (STWJ) south of the Himalayas enforces upper-air convergence and adiabatic sinking over northern India; only when it shifts north of the Tibetan Plateau in early June can upper-air divergence trigger the explosive 'burst' of the Southwest Monsoon.

exp.why: During winter and spring, the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau bifurcate the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet into northern and southern branches. Despite extreme surface temperatures (45°C+) and low surface pressure over Rajasthan and Punjab in May, the monsoon cannot break over the subcontinent until the southern branch of the STWJ withdraws north of the Tibetan Plateau.

Statement-II provides the exact dynamical explanation for Statement-I: the southern branch of the STWJ (centred near 25°N at 200 hPa) induces upper-tropospheric convergence and dynamic subsidence over northern India. This sinking air warms adiabatically, creating a persistent mid-tropospheric inversion that suppresses deep convection and prevents maritime monsoon air from invading the subcontinent until the jet shifts northward.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4; Yin (1949) Journal of Meteorology

stem: During the boreal summer, the upper-tropospheric Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) streams westward across Peninsular India and the Arabian Sea before decelerating and subsiding over the southwestern Indian Ocean near 25°S–30°S latitude. Which one of the following correctly describes the immediate synoptic consequence of this upper-air subsidence?

opts.A: It weakens the Siberian High and initiates the withdrawal of the Northeast Monsoon from the Coromandel coast.
opts.B: It reinforces the semi-permanent Mascarene High, which steepens the trans-equatorial pressure gradient and accelerates the low-level Somali Jet toward India.
opts.C: It intensifies the Azores High, driving Western Disturbances across the Mediterranean Sea into northwestern India.
opts.D: It triggers a persistent cyclonic vortex off the coast of Madagascar that blocks southeast trade winds from crossing the equator.

core: The Indian Summer Monsoon operates as a closed inter-hemispheric Hadley-type circulation loop: upper-level outflow from the Tibetan High via the Tropical Easterly Jet subsides over the Mascarene Islands, strengthening the Mascarene High and driving the low-level Findlater (Somali) Jet back toward India.

exp.why: Option B is correct because the air carried westward at 100–200 hPa by the Tropical Easterly Jet sinks over the Mascarene Islands region (near Madagascar at 25°S–30°S) in the Southern Hemisphere. This upper-air subsidence intensifies the surface Mascarene High. A stronger Mascarene High increases the cross-equatorial pressure gradient toward the Indian Monsoon Trough, accelerating the low-level cross-equatorial Somali (Findlater) Jet at 850 hPa, which pumps vast quantities of moisture into the Arabian Sea branch of the Southwest Monsoon. Options A and C are incorrect as the Siberian High and Azores High are Northern Hemisphere systems unrelated to southern Indian Ocean subsidence. Option D is incorrect because subsidence produces an anticyclonic high-pressure cell, not a cyclonic vortex.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4; Findlater (1969)

stem: With reference to ocean-atmosphere interactions in the Arabian Sea during the Southwest Monsoon season (June–September), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Strong southwesterly monsoon winds blowing parallel to the coasts of Somalia and Oman induce offshore Ekman transport in the upper layer of the western Arabian Sea.
2. This wind-driven circulation causes an accumulation of warm surface water along the Horn of Africa, generating heavy convective rainfall over coastal Somalia during July.

3. As the monsoon winds travel from the western Arabian Sea across the warmer waters of the central and eastern Arabian Sea, the lower-tropospheric thermal inversion weakens and moisture uptake increases substantially.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Strong southwesterly Findlater Jet winds along the Horn of Africa drive offshore Ekman transport and intense coastal upwelling of cold water (the Somali Current), which stabilizes the air over the western Arabian Sea before warm eastern Arabian Sea waters destabilize the air column prior to hitting the Western Ghats.

exp.why: During the Southwest Monsoon, powerful southwesterly winds blow parallel to the coastlines of Somalia and Oman. In the Northern Hemisphere, Ekman transport moves the net surface water layer 90° to the right of the wind direction—meaning away from the coast (offshore) into the open Arabian Sea.

Offshore Ekman transport does not pile up warm water along the coast; instead, it triggers intense coastal upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water along the Somali and Omani coasts, lowering sea surface temperatures by 4°C to 6°C in July. This cold water chills the base of the overlying monsoon air, creating a strong low-level temperature inversion that suppresses cloud growth and keeps coastal Somalia arid.

As the southwesterly airstream moves eastward past 60°E–65°E over the significantly warmer sea surface temperatures of the central and eastern Arabian Sea, heat and latent moisture fluxes from the ocean erode the temperature inversion, deepening the moist boundary layer before the winds ascend the Western Ghats.

ref: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography Ch. 14; Gadgil (2003) Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the impact of El Nino variants on the Indian Summer Monsoon:
items: Statement-I: Both Canonical El Nino and El Nino Modoki events tend to suppress Indian Summer Monsoon rainfall, even though anomalous sea surface warming during an El Nino Modoki is concentrated in the Central Equatorial Pacific rather than along the coast of Peru.

Statement-II: While a Canonical El Nino shifts the single zonal Walker Circulation eastward so that its subsiding limb sits over the Indo-Pacific region, an El Nino Modoki establishes an anomalous two-cell Walker Circulation with an ascending branch over the Central Pacific flanked by descending branches over both the Eastern Pacific and the eastern Indian Ocean.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Both Canonical (Eastern Pacific) El Nino and El Nino Modoki (Central Pacific warming flanked by cooler eastern and western waters) suppress convection over India because both configurations place an anomalous descending branch of the Walker Circulation over the Indo-Pacific Maritime Continent and eastern Indian Ocean.

exp.why: Unlike a Canonical El Nino where maximum warming occurs in the eastern equatorial Pacific off Peru and Ecuador, an El Nino Modoki ('pseudo El Nino') features warm sea surface temperature anomalies in the Central Equatorial Pacific flanked by cooler anomalies in both the eastern and western Pacific. Yet both phenomena are associated with deficient monsoon rainfall over India.

Statement-II explains the physical mechanism behind Statement-I: during a Canonical El Nino, the single Walker cell shifts eastward, placing broad upper-air convergence and atmospheric subsidence over the western Pacific and Indian subcontinent. During an El Nino Modoki, intense convection over the warm Central Pacific splits the anomalous Walker circulation into two cells, with descending (subsiding) limbs over both the cooler Eastern Pacific and the western Pacific/eastern Indian Ocean, thereby suppressing monsoon convection over India.

ref: Ashok et al. (2007) Journal of Geophysical Research; IMD Monsoon Monograph

stem: With reference to the coupled ocean-atmosphere teleconnections influencing the inter-annual and intra-seasonal variability of the Indian Summer Monsoon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) phase is characterized by warmer-than-normal sea surface temperatures in the western Indian Ocean relative to the eastern equatorial Indian Ocean south of Indonesia, which enhances moisture convergence toward the Indian subcontinent.

2. Unlike the stationary Walker Circulation anomalies of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is an intra-seasonal disturbance of coupled clouds, rainfall, and winds that propagates eastward across the global tropics.

3. A shorter periodicity of the Madden-Julian Oscillation cycle of around 30 days, with its active convective phase traversing the Indian Ocean, facilitates vigorous active monsoon spells over India, whereas a prolonged cycle exceeding 45 days is associated with extended monsoon breaks.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A Positive Indian Ocean Dipole (warmer western pole near the Arabian Sea/Somali coast, cooler eastern pole off Sumatra/Java) strengthens cross-equatorial monsoon winds and can neutralize El Niño subsidence, while the eastward-propagating Madden-Julian Oscillation (30–60 day cycle) modulates intra-seasonal active and break monsoon cycles.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. During a Positive IOD event, sea surface temperatures (SSTs) are anomalously warm in the western Indian Ocean (Arabian Sea and Somali coast) and anomalously cool in the eastern equatorial Indian Ocean south of Indonesia. This zonal SST gradient suppresses atmospheric convection over the eastern Indian Ocean and sets up an anomalous easterly wind anomaly along the equator that reduces Ekman transport away from the Indian coast and strengthens moisture convergence into the Indian Summer Monsoon circulation.

Statement 2 is correct. While ENSO involves standing or stationary planetary-scale oscillations in SST and atmospheric pressure between the eastern and western tropical Pacific, the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is a transient, intra-seasonal coupled ocean-atmosphere pulse comprising an enhanced convective (wet) phase and a suppressed (dry) phase that propagates eastward from the western Indian Ocean across the Maritime Continent into the Pacific at roughly 4 to 8 metres per second.

Statement 3 is correct. The MJO operates on an intra-seasonal timescale of 30 to 60 days. When the MJO exhibits a brisk periodicity of around 30 days and its active convective phase passes over the equatorial Indian Ocean, it feeds cyclonic vorticity and moisture into the Monsoon Trough, triggering frequent active monsoon spells. Conversely, a sluggish MJO cycle (>45 days) or a strong suppressed phase lingering over the Indian Ocean promotes large-scale subsidence and prolonged monsoon break conditions.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4; IMD Monsoon Monograph on Teleconnections (IOD & MJO)

stem: Consider the following pairs of pre-monsoon convectional storms in India and their regional agricultural significance:
items: 1. Kalbaisakhi : West Bengal — Beneficial for the cultivation of jute and aus paddy
2. Bordoisila : Karnataka — Triggers the blossoming of coffee flowers
3. Blossom Showers : Assam — Essential for the early flushing of tea leaves
4. Mango Showers : Kerala and Coastal Karnataka — Aids in the early ripening of mangoes
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Pre-monsoon convectional thunderstorms (April–May) arise from intense surface heating meeting moist maritime air currents, acquiring distinct regional names based on their timing and the plantation or kharif crops they sustain.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Kalbaisakhi (Calamity of the month of Baisakh), also known as Nor'westers because the squalls usually approach from the northwest (Chotanagpur plateau), are violent evening thunderstorms in West Bengal and adjoining Odisha/Bangladesh during April and May. The accompanying rainfall is vital for the pre-monsoon sowing and growth of jute and autumn (aus) paddy.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Bordoisila (or Bardoli Chheerha) is the local Assamese name for the pre-monsoon Nor'wester thunderstorms occurring in Assam during April (around Bohag Bihu), where the showers are critical for the tea crop, not coffee in Karnataka.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Blossom Showers (or Cherry Blossom Showers) occur in Kerala and the adjoining coffee-growing highlands of Karnataka (such as Kodagu and Chikmagalur), where pre-monsoon convectional rain triggers the flowering of coffee plantations. In Assam, the pre-monsoon storms beneficial to tea are called Tea Showers or Bordoisila.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Mango Showers (locally called Amra Vrishti) occur toward the close of summer in Kerala and coastal areas of Karnataka, helping in the early ripening of mangoes and preventing premature fruit drop.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4 (Climate - Rhythm of Seasons)

stem: With reference to the branches of the Southwest Monsoon and their interaction with Indian relief features, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Chotanagpur Plateau receives rainfall from the Arabian Sea branch of the Southwest Monsoon via the sub-stream that enters the Narmada and Tapi rift valleys, where it eventually converges with the Bay of Bengal branch.
2. The Bay of Bengal branch enters the Indo-Gangetic plain from the southwest direction after crossing the Odisha coast directly across the eastern peninsular plateau.

3. Among the three sub-streams of the Arabian Sea monsoon branch, only the northernmost stream passing over Saurashtra, Kachchh, and western Rajasthan reaches the Punjab and Haryana plains directly to merge with the Bay of Bengal branch.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Topographic barriers dictate the pathways of both monsoon branches: the Narmada-Tapi rift channels the second Arabian Sea sub-stream into central India and Chotanagpur, while the Arakan Yoma and Himalayas deflect the Bay of Bengal branch to enter the Ganga plains from the southeast.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The second sub-stream of the Arabian Sea branch strikes the coast north of Mumbai and moves eastward through the structural troughs of the Narmada and Tapi river valleys without encountering a major north-south barrier, bringing widespread rainfall to central India and reaching the Chotanagpur Plateau, where it merges with the Bay of Bengal branch.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Bay of Bengal branch strikes the coast of Myanmar and part of southeast Bangladesh, where the Arakan Yoma hills deflect a large portion of the air mass westward toward the Indian subcontinent. Consequently, the monsoon enters West Bengal and Bangladesh from the south and southeast (not from the southwest across the Odisha plateau) and then splits to flow northwestward up the Ganga plain under the channeling influence of the Himalayas and the seasonal low-pressure trough.

Statement 3 is correct. The Arabian Sea monsoon current splits into three distinct streams: the first is obstructed by the Western Ghats and descends as a dry wind over the Deccan; the second enters the Narmada-Tapi valleys toward Chotanagpur; and only the third sub-stream, which strikes the Saurashtra Peninsula and Kachchh and flows parallel to the Aravallis over western Rajasthan, advances northward to Punjab and Haryana, where it joins the Bay of Bengal branch to cause orographic rainfall in the western Himalayas.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4 (Monsoon Winds of the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the climatic aridity of Western Rajasthan during the Southwest Monsoon season:
items: Statement-I: Even when moisture-laden winds of the Arabian Sea monsoon branch pass over western Rajasthan and Kachchh during July and August, vertical convective cloud development and precipitation are strongly inhibited by a persistent lower-tropospheric thermal inversion.
Statement-II: The Aravalli Range is oriented in a southwest-to-northeast direction, which lies nearly parallel to the path of the Arabian Sea monsoon stream moving toward northwestern India.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Western Rajasthan remains arid despite high specific humidity in the lowest atmospheric layer because of two independent factors: (1) lack of orographic lifting due to the parallel orientation of the Aravallis, and (2) an upper-air thermal inversion caused by hot, dry continental air from the Balochistan plateau overriding the shallow moist Arabian Sea current.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. During the Southwest Monsoon, a shallow wedge of moist maritime air from the Arabian Sea (extending only about 1 to 1.5 km above the surface) flows over Kachchh and western Rajasthan. However, at around 1.5 to 3 km altitude, warm and extremely dry continental air flowing from the Balochistan/Iranian plateau and subsiding anticyclonic air overrides the moist surface layer. This creates a sharp temperature inversion (lid) that prevents buoyant thermals from rising to their lifting condensation level, suppressing cumulus cloud growth.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. The Aravalli Range indeed runs southwest-to-northeast, parallel to the Arabian Sea monsoon stream, which explains why there is no mechanical orographic barrier to force the winds upward. However, the orientation of the Aravallis does not cause the lower-tropospheric thermal inversion described in Statement-I, which is thermodynamically driven by the overriding warm, dry continental air mass from the northwest and mid-tropospheric subsidence.

ref: Savindra Singh Climatology; Khullar India: A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 4

stem: With reference to the phenomenon of 'Break in the Monsoon' during the Indian Summer Monsoon season, consider the following statements:
items: 1. When the axis of the Monsoon Trough shifts northward to lie close to the foothills of the Himalayas, rainfall virtually ceases over the central and Gangetic plains while heavy rainfall occurs along the sub-Himalayan belt and increases over parts of Tamil Nadu and Rayalaseema.
2. A break in the monsoon is characterized by a uniform suppression of precipitation across all meteorological subdivisions of India as the cross-equatorial Somali Jet reverses its flow direction.
3. Over the western coast of India, dry break spells occur when the offshore trough intensifies and forces moist westerlies to ascend the Western Ghats perpendicularly.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A 'Break in the Monsoon' is a spatial redistribution—not a nationwide cessation—of rainfall: as the Monsoon Trough migrates to the Himalayan foothills, the core monsoon zone (Central India and Gangetic plains) turns dry, while the Himalayan foothills, Northeast India, and Southeastern Peninsular India experience enhanced rainfall.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. During a classical Monsoon Break in July or August, the axis of the Monsoon Trough shifts northward from its normal position (stretching from Sri Ganganagar to Kolkata) to hug the foothills of the Himalayas. Depressions from the Bay of Bengal cease to form or track across central India, starving the Gangetic plains of rain. Simultaneously, moist southwesterlies are channeled directly against the Himalayas, causing torrential orographic downpours in the sub-Himalayan region (leading to paradoxical flooding in the rivers of North Bihar and Assam while the plains suffer drought), and convective/trough activity enhances rainfall in the rain-shadow regions of Tamil Nadu and Rayalaseema.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Rainfall does not decrease uniformly across all meteorological subdivisions of India during a monsoon break; it shows an out-of-phase dipole where the core monsoon zone dries up while the Himalayan foothills, Northeast India, and southeastern Peninsula receive above-normal rain. Furthermore, the cross-equatorial Somali Jet (Findlater Jet) weakens or shifts position during a break, but it does not reverse its direction until the withdrawal of the Southwest Monsoon.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Along the west coast of India, dry break spells are associated with days when the moist winds blow parallel to the coast and the West Coast offshore trough weakens. Conversely, when the offshore trough intensifies and moist westerlies strike the Western Ghats perpendicularly, vigorous active monsoon conditions and heavy orographic rainfall occur.

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4 (Break in the Monsoon); IMD Glossary

stem: With reference to the synoptic-scale Monsoon Depressions originating over the Bay of Bengal during July and August, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Low-pressure monsoon depressions over the Head Bay of Bengal frequently intensify into severe cyclonic storms during July and August because the strong Tropical Easterly Jet overhead creates a zone of very low vertical wind shear.

2. Once formed over the Head Bay of Bengal, these depressions generally track west-northwestward across the Indian landmass, steered by the orientation of the quasi-stationary Monsoon Trough and upper-tropospheric easterlies.

3. The progressive decrease in seasonal monsoon rainfall from Kolkata toward Delhi along the Ganga plain is driven by the gradual depletion of precipitable moisture as the Bay of Bengal air mass travels further inland away from its oceanic source.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Monsoon depressions in July–August fail to intensify into severe tropical cyclones due to strong vertical wind shear between lower-level southwesterlies and upper-level Tropical Easterly Jet winds, but they act as the primary rain-bearing synoptic systems steering west-northwestward along the Monsoon Trough.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. During the peak monsoon months of July and August, low-pressure systems over the Head Bay of Bengal rarely intensify beyond the stage of a 'Monsoon Depression' into severe cyclonic storms. This is because strong lower-tropospheric southwesterly monsoon winds juxtaposed with strong upper-tropospheric easterlies (the Tropical Easterly Jet) generate very high vertical wind shear over the northern Bay of Bengal, which tilts the vertical vortex and prevents tropical cyclogenesis, compounded by their rapid landfall due to formation close to the coast.

Statement 2 is correct. Monsoon depressions form over the warm waters of the Head Bay of Bengal (often triggered by remnants of typhoons/lows propagating westward from the South China Sea/Gulf of Thailand) and move west-northwestward along the axis of the Monsoon Trough across Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, and the Gangetic plains, steered by upper-tropospheric easterly flow on the southern flank of the Tibetan anticyclone.

Statement 3 is correct. As the Bay of Bengal monsoon stream and its embedded depressions travel up the Indo-Gangetic plain from southeast to northwest, they continuously shed moisture through precipitation without oceanic replenishment. This progressive continentality explains the steady decline in seasonal monsoon rainfall from Kolkata (~120–160 cm) through Patna (~105 cm) and Prayagraj (~90 cm) to Delhi (~55–65 cm).

ref: NCERT Class XI India Physical Environment Ch. 4; IMD Cyclone & Monsoon Depression Manual

stem: With reference to the season of Retreating Monsoon (October and November) in the Indian subcontinent, which one of the following statements best explains the meteorological phenomenon of 'October Heat' and the accompanying shift in cyclonic activity?

opts.A: The gradual withdrawal of the southwest monsoon clears the sky over northern and central India, causing high daytime insolation over land still saturated with soil moisture, while the low-pressure trough migrates southward to the central and southern Bay of Bengal.
opts.B: The abrupt and simultaneous collapse of the monsoon trough across the entire subcontinent induces strong adiabatic compression over the Ganga plains and completely suppresses cyclogenesis in the North Indian Ocean.
opts.C: The rapid southward shift of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet Stream brings warm, humid air masses from Central Asia into the Indo-Gangetic plains, raising both daytime and nocturnal temperatures uniformly.
opts.D: The intensification of the Somali Low-Level Jet during mid-October drives warm equatorial air over the peninsular interior, trapping outgoing terrestrial radiation beneath persistent stratocumulus cloud cover.

core: Unlike the sudden 'burst' of the advancing monsoon, the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon is gradual (spanning nearly three months); in October, clear skies and intense solar heating over waterlogged soils produce oppressive high-temperature and high-humidity conditions known as 'October Heat', even as the low-pressure center shifts to the Bay of Bengal to fuel severe post-monsoon cyclones.

exp.why: Option A is correct: During October and November, as the sun begins its apparent southward movement (dakshinayan), the monsoon trough over the northern plains weakens and is gradually replaced by a high-pressure system. The sky becomes clear and daytime temperatures rise sharply. Because the land is still moist from the preceding rainy season, high insolation causes heavy evaporation, resulting in an oppressive combination of high heat and high relative humidity known as 'October Heat' (though nights become cool and pleasant). Simultaneously, the low-pressure area shifts to the central and southern Bay of Bengal by early November, where high sea-surface temperatures and low vertical wind shear trigger frequent tropical cyclones that strike the eastern coast. Option B is incorrect because monsoon retreat is gradual (taking about three months from September to December) rather than abrupt like its onset, and Bay of Bengal cyclogenesis actually peaks during October-November. Option C is incorrect because Central Asian continental air is cold and dry, and October nights in northern India are cool, not warm. Option D is incorrect because the Somali Jet weakens and reverses after the summer monsoon, and 'October Heat' is driven by clear skies rather than overcast cloud cover.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 4 (Climate); GC Leong Ch. 16

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the seasonal rainfall regime of the Coromandel Coast:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the Malabar Coast, the Coromandel Coast receives the overwhelming majority of its annual rainfall between June and September due to the direct onshore strike of the Bay of Bengal branch of the southwest monsoon.

Statement-II: During the summer monsoon season, the Tamil Nadu coast lies in the rain-shadow zone of the Arabian Sea branch across the Western Ghats and is aligned nearly parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch, whereas from October to December, northeast monsoon winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and blow onshore against the eastern coast.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu and adjoining southern Andhra Pradesh) exhibits a distinct winter/autumn rainfall maximum (Koeppen 'As' climate), remaining anomalously dry during the June-September SW monsoon due to its leeward position relative to the Western Ghats and parallel orientation to the Bay of Bengal monsoon current.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Unlike most of India (including the Malabar Coast), which receives 75-90% of its annual rainfall during the southwest monsoon season (June to September), the Coromandel Coast remains largely dry during these summer months. Instead, it receives nearly 50-60% of its annual precipitation between October and December during the retreating/northeast monsoon season.

Statement-II is correct. Two dual geographic factors explain the summer dryness of the Tamil Nadu coast: first, it lies on the leeward (rain-shadow) side of the Western Ghats with respect to the Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon; second, the coastline of Tamil Nadu runs parallel to the south-westerly Bay of Bengal branch headed toward the Arakan Yoma and Bengal delta, preventing orographic uplift. Conversely, between October and December, the prevailing northeast trade/monsoon winds cross the warm waters of the Bay of Bengal, absorb substantial moisture, and strike the concave Coromandel Coast onshore, supplemented by westward-moving cyclonic depressions.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 4 (Climate)

stem: With reference to 'Western Disturbances' affecting the weather of the Indian subcontinent, consider the following statements:
items: 1. They are warm-core tropical cyclones originating over the Arabian Sea that are steered westward across northwestern India by the Tropical Easterly Jet Stream during the winter solstice.

2. Because they traverse arid continental tracts across West Asia before entering the subcontinent, they do not receive any secondary moisture contribution from water bodies such as the Caspian Sea or the Persian Gulf.

3. The arrival of a Western Disturbance over the northern plains is always marked by an immediate sharp drop in night temperatures ahead of the system, whereas its passage and departure bring warm, humid nights favorable for the harvesting of Kharif crops.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Western Disturbances are extratropical (temperate frontal) cyclonic depressions originating over the Mediterranean region and steered eastward into NW India by the southern branch of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet Stream, bringing warm cloudy nights upon arrival, cold waves after departure, and crucial winter rainfall ('Mahawat') for Rabi crops.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Western Disturbances are non-monsoonal, cold-core extratropical (temperate/frontal) storms originating over the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean, not warm-core tropical cyclones from the Arabian Sea. Furthermore, they are steered eastward (from west to east) into northwestern India by the southern branch of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet Stream (STWJ), not westward by the Tropical Easterly Jet.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While their primary cyclogenesis and moisture source lie over the Mediterranean Sea, as these upper-tropospheric troughs move eastward across Iran, Iraq, and Afghanistan, they regularly draw secondary moisture augmentation from the Caspian Sea in the north and the Persian Gulf (and occasionally the northern Arabian Sea) in the south.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The sequence of temperature change and agricultural utility is reversed. An approaching Western Disturbance brings warm southerly winds in its warm sector along with thick cloud cover that traps outgoing longwave terrestrial radiation, causing a distinct rise in night (minimum) temperatures ahead of the system. Only after the disturbance passes do skies clear and cold, dry northerly winds blow from the freshly snow-clad Himalayas, triggering severe cold-wave and frost conditions. Moreover, this winter rainfall (locally called 'Mahawat') is vital for the vegetative growth of Rabi crops—especially wheat and mustard—rather than the harvesting of Kharif crops.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 4 (Climate); IMD Climatological Monograph

stem: With reference to the spatial distribution and inter-annual variability of rainfall in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In India, the Coefficient of Variation (CV) of annual rainfall exhibits a direct positive relationship with the mean annual precipitation, resulting in the highest percentage variability of over 60% along the windward slopes of the Western Ghats and the Meghalaya plateau.

2. Regions receiving less than 50 cm of mean annual rainfall, such as western Rajasthan and northern Gujarat, exhibit a Coefficient of Variation exceeding 50%, rendering rainfed agriculture highly susceptible to meteorological droughts.

3. Both the interior leeward belt of the Deccan Plateau east of the Sahyadris and the cold desert of Ladakh north of the Great Himalayas fall under the low-rainfall category receiving less than 50 cm of mean annual precipitation.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Coefficient of Variation (CV = [Standard Deviation / Mean] × 100) of Indian rainfall is inversely proportional to total mean annual rainfall: high-rainfall regions (West Coast, Northeast) have the lowest CV (<15%) and highest reliability, whereas arid/semi-arid regions (Thar Desert, Kachchh) have the highest CV (>50-60%) and extreme drought vulnerability.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Coefficient of Variation (CV), which measures inter-annual percentage deviation from normal rainfall, is inversely related (negatively correlated) to mean annual rainfall across India. Areas of heavy precipitation (>200 cm), such as the windward slopes of the Western Ghats, Sub-Himalayan Northeast India, and the Meghalaya plateau, record the lowest CV of less than 15%, meaning rainfall is highly dependable from year to year.

Statement 2 is correct.
