Arid and semi-arid regions receiving scanty annual rainfall (<50 cm), notably western Rajasthan, Kachchh, and northern Gujarat, exhibit the highest Coefficient of Variation in the country (ranging from 50% to over 60%). Because the baseline mean is already very low, even a modest deficit in absolute rainfall translates into a large percentage departure, causing frequent and severe meteorological and agricultural droughts.

Statement 3 is correct. In India's annual rainfall distribution map, precipitation below 50 cm occurs in three distinct geographical pockets: (i) western Rajasthan and adjoining parts of Gujarat, Haryana, and Punjab; (ii) the cold desert of Ladakh behind the orographic barrier of the Great Himalayas; and (iii) the acute rain-shadow pocket of the interior Deccan Plateau (parts of interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Rayalaseema) on the leeward side of the Western Ghats.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 4 (Variability of Rainfall)

stem: With reference to Koeppen's empirical scheme of climatic classification as applied to India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Cwg (Monsoon with dry winter) : Most of the Northern Ganga Plains and eastern Rajasthan
2. As (Monsoon with dry summer) : Konkan and Malabar Coast south of Goa
3. Aw (Tropical Savannah) : Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu
4. Dfc (Cold humid winter with short summer) : Rain-shadow semi-arid steppe belt of interior Peninsular India
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: In Koeppen's classification of Indian climate, 'Amw' denotes the west coast south of Goa (short dry winter), 'As' denotes the Coromandel coast (dry summer, wet autumn/winter), 'Aw' covers the Peninsular plateau (tropical savannah), 'Cwg' covers the Indo-Gangetic plains, 'BShw' covers the semi-arid rain-shadow and steppe zones, and 'Dfc' covers Arunachal Pradesh.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under Koeppen's classification, 'Cwg' stands for Mesothermal (warm temperate) Monsoon climate with a dry winter, where the mean temperature of the coldest month falls below 18°C (marking it 'C' rather than tropical 'A'). This climatic type covers most of the Northern Plains (Ganga plain), eastern Rajasthan, northern Madhya Pradesh, and the Brahmaputra valley.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. 'As' (Tropical Monsoon climate with a dry summer/high-sun season) characterizes the Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu and adjoining coastal Andhra Pradesh, where summer is dry and rainfall occurs in autumn/early winter. The Konkan and Malabar Coast south of Goa is classified as 'Amw' (Monsoon type with a short dry winter season and heavy summer rainfall exceeding 300 cm).

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. 'Aw' (Tropical Savannah climate with a distinct dry winter season) covers most of the Peninsular Plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer (excluding the coastal strips and the semi-arid leeward rain-shadow trough), whereas the Coromandel Coast is classified as 'As'.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. 'Dfc' (Cold, humid winter with a short summer) represents the sub-arctic/microthermal mountain climate of Arunachal Pradesh in the eastern Himalayas. In contrast, the rain-shadow semi-arid steppe belt of interior Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Telangana (as well as the eastern fringes of the Thar desert) is classified as 'BShw' (Semi-arid Steppe climate).

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 4 (Koeppen's Scheme - Climatic Regions of India, Table 4.1)

stem: With reference to Tropical Wet Evergreen and Semi-Evergreen forests in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Tropical Wet Evergreen forests are commercially the most extensively exploited timber forests in India because their softwood trees grow in homogeneous, single-species stands across the Western Ghats and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

2. Unlike Tropical Deciduous species, individual trees in a Tropical Wet Evergreen forest never shed their leaves at any point during the year, requiring mean annual rainfall above 200 cm and mean annual temperatures above 22°C.

3. While Rosewood, Mahogany, Aini and Ebony are the characteristic climax species of Tropical Thorn forests in north-western India, White Cedar, Hollock and Kail exclusively inhabit the sub-alpine pastures of theHigher Himalayas.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Tropical Wet Evergreen forests (>200 cm rainfall, >22°C temperature) feature multi-tiered hardwood trees (Rosewood, Mahogany, Aini, Ebony) that appear evergreen because there is no fixed synchronous season for leaf shedding; despite high biomass, their commercial timber exploitation is limited by extreme species heterogeneity (absence of pure stands) and dense undergrowth.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Although Tropical Wet Evergreen forests occur on the western slopes of the Western Ghats, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and the hills of the Northeastern region, they are commercially much less exploited than Tropical Moist Deciduous (Monsoon) forests. This is because their trees produce very dense, heavy hardwood (not softwood), grow in highly heterogeneous mixed stands (a high diversity of species per hectare rather than pure, single-species stands), and have impenetrable undergrowth of canes, palms, and climbers that hampers logging and transport.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While the climatic thresholds (>200 cm annual rainfall, mean annual temperature above 22°C, and relative humidity exceeding 70%) are accurate, it is a biological misconception that evergreen trees never shed their leaves. Individual trees in Tropical Wet Evergreen forests do shed their old leaves, flower, and bear fruit, but there is no definite, synchronous time of the year for all trees or species to shed leaves simultaneously (unlike deciduous trees, which shed leaves synchronously ahead of the dry season). Consequently, the forest canopy as a whole appears green throughout the year.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Rosewood, Mahogany, Aini, and Ebony are the quintessential climax hardwood species of Tropical Wet Evergreen forests (not Tropical Thorn forests, which are dominated by Babool, Ber, Khejri, and Khair). Similarly, White Cedar, Hollock, and Kail (Kadam) are the characteristic tree species of Tropical Semi-Evergreen forests found in the slightly less rainy transitional fringes alongside wet evergreen forests.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 5 (Natural Vegetation)

stem: With reference to the Tropical Deciduous Forests of India and their characteristic floral assemblages, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Tropical Moist Deciduous forests thrive in regions receiving annual rainfall between 100 cm and 200 cm along the foothills of the Himalayas and the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats, featuring species such as Teak, Sal, Shisham, Hurra, and Kusum.

2. Towards the drier margins of Tropical Dry Deciduous forests (receiving 70 cm to 100 cm rainfall), the closed forest canopy transitions into an open parkland landscape where trees like Tendu, Palas, Amaltas, and Axlewood are interspersed with stretches of grass.
3. Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is a shade-tolerant climax tree species naturally endemic to the Tropical Wet Evergreen forests of the Malabar Coast and the Nilgiri hills.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Tropical Deciduous (Monsoon) forests are bifurcated by the 100 cm isohyet into Moist Deciduous (100–200 cm) and Dry Deciduous (70–100 cm) formations. Red Sanders is not a wet evergreen species of the Western Ghats; it is a light-demanding species strictly endemic to the rocky, dry deciduous tracts of the southern Eastern Ghats.

exp.why: Tropical Moist Deciduous forests occur in regions with 100–200 cm annual rainfall, including the northeastern states, the Himalayan foothills (Bhabar-Terai belt), Jharkhand, western Odisha, Chhattisgarh, and the leeward eastern slopes of the Western Ghats. Teak, Sal, Shisham, Hurra, Mahua, Amla, Semul, Kusum, and Sandalwood are the principal species.

Tropical Dry Deciduous forests cover vast areas of the Peninsular plateau and northern plains receiving 70–100 cm rainfall. In the drier tracts, these forests degrade into a 'parkland' landscape where trees such as Tendu, Palas (Butea monosperma), Amaltas, Bel, Khair, and Axlewood stand amidst open grassy patches, shedding their leaves completely during the dry summer.

Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is neither shade-tolerant nor found in the wet evergreen forests of the Malabar Coast/Nilgiris. It is a refractory, light-demanding species strictly endemic to the rocky, degraded quartzite and shale soils of the Tropical Dry Deciduous forests in the southern Eastern Ghats (specifically the Seshachalam, Palakonda, Veligonda, and Lankamalleswara hills of Andhra Pradesh).

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 5 (Natural Vegetation); Champion & Seth Forest Types of India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the distribution and ecology of Tropical Thorn Forests in India:
items: Statement-I: Apart from the arid and semi-arid tracts of northwestern India, Tropical Thorn Forests and scrubs occupy a continuous crescent-shaped interior zone across the Deccan Plateau covering parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh.

Statement-II: Woody plants in Tropical Thorn Forests exhibit pronounced xerophytic adaptations, including deep phreatophytic root systems, modification of leaf petioles into photosynthetic phyllodes, and succulent stems to conserve moisture.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Tropical Thorn Forests in northwestern India result from continental aridity and weak monsoon penetration, their presence in the interior Deccan crescent is driven by the pronounced leeward rain-shadow effect of the Western Ghats. Xerophytic adaptations are physiological responses to aridity rather than the geographical cause of why that rain-shadow zone exists.

exp.why: Tropical Thorn Forests occur in areas receiving less than 50 cm of annual rainfall. Besides southwest Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat, and dry parts of Madhya Pradesh/Uttar Pradesh, they form a distinct crescent-shaped rain-shadow belt on the leeward side of the Western Ghats across interior Maharashtra (Marathwada/Desh), interior Karnataka (Bayaluseeme), Telangana, and Rayalaseema in Andhra Pradesh.

Species in Tropical Thorn Forests (such as Babool, Ber, Khejri, Wild Date Palm, Khair, Neem, and Euphorbias) survive prolonged desiccation through xerophytic traits: long phreatophytic taproots that tap deep groundwater, tiny leaves or spiny stipules, expanded leaf stalks (phyllodes) that perform photosynthesis with minimal stomatal water loss, and fleshy succulent stems. However, this physiological response to aridity does not explain WHY the interior Deccan Plateau is arid (which is explained by adiabatic descent and moisture depletion on the leeward side of the Western Ghats).

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 5 (Natural Vegetation); Savindra Singh Biogeography

stem: In the context of Himalayan montane biogeography, the altitudinal limits of both the alpine tree line and the permanent snowline are significantly higher in the Eastern Himalayas than in the Western Himalayas, accompanied by a broader vertical belt of wet temperate broadleaf evergreen forests in the East. Which of the following combinations of physical factors best accounts for this asymmetry?

opts.A: Higher winter precipitation from Western Disturbances, steeper rain-shadow gradients on the southern slopes, and greater distance from maritime moisture sources in the Eastern Himalayas.
opts.B: Closer proximity to the Tropic of Cancer (lower latitude), maritime warmth and intense monsoon precipitation from the Bay of Bengal branch, and weaker winter snowfall from Western Disturbances in the Eastern Himalayas.
opts.C: Greater average crustal thickness, predominance of crystalline granitic bedrock with higher geothermal heat flux, and stronger Foehn-like katabatic winds descending from the Tibetan Plateau in the Eastern Himalayas.
opts.D: Absence of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet Stream over the Eastern Himalayas during winter, combined with a narrower latitudinal spread of the Shiwalik foothills that prevents cold-air drainage.

core: The Eastern Himalayas lie at a lower latitude (~27°N–28°N) and closer to the warm Bay of Bengal than the Western Himalayas (~32°N–36°N). Higher summer temperatures, abundant monsoon rainfall (>200 cm), and weaker winter snow accumulation from Western Disturbances push both the tree line (~4,000 m vs ~3,300 m) and snowline (~4,500–5,000 m vs ~4,000–4,200 m) to higher elevations in the East.

exp.why: Option B is correct because three primary climatic drivers govern the East-West Himalayan vegetation and cryospheric asymmetry: (1) Latitude: The Eastern Himalayas lie closer to the Tropic of Cancer (~27°–28°N) compared to the Western Himalayas (~32°–36°N), resulting in higher solar insolation and warmer mean temperatures at equivalent altitudes; (2) Monsoon Moisture & Maritime Influence: The Bay of Bengal branch impinges directly on the Eastern Himalayas, delivering over 200–300 cm of warm summer rainfall that supports dense broadleaf evergreen oaks, laurels, chestnuts, and diverse rhododendrons; and (3) Winter Western Disturbances: The Western Himalayas receive heavy winter snowfall from mid-latitude Western Disturbances, which lowers spring temperatures and depresses both the permanent snowline and the upper limit of tree growth. Option A reverses the Western Disturbance gradient; Option C invokes negligible geothermal/crustal factors; Option D is factually incorrect as the STWJ flows across the entire southern Himalayan flank in winter and the Eastern Himalayas actually lack a continuous Shiwalik range.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 2 & Ch. 5; Majid Husain Geography of India

stem: With reference to the Southern Montane Forests ('Shola-Grassland' ecosystem) found in the high-altitude reaches of the Western Ghats, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the upper montane zones of the Himalayas, the Shola forests occurring above 1,500 metres in the Nilgiri, Anaimalai, and Palani hills lack indigenous coniferous canopies and consist instead of stunted tropical montane broadleaf evergreen trees.

2. The sharp spatial segregation between valley-bound Shola woods and exposed hilltop grasslands is maintained by winter ground frost and desiccating winds on convex ridges, which prevent frost-sensitive tree seedlings from establishing on open slopes.
3. Characteristic tree flora associated with these southern montane wet temperate tracts include Magnolia, Laurel, Cinchona, and Wattle, accompanied by a dense epiphytic growth of mosses and lichens.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Shola-Grassland mosaic above 1,500 m in the southern Western Ghats is a bi-phasic climax ecosystem shaped by microclimatic frost-and-wind dynamics. Sheltered folds retain moisture and escape radiation frost to support stunted tropical broadleaf evergreens (Sholas), whereas exposed rolling downs experience winter ground frost and summer fires that maintain montane C4 grasslands.

exp.why: Because the Nilgiri, Anaimalai, and Palani hills lie in the low tropical latitudes (10°N–12°N) and do not exceed ~2,695 m (Anamudi), they lack snow-adapted native gymnosperms/conifers (such as native Pine, Deodar, or Fir). Instead, their montane wet temperate forests ('Sholas') comprise dwarf, gnarled, densely-crowned broadleaf evergreen trees of tropical ancestry.

During clear winter nights (November to February), radiative cooling on the exposed rolling hilltops causes ground temperatures to drop below 0°C, producing severe ground frost ('hoar frost'). Tropical-origin Shola tree seedlings cannot tolerate frost desiccation or high-velocity winds on convex ridges and are therefore confined to sheltered valleys, folds, and concave depressions where moisture and canopy cover buffer thermal extremes.

As documented in standard biogeographical surveys and NCERT, the prominent tree species in these Southern Montane forests (Nilgiris, Anaimalai, Palani, and Satpura/Maikal/Mahabaleshwar at lower heights) include Magnolia, Laurel, Cinchona, and Wattle (the latter two introduced historically and now naturalized in the landscape), draped with epiphytic mosses, ferns, and orchids.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 5 (Montane Forests); Champion & Seth Class 11A (Southern Montane Wet Temperate Forest)

stem: With reference to the Mangrove ecosystems of India and their geomorphic and physiological characteristics, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Mangrove species overcome the hypoxic conditions of waterlogged intertidal mudflats through negatively geotropic aerial roots (pneumatophores) bearing lenticels, and exhibit viviparous germination where seeds germinate while still attached to the parent tree.

2. Mangrove formations along India's East Coast are much broader and more continuous than those along the West Coast (excluding Gujarat) primarily because East-flowing rivers build gently sloping, sediment-rich deltas, whereas the steeper Western Ghats gradient confines West Coast mangroves to narrow estuaries and tidal creeks.
3. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are devoid of natural mangrove forests due to their steep submarine continental shelf and the absence of large perennial alluvial rivers.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mangroves are halophytes adapted to anoxic, saline intertidal zones via pneumatophores, stilt/prop roots, salt-excreting leaves, and vivipary. Geomorphologically, large prograding deltas on the East Coast (Ganga-Brahmaputra, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) provide vast intertidal mudflats compared to the submerged, cliffed, estuarine West Coast.

exp.why: Intertidal mangrove mud is waterlogged and oxygen-depleted (anoxic/hypoxic). True mangroves (like Avicennia and Sonneratia) grow vertical blind roots called pneumatophores upward out of the mud (negatively geotropic) covered with breathing pores (lenticels) for gas exchange. They also exhibit vivipary, wherein the seed germinates inside the fruit while still attached to the maternal tree, dropping as a buoyant, ready-to-root seedling (propagule).

India's East Coast features a wide, gently sloping continental shelf and massive sediment-laden deltas (Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika/Mahanadi, Coringa/Godavari, Krishna, Pichavaram/Kaveri), creating extensive low-energy mudflats ideal for broad mangrove belts. Conversely, the West Coast south of Gujarat is an emergent/faulted steep coast where swift rivers form narrow funnel-shaped estuaries, restricting mangroves to small patches along creeks and backwaters.

Far from being devoid of mangroves, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands possess the third-largest mangrove area in India (after West Bengal and Gujarat), covering over 600 sq. km. Sheltered tidal creeks, lagoons, and low-energy bays across the archipelago support pristine, species-rich insular mangrove formations.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 5; FSI India State of Forest Report (Mangrove Cover Chapter)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the methodology and legal framework used in the India State of Forest Report (ISFR) published by the Forest Survey of India (FSI):
items: Statement-I: In the biennial ISFR assessment, a state can simultaneously register a net increase in its 'Forest Cover' even while experiencing degradation or loss of natural tree cover inside its 'Recorded Forest Area' (RFA).

Statement-II: Under the ISFR remote-sensing classification, degraded forest lands with a tree canopy density of less than 10 percent are categorized as 'Scrub' and are excluded from the computation of total Forest Cover.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: 'Recorded Forest Area' (RFA) is a purely legal designation (land notified under the Indian Forest Act or State Forest Acts, regardless of whether trees exist on it), whereas 'Forest Cover' is a satellite-based biophysical metric measuring any land patch >= 1 hectare with >= 10% canopy density irrespective of legal ownership or land use (including private orchards, bamboo, palms, and agroforestry).

exp.why: Statement-I is correct because 'Forest Cover' and 'Recorded Forest Area' (RFA) measure two fundamentally different domains. RFA refers strictly to lands legally notified as Reserve Forests, Protected Forests, or Unclassed Forests under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 or state forest laws, even if they are barren or snow-covered. Conversely, 'Forest Cover' measures any patch of land of 1 hectare or more with a tree canopy density of at least 10%, irrespective of legal ownership, land use, or tree species. Consequently, expansion of commercial monoculture plantations, mango/coconut/arecanut orchards, or tea-estate shade trees outside the legal RFA can increase a state's satellite-measured 'Forest Cover' even while natural forests inside the RFA suffer degradation.

Statement-II is also correct: FSI classifies Forest Cover into three canopy-density tiers—Very Dense Forest (canopy density >= 70%), Moderately Dense Forest (40% to <70%), and Open Forest (10% to <40%). Degraded forest lands with canopy density below 10% are mapped separately as 'Scrub' and are not counted as part of 'Forest Cover'. However, Statement-II merely defines the lower canopy threshold for Scrub and does not explain Statement-I, which arises from the legal-versus-biophysical decoupling between RFA and Forest Cover.

ref: Forest Survey of India (FSI) India State of Forest Report (ISFR) Ch. 1 & 2; Indian Forest Act, 1927

stem: With reference to the Myristica swamp ecosystems and traditional sacred groves of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Myristica swamps are relict brackish-water mangrove ecosystems restricted to the estuarine deltas of the Eastern Ghats.
2. Tree species in Myristica swamps possess specialized aerial knee roots and stilt roots with lenticels to survive in waterlogged, anaerobic soils.

3. Among India's community-conserved sacred groves, 'Orans' refer to wet montane forest patches in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, whereas 'Law Kyntang' denotes arid scrubland groves in western Rajasthan.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Myristica swamps are ancient, primitive non-saline freshwater swamp forests found primarily in poorly drained valleys of the Western Ghats, characterized by trees bearing knee roots and stilt roots. India's relict forest patches are frequently preserved as sacred groves, such as Kavu in Kerala, Devarakadu in Karnataka, Orans in Rajasthan, and Law Kyntang in Meghalaya.

exp.why: Myristica swamps are strictly freshwater (non-saline) swamp forests, not brackish estuarine mangroves. They are ancient, primitive relict ecosystems found predominantly in flat-bottomed, poorly drained valleys of the Western Ghats (especially in southern Kerala and Uttara Kannada in Karnataka), with smaller isolated pockets in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Meghalaya.

Because Myristica swamps experience prolonged or perennial freshwater inundation, dominant endemic trees of the family Myristicaceae (wild nutmegs such as Myristica fatua and Gymnacranthera canarica) evolve prominent stilt roots and looping knee roots (pneumatophores) studded with lenticels to facilitate gaseous exchange in oxygen-depleted soils.

The regional terminology is interchanged. 'Orans' (and 'Jogmaya') are traditional community-protected sacred groves and woodland pastures in the arid and semi-arid Thar landscape of Rajasthan, whereas 'Law Kyntang' and 'Law Lyngdoh' are sacred groves preserved by indigenous communities in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya.

ref: Champion & Seth (1968) Forest Types of India (Sub-group 4C: Tropical Freshwater Swamp Forests); ENVIS Centre on Conservation of Ecological Heritage and Sacred Sites of India

stem: Consider the following pairs of Himalayan tree species and their characteristic ecological niches or attributes:
items: 1. Chir Pine (Pinus roxburghii) : Forms gregarious pure stands in the subtropical belt (1000-1800 m) that are highly susceptible to resin-fueled surface forest fires
2. Deodar (Cedrus deodara) : Endemic exclusively to the hyper-humid Eastern Himalayas of Arunachal Pradesh where summer monsoon rainfall exceeds 350 cm
3. Himalayan Birch (Betula utilis) : Characteristic sub-alpine species marking the upper timberline transition below alpine pastures
4. Banj Oak (Quercus leucotrichophora) : Broad-leaved moist temperate species whose dense leaf litter and root network promote mountain spring recharge
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Himalayan vegetation exhibits distinct altitudinal and longitudinal zonation driven by temperature lapse rates and the east-to-west gradient of monsoon versus winter Western Disturbance precipitation. While Chir Pine dominates fire-prone subtropical slopes and Banj Oak sustains moist temperate hydrology, Deodar is a hallmark of the snow-fed Western Himalayas and Birch marks the sub-alpine timberline.

exp.why: Chir Pine occurs extensively in the Himalayan Subtropical Pine Forests between 1000 m and 1800 m. Its thick, flammable carpet of resinous dry needles inhibits understorey growth and makes these stands highly prone to recurring summer surface fires.

Deodar (Cedrus deodara) is a classic temperate conifer of the Western Himalayas (Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand) between 1500 m and 2500 m, where it thrives on well-drained slopes receiving substantial winter snowfall from Western Disturbances and moderate summer rain. It is absent from the hyper-humid Eastern Himalayas.

Himalayan Silver Birch (Bhojpatra, Betula utilis), along with Silver Fir (Abies spectabilis), Rhododendrons, and Junipers, forms the sub-alpine forest belt (roughly 3000-4000 m), representing the highest tree line before transitioning into alpine meadows (Bugyals or Marg).

Banj Oak is a keystone broad-leaved species of the lower moist temperate Himalayan zone (1500-2400 m). Unlike Chir Pine, oak forests produce thick humus-rich litter and deep mycorrhizal root systems that enhance rainwater infiltration and sustain perennial hill springs.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 5 (Natural Vegetation); FSI India State of Forest Report (ISFR)

stem: With reference to the ecological impact of plant species on Indian forest and grassland biomes, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Senna spectabilis and Lantana camara degrade deciduous and shola-grassland mosaics in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve by forming dense thickets and allelopathic litter that suppress native palatable grasses.
2. Mikania micrantha acts as an aggressive perennial climber in the moist forests of Northeast India and the Western Ghats, smothering native tree regeneration by blocking canopy light.
3. Both Prosopis juliflora (Gando Baval) and Prosopis cineraria (Khejri) are invasive alien species introduced from South America that have degraded the Banni Grasslands of Kachchh.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Invasive alien plant species such as Senna spectabilis, Lantana camara, Mikania micrantha, and Prosopis juliflora severely alter fire regimes, soil chemistry, and trophic availability across Indian biomes. Distinguishing invasive exotic species (like Prosopis juliflora) from native congeneric keystone species (like Prosopis cineraria) is critical for ecological restoration.

exp.why: Senna spectabilis (an exotic tree from tropical America) and Lantana camara have extensively invaded the Mudumalai, Wayanad, Bandipur, and Nagarhole landscapes of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve. Their rapid coppicing, shade dominance, and allelopathic chemical exudates arrest the growth of native grasses and bamboo, shrinking forage for wild herbivores.

Mikania micrantha (commonly called 'mile-a-minute' weed) is a neotropical invasive creeper that thrives in high-rainfall openings and moist deciduous to semi-evergreen forests in Northeast India (including Kaziranga) and the Western Ghats, physically blanketing saplings and grass beds.

While Prosopis juliflora (Gando Baval) is indeed an invasive alien mesquite native to Central and South America that has encroached upon the Banni Grasslands of Kachchh and saline wetlands, Prosopis cineraria (Khejri / Shami) is a native, keystone tree of the Indian Thar Desert. Khejri fixes atmospheric nitrogen, stabilizes sand dunes, improves understorey crop yields, and provides vital fodder (Loong) and pods (Sangri).

ref: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) & MoEFCC Reports on Invasive Alien Species in Indian Protected Areas; Botanical Survey of India

stem: Consider the following locations in India:
items: 1. Thiruvananthapuram (Malabar Coast)
2. Great Nicobar (Andaman and Nicobar Islands)
3. Mumbai (Konkan Coast)
4. Jaisalmer (Western Rajasthan)
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the normal onset of the advancing Southwest Monsoon across the locations given above, from the earliest to the latest?
core: Although the Kerala coast marks the onset of the Southwest Monsoon over the Indian mainland around June 1, the Bay of Bengal branch strikes the Andaman and Nicobar Islands roughly ten to twelve days earlier (around May 15-21). Thereafter, the monsoon advances northward along the Konkan coast by June 10-11 and reaches extreme western Rajasthan last, in early to mid-July.

exp.why: Thiruvananthapuram on the southern Kerala coast experiences its normal Southwest Monsoon onset on June 1, making it the second location in the sequence (after the Andaman and Nicobar Islands).

The southern Andaman Sea and Nicobar Islands (including Great Nicobar and Sri Vijaya Puram) receive the very first onset of the advancing Southwest Monsoon in the Indian Union between May 15 and May 21, well before the mainland onset over Kerala.
Progressing northward along the Western Ghats escarpment, the Arabian Sea branch normally reaches Mumbai on the Konkan coast around June 10-11, placing it third in the chronological sequence.
Extreme western Rajasthan (Jaisalmer) is the last region in India to be covered by the advancing Southwest Monsoon isochrone, with normal onset occurring around July 1 to July 15.

ref: India Meteorological Department (IMD) Normal Monsoon Onset Isochrone Map; NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 4

stem: With reference to the ecology, distribution, and statutory regulation of bamboo in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While clump-forming (sympodial) bamboo species predominate across the tropical deciduous forests of Peninsular India, non-clump-forming (monopodial) runner bamboo species occur naturally in the cooler hills of Northeast India.

2. Several Indian bamboo species are monocarpic perennials that undergo synchronized gregarious flowering after multi-decade vegetative cycles, followed by mass seeding and the death of the parent clumps.

3. Following the 2017 amendment to the Indian Forest Act, 1927, bamboo was omitted from the statutory definition of 'tree', thereby exempting bamboo grown in non-forest areas from felling and transit permits while retaining its regulation as 'forest-produce' when found in or brought from a forest.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Botanically a grass (family Poaceae), bamboo exhibits distinct growth habits across India's climatic zones (sympodial clumps in Peninsular deciduous forests versus monopodial runners in cooler Northeastern hills) and unique gregarious flowering cycles. The Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 omitted bamboo from the statutory definition of 'tree' under Section 2(7), deregulating bamboo felling and transit on non-forest lands while retaining forest protection over bamboo found in or brought from forest areas.

exp.why: In Peninsular and Central India's tropical moist and dry deciduous forests, bamboo is overwhelmingly sympodial (pachymorph/clump-forming), such as Dendrocalamus strictus and Bambusa bambos. In contrast, monopodial (leptomorph/non-clump-forming runner) bamboos, such as Phyllostachys and Arundinaria species, thrive naturally in the cooler subtropical and temperate montane belts of Northeast India and the Himalayas.

Many ecologically significant bamboos (such as Melocanna baccifera in Mizoram and Northeast India, which triggers the 'Mautam' ecological phenomenon every 48 years) are monocarpic: entire genetically related cohorts flower simultaneously across vast landscapes, shed massive quantities of seed, and then die back completely to regenerate from seed.

The Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 amended Section 2(7) of the Indian Forest Act, 1927 to omit 'bamboos' from the definition of 'tree'. Because 'timber' (which is forest-produce regardless of whether it is found in a forest or non-forest land under Section 2(4)(a)) includes 'trees', removing bamboo from Section 2(7) meant that bamboo grown in non-forest areas ceased to be 'forest-produce' and no longer requires felling or transit permits. However, under Section 2(4)(b)(ii), 'plants not being trees (including grass...)' remain regulated as 'forest-produce' when found in, or brought from, a forest.

ref: Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 (Sections 2(4) & 2(7) of Indian Forest Act, 1927); FSI India State of Forest Report (Bamboo Resources Chapter)

stem: With reference to the linkages between soil characteristics, hydrology, and natural vegetation in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In India's Tropical Wet Evergreen forests growing over lateritic soils, the vast majority of bio-available plant nutrients are locked within the living biomass and rapidly recycled surface litter rather than in deep mineral soil horizons.

2. Once a Tropical Wet Evergreen forest is clear-felled, the exposed lateritic soil supports high-yield cereal cultivation for decades without fertilizer inputs because heavy monsoon rainfall inhibits the leaching of silica and exchangeable bases.

3. Along the Himalayan foothills, the abrupt vegetational shift from deep-rooted deciduous trees in the Bhabar belt to tall elephant grasses and moist sal forests in the Terai belt is governed by the subterranean disappearance of streams in coarse boulder beds and their surface re-emergence downslope.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Luxuriant Tropical Wet Evergreen forests thrive over nutrient-poor lateritic soils only because of a tight, closed nutrient cycle at the forest floor; clear-felling breaks this cycle and exposes leached iron-aluminium oxides that bake into infertile hardpans. Along the Himalayan piedmont, edaphic permeability variations between the porous Bhabar shingle fan and the marshy Terai spring-line dictate vegetation structure.

exp.why: Under warm temperatures and torrential rainfall (>250 cm), mineral soils beneath Tropical Wet Evergreen forests undergo intense chemical weathering and leaching. The lush multi-tiered canopy survives because shallow root mats and mycorrhizal fungi capture nutrients immediately from decomposing leaf litter before percolating rainwater can flush them down.

Heavy monsoon rainfall strongly promotes—rather than inhibits—the leaching of soluble silica and exchangeable bases (calcium, magnesium, potassium), a process known as desilication or laterization. When the evergreen forest canopy is clear-felled, the thin humus layer oxidizes and erodes rapidly, leaving behind acidic iron and aluminium sesquioxides that harden irreversibly on exposure and render the land infertile for sustained cereal farming.

The Bhabar is a narrow (8-16 km) piedmont belt of coarse pebbles and boulders where Himalayan streams lose surface flow by percolating underground, creating dry edaphic conditions suited to deep-rooted deciduous species (like Khair and Sissoo). Immediately south lies the Terai, where the finer alluvium forces the underground water back to the surface, creating marshy conditions that sustain tall elephant grasses (Saccharum species), cane brakes, and moist deciduous Sal (Shorea robusta) forests.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 2 (Physiography - Bhabar & Terai) & Ch. 5 & 6 (Natural Vegetation & Soils); G.C. Leong Ch. 15

stem: With reference to the agricultural seasons and regional cropping patterns in India, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Unlike Northern and Interior India where Kharif and Rabi seasons support distinct tropical and temperate crops respectively, Southern Peninsular India can cultivate the same tropical crops across both seasons whenever adequate soil moisture is available.

Statement-II: The Coromandel coast of Peninsular India receives the bulk of its annual rainfall during October to December from the retreating Northeast Monsoon and Bay of Bengal cyclonic depressions.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The sharp thermal demarcation between Kharif (tropical) and Rabi (temperate) crops is a continental feature of North India caused by winter temperature drops below the 18°C isotherm. In Peninsular India south of the Tropic of Cancer, maritime moderation and low latitude keep mean winter temperatures above 20°C, making soil moisture—rather than thermal limitation—the primary determinant of year-round tropical crop cultivation.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Northern and Northwestern India, continental winters bring mean monthly temperatures down to 10°C–15°C, necessitating cold-tolerant temperate crops (wheat, barley, mustard, gram) in Rabi and warm-season crops (paddy, maize, cotton, bajra) in Kharif. In Southern Peninsular India, the absence of severe winter cold allows farmers to grow tropical crops like rice, maize, jowar, and groundnut during both Kharif and Rabi seasons if irrigation or residual soil moisture is present.

Statement-II is correct, as the Tamil Nadu/Coromandel coast receives winter rainfall from the Northeast Monsoon picking up moisture over the Bay of Bengal. However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: the ability of Peninsular India to grow tropical crops across all seasons is explained by its tropical thermal regime (lack of a continental winter temperature drop south of the Tropic of Cancer), not merely the seasonal rainfall distribution along the Coromandel coast.

ref: NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 5 (Land Resources and Agriculture)

stem: With reference to the agro-climatic and physiological requirements of Rabi wheat cultivation in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A cool and moist weather regime during the vegetative phase satisfies the vernalization requirement and promotes profuse synchronous tillering.
2. Light winter precipitation brought by Western Disturbances over Northwestern India supplements soil moisture during the critical crown root initiation and jointing stages.
3. An abrupt surge in daytime temperatures above 32°C accompanied by high atmospheric humidity during late February and March accelerates starch synthesis and increases individual grain weight.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Wheat is a temperate C3 Rabi crop requiring cool temperatures (10°C–15°C) during vegetative tillering and warm, dry, cloud-free weather (21°C–26°C) during grain ripening. Sudden spring heatwaves above 30°C–32°C during the milky and dough stages trigger 'terminal heat stress', which inhibits starch synthase activity, accelerates leaf senescence, and causes premature shriveling of grains.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Winter/Rabi wheat requires cool temperatures during its early vegetative stage to fulfill vernalization (low-temperature induction of flowering competence) and to prolong the tillering window, which directly increases the number of ear-bearing shoots per plant.

Statement 2 is correct. Extra-tropical cyclonic depressions originating over the Mediterranean region (Western Disturbances) bring light winter rainfall across Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, and Western Uttar Pradesh between December and February, providing crucial moisture during the crown root initiation (CRI) and stem elongation/jointing stages.

Statement 3 is incorrect. An abrupt spike in daytime temperatures above 30°C–32°C during late February and March causes 'terminal heat stress' during the grain-filling (milky to dough) stage. High thermal stress deactivates soluble starch synthase enzymes, increases respiratory carbon loss, shortens the grain-filling duration, and produces shriveled, low-weight grains. Furthermore, high humidity during maturity promotes yellow and brown rust fungal infections rather than healthy ripening.

ref: ICAR Handbook of Agriculture; NCERT Class XII India People and Economy, Ch. 5

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the agronomic and edaphic conditions of rice cultivation in India:
items: 1. In the lower Gangetic plains and Assam valley, 'Aman' is the principal winter-harvested paddy crop sown during the Southwest Monsoon, whereas 'Boro' is the summer-harvested irrigated paddy crop sown in winter.
2. Lowland transplanted paddy cultivation performs best on deep, coarse-textured sandy-loam soils with high vertical percolation rates that prevent root-zone hypoxia.
3. Unlike wheat, rice is a strictly stenothermal lowland crop that cannot be cultivated above an altitude of 800 metres in the Indian subcontinent.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Rice exhibits remarkable agro-ecological plasticity in India, spanning from below sea level in Kuttanad to over 2,000 m in the Himalayas, and across three seasonal cycles (Aus, Aman, Boro) in humid Eastern India. Edaphically, lowland puddled rice requires clayey or clay-loam soils with an impervious subsoil horizon to minimize percolation loss and retain standing water.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In West Bengal, Assam, and coastal Odisha, three seasonal rice crops are grown: 'Aus' (sown in May–June, harvested in September–October/autumn), 'Aman' (sown in June–July during the Southwest Monsoon and harvested in November–December/winter, accounting for the largest acreage), and 'Boro' (sown in November–December under irrigation and harvested in March–May/summer).

Statement 2 is incorrect. Coarse-textured sandy soils have excessive hydraulic conductivity and vertical percolation, making it impossible to maintain a ponded water layer without massive water and nutrient leaching losses. Lowland transplanted paddy requires heavy clayey or clay-loam soils with a compact, low-permeability subsoil pan (created via puddling) to hold standing water; rice roots naturally overcome soil hypoxia through specialized lysigenous aerenchyma tissue that transports atmospheric oxygen from the shoots to the roots.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Rice has wide genetic and ecological adaptability across altitudes and moisture regimes in India. It is successfully cultivated from below sea level in the Kuttanad backwaters of Kerala to altitudes exceeding 1,800–2,000 metres in the Kashmir Valley and terraced Himalayan slopes using cold-tolerant Japonica and Indica-Japonica landraces.

ref: NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 5; D.R. Khullar: India A Comprehensive Geography

stem: With reference to Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) and the System of Rice Intensification (SRI) in comparison to conventional puddled transplanted rice, consider the following statements:
items: 1. By eliminating wet puddling operations, Direct Seeded Rice preserves soil macroporosity and reduces sub-surface hardpan compaction for the succeeding Rabi crop.

2. Because DSR fields lack a continuous stagnant water layer during the early vegetative stage, they face higher weed competition and a greater susceptibility to iron deficiency chlorosis than flooded paddy.

3. Replacing continuous soil submergence with aerobic soil regimes or alternate wetting and drying in DSR and SRI consistently reduces both methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from paddy fields.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Transitioning from flooded puddled rice to Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) or alternate wetting and drying (SRI) saves irrigation water, preserves soil structure for subsequent Rabi crops, and suppresses anaerobic methanogenesis (CH4). However, aerobic soil conditions create three agronomic trade-offs: heavier weed infestation, oxidation of soluble ferrous iron (Fe2+) into unavailable ferric iron (Fe3+), and elevated nitrous oxide (N2O) fluxes due to fluctuating nitrification-denitrification cycles.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Conventional puddling breaks down soil aggregates and creates a dense, compacted plough pan that restricts deep root penetration and causes waterlogging for the succeeding Rabi wheat crop. DSR sows seeds directly into unpuddled soil, conserving 15–30% irrigation water and maintaining favourable soil physical structure for zero-till Rabi crops.

Statement 2 is correct. In conventional transplanted rice, the 5–10 cm standing water layer physically suppresses aerobic weed germination and creates reducing (anaerobic) conditions that reduce insoluble ferric iron (Fe3+) into plant-available ferrous iron (Fe2+). In DSR, the absence of early flooding allows simultaneous emergence of competitive grassy weeds and keeps soil iron oxidized as insoluble Fe3+ (especially in alkaline/calcareous soils), frequently triggering iron-deficiency chlorosis.

Statement 3 is incorrect. While aerobic soil regimes in DSR and alternate wetting and drying (AWD) in SRI inhibit strict anaerobic methanogenic archaea—substantially lowering methane (CH4) emissions—they do not reduce nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions. Instead, alternating aerobic and anaerobic soil moisture regimes accelerate coupled nitrification and incomplete denitrification, which typically spikes nitrous oxide (N2O) fluxes, creating a well-documented greenhouse gas trade-off.

ref: ICAR-NRRI Technical Bulletins on DSR & SRI; IPCC Wetland Supplement on Paddy GHG Fluxes

stem: With reference to the agro-climatic and edaphic niches of major and minor millets (Shree Anna) in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Jowar (Sorghum) : Grown exclusively as a rainfed Kharif crop on acidic red and lateritic hill soils of Southern India
2. Bajra (Pearl Millet) : Cultivated predominantly as a drought-hardy Kharif crop on sandy and shallow upland soils of Northwestern and Western India
3. Ragi (Finger Millet) : Requires deep calcareous Vertisols and cannot tolerate sub-humid hill climates or acidic soils
4. Kodo Millet : Hardy minor millet cultivated on marginal, gravelly and skeletal upland soils of the Central Indian plateau
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Among India's major millets, Jowar is uniquely adapted to moisture-retentive black Vertisols of the Deccan Plateau across both Kharif and Rabi seasons, Bajra dominates arid/semi-arid sandy Aridisols and Inceptisols in Northwestern India, and Ragi thrives on red, lateritic, and acidic upland soils in Southern and Himalayan hill states.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. Jowar (Sorghum bicolor) is cultivated as both a Kharif and a Rabi crop, and it thrives on medium-to-deep moisture-retentive black clayey soils (Vertisols) of the Deccan Plateau (Maharashtra and Northern Karnataka). In fact, post-monsoon Rabi Jowar grown on residual soil moisture in black soils accounts for roughly half of Maharashtra's sorghum acreage.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Bajra (Pennisetum glaucum) is the most drought- and heat-tolerant major millet, thriving in low-rainfall (40–60 cm) arid and semi-arid regions with light-textured sandy, loamy-sand, and shallow black/red upland soils across Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Gujarat, and Maharashtra.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Ragi (Eleusine coracana) is remarkably tolerant of acidic soils (pH 4.5–6.5) and flourishes on red, lateritic, and shallow hilly upland soils in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand, and Odisha. It also tolerates higher rainfall (up to 100 cm) and cooler sub-humid hill altitudes up to 2,000 metres compared to Bajra.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Kodo millet (Paspalum scrobiculatum) is an indigenous drought-resilient minor millet extensively grown on poor, gravelly, skeletal, and shallow marginal soils in the tribal belts of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu.

ref: ICAR-IIMR (Indian Institute of Millets Research) Compendium on Shree Anna; NCERT Class XII

stem: With reference to the botanical classification and photosynthetic physiology of millets and pseudocereals in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Kodo, Kutki (Little millet) and Sanwa (Barnyard millet) are true monocotyledonous grasses belonging to the family Poaceae, Kuttu (Buckwheat) and Rajgira (Amaranth) are dicotyledonous pseudocereals.

2. True millets such as Sorghum, Pearl Millet and Foxtail Millet utilize the C4 photosynthetic pathway with specialized Kranz leaf anatomy, which concentrates carbon dioxide around the RuBisCO enzyme and suppresses photorespiration under high temperatures.

3. Because C4 carbon fixation sustains high photosynthetic rates even under partial stomatal closure, true millets exhibit a lower transpiration ratio and superior water-use efficiency compared to C3 cereals like rice and wheat.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: True millets are monocot grasses (family Poaceae) possessing C4 Kranz anatomy, which spatially separates initial carbon fixation (via PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells) from the Calvin cycle (in bundle-sheath cells). By contrast, Kuttu (Buckwheat) and Rajgira (Amaranth)—though grouped commercially with Nutri-cereals—are broadleaf dicotyledonous pseudocereals.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. True minor millets—such as Kodo millet (Paspalum scrobiculatum), Kutki/Little millet (Panicum sumatrense), Sanwa/Barnyard millet (Echinochloa frumentacea), Kangni/Foxtail millet (Setaria italica), and Chena/Proso millet (Panicum miliaceum)—are monocotyledonous grasses of the family Poaceae. In contrast, Kuttu/Buckwheat (Fagopyrum esculentum, family Polygonaceae) and Rajgira/Chaulai/Amaranth (Amaranthus spp., family Amaranthaceae) are non-grass dicotyledonous plants whose starchy seeds are consumed like cereal grains, making them pseudocereals.

Statement 2 is correct. True millets are C4 plants characterized by Kranz leaf anatomy (concentric rings of mesophyll cells around thick-walled bundle-sheath cells). Primary carbon fixation in the mesophyll is catalyzed by PEP carboxylase (which has no oxygenase activity), pumping four-carbon organic acids into the bundle-sheath cells where decarboxylation creates a high local CO2 concentration around RuBisCO, virtually eliminating wasteful photorespiration even under high heat and drought.

Statement 3 is correct. Because the C4 CO2-concentrating mechanism maintains a steep inward CO2 diffusion gradient even when stomata partially close during moisture stress, millets lose far less water vapour per unit of carbon fixed. Consequently, C4 millets have a low transpiration ratio (requiring roughly 250–350 g of water per gram of dry biomass produced) compared to C3 cereals like wheat and rice (which require 500–650 g of water per gram of dry biomass).

ref: FSSAI & Ministry of Agriculture Notification on Nutri-Cereals (Shree Anna); NCERT Class XI Biology (Photosynthesis in Higher Plants)

stem: With reference to the agronomy and spatial distribution of pulse crops in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Gram (Chickpea) requires frequent heavy irrigation and prolonged standing water in the root zone during its flowering and pod-setting stages.
2. The expansion of assured canal and tubewell irrigation for high-yielding wheat varieties across the Indo-Gangetic plains displaced Gram cultivation towards the rainfed central and Deccan plateaus.
3. Tur (Pigeonpea) is predominantly cultivated as a Kharif crop possessing a deep taproot system that confers drought resilience, whereas Masoor (Lentil) is cultivated as a Rabi crop.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Gram (Chickpea) is a subtropical winter pulse adapted to residual soil moisture that suffers severe flower drop and wilt under heavy irrigation or rain during flowering. Post-Green Revolution expansion of irrigated HYV wheat pushed pulses out of the Indo-Gangetic plains into rainfed central India.

exp.why: Gram (Chickpea) is a hardy dryland Rabi crop cultivated primarily on conserved residual soil moisture, requiring at most one or two light irrigations (pre-flowering and pod development). Heavy irrigation, winter cloudiness, or waterlogging during the flowering stage impairs root aeration, induces excessive vegetative growth at the expense of pod formation, triggers flower shedding, and promotes Fusarium wilt.

Following the Green Revolution in the late 1960s and 1970s, the combination of assured irrigation, input subsidies, and Minimum Support Price procurement for high-yielding wheat varieties rendered low-yielding, risk-prone Gram uncompetitive in Punjab, Haryana, and Western Uttar Pradesh, shifting its core production belt to rainfed Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan.

Tur (Arhar/Pigeonpea) is a long-duration, predominantly rainfed Kharif pulse whose deep, extensive taproot extracts moisture from deeper soil horizons and breaks hardpans, whereas Masoor (Lentil) is a cool-season leguminous Rabi crop grown across central and eastern India.

ref: NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 3 (Land Resources and Agriculture); ICAR Handbook of Agriculture

stem: With reference to the agro-climatic thresholds and seasonal distribution of oilseed crops in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Sesamum (Til) is cultivated primarily as a winter Rabi crop in Northern India and as a rainfed Kharif crop in Southern India due to its high tolerance to winter frost.

2. Rapeseed and mustard are tropical oilseeds requiring high temperatures and heavy monsoon rainfall during their vegetative phase, whereas groundnut is a subtropical winter crop that thrives under cool temperatures and mild frost.
3. Soybean is predominantly cultivated in India as an irrigated Rabi crop across the arid plains of Western Rajasthan, whereas Castor seed cultivation is confined to temperate Himalayan valleys.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Oilseed crops in India exhibit sharp thermal and photoperiodic zoning: tropical crops like Sesamum and Castor flip from Kharif in frost-prone North India to Rabi in milder South India, while subtropical Rapeseed-Mustard is strictly a cool-season Rabi crop.

exp.why: Sesamum (Til) is a tropical crop that requires warm temperatures (25°C–30°C) and is highly susceptible to frost and prolonged cold. Consequently, it is grown as a rainfed Kharif crop in North India (before winter frost sets in) and as a Rabi crop in South India (where winter temperatures remain warm enough to support growth).

This reverses the climatic requirements of the two oilseeds. Rapeseed and mustard are subtropical Rabi crops grown during the cool, dry winter season across northwestern and central India (15°C–25°C), whereas Groundnut is predominantly a tropical rainfed Kharif crop (accounting for over 80% of output, with a minor summer/Rabi share in South India) that is highly vulnerable to frost and prolonged cold.

Soybean in India is overwhelmingly a rainfed Kharif crop concentrated in the medium-to-deep black soils (Vertisols) of the Malwa Plateau in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and southeastern Rajasthan. Castor seed is a warm-climate tropical/semi-arid oilseed grown as both a Kharif and Rabi crop primarily in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Andhra Pradesh/Telangana, not in temperate Himalayan valleys.

ref: NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 3; Khullar: India A Comprehensive Geography (Agriculture)

stem: With reference to the agro-climatic and edaphic conditions governing the cultivation of Cotton in India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It requires frequent showers and high atmospheric humidity during the boll-bursting and harvesting stages to prevent fibre brittle-fracture.
opts.B: Its rainfed cultivation across the Deccan Trap depends on lateritic soils that rapidly drain sub-soil moisture at the end of the southwest monsoon.
opts.C: It requires a minimum growing window of about 210 frost-free days, abundant sunshine during boll opening, and soils capable of retaining sub-soil moisture without waterlogging.
opts.D: Unlike the New World tetraploid species, the indigenous Old World diploid species of cotton possess extra-long staple fibres but lack natural tolerance to drought and sucking pests.

core: Cotton is a tropical/subtropical fibre crop requiring at least 210 frost-free days, moderate rainfall (50–100 cm), moisture-retentive Vertisols (Regur) or irrigated alluvial soils, and dry, sunny skies during boll bursting to prevent fungal boll rot and lint discolouration.

exp.why: Option C is correct because Cotton is highly sensitive to frost, requiring a minimum of ~210 frost-free days and warm temperatures (21°C–30°C). During the boll-opening and picking stages, clear skies and bright sunshine are vital; rainfall or high humidity at maturity (Option A) stains the lint, induces fungal boll rot, and degrades fibre quality. In the Deccan Trap, rainfed cotton thrives on Black soils/Vertisols (Regur), not lateritic soils (Option B), because montmorillonite clay swells when wet and retains sub-soil moisture deep into the post-monsoon dry season. Furthermore, indigenous Old World diploid species (Gossypium arboreum and G. herbaceum) have short-to-medium staple fibres and high inherent resistance to drought and pests, whereas New World tetraploid species (G. hirsutum and G. barbadense) yield long and extra-long staple fibres (making Option D incorrect).

ref: NCERT Class X: Contemporary India-II, Ch. 4; NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the cultivation and processing of Jute in India:
items: Statement-I: Commercial jute cultivation in India remains heavily concentrated in the lower Gangetic plain, the Brahmaputra valley, and the Mahanadi delta because the crop rapidly exhausts soil nutrients and relies on annual silt replenishment by floodwaters.

Statement-II: The post-harvest retting of jute requires immersing the stalks in fast-flowing, brackish coastal waters so that dissolved salts chemically dissolve the pectin matrix without microbial intervention.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Jute is a nutrient-exhaustive hot-and-humid crop requiring annual alluvial silt renewal (Khadar) for vegetative growth and abundant, warm, slow-flowing soft freshwater for biological retting by pectinolytic microbes.

exp.why: Jute rapidly depletes soil nitrogen and mineral nutrients during its intense 120-day vegetative growth cycle. Therefore, it performs best on fresh alluvial loams (Khadar) of the Hooghly basin, lower Assam/Brahmaputra valley, North Bihar, and Mahanadi delta that receive annual renewal of fertile silt through seasonal flooding.

Retting is not an abiotic chemical reaction in brackish water; it is a biological fermentation process mediated by aerobic and anaerobic pectinolytic bacteria and fungi that decompose the pectin and hemicellulose gums binding the bast fibres to the woody core (hurd). It requires abundant, warm (around 30°C–34°C), slow-flowing, soft freshwater; brackish/saline or iron-laden water inhibits microbial retting and stains the fibre dark grey ('shyamla'), destroying its golden lustre.

ref: NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 3; Central Research Institute for Jute and Allied Fibres (ICAR-CRIJAF)

stem: With reference to the regional contrast between Tropical (Peninsular) and Subtropical (Indo-Gangetic) sugarcane cultivation in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Compared to Peninsular India, the Indo-Gangetic plains achieve a higher average sucrose recovery percentage and a longer mill-crushing season due to perennial canal irrigation.
2. During the ripening and pre-harvest stage, sugarcane requires cool, dry, and sunny weather to arrest vegetative elongation and promote sucrose accumulation in the stalks.

3. The absence of desiccating summer 'Loo' winds and winter frost in Peninsular India prevents sucrose inversion and stalk shrinkage, contributing to higher per-hectare cane productivity than in North India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although the subtropical Indo-Gangetic belt accounts for the largest area under sugarcane, tropical Peninsular India achieves higher per-hectare yields, superior sucrose content, and a longer crushing season due to maritime moderation free of summer Loo winds and winter frost.

exp.why: Despite Uttar Pradesh having the largest area under sugarcane, Peninsular states (Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu) achieve a significantly higher average sucrose recovery rate and a much longer crushing season (often 7 to 8 months in the South compared to 4 to 6 months in the North) because moderate tropical temperatures allow staggered planting (Adsali, Eksali, and Suru crops) and prevent thermal extremes.

While sugarcane requires warm temperatures (21°C–27°C) and high moisture during its vegetative grand-growth phase, the ripening phase requires cool, dry, frost-free, and sunny weather with a distinct diurnal temperature range. Heavy rainfall or high temperatures during ripening sustain vegetative growth and convert stored sucrose back into reducing sugars, lowering juice quality.

In the subtropical North Indian plains, scorching summer 'Loo' winds temporarily arrest stalk growth and increase fibre coarseness, while winter frost kills apical buds and triggers enzymatic inversion of sucrose into glucose and fructose, reducing both per-hectare yield and crystalline sugar recovery compared to Peninsular India.

ref: NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 3; Majid Husain: Geography of India (Agriculture)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the phenology and geomorphic requirements of Tea cultivation in India:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the tea estates of the Nilgiri and Cardamom hills in Southern India that undergo a prolonged winter dormancy, tea plantations in the Brahmaputra valley and Darjeeling hills permit continuous leaf plucking throughout all twelve months of the year.

Statement-II: Although the tea bush requires 150 to 300 cm of well-distributed annual rainfall, its root system cannot tolerate stagnant water and requires well-drained hill slopes with deep, friable, acidic soils devoid of free calcium carbonate.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Tea is a calcifuge plantation crop requiring heavy rainfall on well-drained acidic slopes (pH 4.5–5.5) to prevent root asphyxiation. Subtropical North-Eastern tea estates enter winter dormancy ('banjhi') from December to February, whereas tropical South Indian hill estates flush and are plucked year-round.

exp.why: This statement reverses the regional phenology of tea in India. In North-Eastern India (Assam valley, Dooars, and Darjeeling), the drop in winter minimum temperatures below 13°C–16°C and shorter winter day-lengths induce a pronounced winter dormancy period from December to late February/March during which vegetative flushing stops and no plucking takes place. Conversely, in the Nilgiri, Anamalai, and Cardamom hills of Southern India, lower latitudes and equitable montane temperatures without severe winter cold enable continuous flushing and plucking throughout the year.

Tea requires high, evenly distributed rainfall (150–300 cm) to stimulate continuous sprouting of tender apical buds ('two leaves and a bud'), but its feeder roots are extremely sensitive to oxygen deprivation caused by waterlogging. Hence, it is grown on undulating hill slopes or drained terraces ('bheels' with drainage trenches) with deep, humus-rich, acidic soils (pH 4.5–5.5) free of lime/calcium carbonate.

ref: NCERT Class XII: India People and Economy, Ch. 3; G.C. Leong: Certificate Physical and Human Geography (Plantation Agriculture)

stem: With reference to the agro-climatic requirements and cultivation of coffee in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Compared to Coffea arabica, Coffea canephora (Robusta) requires higher and cooler elevations between 1,000 and 1,500 metres, heavier two-tier canopy shade, and is substantially more susceptible to leaf rust and white stem borer.

2. In the coffee tracts of the Western Ghats, a spell of dry winter weather is essential to induce floral bud dormancy, which is subsequently broken by pre-monsoon convective 'Blossom Showers' in March–April to trigger synchronized flowering.

3. Beyond its traditional core in the Western Ghats of Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu, shade-grown Arabica coffee has been successfully established on the bauxite-capped lateritic hills of the Araku Valley in the Eastern Ghats.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Coffea arabica is a high-altitude (1,000–1,500 m), cooler-climate (15°C–25°C), shade-demanding species sensitive to leaf rust and white stem borer, whereas Coffea canephora (Robusta) thrives at lower, warmer, more humid elevations (500–1,000 m) with greater pest resilience. Both species rely on winter moisture stress followed by pre-monsoon 'Blossom Showers' (and subsequent 'Backing Showers') to initiate uniform anthesis and berry setting.

exp.why: Statement 1 swaps the ecological profiles of Arabica and Robusta coffee. Coffea arabica requires higher, cooler elevations (1,000–1,500 metres above mean sea level), an equable temperature range of 15°C–25°C, heavier shade, and is highly vulnerable to coffee leaf rust (Hemileia vastatrix) and Xylotrechus quadripes (white stem borer). Conversely, Coffea canephora (Robusta) thrives at lower, warmer, and more humid altitudes (500–1,000 metres) with temperatures of 20°C–30°C, requires lighter shade, and exhibits markedly higher resistance to leaf rust and stem borer.

Statement 2 is correct. Coffee physiology requires a distinct rainless period of 60–90 days during winter (December–February) so that floral buds mature and enter dormancy. Light pre-monsoon convectional rains in March–April (known in Karnataka and Kerala as 'Blossom Showers' or 'Mango Showers') relieve moisture tension inside the buds, triggering synchronized blossoming within 8–10 days.

Statement 3 is correct. While the Western Ghats (Bababudangiri, Kodagu, Chikmagalur, Wayanad, and Nilgiris) account for the bulk of Indian coffee output, non-traditional areas in the Eastern Ghats—most notably the Araku Valley and Chintapalli tracts of Andhra Pradesh and Koraput in Odisha (at elevations of 900–1,200 m with red lateritic soils)—cultivate GI-tagged, shade-grown Arabica coffee under tribal agroforestry systems.

ref: Coffee Board of India Agronomy Guide; NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5; Khullar India: A Comprehensive Geography

stem: Consider the following pairs associating high-value specialized crops in India with their characteristic geomorphic and edaphic habitats:
items: 1. Saffron (Crocus sativus) : Glacio-fluvial-lacustrine Karewa terraces of the Kashmir Valley
2. Small Cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum) : Humid, shaded evergreen forest understoreys of the Southern Western Ghats
3. Natural Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) : Semi-arid, frost-prone basaltic plateaus of the rain-shadow Deccan interior
4. Cashew (Anacardium occidentale) : Waterlogged, heavy alkaline clay-pan depressions of the central Indo-Gangetic plains
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Specialized plantation and spice crops in India occupy tightly defined geomorphic and micro-climatic niches governed by drainage, soil pH, frost sensitivity, and humidity. While Saffron requires well-drained calcareous Karewa lacustrine tablelands and Small Cardamom thrives in filtered evergreen forest shade, Natural Rubber and Cashew require warm, frost-free, well-drained acidic lateritic slopes rather than semi-arid Deccan plateaus or waterlogged alkaline plains.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Pampore and adjoining tracts in the Kashmir Valley cultivate GI-tagged Kashmir Saffron (Zafran) on Karewas—thick Pleistocene unconsolidated gravel, sand, and silt-clay deposits of glacio-fluvial-lacustrine origin. Their elevated terrace topography ensures rapid sub-surface drainage (preventing corm rot) alongside cold snowy winters and warm dry autumns.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Small Cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum) is indigenous to the moist evergreen forests of the Western Ghats (notably the Cardamom Hills of Idukki in Kerala, Kodagu in Karnataka, and Anamalai/Palani hills in Tamil Nadu) at 600–1,500 m elevation. It requires filtered canopy shade, organic-rich forest loams with pH 5.0–6.5, and high relative humidity.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Natural Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) is an equatorial tree crop requiring deep, well-drained, acidic lateritic or red alluvial soils (pH 4.5–6.0), equable warm temperatures (25°C–34°C), high relative humidity, and over 200 cm of well-distributed annual rainfall without frost. It is grown in the foothills of Kerala and Kanyakumari, as well as in Tripura, Assam, and Meghalaya using cold-tolerant clones—not on semi-arid, frost-prone basaltic Deccan rain-shadow plateaus.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Cashew is a tropical, frost-sensitive tree crop that thrives on well-drained coastal sandy dunes, red loams, and lateritic hill slopes along the West Coast (Konkan, Malabar, Goa, Dakshina Kannada) and East Coast (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu). It cannot tolerate severe winter frost, poor drainage, or heavy waterlogged alkaline clay pans.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 2; ICAR Handbook of Horticulture; Spices Board & Rubber Board of India

stem: With reference to the methodological frameworks used to classify India into 15 Agro-Climatic Zones and 20 Agro-Ecological Regions, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the erstwhile Planning Commission delineated India into 15 Agro-Climatic Zones for decentralized regional agricultural planning, the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP) classified the country into 20 Agro-Ecological Regions.

2. The bioclimate parameter of 'Length of Growing Period' (LGP)—defined as the continuous number of days in a year when soil moisture availability and temperature permit crop growth—was the primary quantitative criterion used by the Planning Commission for its 15 Agro-Climatic Zones, whereas NBSS&LUP excluded soil moisture regimes from its 20 Agro-Ecological Regions.

3. Under the NBSS&LUP framework, two areas receiving identical annual rainfall can be placed in different Agro-Ecological Regions if their dominant soil types differ substantially in water-holding capacity, such as deep black Vertisols versus shallow red Alfisols.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's 15 Agro-Climatic Zones (Planning Commission, 1989) were delineated primarily using macro-level physiography, climate (rainfall/temperature), and administrative boundaries for Seventh Plan resource allocation. In contrast, the 20 Agro-Ecological Regions (NBSS&LUP / ICAR) integrate four homogeneous bio-physical layers—Physiography, Soils (soil-scape), Bioclimate, and Length of Growing Period (LGP)—capturing how soil water retention modifies effective moisture availability.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. During the mid-term appraisal of the Seventh Five-Year Plan (1989), the Planning Commission divided India into 15 broad Agro-Climatic Zones (later subdivided by NARP/ICAR into 127 sub-zones) for decentralized regional agricultural planning. Subsequently, the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP) under ICAR delineated 20 Agro-Ecological Regions (and 60 Agro-Ecological Sub-Regions).

Statement 2 is incorrect because it reverses the methodological criteria of the two frameworks. Length of Growing Period (LGP)—the period in days when precipitation plus soil moisture storage exceeds half of potential evapotranspiration (0.5 PET) under conducive temperatures—is the core quantitative cornerstone of the NBSS&LUP's 20 Agro-Ecological Regions, NOT the Planning Commission's 15 Agro-Climatic Zones.

Statement 3 is correct. Because LGP depends not merely on rainfall receipt but also on post-rainy season moisture stored in the soil profile, a region with deep, clayey black Vertisols (capable of holding 200–250 mm of available water per metre depth) sustains a significantly longer LGP than an adjacent region with shallow, gravelly red Alfisols (holding <100 mm) under the exact same rainfall regime, placing them in distinct Agro-Ecological Regions.

ref: NBSS&LUP Publication No. 24 (Agro-Ecological Regions of India); ICAR Handbook of Agriculture; Planning Commission Agro-Climatic Regional Planning Report

stem: In large rainfed lowland tracts of eastern and central India (such as Bihar, West Bengal, Odisha, and Chhattisgarh), farmers broadcast the seeds of short-duration winter pulses or oilseeds—such as lentil, lathyrus (khesari), or linseed—directly into the standing, maturing Kharif paddy crop about two weeks prior to its harvest. This enables the succeeding Rabi crop to germinate and establish using residual surface moisture without any intermediate ploughing, thereby overcoming terminal moisture stress and turnaround-time delays. In agronomic terminology, this sequential cropping system is known as:

opts.B: Relay cropping (locally termed Paira or Utera cultivation)

core: Relay cropping (known as Paira in Bihar/West Bengal/Odisha and Utera in Chhattisgarh/Madhya Pradesh) is a sequential multiple-cropping system in which the second crop is sown into the first crop after the first crop has reached its reproductive stage (flowering) but before it is harvested. It maximizes resource-use efficiency in rainfed rice-fallow ecosystems by capturing rapidly receding post-monsoon soil moisture without tillage.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. Relay cropping is analogous to a relay race where the first crop hands over the land to the next crop before leaving the field. In eastern and central India's rainfed lowland paddy ecosystems, ploughing heavy puddle-cracked clay soils after paddy harvest causes rapid evaporation of residual moisture and delays Rabi sowing into winter cold. By broadcasting seeds of hardy pulses (lentil, lathyrus, chickpea, field pea) or oilseeds (linseed) into standing paddy 10–15 days before harvest (called Paira or Utera cropping), seedlings establish under the humid paddy canopy and grow on residual moisture. Option (A) Alley cropping involves growing arable crops in alleys between rows of perennial woody leguminous shrubs/trees (e.g., Leucaena). Option (C) Ratoon cropping involves raising a fresh crop from the regrowth of basal stubble/suckers of a harvested crop (e.g., sugarcane, banana, sorghum) without replanting seeds. Option (D) Strip intercropping involves growing two or more crops simultaneously in wide, alternating strips that permit independent mechanical cultivation.

ref: ICAR Textbook of Agronomy (Reddy & Reddy); National Food Security Mission (NFSM) Rice-Fallow Pulse Guidelines

stem: With reference to agricultural land-use metrics and crop-water relationships in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Since Cropping Intensity is a measure of horizontal agricultural expansion, a State can increase its Cropping Intensity only by bringing additional cultivable wasteland or fallow land into its Net Sown Area (NSA).

2. The 'Consumptive Use' of water by a crop encompasses the water lost through evaporation from the adjacent soil surface, transpiration through plant stomata, and the water metabolically incorporated into plant tissues.

3. For any irrigated field crop in a dry season, the gross 'Irrigation Requirement' at the field head is always numerically lower than its 'Consumptive Use' because soil leaching and application losses reduce the volume of water that must be supplied.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Cropping Intensity—defined as (Gross Cropped Area / Net Sown Area) × 100—measures vertical land-use intensification via multiple cropping on the same plot during an agricultural year, rather than horizontal expansion of Net Sown Area. In crop-water accounting, Field Irrigation Requirement in dry seasons exceeds Consumptive Use (Evapotranspiration + metabolic water) because percolation, conveyance/application losses, and salt-leaching demands must be supplied over and above net plant evapotranspiration.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Cropping Intensity is calculated as (Gross Cropped Area / Net Sown Area) × 100. It measures vertical (intensive) agricultural land utilization—how many times a given physical unit of Net Sown Area is cultivated within a single agricultural year (July to June). By raising two or three sequential crops (Kharif, Rabi, Zaid) on the exact same plot through assured irrigation and short-duration varieties, Gross Cropped Area rises while Net Sown Area remains unchanged, thereby increasing Cropping Intensity without any horizontal expansion into forests or wastelands.

Statement 2 is correct.
