In irrigation agronomy, 'Consumptive Use' (CU) represents the total quantity of water consumed by a crop for survival and biomass synthesis: (a) evaporation from the cropped soil/water surface, (b) transpiration through plant foliage, and (c) water retained metabolically for building plant tissues (which normally constitutes less than 1% of total evapotranspiration, making CU practically nearly equal to Evapotranspiration).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Crop Water Requirement (CWR) equals Consumptive Use plus water needed for special operations (such as puddling, land preparation, and leaching of root-zone salts) plus unavoidable percolation and application losses. Field Irrigation Requirement equals (CWR minus Effective Rainfall) divided by field application efficiency. During a dry season when effective rainfall is zero or negligible, soil leaching and application losses increase (rather than decrease) the gross volume of water needed, making the gross Irrigation Requirement substantially higher than Consumptive Use.

ref: NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5; ICAR Principles of Agronomy (S.R. Reddy)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the regional distribution of surface irrigation systems in India:
items: Statement-I: In the interior Peninsular plateau of southern India, surface water storage through earthen and masonry tanks is hydro-geologically viable because the undulating terrain is underlain by hard, impermeable Archaean crystalline rocks that prevent the rapid downward seepage of impounded rainwater.

Statement-II: Unlike the youthful, actively down-cutting Himalayan rivers that frequently shift their courses across unconsolidated plains, the east-flowing rivers of the Peninsular plateau have reached a senile stage of grading and form extensive, fertile deltas along the Bay of Bengal coast.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Tank irrigation thrives across the interior Peninsular plateau (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka) due to three local controls: impermeable crystalline gneissic/granitic bedrock preventing percolation loss, undulating relief offering natural depressions for bunding, and torrential seasonal monsoon streams requiring storage. Conversely, the graded deltas of east-flowing Peninsular rivers along the Bay of Bengal explain the development of coastal deltaic canal networks rather than interior plateau tanks.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Tank irrigation has historically flourished across the Peninsular Deccan because: (1) the underlying Archaean gneisses, granites, and schists are hard and non-porous, minimizing downward seepage losses from shallow surface reservoirs; (2) the undulating topography naturally forms shallow basins that can be impounded easily by constructing earthen bunds across seasonal streams; and (3) hard rock makes digging deep canals and tube-wells costly.

Statement-II is also correct. Major east-flowing Peninsular rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) flow through broad, graded, senile valleys with low gradients and build extensive alluvial deltas along the Eastern Coastal Plain. However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: the delta-building character of east-flowing rivers along the coastal plain accounts for dense deltaic canal irrigation (such as the Kaveri, Godavari, and Krishna delta canal systems), whereas interior plateau tank irrigation is governed by impermeable crystalline lithology, undulating relief, and seasonal rainfed streams.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment Ch. 3; Khullar India: A Comprehensive Geography Ch. on Irrigation

stem: Consider the following statements regarding soil degradation in the irrigated tracts of India:
items: Statement-I: Extensive tracts of fertile alluvial and arid soils in the canal command areas of north-western India have degraded into saline and alkaline efflorescences locally known as Reh, Kallar, or Usar.

Statement-II: In semi-arid canal command areas where annual potential evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation, continuous seepage from unlined perennial canals depresses upward capillary movement in the soil profile and leaches soluble sodium, calcium, and magnesium salts below the root zone.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Secondary salinization in semi-arid canal command areas occurs when seepage from unlined canals and flood over-irrigation raise the water table within the critical capillary fringe (2 to 3 metres below the surface). High atmospheric evaporative demand then draws groundwater laden with dissolved sodium, calcium, and magnesium salts upward through soil capillaries, leaving white saline-alkaline crusts (Reh or Kallar) upon evaporation.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Intensive perennial canal irrigation in semi-arid regions such as Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, and the Indira Gandhi Canal command area in northern Rajasthan has led to widespread waterlogging and secondary salinization/alkalinization, rendering once-productive soils infertile under surface salt encrustations locally termed Reh, Kallar, Usar, or Thur.

Statement-II is incorrect as it reverses the vertical direction of soil-water and solute movement. Seepage from unlined perennial canals elevates the shallow groundwater table close to the land surface. Because annual potential evapotranspiration greatly exceeds rainfall in semi-arid climates, a strong upward hydraulic gradient is established; dissolved sodium, calcium, and magnesium salts are drawn upward by capillary action into the topsoil rather than being leached downward, precipitating as surface crusts when the moisture evaporates.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch. 6 (Soils); Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) Handbook of Agriculture on Saline and Alkali Soils

stem: With reference to the hydraulic and agronomic suitability of pressurized micro-irrigation systems in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. On undulating sandy terrain with excessively high infiltration rates, sprinkler irrigation prevents the deep percolation losses and land-levelling costs associated with conventional surface flood irrigation.

2. When irrigating crops with moderately saline groundwater in high-wind arid regions, overhead sprinkler systems are agronomically superior to drip irrigation because aerial spraying dilutes dissolved salts before the water reaches the crop canopy.

3. In drip irrigation systems, soluble fertilizers applied through fertigation are delivered directly into the active root zone, which minimizes both weed proliferation in inter-row spaces and nutrient leaching below the rhizosphere.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sprinkler irrigation mimics rainfall and is well suited to undulating, highly permeable sandy soils where surface flooding causes rapid percolation losses, but it suffers from high wind-drift evaporation and causes foliar salt burn when saline water is used. Drip irrigation applies water directly to the root zone at low tension, preventing leaf wetting and pushing salts to the outer periphery of the wetting bulb.

exp.why: Sandy and loamy-sand soils on undulating topography (such as the stabilized dunes and bagar tracts of Rajasthan and southern Haryana) have very high infiltration rates and low water-holding capacity. Surface flood irrigation on such land fails because water percolates rapidly near the field inlet before reaching the tail end, whereas overhead sprinklers distribute controlled water depth uniformly without requiring expensive land levelling.

Overhead sprinkler irrigation is contraindicated when using moderately saline groundwater in hot, high-wind arid environments. High wind drift and partial in-flight evaporation actually increase the salt concentration of the falling droplets, coating the crop leaves with toxic sodium and chloride ions that cause severe foliar scorching and necrosis. Conversely, drip irrigation is far superior for saline water management because it avoids wetting the foliage and maintains constantly high soil moisture (high matric potential) inside the root zone while displacing salts toward the perimeter of the wetted zone.

Drip fertigation injects water-soluble nutrients directly into the rhizosphere in small, synchronized splits matching crop uptake stages. Because the inter-row soil surface remains dry and deep drainage is prevented, weed germination between crop rows is suppressed and nitrate/potash leaching losses are minimized.

ref: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) Operational Guidelines on Per Drop More Crop; ICAR Textbook of Irrigation Agronomy

stem: Consider the following pairs of indigenous hydro-agricultural and water-harvesting systems in India and their corresponding functional mechanisms and regions:
items: 1. Zabo : Impounding hill runoff through an integrated spatial cascade of hilltop forest catchment, mid-slope livestock enclosures, and valley-bottom paddy-cum-fish terraces in Nagaland
2. Ahar-Pyne : Horizontal tunnel adits excavated into porous lateritic hillocks to tap sub-surface seepage by gravity in the Northern Malabar region
3. Surangam : Earthen embankment constructed across lower hill slopes to arrest monsoon runoff and silt over rocky sandstone catchments in Jaisalmer
4. Khadin : Floodwater diversion channels leading from seasonal rivers into three-sided embanked retention basins in the South Bihar plains
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: India's traditional water-harvesting architectures are finely calibrated to local lithology and monsoon regimes: Zabo integrates forestry, cattle manuring, and wet-rice terracing in Nagaland; Ahar-Pyne diverts flashy river floods into retention basins in South Bihar; Surangam taps lateritic groundwater via horizontal adits in Kasargod/Northern Malabar; and Khadin traps sheet runoff behind earthen bunds in arid Jaisalmer.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The Zabo (or Ruza) system practiced by the Chakhesang tribe in Phek district of Nagaland is an indigenous watershed system on steep hill slopes where protected hilltop forests serve as the catchment, runoff passes through mid-slope water-harvesting ponds and cattle corrals (picking up organic manure), and finally irrigates and fertilizes paddy-cum-fish fields at the foot of the slope.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Ahar-Pyne is the indigenous floodwater-harvesting irrigation system of South Bihar (Magadh plains), where Pynes are artificial diversion channels drawn from seasonal rivers and Ahars are rectangular catchment basins embanked on three sides to store water for Kharif paddy and Rabi crops. Horizontal tunnel adits dug into laterite hills in Northern Malabar (Kasargod) describe the Surangam system.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Surangam is a traditional subterranean water-harvesting system found in the lateritic hillocks of Kasargod district in northern Kerala and Dakshina Kannada in Karnataka. The earthen embankment (dhora) built across lower slopes to trap runoff and silt over rocky catchments in Jaisalmer (western Rajasthan) describes the Khadin system.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Khadin is an arid runoff-farming system designed by the Paliwal Brahmins in Jaisalmer, western Rajasthan, where monsoon sheet wash from gravelly uplands is impounded behind a crescent-shaped earthen bund, saturating the alluvial bed so crops can be grown on residual soil moisture. Floodwater diversion channels and retention basins in South Bihar describe the Ahar-Pyne system.

ref: NCERT Class XII India: People and Economy, Ch. 6 (Water Resources); CSE Dying Wisdom: Rise, Fall and Potential of India's Traditional Water Harvesting Systems

stem: In the official agronomic classification of unirrigated agriculture in India, which one of the following accurately distinguishes 'Dry Farming', 'Dryland Farming', and 'Rainfed Farming'?

opts.A: Dry Farming is practiced in semi-arid regions receiving 750 mm to 1,150 mm of annual rainfall with protective canal irrigation, Dryland Farming in arid regions receiving less than 750 mm relying entirely on dew and soil mulching, and Rainfed Farming in sub-humid regions receiving over 1,150 mm where multi-tier groundwater extraction is mandatory.
opts.B: Dry Farming is practiced in humid regions receiving over 1,150 mm of annual rainfall during the post-monsoon dry season, Dryland Farming in semi-arid regions receiving 750 mm to 1,150 mm with a primary focus on leaching saline soils, and Rainfed Farming in arid zones receiving less than 750 mm where drought-escaping ephemerals are cultivated.
opts.C: Dry Farming is practiced in arid regions with a crop-growing season exceeding 200 days under zero-tillage regimes, Dryland Farming in sub-humid regions with a crop-growing season of 120 to 180 days requiring subsurface tile drainage, and Rainfed Farming in semi-arid plateaus with a crop-growing season of less than 75 days.
opts.D: Dry Farming is practiced in arid regions receiving less than 750 mm of annual rainfall with a primary focus on moisture conservation, Dryland Farming in semi-arid regions receiving 750 mm to 1,150 mm requiring both moisture conservation and drainage, and Rainfed Farming in humid/sub-humid regions receiving over 1,150 mm where disposal of excess water is vital.

core: Unirrigated agriculture in India is stratified into three agronomic regimes based on annual precipitation, length of growing period (LGP), and water-management priorities: Dry Farming (<750 mm, arid, <75 days LGP, acute moisture stress), Dryland Farming (750–1,150 mm, semi-arid, 75–120 days LGP, dual conservation and drainage need), and Rainfed Farming (>1,150 mm, sub-humid to humid, >120 days LGP, drainage of excess runoff and erosion control).

exp.why: Option D is correct. According to the National Commission on Agriculture and ICAR agronomic classification: (1) Dry Farming covers arid regions receiving less than 750 mm annual rainfall, characterized by a short growing season (<75 days), frequent crop failures due to prolonged dry spells, single cropping, and an absolute priority on in-situ soil moisture conservation; (2) Dryland Farming covers semi-arid regions receiving 750–1,150 mm annual rainfall (growing season 75–120 days), where dry spells occur alongside occasional intense storms on black or red soils, necessitating both moisture conservation and safe surface drainage for intercropping/single cropping; and (3) Rainfed Farming covers sub-humid and humid regions receiving >1,150 mm rainfall (growing season >120 days), where water deficiency is rare and agronomic management prioritizes drainage of excess water, control of sheet/gully erosion, and management of soil acidity. Options A, B, and C invert the rainfall thresholds, irrigation status, and length of growing periods.

ref: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment; ICAR Handbook of Dryland Agriculture

stem: With reference to the physiological and ecological requirements of specialized horticultural and commercial crops in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Temperate pome and stone fruits such as apple and cherry cultivated in the Western Himalayas require uninterrupted warm winter temperatures above 15°C to prevent bud dormancy and initiate uniform spring blossoming.
2. Foxnut (Makhana), predominantly cultivated in the Mithila region of North Bihar, is a deep-water lotic crop that requires fast-flowing, well-oxygenated river channels to prevent seed decay.

3. Owing to its deep taproot architecture and waxy fronds, Oil Palm (Elaeis guineensis) has a significantly lower annual evapotranspiration demand than dryland oilseeds like mustard, making it naturally adapted to unirrigated semi-arid plateaus.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Specialized Indian crops exhibit strict ecophysiological niches: temperate Himalayan pome/stone fruits require cumulative winter chilling hours (<7°C) to break endodormancy; Foxnut (Makhana) thrives exclusively in shallow, stagnant lentic wetlands rich in organic detritus; and Oil Palm is a water-intensive humid tropical crop requiring high year-round soil moisture and humidity.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Temperate pome fruits (apple, pear) and stone fruits (cherry, plum, peach) enter physiological winter dormancy to survive freezing conditions and strictly require a cumulative quota of 'chilling hours'—typically 800 to 1,500 hours of winter temperatures below 7°C (45°F)—to break endodormancy and trigger synchronized spring bud-break and flowering. Winter warming above 7°C in lower Himalayan valleys disrupts chill accumulation, leading to delayed, erratic blossoming and prompting farmers to shift apple orchards to higher elevations or adopt low-chill cultivars.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Foxnut or Gorgon nut (Euryale ferox) is strictly a shallow, stagnant 'lentic' wetland crop—not a fast-flowing 'lotic' river crop. It thrives in stationary perennial water bodies, oxbow lakes (mauns), floodplain depressions (chaurs), and shallow farm ponds (1 to 1.5 metres water depth) containing a thick, nutrient-rich organic muck/sludge bottom in the Kosi-Mithila plains of North Bihar.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Oil Palm (Elaeis guineensis) possesses a fibrous adventitious root system concentrated largely in the top 50–60 cm of soil rather than a deep drought-escaping taproot. It is a humid tropical perennial with an exceptionally high year-round evapotranspiration demand (requiring 150–200 mm of well-distributed precipitation per month, or ~2,000 mm annually, without prolonged dry spells), meaning its cultivation outside humid zones in peninsular India requires assured year-round micro-irrigation, unlike low-water-demand dryland oilseeds such as mustard or sesamum.

ref: ICAR Handbook of Horticulture; National Mission on Edible Oils - Oil Palm (NMEO-OP) Agronomic Guidelines

stem: With reference to the ecophysiology and cropping patterns of coarse cereals in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Modern hybrid cultivars of maize are predominantly photo-insensitive and thermo-insensitive, enabling the crop to be cultivated across Kharif, Rabi, and Spring seasons in different agro-climatic regions of India.

2. While maize possesses well-developed aerenchyma tissues that allow it to withstand prolonged root-zone waterlogging in heavy clay soils, barley is highly susceptible to soil salinity and alkalinity.

3. In the lower-middle Gangetic plains of Bihar and across peninsular India, Rabi maize consistently achieves higher average grain yields per hectare than Kharif maize due to longer sunshine duration, lower pest incidence, and controlled irrigation.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Maize (Zea mays) is a C4 crop whose photo-thermo-insensitive hybrids allow year-round cultivation (Kharif, Rabi, and Spring), with Rabi maize outyielding Kharif maize due to cloud-free solar radiation and absence of monsoon waterlogging. However, maize is acutely sensitive to root-zone hypoxia from waterlogging, whereas barley (Hordeum vulgare) is the most salt- and alkali-tolerant winter cereal.

exp.why: Known as the 'Queen of Cereals' due to its high genetic yield potential among cereals, modern single-cross maize hybrids bred in India are largely day-neutral (photo-insensitive) and adaptable across wide thermal regimes, permitting cultivation in Kharif (monsoon), Rabi (winter in frost-free Bihar and peninsular India), and Zaid/Spring seasons.

Statement 2 swaps the edaphic stress tolerances of maize and barley. Maize lacks functional aerenchyma for prolonged submergence and is extremely sensitive to root-zone waterlogging and oxygen depletion (especially during the seedling to knee-high stages); standing water for even 24 to 48 hours severely stunts root respiration and nitrogen uptake. Conversely, barley (Hordeum vulgare) has exceptional tolerance to drought, soil salinity, and alkalinity, making it the preferred winter cereal on marginal Usar/saline soils where wheat fails.

Although Kharif accounts for the largest share of maize acreage in India, Rabi maize (grown extensively in Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka) achieves substantially higher productivity per hectare. Mild winter temperatures reduce respiratory losses, clear skies provide 7 to 9 hours of bright sunshine for C4 photosynthesis, controlled irrigation prevents monsoon waterlogging and nitrogen leaching, and weed/pest pressure is significantly lower.

ref: ICAR Indian Institute of Maize Research (IIMR) Agronomic Package of Practices; NCERT Class XII India: People and Economy, Ch. 5 (Land Resources and Agriculture)

stem: With reference to the edaphic and climatic requirements of commercial plantation and cash crops in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Premium Flue-Cured Virginia (FCV) cigarette tobacco requires heavy, nitrogen-rich clayey soils to develop thin, bright lemon-yellow leaves with mild aroma and superior combustibility.
2. Tobacco is highly sensitive to both frost and waterlogging, requiring a frost-free growing period of 100 to 120 days and well-aerated root zones.
3. Unlike the coconut palm, the arecanut palm thrives best in semi-arid rainfed plateaus characterized by wide diurnal temperature ranges and alkaline calcareous soils.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Flue-Cured Virginia (FCV) tobacco exhibits an inverse soil-nitrogen quality relationship where excess nitrogen and heavy clay produce coarse, pungent, poorly burning leaves; hence it prefers light, well-drained sandy or red loams low in organic nitrogen. Arecanut is a humid tropical crop requiring high moisture and shaded, well-drained lateritic or loamy valleys.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the edaphic requirement for quality cigarette tobacco. Excess soil nitrogen and heavy clayey soils promote luxuriant vegetative growth, resulting in thick, dark, coarse leaves with high nicotine, pungent smoke, and poor combustibility (burn rate). Premium Flue-Cured Virginia (FCV) tobacco requires light-textured, well-drained red sandy loams low in organic matter and nitrogen so that nitrogen is depleted as the leaf matures, enabling uniform yellowing during flue-curing.

Statement 2 is correct. Tobacco is a frost-sensitive crop requiring a frost-free period of 100 to 120 days with mean temperatures between 20°C and 27°C. Its root system is highly susceptible to oxygen deprivation and soil-borne pathogens (such as black shank) under waterlogged conditions.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Arecanut (Areca catechu) is a humid tropical palm that requires heavy, well-distributed rainfall (1500–3000 mm) or copious perennial irrigation, high relative humidity, and a narrow temperature range (15°C–35°C) free from extreme heat or frost. It thrives in well-drained acidic to neutral lateritic, red loamy, and alluvial soils (such as the Malnad valleys of Karnataka, Kerala, and Assam) and is intolerant of alkaline calcareous soils.

ref: ICAR Handbook of Agriculture; NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the pedological dynamics and regional nomenclature of shifting cultivation (slash-and-burn agriculture) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In tropical wet hill ecosystems where native soils are heavily leached and acidic, the burning of slashed forest biomass initially causes a temporary rise in topsoil pH and a flush of plant-available basic cations such as potassium, calcium, and magnesium.

2. The rapid decline in crop productivity after one or two cropping cycles in slash-and-burn plots is driven by the volatilization of nitrogen and sulfur during combustion, followed by accelerated surface runoff and leaching of soluble ash nutrients under torrential monsoon rains.
3. Shifting cultivation is traditionally known as 'Podu' in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, 'Bewar' or 'Dahiya' in Madhya Pradesh, and 'Kumari' in the Western Ghats.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Slash-and-burn cultivation in tropical hills relies on ash deposition to temporarily neutralize soil acidity and release exchangeable basic cations (Ca, Mg, K). However, exposure of steep slopes to intense monsoon rainfall rapidly leaches these soluble bases and erodes topsoil, forcing plot abandonment within 2–3 years.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Tropical hill soils (Oxisols and Ultisols) in high-rainfall zones are naturally acidic and deficient in available bases due to intense weathering. Incorporating alkaline wood ash from burned biomass acts as a temporary liming agent, raising topsoil pH, reducing aluminium toxicity, and releasing a sudden flush of soluble potassium, calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus.

Statement 2 is correct. During the burning phase, most of the aboveground organic carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur are lost to the atmosphere as gases. Once the forest canopy and litter layer are removed, torrential monsoon rains directly strike the bare hill slopes, causing rapid leaching of water-soluble ash nutrients (especially potassium) and severe sheet erosion.

Statement 3 is correct. In India, shifting cultivation is known as Jhum in the North-Eastern states, Podu (or Penda/Koman/Bringa) in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, Bewar or Dahiya in Madhya Pradesh, Kumari in the Western Ghats, and Waltre in south-eastern Rajasthan.

ref: NCERT Class X Contemporary India-II Ch. 4; Brady & Weil 'The Nature and Properties of Soils'

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the sustainability of the rice-wheat cropping system in the Trans-Gangetic Plains (Agro-Climatic Zone VI):
items: Statement-I: In the continuous rice-wheat rotation of the Trans-Gangetic Plains, the succeeding Rabi wheat crop frequently suffers from restricted root proliferation, temporary surface waterlogging upon irrigation, and induced micronutrient stress.

Statement-II: Repeated wet tillage (puddling) for transplanted Kharif paddy disperses clay particles and destroys soil macro-aggregates, creating a dense, compacted subsurface plough-pan at a depth of 15 to 20 cm.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In the rice-wheat monoculture of the Trans-Gangetic Plains, wet puddling for Kharif rice intentionally breaks down soil structure to reduce water percolation, forming a compacted subsurface hardpan at 15–20 cm depth. This edaphic alteration severely impedes deep root penetration, aeration, and water infiltration for the succeeding aerobic Rabi wheat crop.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Wheat is an aerobic upland crop requiring well-aggregated, porous soil for deep root growth and oxygen diffusion. When grown continuously after puddled transplanted rice in Punjab, Haryana, and Western Uttar Pradesh, wheat exhibits shallow rooting, yellowing after winter irrigation due to temporary oxygen depletion, and reduced uptake of immobile micronutrients like zinc, iron, and manganese.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Wet puddling (churning saturated soil with tractors) destroys natural soil aggregates and disperses clay particles, which settle and clog transmission pores while mechanical pressure compacts the soil at 15–20 cm depth into an impermeable plough-pan. While this hardpan reduces percolation losses during flooded paddy cultivation, it acts as a physical and hydraulic barrier for the subsequent Rabi wheat crop.

ref: Economic Survey (Agriculture Chapters); ICAR Report on Rice-Wheat Cropping System in Indo-Gangetic Plains

stem: With reference to biological nutrient management and conservation agriculture practices in Indian cropping systems, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While symbiotic Rhizobium bacteria are the primary biological nitrogen fixers in anaerobic, waterlogged lowland paddy fields, the Azolla-Anabaena symbiosis and free-living Cyanobacteria require well-aerated dryland pulse soils for nitrogenase activity.

2. In the rice-wheat belt of north-western India, zero-tillage seeding of wheat directly into standing rice stubbles conserves residual soil moisture, advances wheat sowing to mitigate terminal heat stress in March, and suppresses the emergence of the weed Phalaris minor.

3. Phosphorus-Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) such as Bacillus megaterium and Pseudomonas striata enhance crop phosphorus availability not by fixing atmospheric phosphorus, but by secreting organic acids that dissolve insoluble soil phosphates.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Biological nitrogen-fixing biofertilizers occupy distinct redox niches: Rhizobium requires aerobic leguminous root nodules where leghemoglobin regulates oxygen, whereas Azolla-Anabaena and Cyanobacteria thrive in flooded anaerobic paddy fields. Zero-tillage wheat sowing in rice residue conserves soil moisture, prevents terminal heat stress, and suppresses Phalaris minor.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the ecological niches of these biofertilizers. Symbiotic Rhizobium bacteria form nodules on the roots of leguminous pulses in well-aerated upland soils (using leghemoglobin to buffer oxygen for the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase enzyme) and fail under prolonged waterlogging. Conversely, the aquatic fern Azolla (harboring the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae) and free-living Blue-Green Algae (Cyanobacteria) are adapted to flooded, waterlogged lowland paddy ecosystems.

Statement 2 is correct. Zero-tillage (including Happy Seeder technology) allows direct drilling of wheat seeds into unploughed paddy fields immediately after harvest. This eliminates the 10–15 day turnaround time required for conventional tillage, ensuring timely November sowing that helps the wheat crop reach grain maturity before the onset of terminal heat stress in March, while minimal soil disturbance and surface mulch inhibit the germination of Phalaris minor (little seed canary grass).

Statement 3 is correct. Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus has no gaseous atmospheric pool for biological fixation. Most applied phosphorus gets chemically fixed in the soil as insoluble tricalcium phosphate (in alkaline soils) or iron/aluminium phosphates (in acidic soils). Phosphorus-Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) secrete low-molecular-weight organic acids (such as gluconic and citric acid) and phosphatase enzymes that chelate cations and convert insoluble phosphates into plant-available orthophosphate ions.

ref: NCERT Class XII Biology Ch. 10 (Microbes in Human Welfare); ICAR Conservation Agriculture Guidelines

stem: Consider the following major crops cultivated in India:
items: 1. Wheat
2. Sugarcane
3. Pearl Millet (Bajra)
4. Rice (Transplanted Paddy  - single season crop cycle )
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct ascending order of the above crops in terms of their total seasonal Consumptive Water Requirement (in mm) over their complete crop growth cycle?
core: Total seasonal consumptive water requirement (mm of evapotranspiration over the entire crop life cycle) depends on both daily transpiration intensity and total crop duration in the field. Because sugarcane remains in the field for 12 to 18 months spanning the peak summer evaporative period, its cumulative seasonal water requirement (1500–2500 mm) exceeds that of a single 120-day season of transplanted rice (1100–1400 mm).

exp.why: Wheat is a cool-season Rabi C3 cereal grown during winter when potential evapotranspiration is moderate. Its total seasonal consumptive water requirement ranges between 450 mm and 650 mm (typically delivered across 4 to 6 irrigations at critical physiological stages such as Crown Root Initiation, jointing, flowering, and milking), placing it second from the bottom after Pearl Millet.

Sugarcane has the highest cumulative seasonal consumptive water requirement (1500 mm to 2500 mm) among the listed crops because it is a long-duration (12 to 18 months) high-biomass crop whose formative and grand growth phases span the hot, dry summer months of April to June. Candidates frequently confuse daily water application intensity in flooded paddy with total full-lifecycle water depth.

Pearl Millet (Bajra) is a short-duration (75 to 90 days), drought-hardy C4 Kharif millet with high photosynthetic water-use efficiency and xerophytic leaf adaptations. It has the lowest total seasonal water requirement among the four crops, needing only 250 mm to 350 mm of moisture.

Transplanted lowland Rice (Paddy) has a high daily water requirement due to puddling, surface evaporation, and percolation in standing water, totaling 1100 mm to 1400 mm over a single 100 to 140 day cropping season. This places it above Wheat (450–650 mm) but below long-duration Sugarcane (1500–2500 mm), yielding the ascending sequence 3 - 1 - 4 - 2.

ref: ICAR Handbook of Agriculture (Water Management Chapter); Reddy & Reddi 'Principles of Agronomy'

stem: With reference to the physiological and agro-ecological impacts of climate change and elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide on Indian agriculture, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations (in the absence of extreme thermal stress), C4 crops such as maize, pearl millet, sorghum, and sugarcane exhibit a much stronger photosynthetic boost from the CO2 fertilization effect than C3 crops such as rice, wheat, and pulses.

2. Elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide levels induce a 'nutritional dilution' effect in C3 staple grains like wheat and rice, lowering the grain concentrations of protein and essential micronutrients such as iron and zinc.

3. Rising winter temperatures in the Western Himalayas have reduced cumulative winter chilling hours in lower valleys, driving an upward altitudinal shift of the commercial temperate apple belt toward higher elevations.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: C3 crops (rice, wheat, pulses) experience a stronger photosynthetic CO2 fertilization response than C4 crops (maize, sorghum, bajra, sugarcane) because elevated CO2 suppresses photorespiration in RuBisCO, whereas C4 plants already concentrate CO2 in bundle-sheath cells. However, elevated CO2 causes carbohydrate-driven nutritional dilution of protein, iron, and zinc in C3 grains.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the physiological response of C3 and C4 pathways to elevated CO2. In C3 plants (rice, wheat, barley, pulses), the RuBisCO enzyme is not CO2-saturated at ambient levels and loses significant carbon to photorespiration; hence elevated atmospheric CO2 suppresses photorespiration and strongly stimulates net photosynthesis. In contrast, C4 crops (maize, sorghum, pearl millet, sugarcane) possess an internal biochemical CO2 pump (PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells) that already saturates RuBisCO in bundle-sheath cells, so they show minimal direct photosynthetic stimulation from rising atmospheric CO2.

Statement 2 is correct. Free-Air CO2 Enrichment (FACE) studies demonstrate that when C3 cereals like wheat and rice grow under elevated atmospheric CO2, accelerated starch synthesis and reduced stomatal conductance (which lowers transpiration-driven mass flow of soil nitrogen and minerals) cause a 'nutritional dilution' effect, reducing grain concentrations of protein, iron (Fe), and zinc (Zn) by 5% to 15%.

Statement 3 is correct. Temperate apple cultivars require 800 to 1,200+ cumulative winter chilling hours (temperatures below 7°C) to break winter dormancy and induce normal spring flowering. Warming winters in the lower mid-hills of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir (1,200–1,800 m) have created chilling deficits and erratic blossoming, shifting commercial apple cultivation upward above 2,200–2,500 m into higher cold-arid valleys such as Kinnaur, Lahaul, and Spiti.

ref: IPCC AR6 WGII Ch. 5 (Food, Fibre, and Other Ecosystem Products); ICAR-NICRA Climate Change Impact Reports

stem: With reference to the lithological and stratigraphic controls on mineral distribution across the geological provinces of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Archaean-Proterozoic Dharwar greenstone-schist belts serve as the principal geological host for India's Banded Iron Formations (BIFs) and polymetallic gold-bearing quartz reefs.

2. The Purana sedimentary basins of the Vindhyan Supergroup are extensively mineralized with hydrothermal base-metal sulphide veins of copper, lead, and zinc, while remaining largely devoid of flux-grade limestones.
3. The Permo-Carboniferous Gondwana Supergroup preserved within intracratonic faulted grabens along river valleys accounts for over ninety-five percent of India's bituminous coal reserves.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's mineral geography is strictly governed by stratigraphic evolution: ancient crystalline cratons (Dharwar and Aravalli-Delhi systems) host metallic ores and base-metal sulphides, Proterozoic Vindhyan basins yield non-metallic limestones and kimberlite diamonds, and Gondwana intracratonic grabens preserve bituminous coal.

exp.why: The Archaean-Proterozoic Dharwar Supergroup (comprising volcano-sedimentary greenstone belts and schists in Karnataka, alongside equivalent Iron Ore Group formations in Singhbhum-Odisha and Bailadila) underwent intense metamorphism and hydrothermal activity, hosting the bulk of India's high-grade Banded Iron Formations (BIFs), manganese, and auriferous (gold-bearing) quartz reefs such as Kolar and Hutti.

This statement swaps the metallogenic signature of the Vindhyan system with that of the Aravalli-Delhi and Dharwar systems. The Vindhyan Supergroup consists predominantly of unmetamorphosed marine and fluviatile shales, sandstones, and limestones; it is famous for non-metallic minerals—specifically cement-grade and steel-flux-grade limestone, ornamental building stones, and diamondiferous kimberlite/conglomerate pipes (Panna belt)—and is virtually devoid of metalliferous base-metal sulphide veins.

Over 98% of India's total coal reserves (and virtually all of its metallurgical and thermal bituminous coal) belong to the Permo-Carboniferous Lower Gondwana formations (Damuda series: Karharbari, Barakar, and Raniganj stages) preserved within down-faulted intracratonic trough basins (grabens) aligned along the Damodar, Son-Mahanadi, and Pranhita-Godavari river valleys.

ref: NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5; D.R. Khullar 'India: A Comprehensive Geography' Ch. 3 & 19

stem: With reference to the major iron ore belts of India, their mining ranges, and export port linkages, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The high-grade hematite deposits of the Badampahar-Gorumahisani range in Mayurbhanj and the Gua-Noamundi range in Singhbhum form integral parts of the Odisha-Jharkhand iron ore belt.
2. Iron ore mined from the Bailadila range in the Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt is transported primarily via a dedicated slurry pipeline and rail corridor to Paradip Port for export.

3. Despite possessing relatively lower average iron content than the Bailadila and Singhbhum ores, the deposits of the Maharashtra-Goa belt remain viable for export due to their friable nature amenable to beneficiation and short inland waterway connectivity to Mormugao Port.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's four principal iron ore belts exhibit distinct grade profiles and dedicated port hinterlands: Bailadila (Chhattisgarh) is linked to Visakhapatnam, Daitari-Keonjhar (Odisha) to Paradip, Ballari-Hospet to Mangaluru/Chennai/Ennore, and the lower-grade coastal Goa-Ratnagiri ores to Mormugao.

exp.why: The Odisha-Jharkhand belt represents one of India's oldest and richest hematite provinces. It encompasses the Badampahar, Sulaipat, and Gorumahisani hills in Mayurbhanj district (which historically supplied Tata Iron and Steel Company), the Bonai-Keonjhar-Sundargarh horse-shoe synclinorium in Odisha, and the Gua and Noamundi mines in West Singhbhum district of Jharkhand.

The super-high-grade hematite deposits of the Bailadila range (meaning 'hump of an ox') in Dantewada district of Chhattisgarh (part of the Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt) are evacuated to Visakhapatnam Port in Andhra Pradesh—not Paradip Port—via the Kottavalasa-Kirandul (K-K) railway line and the Kirandul-Visakhapatnam slurry pipeline. Paradip Port primarily handles iron ore from the Daitari, Sukinda, and Keonjhar ranges of Odisha.

The Maharashtra-Goa belt (covering Goa and Ratnagiri/Sindhudurg districts of Maharashtra) contains mostly friable, powdery (blue dust/lateritic) iron ores of moderate to lower grade (typically 50–58% Fe). However, cheap riverine barge transport along the Mandovi and Zuari rivers directly to the natural harbour at Mormugao Port, combined with ease of crushing and pelletization/sintering, makes these ores highly competitive in international export markets.

ref: NCERT Class X Contemporary India-II Ch. 5; NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the distribution and industrial utilization of Hematite and Magnetite iron ores in India:
items: Statement-I: Because pure magnetite mineral crystals possess a higher theoretical stoichiometric iron content than pure hematite, domestic integrated blast-furnace steel plants in India rely predominantly on magnetite deposits of the southern craton rather than the hematite deposits of the eastern belt.

Statement-II: In India, natural magnetite resources occur predominantly in the southern states as lower-grade metamorphosed banded magnetite-quartzite rocks requiring intensive grinding and magnetic separation, whereas the eastern cratonic belt hosts naturally enriched, high-grade direct-shipping hematite ores.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Although pure stoichiometric magnetite (Fe3O4, 72.4% Fe) has a higher theoretical iron percentage than pure hematite (Fe2O3, 69.9% Fe), Indian bulk rock geology reverses this advantage: India's eastern and central cratons hold naturally leached, high-grade direct-shipping hematite (58–66% Fe), whereas Indian magnetite occurs as low-grade quartz-magnetite metamorphic rock (30–40% Fe) in the ecologically fragile Western Ghats.

exp.why: Statement-I confuses the theoretical chemical formula of pure mineral crystals with the bulk grade of natural ore bodies mined in India. Even though pure stoichiometric Fe3O4 contains 72.4% Fe compared to 69.9% Fe in pure Fe2O3, domestic integrated steel plants in India rely overwhelmingly on Hematite from the eastern and central belts (Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and the Ballari-Hospet sector of Karnataka) rather than Magnetite.

Statement-II accurately explains the geological reality in India. Over 90% of India's magnetite resources are located in the southern belt (Karnataka's Bababudan-Kudremukh belt, Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu's Salem-Kanjamalai belt). In these formations, magnetite is finely disseminated within hard, metamorphosed banded magnetite-quartzite (BMQ) rocks averaging only 30–40% Fe in situ, requiring energy-intensive fine grinding and wet magnetic separation—and many deposits lie inside ecologically sensitive Western Ghats zones. Conversely, supergene leaching of silica from Banded Hematite Quartzites in eastern and central India produced massive pockets of high-grade direct-shipping hematite (58–66% Fe).

ref: Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) Indian Minerals Yearbook: Iron Ore; Geological Survey of India (GSI) Special Publication on Iron Ore

stem: In the context of Indian economic geology, high-grade bauxite deposits—such as those at Panchpatmali in Koraput, the Amarkantak-Maikal plateau, and the 'Pat' lands of Lohardaga—characteristically occur as blanket cappings atop flat-topped plateaus and hill summits rather than in deep valley bottoms. Which of the following best explains this geomorphological and geochemical pattern?

opts.A: Bauxite precipitates exclusively from ascending hydrothermal fluids along deep-seated fault scarps during continental rifting, after which differential erosion removes the softer valley sediments to leave inverted plateau caps.
opts.B: Bauxite is a marine evaporite mineral formed in hypersaline coastal lagoons that were subsequently uplifted by epeirogenic movements into flat-topped mesas across Peninsular India.
opts.C: Aluminous silicates undergo mechanical frost-shattering and aeolian winnowing on high windward ridges, concentrating heavy aluminium oxide grains while lighter quartz grains are blown into adjacent valleys.
opts.D: Warm tropical monsoon climates with alternating wet and dry seasons promote intense in-situ chemical weathering on gently sloping, well-drained plateau surfaces, enabling percolating rainwater to leach away mobile silica and alkali bases while leaving insoluble hydrated aluminium oxides behind as residual lateritic caps.

core: Bauxite is a residual weathering deposit formed by tropical lateritization (desilication) of aluminium-rich parent rocks such as Deccan Trap basalts and Eastern Ghats khondalites. Gently undulating, flat-topped plateaus ('pats') provide the exact hydrological balance needed: low surface runoff allows deep rainwater infiltration, while high elevation above the regional water table ensures rapid subsurface drainage that flushes out dissolved silica.

exp.why: Option D is correct because bauxite (hydrated aluminium oxides: gibbsite, boehmite, and diaspore) forms through in-situ chemical weathering (lateritization/desilication) of aluminous silicate rocks—primarily Deccan Trap basalts in central/western India (Amarkantak, Maikal, Lohardaga pats, Kolhapur) and Khondalite-Charnockite suites in the Eastern Ghats (Panchpatmali, Gandhamardan, Baphlimali in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh). Under a hot tropical monsoon climate with alternating wet and dry seasons, warm alkaline groundwater during the wet season dissolves and flushes out mobile silica (SiO2) and alkali/alkaline-earth bases (Na, K, Ca, Mg), while insoluble oxides of aluminium (Al2O3) and iron (Fe2O3) remain behind as a residual enrichment blanket. Flat-topped plateaus are geomorphologically ideal because steep slopes suffer excessive mechanical sheet erosion before chemical leaching can complete, whereas poorly drained valley bottoms remain waterlogged with silica-saturated groundwater that re-silicates clay into kaolinite rather than bauxite. Options A, B, and C are incorrect as bauxite is neither a hydrothermal vein mineral, nor a marine evaporite, nor a periglacial/aeolian placer.

ref: NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5; Savindra Singh Physical Geography (Weathering & Lateritization)

stem: With reference to the geological occurrence and spatial distribution of Manganese ore in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Primary manganese ore deposits in India are closely associated with the Precambrian Dharwar system, occurring notably in the metamorphosed Gondite series and the hybrid Kodurite series.
2. The contiguous Balaghat-Bhandara-Nagpur arc stretching across Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra represents a premier manganese-producing belt where the ore is hosted within the Sausar group of rocks.
3. While Madhya Pradesh possesses the single largest share of India's total recoverable geological reserves of manganese ore, Odisha consistently leads all states in annual mine production.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Indian manganese occurs primarily in Precambrian Dharwar metasediments as syngenetic Gondite deposits (Madhya Pradesh-Maharashtra), hybrid Kodurite deposits (Eastern Ghats), and supergene lateritic concentrations (Odisha and Karnataka). Crucially, Odisha holds the largest share of India's total geological resources/reserves (~44%), whereas Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra lead in annual mine production.

exp.why: Geologically, India's manganese deposits belong overwhelmingly to the Archaean-Proterozoic Dharwar Supergroup. They are classified into three main genetic types: (i) the Gondite series (metamorphosed manganiferous sandy-argillaceous sediments rich in spessartine garnet and rhodonite, typical of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat), (ii) the Kodurite series (formed by reaction between manganiferous sediments and granitic/charnockitic intrusions in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha), and (iii) supergene lateritoid deposits formed by surface enrichment over Dharwarian shales/phyllites (Bonai-Keonjhar in Odisha and Sandur-Ballari in Karnataka).

The roughly 200-km-long arcuate belt stretching across Balaghat and Chhindwara districts in Madhya Pradesh and Bhandara and Nagpur districts in Maharashtra (hosted in the Proterozoic Sausar Group of metasediments, including the famous Bharweli and Dongri Buzurg mines) constitutes India's foremost underground and open-cast manganese mining belt.

This statement reverses the statistical relationship between geological reserves/resources and annual production across states. According to the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) National Mineral Inventory, Odisha holds the single largest share of India's total geological manganese ore resources (approximately 44%), followed by Karnataka (22%) and Madhya Pradesh (12%). Conversely, in terms of annual mine production, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra are the leading producers, together accounting for well over half of India's annual output, while Odisha ranks third.

ref: Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) Indian Minerals Yearbook: Manganese Ore; NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5

stem: Consider the following pairs of major metalliferous mining centres in India, their geological settings, and their primary metallic commodities:
items: 1. Malanjkhand (Madhya Pradesh) : Stratiform sediment-hosted Bhilwara Supergroup deposit producing Lead, Zinc, and by-product Silver
2. Rampura-Agucha (Rajasthan) : Open-pit granitic porphyry deposit hosted in fractured Bundelkhand-Bastar cratonic granitoids producing Copper
3. Sukinda Valley (Odisha) : Layered ultramafic complex hosting over ninety percent of India's recoverable Chromite resources
4. Khetri-Singhana (Rajasthan) : Proterozoic Delhi Supergroup metasedimentary belt hosting major sulphide Copper mineralization
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: India's base-metal and ferro-alloy provinces occupy distinct tectonic niches: Malanjkhand (MP) is a granitic porphyry-type open-pit copper deposit, Khetri (Rajasthan) and Singhbhum (Jharkhand) are Proterozoic metasedimentary/shear-zone copper belts, Rampura-Agucha and Zawar (Rajasthan) are sediment-hosted Pb-Zn-Ag deposits, and Sukinda (Odisha) is an ultramafic chromite-nickel complex.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched because the geological descriptions of Malanjkhand and Rampura-Agucha have been interchanged. Malanjkhand in Balaghat district of Madhya Pradesh is India's largest open-pit (now transitioning to underground) copper mine, where chalcopyrite mineralization occurs in thick quartz reefs filling fracture zones within Proterozoic granitoids, accounting for over 70% of Hindustan Copper Limited's production.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Rampura-Agucha in Bhilwara district of Rajasthan (along with the Zawar, Rajpura-Dariba, and Kayad mines in the Aravalli-Bhilwara fold belts) is one of the world's largest stratiform, sediment-hosted Lead-Zinc (galena and sphalerite) deposits, which also yields the overwhelming majority of India's primary by-product Silver and Cadmium.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. The Sukinda ultramafic belt (composed of serpentinized dunite and peridotite along the Damsal valley across Jajpur, Dhenkanal, and Keonjhar districts of Odisha) hosts over 95% of India's total recoverable chromite (FeCr2O4) resources as well as significant lateritic nickel occurrences.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. The Khetri-Singhana belt (spanning Jhunjhunu and Sikar districts in Rajasthan, including the Khetri, Kolihan, and Chandmari mines) is hosted within Proterozoic garnetiferous schists, phyllites, and quartzites of the Delhi Supergroup and constitutes one of India's three principal copper provinces alongside Malanjkhand (MP) and the Singhbhum Thrust Belt (Rakha, Mosaboni, Surda in Jharkhand).

ref: NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5; Geological Survey of India (GSI) Base Metal & Chromite Commodity Dossiers

stem: With reference to the geological distribution and metallurgy of strategic ferro-alloy and precious metals in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Over 90 percent of India's total recoverable resources of both Chromite and Nickel are overwhelmingly concentrated in a single state within the Sukinda ultramafic belt.
2. India meets a significant share of its domestic primary nickel smelter demand from polymetallic sulphide ores mined in the Aravalli belt of Rajasthan.

3. In Peninsular India, prospective occurrences of Platinum Group Elements (PGE) are geologically hosted in layered mafic-ultramafic igneous complexes such as Boula-Nuasahi in Odisha, Sittampundi in Tamil Nadu, and Hanumalpura in Karnataka.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's Chromite (>95%) and Nickel (~93%) resources are heavily co-located in the Sukinda ultramafic complex of Odisha, while PGE mineralization is similarly tied to Precambrian layered mafic-ultramafic intrusions. However, because Sukinda nickel occurs as refractory low-grade limonitic/lateritic oxide overburden rather than easily smeltable sulphide ore, India has negligible primary nickel production.

exp.why: According to the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) National Mineral Inventory, Odisha accounts for more than 95% of India's chromite resources and about 93% of its nickel resources, both overwhelmingly concentrated in the Sukinda Valley ultramafic belt (Jajpur district), with minor chromite/nickel occurrences in Keonjhar, Dhenkanal, Jharkhand (Singhbhum), and Manipur/Nagaland ophiolites.

India produces no primary refined nickel from Rajasthan and remains almost entirely import-dependent for primary nickel. In the Sukinda Valley, nickel occurs as low-grade (0.5% to 0.9% Ni) refractory lateritic/limonitic oxide ore intimately disseminated within goethite in the chromite overburden, for which commercial hydrometallurgical extraction at scale has remained technologically challenging. Historically, only tiny quantities of by-product nickel sulphate were recovered during copper refining at Ghatsila (Jharkhand).

Platinum Group Elements (Platinum, Palladium, Rhodium, Iridium, Osmium, Ruthenium) are magmatic siderophile/chalcophile elements hosted in layered mafic-ultramafic chromitite-anorthosite complexes. The three flagship GSI-explored PGE prospects in India are the Boula-Nuasahi igneous complex (Keonjhar, Odisha), the Sittampundi anorthosite complex (Namakkal, Tamil Nadu), and the Hanumalpura mafic-ultramafic complex (Davanagere, Karnataka).

ref: IBM Indian Minerals Yearbook (Chromite, Nickel & Platinum Group Metals); GSI Special Publication on Mafic-Ultramafic Complexes

stem: With reference to the geological origin and industrial utility of non-metallic minerals in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. High-grade sheet mica in the Koderma-Hazaribagh and Nellore belts is geologically formed through the contact metamorphism of dolomitic limestone by basaltic lava flows.

2. Natural mineral gypsum in India is predominantly an evaporite deposit formed in arid marine and lacustrine basins, with Rajasthan's Nagaur-Bikaner-Jaisalmer tract accounting for over 80 percent of the national resources.
3. Unlike limestone, dolomite is completely avoided in the iron and steel industry because its magnesium carbonate content prevents slag fluidity and corrodes furnace linings.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Non-metallic industrial minerals occupy distinct petrogenetic niches: muscovite sheet mica crystallizes from volatile-rich granitic pegmatite veins, whereas gypsum precipitates as an arid-basin chemical evaporite. In metallurgy, dolomite is vital both as a blast-furnace/sinter flux and as a basic refractory brick lining.

exp.why: Sheet mica (principally muscovite and phlogopite) in the Koderma-Giridih-Hazaribagh belt (Jharkhand), Nellore belt (Andhra Pradesh), and Bhilwara belt (Rajasthan) is formed during the late-stage fractional crystallization of volatile-rich granitic pegmatite veins intruding into Precambrian mica-schists and gneisses. Contact metamorphism of siliceous dolomitic limestone by basic sills instead produces chrysotile asbestos and steatite/talc (as seen in the Cuddapah basin).

Natural gypsum (hydrated calcium sulphate) is a sedimentary evaporite formed by chemical precipitation in shallow lagoonal marine and arid lacustrine (playa/rann) basins. Rajasthan (led by Nagaur, Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, and Sri Ganganagar districts) holds over 81% of India's natural gypsum resources, followed by Jammu & Kashmir and Tamil Nadu.

The iron and steel industry is the single largest consumer of dolomite in India, accounting for over 80% of domestic consumption. Dolomite (calcium magnesium carbonate) is actively added in sinter plants and blast furnaces as a flux (where regulated MgO levels actually improve slag fluidity) and is calcined/dead-burnt to manufacture basic refractory linings for Basic Oxygen Furnaces (LD converters) and steel ladles.

ref: NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 7; IBM Indian Minerals Yearbook (Mica, Gypsum & Dolomite)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the geochemical characteristics and industrial suitability of Tertiary coals in Northeast India:
items: Statement-I: Because the Oligocene Tertiary coals of the Makum coalfield in Assam possess strong caking properties and low inherent ash content, they are directly utilized without blending as the primary metallurgical fuel in conventional blast furnaces for pig iron production in eastern India.

Statement-II: Coal seams formed under marine-influenced lagoonal and paralic depositional environments during the Tertiary period in Northeast India contain high proportions of organic and pyritic sulphur (3% to 8%), which induces brittle 'hot-shortness' in iron and corrodes blast furnace linings.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Northeast India's Tertiary coals (such as the Barail Group seams of Makum, Assam) present a geochemical paradox: tectonic folding gave them high caking indices and low ash content, yet their paralic/lagoonal marine origin imparted extremely high organic sulphur (3–8%). Because organic sulphur cannot be removed by physical coal washing and causes hot-shortness in steel, they cannot be directly used as primary blast-furnace coke.

exp.why: Although the Oligocene coals of the Makum coalfield (Tinsukia, Assam) exhibit anomalously strong caking/swelling properties, high volatile matter, and low inherent ash content (4% to 10%), they cannot be used directly as the primary metallurgical fuel in conventional blast furnaces. At most, only very small proportions (5% to 10%) can be blended with low-sulphur Gondwana coking coals because of their prohibitively high sulphur content and low ash-fusion temperature.

Unlike freshwater continental Gondwana coals (which contain <0.6% sulphur), the Eocene-Oligocene Tertiary coals of Assam, Meghalaya, and Arunachal Pradesh accumulated in marine-influenced paralic and lagoonal swamps rich in sulphate-reducing bacteria. Consequently, they contain 3% to 8% sulphur (predominantly chemically bound organic sulphur that resists gravity washing). In a blast furnace, excess sulphur enters the hot metal as iron sulphide (FeS), forming low-melting eutectics along grain boundaries that cause brittle cracking during hot rolling ('hot-shortness' or 'red-shortness') and corrode furnace structures.

ref: GSI Coal Wing Bulletins on Tertiary Coalfields of Northeast India; Khullar India A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 17

stem: Consider the following major Gondwana coalfields of Peninsular India:
items: 1. Talcher Coalfield (Brahmani-Mahanadi Basin)
2. Singrauli Coalfield (Son Valley Basin)
3. Singareni-Kothagudem Coalfield (Pranhita-Godavari Basin)
4. Korba Coalfield (Hasdeo-Mahanadi Basin)
prompt: What is the correct sequence of the coalfields given above when arranged from North to South?
core: India's Gondwana coalfields follow major structurally faulted river-basin grabens arranged along well-defined latitudinal belts: the Damodar-Son axis lies farthest north (~23.5°N–24.2°N), the Hasdeo-Mahanadi basin of Chhattisgarh (Korba ~22.3°N) lies north of Odisha's Brahmani-Mahanadi graben (Talcher ~21.0°N), and the Pranhita-Godavari valley (Singareni/Kothagudem ~17.5°N) extends farthest south.

exp.why: Talcher Coalfield in Angul district of Odisha (Brahmani-Mahanadi Basin) is located at approximately 20.9°N to 21.1°N latitude, making it the third from the north among the given coalfields.

Singrauli Coalfield straddling the Madhya Pradesh (Singrauli district) and Uttar Pradesh (Sonbhadra district) border in the Son Valley Basin lies at approximately 24.0°N to 24.2°N latitude, making it the northernmost among the four.
Singareni-Kothagudem Coalfield in Telangana (Pranhita-Godavari Valley Basin) lies at approximately 17.5°N latitude, making it the southernmost major Gondwana coal belt among the four.

Korba Coalfield in the Hasdeo River basin (a northern tributary of the Mahanadi in Chhattisgarh) is situated at approximately 22.3°N to 22.4°N latitude, placing it south of Singrauli (24.2°N) and decisively north of Talcher (21.0°N). Thus, the exact North-to-South sequence is 2 - 4 - 1 - 3.

ref: Ministry of Coal / CMPDI Coal Atlas of India; Oxford School Atlas (Mineral & Fuel Map of India)

stem: Despite possessing one of the world's largest geological reserves of bituminous Gondwana coal, India faces a structural shortage of prime metallurgical coking coal. In this context, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Indian Gondwana coal seams are predominantly of 'drift' (allochthonous) origin, where uprooted vegetation was transported by rivers into faulted graben basins, resulting in fine mineral sediment getting intimately inter-grown with the plant matter.

2. Because Indian Gondwana basins experienced repeated marine transgressions during the Permo-Carboniferous period, Gondwana coal suffers from excessively high sulphur content (over 3%) and low ash-fusion temperatures.

3. The high proportion of finely disseminated 'inherent' ash in Indian Gondwana coking coal reduces its washability efficiency in coal beneficiation plants, compelling Indian integrated steel plants to rely heavily on imported low-ash prime coking coal.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The primary structural handicap of Indian Gondwana coal is its allochthonous ('drift') origin in continental fluvio-lacustrine basins, which embedded microscopic clay and silt directly into the organic maceral matrix as 'inherent ash'. While Indian Gondwana coal enjoys very low sulphur (<0.6%) and high ash-fusion temperatures, its finely disseminated ash makes gravity-based washing difficult and limits prime coking coal availability strictly to the Jharia coalfield.

exp.why: Unlike the Carboniferous coals of Europe and North America—which formed 'in-situ' (autochthonous origin) in undisturbed coastal peat swamps with very little clastic sediment influx—Indian Lower Gondwana (Barakar and Raniganj stage) coals are predominantly of 'drift' (allochthonous) origin. Glossopteris flora was washed down by turbulent river systems into subsiding intracratonic rift grabens, thoroughly mixing fine clay and quartz silt with the decaying plant debris.

Indian Gondwana coal accumulated in freshwater continental fluvio-lacustrine basins. Consequently, its sulphur content is remarkably low (typically below 0.5% to 0.6%) and its ash-fusion temperature is high (above 1350°C), which prevents clinkering in pulverized thermal boilers. High sulphur (>3%) and low ash-fusion temperatures are the hallmarks of Northeast India's marine-influenced Tertiary coals, not Peninsular Gondwana coals.

In coal beneficiation, 'extraneous/adventitious' dirt bands are easily separated by specific-gravity washing, whereas 'inherent' (finely inter-grown) ash requires ultra-fine crushing and yields low clean-coal recovery. Because Indian coking coal contains 22% to 35% raw ash of predominantly inherent character—and prime coking coal reserves are geographically restricted solely to the Jharia coalfield (much of which is affected by underground seam fires)—Indian blast-furnace steelmakers must import low-ash prime coking coal (mainly from Australia) to blend down ash levels to 12–15%.

ref: Ministry of Coal Expert Committee Reports on Coal Beneficiation; GSI Geology of Indian Coal Basins

stem: With reference to the geological occurrence, mining hydrology, and utilization of Lignite (Brown Coal) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Raw lignite possesses high bed moisture (30% to 55%), low calorific value, and a strong susceptibility to friability and spontaneous exothermic oxidation upon air exposure, which restricts its use predominantly to pit-head thermal power generation.
2. In the Neyveli lignite field of the Cauvery basin, open-cast mining is simplified by the complete absence of sub-surface groundwater aquifers beneath the lignite seam.
3. While the Panandhro and Tadkeshwar lignite fields are located in the Barmer-Bikaner basin of Rajasthan, the Kapurdi and Jalipa lignite fields are situated in the Kutch peninsula of Gujarat.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Lignite in India (concentrated ~80% in Tamil Nadu, followed by Rajasthan and Gujarat) is a young Tertiary fuel with high moisture and volatile matter, making long-distance transport both uneconomical and hazardous due to spontaneous self-heating. Furthermore, open-cast mining at Neyveli requires continuous depressurization pumping of the underlying Cuddalore artesian aquifer.

exp.why: Raw lignite contains 30% to 55% bed moisture and has a low gross calorific value (2,500–3,200 kcal/kg). When exposed to the atmosphere during storage or transit, it rapidly loses moisture, slacks (crumbles) into reactive fine particles, and undergoes low-temperature exothermic oxidation leading to spontaneous combustion. Hence, lignite is overwhelmingly utilized in specialized pit-head circulating fluidized bed combustion (CFBC) or pulverized lignite thermal power stations.

Open-cast lignite mining in the Neyveli field (Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu, holding India's largest lignite reserves alongside Mannargudi) faces a classic hydrogeological challenge: the lignite seam rests directly above a powerful, high-pressure confined (artesian) aquifer in the Cuddalore sandstones. Continuous, large-scale groundwater depressurization pumping is mandatory around the clock to prevent upward artesian pressure from rupturing the mine floor and flooding the open-cast pits.

The state locations are interchanged: Panandhro, Akrimota, and Mata-no-Madh (in Kutch district) along with Tadkeshwar (in Surat district) and Vastan/Rajpardi (Bharuch) are major Tertiary lignite fields in Gujarat. Conversely, Kapurdi, Jalipa, and Giral (in Barmer district) along with Palana, Barsingsar, and Gurha (in Bikaner district) are located in Rajasthan.

ref: Ministry of Coal / NLC India Limited Hydrogeological Reports; NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the geological controls and extraction mechanics of Coal Bed Methane (CBM) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike conventional natural gas reservoirs where gas occupies intergranular pore spaces as a free phase, methane in coal seams is stored predominantly in a physically adsorbed state on the internal surfaces of micropores within the coal matrix.

2. Commercial extraction of Coal Bed Methane requires injecting high-pressure water or steam into the target coal seam to increase hydrostatic pressure, thereby forcing methane to desorb into the natural fracture network (cleats).

3. India's principal producing and prospective Coal Bed Methane blocks—including Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, and Sohagpur—are hosted within Lower Gondwana bituminous to sub-bituminous coal seams of the Damodar and Son-Mahanadi valleys.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Coal Bed Methane (CBM) is an unconventional gas system in which coal acts as both the source rock and the reservoir rock, holding methane via physical adsorption on micropore surfaces under hydrostatic pressure. Production requires dewatering the coal seam to lower hydrostatic pressure below the critical desorption pressure, predominantly within high-rank Gondwana seams of eastern and central India.

exp.why: Coal has a dual-porosity system consisting of a microporous matrix and a network of orthogonal natural fractures called cleats (face cleats and butt cleats). More than 90–95% of Coal Bed Methane is held in a physically adsorbed monomolecular layer on the internal surfaces of the coal matrix micropores, giving coal the ability to store several times more gas per unit volume than a conventional sandstone reservoir at equivalent pressure.

This statement reverses the physical extraction mechanism. Methane remains adsorbed onto the coal matrix as long as the surrounding formation water maintains high hydrostatic pressure. To extract CBM, submersible pumps must first pump out the formation water (a process known as dewatering) to reduce hydrostatic pressure in the seam. Once reservoir pressure drops below the critical desorption pressure, methane desorbs from the micropore surfaces, diffuses through the matrix according to Fick's law, and flows through the cleat network according to Darcy's law toward the wellbore.

Thermal maturity (coal rank) strongly governs methane generation and adsorption capacity. Lower Gondwana (Permian) bituminous seams of the Damodar Valley (Raniganj in West Bengal; Jharia and Bokaro in Jharkhand) and the Son-Mahanadi Valley (Sohagpur in Madhya Pradesh) possess optimal vitrinite reflectance, gas content, and cleat permeability, making them the core of India's CBM production.

ref: Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) Unconventional Hydrocarbon Reports; GSI Coal & Lignite Bulletins; NCERT India People and Economy Ch. 5

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the geological accumulation of conventional hydrocarbons in structural traps:
items: Statement-I: Within an undisturbed anticlinal hydrocarbon trap containing formation water, crude oil, and free natural gas, a vertical well drilled into the highest structural crest of the fold encounters the crude oil zone first before reaching the free natural gas zone.
Statement-II: Within a porous and permeable reservoir rock sealed by an impermeable caprock, immiscible reservoir fluids segregate vertically by buoyancy in inverse order of their specific gravities.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Conventional structural traps such as anticlines require a porous and permeable reservoir rock (sandstone or fractured limestone) overlain by an impermeable seal (shale or evaporite). Inside the trap, fluids stratify by density: free natural gas forms the uppermost gas cap at the structural crest, underlain by the crude oil zone, which in turn floats above saline formation water.

exp.why: In an undisturbed anticlinal trap containing all three phases (free gas, crude oil, and saline water), free natural gas has the lowest density and therefore migrates to the highest structural apex (crest) of the fold, forming a gas cap. Consequently, a vertical well drilled directly into the highest crest of the anticline encounters the free natural gas cap first, followed downward across the gas-oil contact (GOC) by the crude oil zone, and finally across the oil-water contact (OWC) into the saline aquifer.

Secondary migration and accumulation of hydrocarbons inside a porous, permeable reservoir unit (such as Tertiary sandstones or shelf limestones) beneath an impermeable caprock (such as marine shale or anhydrite) are governed by buoyancy forces. Immiscible fluids naturally segregate vertically in inverse order of their specific gravities, placing the least dense fluid (natural gas) at the top, intermediate-density crude oil in the middle, and denser brine at the base.

ref: G.C. Leong Certificate Physical and Human Geography; NCERT Class XII India People and Economy Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the major hydrocarbon fields of India and their geological settings, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Mangala Oilfield : Barmer-Sanchore Intracratonic Rift Basin
2. Ravva Oil and Gas Field : Offshore Cauvery Basin along the Coromandel Coast
3. Naharkatiya Oilfield : Upper Assam Shelf Foreland Basin
4. Kalol Oilfield : Jaisalmer Pericratonic Basin in Western Rajasthan
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: India's Category-I producing sedimentary basins span diverse tectonic settings: intracratonic/pericratonic rifts in western India (Barmer-Sanchore and Cambay), foreland shelf-thrust belts in the northeast (Assam-Arakan), and passive margin deltaic-rift basins along the eastern coast (Krishna-Godavari and Cauvery).

exp.why: The Mangala, Bhagyam, and Aishwariya (MBA) oilfields are major onshore discoveries located in the Barmer-Sanchore Basin of western Rajasthan, an intracratonic Tertiary rift basin containing high-paraffin waxy crude in Palaeocene-Eocene Fatehgarh sandstones.

The Ravva oil and gas field is located offshore in the Krishna-Godavari (KG) Basin along the Andhra Pradesh coast (near Amalapuram/Kakinada), not in the Cauvery Basin. The Cauvery Basin in Tamil Nadu hosts fields such as Narimanam, Nagapattinam, and PY-1/PY-3.

Naharkatiya, along with Digboi, Moran, Hugrijan, and Rudrasagar, lies in the Upper Assam Shelf sub-basin of the Assam-Arakan foreland basin system in the Brahmaputra valley, producing from Oligocene Barail and Miocene Tipam sandstone reservoirs.

Kalol (along with Ankleshwar, Mehsana, Nawagam, and Kosamba) is a major onshore hydrocarbon field situated in the Cambay Basin of Gujarat (a Cenozoic intracratonic graben), not in the Jaisalmer Basin of western Rajasthan.

ref: Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) India's Hydrocarbon Outlook; Khullar India: A Comprehensive Geography Ch. 17

stem: With reference to the geological types and spatial distribution of Uranium mineralization in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The uranium deposits of the Singhbhum Shear Zone—including Jaduguda, Narwapahar, and Turamdih—are structurally controlled hydrothermal vein-type deposits hosted within Proterozoic metamorphic rocks.

2. Unlike the metamorphic vein-type deposits of Jharkhand or the coastal monazite placers of Kerala, the Tummalapalle uranium deposit in the Cuddapah Basin is a stratabound carbonate-hosted deposit occurring within phosphatic siliceous dolostones.

3. The Domiasiat and Wahkyn uranium deposits in Meghalaya are sandstone-hosted deposits formed in Cretaceous fluvial-to-marginal-marine sediments of the Mahadek Basin, whereas the Rohil deposit in Rajasthan is associated with metasomatic albitite zones.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's uranium resources belong to distinct genetic classes across geological provinces: Proterozoic shear-zone hydrothermal veins in the Singhbhum Thrust Belt (Jharkhand), stratabound carbonate-hosted dolostone deposits in the Cuddapah Basin (Andhra Pradesh), Cretaceous sandstone-hosted deposits in the Mahadek Basin (Meghalaya), and metasomatic albitite-hosted deposits in the North Delhi Fold Belt (Rajasthan).

exp.why: The Singhbhum Shear Zone (Singhbhum Thrust Belt) in Jharkhand is India's oldest uranium mining province. Deposits such as Jaduguda, Bhatin, Narwapahar, Turamdih, Bagjata, and Banduhurang are structurally controlled, metamorphite-hosted hydrothermal disseminated and vein-type deposits within Proterozoic quartz-chlorite-biotite schists.

The Tummalapalle-Rachakuntapalle belt in the southwestern part of the Mesoproterozoic Cuddapah Basin (Andhra Pradesh) is one of the largest single stratabound carbonate-hosted uranium reserves in the world. Here, pitchblende and coffinite mineralization is syngenetically and diagenetically hosted within impurity-rich phosphatic siliceous dolostones of the Vempalle Formation, completely distinct from littoral thorium-rich monazite placers.

In Meghalaya (West Khasi Hills), deposits like Domiasiat (Kylleng-Pyndengsohiong-Mawthabah) and Wahkyn are classic sandstone-type uranium deposits hosted in Upper Cretaceous arkosic sandstones of the Mahadek Formation, where organic matter acted as a reductant to precipitate uranium from groundwater. Conversely, the Rohil deposit in Sikar district, Rajasthan, is an albitite-hosted (Na-metasomatism) deposit along the Kaliguman Lineament in the North Delhi Fold Belt.

ref: Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD) Geological Reports; Indian Minerals Yearbook (IBM) - Uranium & Rare Earths

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Beach Sand Minerals (BSM) and coastal placer deposits in India:
